records.name: CN III Oculomotor nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal segment lies between the posterior cerebral artery (vasc-posterior-cerebral-artery) and the superior cerebellar artery (vasc-superior-cerebellar-artery), both of which give it small branches and both of which can compress it: a posterior-communicating-artery aneurysm at the internal carotid (vasc-posterior-communicating-artery) is the classic compressive lesion, because the artery crosses immediately above the nerve in the cistern and the aneurysm's dome points down onto the pupillomotor fibres that run on the nerve's superomedial surface. In the cavernous sinus the nerve is supplied by the meningohypophyseal trunk and the inferolateral trunk of the internal carotid, which is why a cavernous-sinus lesion spares the pupil (the pupillomotor fibres lie peripherally in the cisternal segment but are less exposed in the sinus) and why ischaemic palsy from diabetic small-vessel disease typically spares it too.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.syndrome: Complete oculomotor palsy — "down and out" with ptosis and mydriasis
before.findings: Ptosis from levator failure, a dilated unreactive pupil from sphincter paralysis, and an eye that rests down and out (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique) with impaired adduction, elevation and depression: the patient has diplopia in all directions except outward gaze, and the ptosis may hide it. The palsy localizes to this nerve anywhere along its course, and the FIRST question is whether the pupil is involved, because a pupil-involving palsy is compressive (aneurysm, uncal herniation, tumour) and a pupil-sparing palsy in a vasculopath is usually ischaemic.
before.vascular: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm (internal carotid) or diabetic microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum
before.note: The pupillomotor fibres are the most superficial in the cisternal nerve, where the posterior communicating artery crosses it — that arrangement, not the size of the lesion, is why compression dilates the pupil early.

before.syndrome: Weber syndrome (syn-weber) — fascicular CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
before.findings: A midbrain lesion of the fascicles as they cross the crus cerebri produces ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal fibres): the palsy and the weakness are on opposite sides, which is what identifies the lesion as fascicular rather than at the nerve's exit.
before.vascular: Paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery, or a small midbrain haemorrhage/infarct
before.note: The pupil may or may not be involved depending on whether the Edinger-Westphal fibres are caught; the crossed hemiparesis, not the pupil, is the localizing sign.

before.syndrome: Benedikt, Claude and Nothnagel syndromes (syn-benedikt, syn-claude, syn-nothnagel)
before.findings: Fascicular CN III palsy with a contralateral tremor and extrapyramidal rigidity is Benedikt (red nucleus and cerebellothalamic fibres); with contralateral ataxia and no weakness is Claude (red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle); and with ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia of the limbs plus contralateral hemianesthesia is Nothnagel (tectum and quadrigeminal region). All three share the oculomotor palsy and separate by the adjacent structure the lesion has taken.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery perforators and the superior cerebellar artery territory
before.note: These are the named midbrain syndromes that make a fascicular third-nerve palsy a localizing sign rather than a nerve sign.

before.syndrome: Uncal herniation with a blown pupil
before.findings: Expanding supratentorial mass shifts the uncus over the tentorial edge and stretches the cisternal oculomotor nerve against the posterior clinoid and the petroclinoid ligament: the first sign is an ipsilateral dilated pupil that reacts poorly (the superficial pupillomotor fibres fail first), then a complete palsy of the nerve with ptosis and a down-and-out eye, then contralateral hemiparesis from peduncular compression. It is a neurosurgical emergency and the pupil is the earliest reliable sign.
before.vascular: Compressive (mass effect); the posterior cerebral artery can also be occluded at the same time, adding an occipital infarct
before.note: Pupil first, then palsy, then weakness — the pupil's early involvement is the anatomical consequence of the fibre arrangement in the nerve.

before.findings: A lesion of the cavernous sinus (aneurysm, meningioma, pituitary apoplexy, thrombosis, Tolosa-Hunt) adds CN IV, CN V1 and CN V2 involvement to the CN III palsy, often with proptosis and chemosis, and characteristically spares the pupil or involves it later; the combination of a third-nerve palsy with facial pain in the V1 distribution is the localizing clue to the sinus rather than the orbit or the cistern.
before.vascular: Internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) aneurysm, carotid-cavernous fistula, or meningohypophyseal-trunk supply to the nerve

after.findings: Ptosis, diplopia and impaired adduction/elevation/depression may occur, with a down-and-out eye in a complete somatic palsy. Pupil constriction and accommodation may also be impaired. Pupil sparing does not exclude a compressive lesion such as an aneurysm.

An ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral weakness or ataxia suggests accompanying midbrain motor or crossed cerebellar-output involvement. Weber, Claude and Benedikt labels describe overlapping patterns rather than mandatory full syndromes.
Combined III/IV/VI and trigeminal deficits can arise from cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure lesions. Pupil involvement is variable and cannot distinguish the site by itself.

Acute third-nerve dysfunction can accompany posterior communicating aneurysm or transtentorial herniation. The clinical sequence is variable; a fixed pupil-first, palsy-second, weakness-third progression is not reliable.

afferent: Oculomotor nucleus (nuc-oculomotor) — the somatic motor neurons whose axons form this nerve
Edinger-Westphal nucleus (nuc-edinger-westphal) — the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons; the child record of nuc-oculomotor in the registry, which is why the two are named together

Supranuclear drive from the frontal eye fields (ctx-frontal-eye-fields) and the paramedian pontine reticular formation (nuc-pprf) reaches this nerve only through the nucleus; the nerve itself carries no afferent fibres
Pretectal area (nuc-pretectal) projects to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and is the relay that closes the pupillary light-reflex loop on this nerve
efferent: Superior division to the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris
Inferior division to the medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the ciliary ganglion, then the short ciliary nerves to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle

Rootlets leave the midbrain through the interpeduncular fossa at `surf-cn3-exit` and the nerve traverses the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus with the internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) and the posterior communicating artery (vasc-posterior-communicating-artery)

afferent: Axons arise from oculomotor somatic motor neurons and Edinger-Westphal preganglionic neurons; supranuclear inputs terminate centrally rather than traveling in the nerve.
efferent: Superior division: superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris
Inferior division: medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to ciliary ganglion

course.before: From the oculomotor nucleus (nuc-oculomotor) and the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (nuc-edinger-westphal) in the midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, the fascicles pass ventrally through the red nucleus and the medial part of the crus cerebri, emerging in the interpeduncular fossa at the medial edge of the cerebral peduncle — the surface landmark `surf-cn3-exit` — from where the cisternal segment runs forward and laterally through the interpeduncular and crural cisterns, between the posterior cerebral artery above and the superior cerebellar artery below. It then pierces the dura lateral to the posterior clinoid process, runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus (holding the highest position in the wall throughout, with CN IV descending below it as the two nerves run forward), and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure — the foramen this nerve uses — dividing into a superior division (superior rectus, levator palpebrae) and an inferior division (medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique, and the preganglionic parasympathetic root to the ciliary ganglion).
course.after: Motor and parasympathetic fascicles arise in the rostral midbrain, pass ventrally and emerge in the interpeduncular fossa. The cisternal nerve passes between PCA and SCA, traverses the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. Superior and inferior divisions supply extraocular/eyelid muscles and the ciliary ganglion.

function.before: The principal motor nerve of the eye: it innervates the medial rectus (adduction), the superior and inferior recti (elevation in adduction and depression in adduction), the inferior oblique (elevation in abduction with extorsion) and the levator palpebrae superioris (eyelid opening), and it supplies the parasympathetic fibres that constrict the pupil and accommodate the lens. Its Edinger-Westphal fibres synapse in the ciliary ganglion and reach the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle, which is why a lesion of this nerve produces mydriasis and loss of accommodation as well as diplopia and ptosis. Because the fascicles travel through the red nucleus and the crus cerebri, an intrinsic midbrain lesion adds contralateral hemiparesis or tremor to the palsy — the anatomical basis of the Weber, Benedikt, Claude and Nothnagel syndromes at the bottom of this record. The nerve is the efferent limb of both the pupillary light reflex and the near triad.
function.after: Supplies medial, superior and inferior rectus, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris. Superior/inferior recti are tested for elevation/depression with the eye abducted; inferior oblique elevates the adducted eye. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers synapse in the ciliary ganglion; short ciliary nerves then supply sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. Pupil involvement varies by lesion.

modality.before: Motor (somatic motor to four extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae) plus parasympathetic (visceral motor, preganglionic, to the pupillary sphincter and the ciliary muscle); no sensory component
modality.after: General somatic efferent and preganglionic parasympathetic (general visceral efferent).

records.name: CN IV Trochlear nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal segment is supplied by small branches of the superior cerebellar artery (vasc-superior-cerebellar-artery) and the posterior cerebral artery (vasc-posterior-cerebral-artery), the two vessels it passes between; a dolichoectatic or elongated superior cerebellar artery can compress the nerve and produce a chronic trochlear palsy with diplopia. In the cavernous sinus it is supplied by the meningohypophyseal trunk of the internal carotid (vasc-internal-carotid-artery). Because the nerve is thin and its supply is segmental, microvascular ischaemia of the nerve (diabetes, hypertension) is a common cause of an isolated, pupil-sparing trochlear palsy that recovers over months.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.syndrome: Trochlear (superior oblique) palsy — vertical diplopia with a head tilt
before.findings: Failure to depress the adducted eye produces vertical diplopia that is worst on downward gaze and on the side of the lesion's field; the patient tilts the head AWAY from the affected side to fuse (Bielschowsky head-tilt test: the hypertropia worsens when the head is tilted toward the affected side). A long-standing palsy produces a compensatory facial asymmetry and neck tilt that can be mistaken for a congenital torticollis.
before.vascular: Microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum (diabetes, hypertension) is the commonest cause of an isolated palsy; compression by the superior cerebellar artery is the commonest cause of a chronic one
before.note: The head tilt is the diagnostic sign and its direction distinguishes a trochlear palsy from a skew deviation, which is a brainstem sign rather than a nerve sign.

before.findings: Closed head injury — even a modest one — tears the thin cisternal nerve against the tentorial edge or the petroclinoid ligament, because its long course around the midbrain is unprotected; the palsy may be bilateral after severe trauma, and it is the commonest traumatic ocular motor palsy in some series.
before.note: Mechanical; the nerve's dorsal exit and long cisternal course are the anatomical reason it, and not CN III or VI, is the nerve most often torn in head injury

before.syndrome: Nuclear versus fascicular trochlear palsy (crossed palsy)
before.findings: A lesion of the trochlear NUCLEUS (or of the decussating fibres in the anterior medullary velum) paralyses the superior oblique of the opposite eye — a crossed palsy that also involves the contralateral superior oblique in a bilateral nuclear lesion; a lesion of the fascicle or the cisternal nerve paralyses the ipsilateral muscle. The distinction localizes the damage inside the midbrain rather than outside it, and it is the only cranial nerve for which the rule is inverted.
before.vascular: Dorsal midbrain infarct or haemorrhage (posterior cerebral artery perforators)
before.note: A nuclear lesion never occurs alone in practice: look for an associated internuclear ophthalmoplegia, Horner syndrome or ataxia of the adjacent structures.

before.syndrome: Trochlear palsy in the cavernous sinus and orbit
before.findings: In the sinus or the orbital apex the nerve is part of a combined ophthalmoplegia with CN III, CN V1/V2 and CN VI, often with proptosis and periorbital pain; the palsy is then not localizing on its own. A tumour of the superior orbital fissure can produce an isolated trochlear palsy with orbital pain before any other sign.
before.vascular: Internal carotid artery aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula in the sinus; superior orbital fissure syndrome

after.findings: Vertical/torsional diplopia and hypertropia may be more evident looking down with the eye adducted. Head tilt toward the affected side can worsen hypertropia and patients may compensate by tilting away. This pattern is helpful but not uniquely diagnostic; skew deviation and other ocular conditions can mimic it.

A lesion of the nucleus or fibers before their decussation affects the contralateral superior oblique. A lesion after crossing affects the ipsilateral eye; a midline decussation lesion can affect both. Trauma, congenital disorders, microvascular disease and other causes can produce trochlear palsy.

afferent: Trochlear nucleus (nuc-trochlear) — the somatic motor neurons, the sole source of the nerve's fibres; the nucleus lies at the level of the inferior colliculus and its fibres decussate in the anterior medullary velum before exiting
Supranuclear input reaches the nucleus from the medial longitudinal fasciculus and the paramedian pontine reticular formation (nuc-pprf) for vertical gaze; the nerve itself carries no afferents

The mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus (nuc-mesencephalic-v) and its tract (tract-mesencephalic-v) run in the same dorsal midbrain region and are the proprioceptive companion of the extraocular muscles, but they are NOT the trochlear nerve's afferents — the eye muscles' proprioception travels with CN V
efferent: Superior oblique muscle of the ipsilateral eye (contralateral to the nucleus, because of the dorsal decussation)
Rootlets emerge dorsally at `surf-cn4-exit` — the dorsal exit is the anatomical oddity that makes a trochlear palsy after head trauma a recognisable clinical story

The cisternal nerve passes the ambient cistern and the lateral cavernous-sinus wall alongside the internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) before entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure

afferent: Trochlear motor nucleus; central ocular motor inputs reach the nucleus, not the peripheral nerve.
efferent: Superior oblique of the ipsilateral orbit relative to the post-crossing nerve

course.before: From the trochlear nucleus (nuc-trochlear) in the midbrain tegmentum just caudal to the oculomotor nucleus, the fibres run dorsolaterally around the periaqueductal gray and emerge on the DORSAL surface of the midbrain below the inferior colliculus — the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally — where the landmark `surf-cn4-exit` marks the crossing of the fibres in the anterior medullary velum. The cisternal (subarachnoid) segment then runs a long, slim course around the cerebral peduncle, passing between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries through the ambient (perimesencephalic) cistern, then forward to pierce the tentorium and run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus (holding its position below CN III throughout that wall), to enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure — the foramen this nerve uses — and reach the superior oblique.
course.after: Axons from the inferior-collicular-level trochlear nucleus pass dorsally and cross in the superior (anterior) medullary velum, then emerge below the inferior colliculus. The nerve courses around the midbrain, passes through the cavernous sinus lateral wall and superior orbital fissure, and supplies the superior oblique on the same side as the exiting peripheral nerve.

function.before: Innervates only the superior oblique muscle, whose tendon runs through the trochlea and whose action is to depress the eye in adduction, intort it, and abduct it slightly; the nerve's action therefore appears as a failure of depression when the eye is adducted, which is why the patient with a trochlear palsy complains of vertical diplopia that is worst going down stairs or reading, and why the compensatory head tilt is away from the side of the lesion. The trochlear nucleus is the only cranial-nerve nucleus whose fibres decussate completely before exiting, so a nuclear lesion produces a palsy of the CONTRALATERAL superior oblique while a fascicular or cisternal lesion produces an ipsilateral one. Its long cisternal course makes it the most vulnerable of the ocular motor nerves to closed head injury.
function.after: Supplies superior oblique, which intorts the eye and depresses it most effectively when adducted, with an abducting component. The nucleus supplies the contralateral superior oblique because its fibers cross before dorsal emergence.

modality.before: Motor (somatic motor to the superior oblique only); no sensory and no parasympathetic component

records.name: CN V Trigeminal nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal segment and the root entry zone are supplied by small branches of the basilar artery (vasc-basilar-artery), the superior cerebellar artery (vasc-superior-cerebellar-artery) and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery), which cross the nerve in the cerebellopontine angle; the trigeminal ganglion and the divisions are supplied by the middle meningeal artery, the accessory meningeal artery and the internal carotid's meningohypophyseal branches. The arterial relationship at the root entry zone is the whole mechanism of trigeminal neuralgia from neurovascular compression, and the same relationship explains why an aneurysm of the basilar or superior cerebellar artery can present as facial pain before any weakness — the artery touches the nerve before it touches the brainstem.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.findings: Paroxysmal, electric-shock-like unilateral facial pain in one or more divisions (V2 and V3 most often), triggered by chewing, brushing the teeth, a cold wind or touching a trigger zone, with a completely normal neurological examination between attacks. It is a disease of the root entry zone: in most cases an elongated superior cerebellar artery loops against the nerve, and in a younger patient or with sensory loss it means a demyelinating plaque, a tumour of the cerebellopontine angle or Meckel's cave, or a vascular malformation.
before.vascular: Superior cerebellar artery (or AICA, or a dolichoectatic basilar artery) compressing the trigeminal root entry zone; the microvascular-decompression operation is the anatomical treatment
before.note: Sensory loss ON the same side as the pain, or a corneal reflex reduction, means the pain is secondary (a lesion), not idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia.

before.syndrome: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy — the division pattern localizes the foramen
before.findings: Loss in V1 alone points to the superior orbital fissure or the cavernous sinus; V2 alone to the foramen rotundum or the sinus; V3 alone to the foramen ovale or the infratemporal fossa; all three with a numb chin point to the ganglion, Meckel's cave or the brainstem. The corneal reflex is the most sensitive bedside test of the V1 limb, and its loss with a normal ipsilateral facial motor response (CN VII intact) puts the lesion on the trigeminal side.
before.note: A numb chin with a normal examination otherwise is a classic presentation of a metastatic lesion at the petrous apex or the mandible, not of a benign trigeminal neuropathy.

before.syndrome: Trigeminal motor palsy — jaw deviation and a flaccid bite
before.findings: Weakness of the pterygoid muscles makes the jaw deviate TOWARD the side of the lesion on opening (the intact contralateral lateral pterygoid pushes the jaw across), and the masseter and temporalis waste with a reduced jaw jerk; it is almost never isolated, because the motor fibres leave through the foramen ovale with the sensory root, so an isolated motor palsy localizes to the motor nucleus in the pons or to a lesion at the foramen ovale.
before.note: The jaw-jerk reflex is the brainstem correlate: it is reduced by an ipsilateral motor lesion and exaggerated by a corticobulbar (supranuclear) lesion.

before.findings: A lateral medullary infarct destroys the descending spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus and produces ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss in the onion-skin pattern, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature from the body (spinothalamic tract) — the classical crossed sensory deficit. A midpontine lesion produces IPSILATERAL facial sensory loss with CONTRALATERAL hemiparesis and hemisensory loss (Millard-Gubler/Foville territory with trigeminal involvement), because the trigeminal fibres reach the pons at the level of the motor and principal sensory nuclei and the corticospinal tract is already there.
before.vascular: PICA and vertebral artery for the medullary pattern; paramedian and circumferential basilar branches for the pontine one
before.note: The corneal reflex is often the only sign of a small lateral medullary infarct; testing it is not optional.

after.findings: Lesions can impair sensation in one or more divisions and reduce the V1 afferent corneal reflex. Pterygoid weakness can cause the jaw to deviate toward the weak side on opening. Division patterns narrow localization but do not uniquely identify one foramen.

Brief recurrent shock-like facial pain may be triggered by innocuous stimuli. Neurovascular compression is one recognized mechanism; secondary causes include demyelination or mass lesions. Sensory deficits prompt investigation but no age or examination rule proves a particular cause.

Spinal trigeminal injury can cause ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss together with contralateral body pain-temperature loss when adjacent ascending body pathways are involved. Concentric facial loss is possible but not obligatory.

afferent: Trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion — the cell bodies of the general sensory fibres, from which the three divisions V1, V2 and V3 collect; note that no `nuc-` record exists for the ganglion, so it is named here in prose
Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus (nuc-mesencephalic-v) and its tract (tract-mesencephalic-v) — the proprioceptive fibres of the jaw and extraocular muscles, whose cell bodies lie in the brainstem
Principal (main) sensory trigeminal nucleus (nuc-principal-sensory-v) — discriminative touch and pressure from the face, projecting to the thalamus (nuc-vpm)

Spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal) and tract (tract-spinal-trigeminal) — pain and temperature, organized in the onion-skin pattern (perioral fibres most rostral, periauricular fibres most caudal), which is why a caudal lesion produces the peripheral facial numbness of the lateral medullary syndrome while a rostral one spares the face's periphery
Mesencephalic rootlets also carry the afferent limb of the jaw-jerk reflex, whose efferent limb is the motor nucleus below
efferent: Trigeminal motor nucleus (nuc-trigeminal-motor) — the branchial motor neurons, whose fibres leave with the sensory root through the foramen ovale to the muscles of mastication and the four accessory muscles

Rootlets leave the lateral pons at `surf-cn5-exit`; the cisternal segment then runs to Meckel's cave, where the ganglion lies against the petrous apex and the internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) passes just below and medial to it

Central processes synapse in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei; the ascending projection is the trigeminothalamic tract to the ventral posteromedial nucleus (nuc-vpm) and, for pain, to the intralaminar and posterior thalamic nuclei

The reflex circuits close inside the brainstem (corneal reflex: spinal trigeminal afferent to the facial nucleus; jaw jerk: mesencephalic afferent to the motor nucleus), so they test the nerve AND the brainstem level together

afferent: Peripheral sensory axons associated with trigeminal ganglion neurons
Jaw proprioceptive primary afferents associated with the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus
efferent: Central sensory processes to principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei; proprioceptive connections to mesencephalic/motor circuits
Motor axons from trigeminal motor nucleus through V3 to first-pharyngeal-arch muscles

course.before: A large sensory root and a small motor root emerge from the lateral surface of the mid-pons at the junction of the pons and the middle cerebellar peduncle — the landmark `surf-cn5-exit` — and run forward in the cerebellopontine and prepontine cisterns (the cisternal segment, at the trigeminal root entry zone, where a looping artery can compress the nerve) to the petrous apex, where they pass beneath the tentorial attachment through Meckel's cave and the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion. From the ganglion the nerve divides into three divisions: V1 (ophthalmic) leaves through the superior orbital fissure, V2 (maxillary) through the foramen rotundum, and V3 (mandibular) through the foramen ovale — the three skull-base foramina that name the nerve's divisions and that make the pattern of sensory loss localizing. V3 alone carries the motor fibres, which run with the sensory root through the foramen ovale.
course.after: Large sensory and smaller motor roots emerge at the lateral mid-pons. Most primary sensory neurons are in the trigeminal ganglion; jaw-proprioceptive neurons are in the mesencephalic nucleus. V1 enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure, V2 passes through foramen rotundum and V3 through foramen ovale. The motor root joins V3.

function.before: The great sensory nerve of the head: it supplies the face, the scalp as far back as the vertex, the cornea and conjunctiva, the nasal and oral mucosae, the teeth and gingivae, the dura of the anterior and middle cranial fossae, and the meninges of the tentorium, and it carries the afferent limb of the corneal blink reflex, the sneeze reflex and the jaw-jerk reflex. Its branchial motor fibres innervate the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), the tensor tympani (which damps loud sound), the tensor veli palatini (which opens the Eustachian tube) and the mylohyoid and anterior digastric (which elevate the floor of the mouth in swallowing). Uniquely, its proprioceptive fibres for the jaw and the extraocular muscles have their cell bodies in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus (nuc-mesencephalic-v) inside the brainstem rather than in the ganglion — the only primary sensory neurons in that position — and their axons form the mesencephalic trigeminal tract (tract-mesencephalic-v). Its central processes descend to the spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal) and its tract (tract-spinal-trigeminal) for pain and temperature, and synapse in the principal sensory nucleus (nuc-principal-sensory-v) for discriminative touch.
function.after: Carries general sensation from much of the face, cornea, oral/nasal cavities, teeth and cranial dura. V3 motor fibers supply mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini. CN V supplies the afferent limb of the corneal blink reflex; CN VII supplies its motor limb.

records.name: CN VI Abducens nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal segment is supplied by small branches of the basilar artery (vasc-basilar-artery) and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery), which run through the prepontine cistern beside it; the petrous and cavernous portions are supplied by the dorsal meningeal and meningohypophyseal branches of the internal carotid (vasc-internal-carotid-artery). The ascending course beside the basilar artery is the anatomical reason it is the first nerve to be compressed by a vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia, and the reason an AICA or basilar aneurysm can present with an isolated abducens palsy.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.syndrome: Abducens palsy — failure of abduction with horizontal diplopia
before.findings: The eye cannot be abducted past the midline (or abducts incompletely), diplopia is maximal on gaze to the affected side and is horizontal, and the patient turns the head to fuse. The palsy localizes to the nerve anywhere from the nucleus to the orbit, and an isolated, pupil-sparing sixth-nerve palsy in a patient over 50 with vascular risk factors is usually microvascular and recovers in three months.
before.vascular: Microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum (diabetes, hypertension); or compression by a dolichoectatic basilar artery (vasc-basilar-artery)
before.note: An isolated sixth-nerve palsy is the commonest false localizing sign: it can be the presenting sign of raised intracranial pressure, a pontine glioma, a nasopharyngeal carcinoma at the petrous apex or a Gradenigo syndrome, so imaging is the rule.

before.syndrome: False localizing abducens palsy of raised intracranial pressure
before.findings: Raised pressure displaces the brainstem caudally and stretches the long, fixed, ascending cisternal nerve against the clivus and the petrosphenoidal ligament, producing a (usually bilateral) abduction palsy with no lesion in the nerve's own pathway; it is accompanied by the other signs of raised pressure (headache, papilloedema, a false localizing sign in a patient whose CT is otherwise normal).
before.note: The nerve's anatomy, not its pathology, is the localizing point: a long nerve tethered at both ends is stretched by displacement of either end.

before.syndrome: Nuclear (gaze palsy) versus fascicular (crossed) sixth-nerve lesions
before.findings: A nuclear lesion destroys motor and internuclear neurons together, producing an ipsilateral horizontal GAZE palsy with facial palsy on the same side (because the facial fibres loop around the nucleus at that level); a fascicular lesion as the fibres cross the corticospinal tract produces the Foville and Millard-Gubler syndromes — ipsilateral abducens (or gaze) palsy with CONTRALATERAL hemiparesis, often with an ipsilateral facial palsy.
before.vascular: Paramedian branches of the basilar artery (pontine infarct); Millard-Gubler and Foville are the classic brainstem localizers (syn-millard-gubler, syn-foville)
before.note: The one-and-a-half syndrome (syn-one-and-a-half) is the neighbouring lesion: a PPRF/MLF lesion adds an internuclear ophthalmoplegia to the ipsilateral gaze palsy, leaving only abduction of the contralateral eye.

before.findings: Petrous apicitis or a petrous-apex tumour involving the Dorello canal and Meckel's cave produces the triad of an ipsilateral abducens palsy, deep facial or retro-orbital pain (V1/V2) and hearing loss or otorrhoea — the anatomical combination of the structures that share the petrous apex.
before.note: The petrous apex is where the sixth nerve and the trigeminal ganglion meet; a patient with diplopia, facial pain and ear symptoms has a lesion there, not in the orbit.

after.findings: Impaired abduction produces horizontal diplopia, often greater toward the weak side. Nuclear injury instead usually impairs conjugate gaze toward that side because motor and internuclear neurons are affected.

after.syndrome: Raised intracranial pressure or local injury
after.findings: The long intracranial course can be affected by raised pressure as a false-localizing sign, skull-base disease, cavernous sinus lesions, trauma or microvascular disease. Laterality and recovery are variable.

afferent: Abducens nucleus (nuc-abducens) — the motor neurons for the lateral rectus plus the internuclear neurons that cross to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus (nuc-oculomotor) through the medial longitudinal fasciculus
Paramedian pontine reticular formation (nuc-pprf) and the medial vestibular nucleus (nuc-vestibular-medial) drive the nucleus for horizontal gaze; the nerve itself carries no afferents
Frontal eye fields (ctx-frontal-eye-fields) reach the nucleus through the PPRF — the supranuclear route that a nuclear lesion is tested against
efferent: Lateral rectus muscle of the ipsilateral eye

Rootlets emerge at the pontomedullary junction at `surf-cn6-exit`, then the nerve passes through the Dorello canal under the petrosphenoidal ligament — the choke point where raised intracranial pressure and clival lesions act

In the cavernous sinus the nerve lies lateral to the internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) and receives sympathetic fibres from the carotid plexus that it carries into the orbit (the anatomical reason for the occasional oculosympathetic paresis with a cavernous-sinus lesion)

Internuclear neurons from the nucleus cross the midline and ascend in the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus, which is what makes conjugate gaze and what makes a nuclear lesion a gaze palsy

afferent: Abducens somatic motor neurons; gaze-control input reaches the nucleus centrally.
efferent: Ipsilateral lateral rectus

course.before: From the abducens nucleus (nuc-abducens) in the caudal pons, beneath the facial colliculus of the fourth-ventricle floor, the fibres run ventrally, laterally and caudally through the pontine tegmentum — passing the facial nucleus's fibres that loop around the nucleus (the internal genu of CN VII) — and emerge at the pontomedullary junction just lateral to the corticospinal pyramid, at the landmark `surf-cn6-exit`. The cisternal segment then ascends almost vertically through the prepontine cistern, hugging the clivus, and passes through the narrow Dorello canal beneath the petrosphenoidal (Gruber) ligament into the cavernous sinus; it then runs in the sinus lateral to the internal carotid artery and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure — the foramen this nerve uses — to reach the lateral rectus. No other cranial nerve has such a long, fixed, ascending cisternal course, which is why it is the nerve most often stretched by raised intracranial pressure and by downward displacement of the brainstem.
course.after: Motor fascicles from the caudal pontine abducens nucleus emerge at the pontomedullary sulcus near the midline. The nerve ascends along the clivus through Dorello canal, traverses the cavernous sinus near the internal carotid and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.

function.before: Innervates only the lateral rectus, the muscle that abducts the eye; failure of the nerve therefore produces an inability to abduct the eye past the midline with horizontal diplopia that is worst on gaze to the affected side — the patient turns the head instead. Because the abducens nucleus contains both the motor neurons for the lateral rectus and the internuclear neurons that cross the midline to the contralateral medial-rectus subnucleus of CN III, a NUCLEAR lesion produces an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy (neither eye crosses the midline) rather than an isolated abduction deficit, which is the single most useful distinction between a nuclear and a nerve lesion. The nucleus is also the target of the paramedian pontine reticular formation (nuc-pprf) for horizontal conjugate gaze.
function.after: Supplies ipsilateral lateral rectus for eye abduction. Abducens internuclear neurons cross and ascend in the opposite MLF to the oculomotor nucleus; those axons are central gaze connections and are not carried in CN VI.

modality.before: Motor (somatic motor to the lateral rectus only); no sensory and no parasympathetic component

records.name: CN VII Facial nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal segment and the root exit zone are crossed by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery), whose loop in the cerebellopontine angle is the vessel that compresses this nerve's root entry zone in hemifacial spasm — the facial-nerve analogue of trigeminal neuralgia. The intratemporal nerve is supplied by the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery and by the stylomastoid branch of the posterior auricular artery; in the parotid it is supplied by the superficial temporal and transverse facial arteries. The artery at the root exit zone is load-bearing clinically: an AICA loop causes hemifacial spasm, and the same vessel occluding produces an AICA syndrome with facial palsy, deafness and vertigo together.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.syndrome: Peripheral facial palsy (Bell's palsy and its mimics)
before.findings: A complete lower-motor-neuron palsy paralyses the whole ipsilateral face: the forehead cannot be wrinkled, the eye cannot be closed (with a risk of exposure keratitis), the mouth droops and the patient cannot whistle or hold liquid on that side; hyperacusis, loss of taste in the anterior tongue and a dry eye accompany it when the lesion is inside the facial canal (the geniculate and chorda segments), and are absent when the lesion is distal to the stylomastoid foramen. Bell's palsy is idiopathic and self-limiting in most cases; the mimics that must be excluded are a parotid tumour, cholesteatoma, temporal-bone fracture, sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome and a pontine lesion.
before.vascular: Microvascular ischaemia and viral inflammation of the nerve inside the facial canal; the diagnosis of exclusion is the reason imaging is advised when the palsy is progressive, painful or recurrent
before.note: The site of the lesion is read off the associated signs: loss of tearing (greater petrosal), hyperacusis (stapedius), loss of taste (chorda tympani), loss of saliva (chorda tympani) — a stepwise localization along the facial canal.

before.syndrome: Central (supranuclear) facial palsy with forehead sparing
before.findings: A corticobulbar lesion above the pons spares the upper face, because the motor neurons for the frontalis and orbicularis oculi receive bilateral cortical input while the lower-face neurons receive only contralateral input: the patient has a drooping mouth but can still wrinkle the forehead and close the eye tightly. It is the single most useful bedside distinction between a hemispheric or capsular lesion and a brainstem or nerve lesion, and it is accompanied by the other signs of the causal lesion (hemiparesis, aphasia, hemianopia or a brainstem crossed syndrome).
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery or internal capsule territory (with hemiparesis); a pontine lesion produces the peripheral type instead, with the crossed pattern of Millard-Gubler (syn-millard-gubler)
before.note: The rule is anatomical, not clinical folklore: bilateral corticobulbar supply to the upper-face motor neurons is what spares the forehead.

before.findings: Intermittent, involuntary, unilateral clonic contractions of the muscles of facial expression, beginning around the orbicularis oculi and spreading to the mouth, that persist in sleep and can be triggered by voluntary movement; it is usually caused by an arterial loop (most often AICA or the posterior inferior cerebellar artery) compressing the facial nerve at its root exit zone, and microvascular decompression is curative.
before.vascular: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery), occasionally the vertebral or basilar artery
before.note: The facial-nerve twin of trigeminal neuralgia: both are diseases of the root entry zone, and both are treated by moving the artery rather than by cutting the nerve.

before.syndrome: Ramsay Hunt syndrome and other intratemporal causes
before.findings: Varicella-zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion produces a facial palsy with severe ear pain, vesicles in the external canal or the concha (the sensory zone of CN VII), hearing loss and vertigo — the combination that localizes the lesion to the geniculate ganglion and the meatus rather than to the canal alone.
before.note: The vesicles sit exactly in the nerve's own sensory distribution, which is why their presence names the diagnosis; a facial palsy with sensorineural hearing loss should always raise the meatus as the site.

after.findings: Nuclear, fascicular or peripheral motor injury can weaken the entire ipsilateral face, including forehead and eye closure. More proximal lesions may add hyperacusis, taste or secretomotor changes; these are not universal.

Unilateral supranuclear lesions often predominantly affect the contralateral lower face because upper facial input is more bilateral. Forehead sparing is a useful relative pattern, not an absolute rule. A pontine lesion can produce a peripheral-pattern palsy with other brainstem signs.
Bell palsy, infection, inflammatory disease, tumor and traumatic injury are among possible peripheral causes. A facial-weakness pattern alone does not establish Bell palsy.

afferent: Facial nucleus (nuc-facial) — the branchial motor neurons, whose axons run in the motor root; the nucleus receives bilateral corticobulbar input for the upper face and contralateral-dominant input for the lower face
Superior salivatory nucleus (nuc-superior-salivatory) — the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons for the lacrimal, nasal, submandibular and sublingual glands
Nucleus solitarius, rostral gustatory part (nuc-solitarius-rostral) — the central target of the taste fibres carried in the nervus intermedius
Spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal) — the central target of the small general sensory zone of the concha and the external auditory canal
Trigeminal afferents (CN V, nrv-cn5-trigeminal) supply the corneal reflex's afferent limb; this nerve supplies the efferent limb, so the reflex tests both
efferent: Muscles of facial expression through the five parotid branches, plus stapedius, stylohyoid and the posterior digastric
Greater petrosal nerve to the pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal and nasal glands) and chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion (submandibular and sublingual glands)

Taste fibres from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and soft palate turn centrally into the rostral nucleus solitarius, which then projects to the thalamus (nuc-vpm) and the insula for conscious taste

Rootlets leave at the pontomedullary junction at `surf-cn7-exit` and the nerve crosses the cerebellopontine angle with CN VIII (nrv-cn8-vestibulocochlear) into the internal acoustic meatus — the two nerves share a foramen and therefore fail together when a lesion is at the meatus

The nerve carries preganglionic fibres that turn into the facial canal toward the geniculate ganglion, the anatomical reason a lesion in the canal produces loss of tearing and taste in addition to the palsy (a lesion outside the stylomastoid foramen does not)

afferent: Taste and small general sensory afferents with cell bodies in geniculate ganglion; central taste input reaches rostral solitary nucleus and general sensory input spinal trigeminal complex.
efferent: Branchial motor axons from facial nucleus to second-pharyngeal-arch muscles
Superior salivatory/lacrimal preganglionic axons to pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia

course.before: The motor root and the smaller nervus intermedius emerge at the pontomedullary junction, lateral to the abducens rootlets, in the cerebellopontine angle — the landmark `surf-cn7-exit` — and pass with CN VIII into the internal acoustic meatus (the foramen this nerve uses at the skull base) and then into the facial canal of the petrous temporal bone. In the canal the fibres reach the geniculate ganglion, where the greater petrosal nerve leaves for the pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal and nasal glands) and the nerve turns posteriorly (the external genu over the oval window), giving off the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani (taste from the anterior tongue plus secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands) before exiting the skull through the stylomastoid foramen. Outside the skull it enters the parotid gland and divides into the temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches to the muscles of facial expression. The cisternal segment between the brainstem and the meatus is the short one that neurovascular compression acts on.
course.after: Facial motor fibers loop around the abducens nucleus, then emerge with the nervus intermedius at the pontomedullary/cerebellopontine angle. The nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus and facial canal. Greater petrosal and chorda tympani branches carry parasympathetic/taste fibers; motor fibers exit the stylomastoid foramen and branch within the parotid gland.

function.before: Three nerves in one sheath. Its branchial motor fibres innervate all the muscles of facial expression (orbicularis oculi and oris, buccinator, the muscles of the nose and the platysma), plus stapedius (which damps loud sound, so its paralysis causes hyperacusis), stylohyoid and the posterior belly of the digastric — so the nerve closes the eye, seals the lips, produces the social face and the corneal reflex's efferent limb. Its parasympathetic fibres run from the superior salivatory nucleus (nuc-superior-salivatory) to the pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia for tear and saliva production, which is why a dry eye and a dry mouth accompany a complete lesion. Its special sensory fibres carry taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the soft palate, with cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion and central processes that join the nervus intermedius to the rostral nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-rostral). The long intratemporal course is the reason a facial palsy can be the first sign of a parotid tumour, a temporal-bone fracture, cholesteatoma or Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
function.after: Supplies facial-expression muscles, stapedius, posterior digastric and stylohyoid; conveys anterior-two-thirds tongue taste; provides parasympathetic supply to lacrimal/nasal/palatal glands through pterygopalatine ganglion and submandibular/sublingual glands through submandibular ganglion. Passing through the parotid does not give it parotid secretomotor function.

modality.before: Mixed — branchial motor (muscles of facial expression plus stapedius, stylohyoid and the posterior digastric), general sensory (a small concha/ear-canal zone), special sensory (taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue) and visceral motor (parasympathetic secretomotor to the lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual and nasal glands)
modality.after: Branchial motor, preganglionic parasympathetic, taste (special visceral afferent), and a small general sensory component.

records.name: CN VIII Vestibulocochlear nerve

bloodSupply.before: The nerve and the inner ear it serves are supplied by the labyrinthine artery, a branch of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery) that runs with the nerve through the internal acoustic meatus; the labyrinthine artery is an end artery, so its occlusion causes sudden, permanent sensorineural deafness with vestibular failure rather than a transient deficit. The AICA's territory is the reason an AICA infarct produces the combination of vertigo, deafness, tinnitus, facial palsy and ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, and the reason the nerve's blood supply, not just its structure, is what fails in sudden deafness in the elderly.
bloodSupply.after: The inner ear and intrameatal nerve are supplied by the labyrinthine artery, usually arising from AICA but sometimes from the basilar artery. The central cochlear/vestibular nuclear region has separate overlapping vertebrobasilar branches.

before.syndrome: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at the internal acoustic meatus
before.findings: A slow-growing tumour of the vestibular division produces unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with poor speech discrimination, tinnitus, and later imbalance; because the meatus is shared, growth eventually adds a facial palsy (CN VII), a reduced corneal reflex and facial numbness (CN V). The early picture is a hearing loss out of proportion to the audiogram's apparent severity, which is why speech discrimination testing is the key bedside finding.
before.note: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas mean neurofibromatosis type 2; the shared meatus is the anatomical reason this tumour has a syndromic signature at all.

before.syndrome: Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis (acute unilateral vestibular failure)
before.findings: Acute, severe, continuous vertigo with nausea and vomiting, horizontal-torsional nystagmus that beats away from the affected ear, and a positive head-impulse test on the affected side, with NO hearing loss (neuritis) or WITH hearing loss and tinnitus (labyrinthitis). The absence of the other brainstem signs is what separates it from a lateral medullary or AICA infarct, and the head-impulse test is the sign that localizes the failure to the vestibular nerve.
before.vascular: Post-viral inflammation of the vestibular division; an AICA infarct is the vascular mimic and is suggested by the additional deafness, facial palsy or ataxia
before.note: The HINTS examination (head impulse, nystagmus type, test of skew) separates a peripheral from a central cause at the bedside, because a central lesion can present as isolated vertigo.

before.findings: Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery produces vertigo with vomiting, ipsilateral sensorineural deafness and tinnitus, ipsilateral facial palsy, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, and a crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body) — the whole output of this nerve's compartment failing at once, because the labyrinthine branch and the facial and vestibular nerve roots share it.
before.note: The combination of deafness and vertigo with a facial palsy and ataxia is the reason a patient with 'labyrinthitis' who also has a facial droop needs urgent imaging.

before.syndrome: Sensorineural hearing loss — cochlear versus retrocochlear localization
before.findings: A cochlear lesion (hair-cell loss from noise, ototoxic drugs or Menière disease) produces recruitment and preserved or disproportionate speech discrimination, while a retrocochlear lesion of this nerve or the meatus produces poor discrimination, a disproportionate loss of speech understanding and often an abnormal auditory brainstem response; the distinction is the bedside version of the question 'inner ear or nerve?', and it decides whether the patient needs an MRI of the meatus.
before.vascular: Labyrinthine artery occlusion (an AICA branch) causes sudden retrocochlear-pattern deafness; the vascular cause is an emergency for the ear as well as for the brainstem

after.findings: Peripheral cochlear/nerve injury can cause ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus or imbalance; vestibular injury can cause vertigo and nystagmus. Central and peripheral patterns overlap and the symptoms do not establish one site on their own.
Vestibular schwannoma and other masses may affect hearing/balance and, with extension, adjacent nerves or brainstem. Hearing loss need not be the first or only finding.

AICA/labyrinthine ischemia can mimic peripheral vestibular illness, sometimes with hearing loss. Acute vestibular examination requires the appropriate clinical setting and expertise; an atlas pattern is insufficient to exclude stroke.

afferent: Ventral cochlear nucleus (nuc-cochlear-ventral) and dorsal cochlear nucleus (nuc-cochlear-dorsal) — the first central relays of hearing; the ventral nucleus projects to the superior olivary complex (nuc-superior-olivary) for sound localization, the dorsal nucleus to the contralateral inferior colliculus (nuc-inferior-colliculus)

Superior vestibular nucleus (nuc-vestibular-superior), medial vestibular nucleus (nuc-vestibular-medial), lateral vestibular nucleus (nuc-vestibular-lateral) and inferior vestibular nucleus (nuc-vestibular-inferior) — the four first-order vestibular relays, whose central targets are the abducens nucleus (nuc-abducens) via the medial longitudinal fasciculus, the cerebellum and the thalamus
Note on the registry: no `nuc-` record exists for the spiral or vestibular ganglia, so those first-order cell groups are named here in prose rather than linked
Rootlets enter the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction at `surf-cn8-exit`, immediately dorsal to the facial nerve's rootlets, which is why a lesion at the meatus involves both nerves
efferent: The vestibular nerve is classically afferent-only, but it does carry the efferents of the olivocochlear bundle from the superior olivary complex to the outer hair cells, and the vestibular nuclei give the reflex efferents (to CN III, IV and VI through the MLF and to the spinal cord through the vestibulospinal tracts) that stabilise gaze and posture
The efferent limb of the vestibular reflex arcs is therefore the ocular motor nerves (nrv-cn3-oculomotor, nrv-cn4-trochlear, nrv-cn6-abducens) and the vestibulospinal tracts, not this nerve
Its afferents together with the cochlear nuclei form the auditory pathway that reaches the auditory cortex (ctx-a1) through the inferior colliculus and the medial geniculate nucleus (nuc-mgn)

afferent: Spiral ganglion neurons receiving cochlear hair-cell input
Vestibular ganglion neurons receiving semicircular-canal and otolith input
efferent: Central primary afferents to cochlear nuclei, vestibular nuclei and cerebellar targets
Small olivocochlear and vestibular efferent systems return from the brainstem toward inner-ear targets

contextNote.after: Authored schematic course represents the common intracranial path, not each inner-ear branch or a validated labyrinth. Sensory nerve central projections and reflex efferents are distinguished.

course.before: The two divisions emerge together from the pontomedullary junction at the lateral end of the sulcus between the pons and the medulla, alongside CN VII, at the landmark `surf-cn8-exit`, and cross the cerebellopontine angle as a short cisternal segment (about 1 cm) to enter the internal acoustic meatus — the foramen this nerve uses at the skull base — where the facial nerve runs with them. Inside the meatus the cochlear division passes to the spiral ganglion and the organ of Corti through the modiolus of the cochlea, and the vestibular division passes to the vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion and then to the utricle, saccule and the three semicircular canals. The meatus is a tight, shared compartment, which is why a lesion there (acoustic neuroma, meningioma, meatal fracture) produces deafness, vertigo AND a facial palsy together — the anatomical reason for the classic combination.
course.after: Cochlear and vestibular divisions connect the inner ear through the internal acoustic meatus to the lateral pontomedullary/cerebellopontine-angle region. Primary cochlear neurons reside in spiral ganglion and vestibular neurons in vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion.

function.before: Carries the two special senses of the inner ear. The cochlear division transmits the tonotopically organized output of the organ of Corti (hair cells to spiral ganglion to the cochlear nuclei, nuc-cochlear-ventral and nuc-cochlear-dorsal), which is the first stage of the auditory pathway to the superior olivary complex (nuc-superior-olivary), the inferior colliculus (nuc-inferior-colliculus) and the auditory cortex (ctx-a1); its fibres are organized by frequency, so a lesion produces a sensorineural hearing loss with impaired speech discrimination rather than the conductive pattern of a middle-ear lesion. The vestibular division carries head-acceleration and head-position signals from the semicircular canals and otolith organs to the four vestibular nuclei (nuc-vestibular-superior, -medial, -lateral and -inferior) and, through the cerebellum (nuc-dentate and the flocculonodular lobe), drives the vestibulo-ocular reflex for gaze stabilization, the vestibulospinal reflexes for posture, and the conscious sense of head orientation that reaches the thalamus and the parietal cortex. An acute imbalance of its two sides produces the cardinal vestibular syndrome of vertigo, nystagmus and postural instability.
function.after: Cochlear fibers transmit sound information to cochlear nuclei. Vestibular fibers carry head-motion/position signals to vestibular nuclei and directly to cerebellar circuitry, supporting balance and vestibulo-ocular reflexes. The downstream ocular motor or spinal output of those reflexes is carried by other pathways.

modality.before: Special sensory — hearing (cochlear division) and balance/head position (vestibular division); no motor component of any kind
modality.after: Special somatic afferent; small peripheral auditory/vestibular efferent components also exist.

records.name: CN IX Glossopharyngeal nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal root is supplied by small perforating branches of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery) and the vertebral artery (vasc-vertebral-artery), and the nerve descends into the neck immediately medial to the internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) at its bifurcation — an anatomical relationship that makes the nerve vulnerable during carotid endarterectomy (where its injury causes dysphagia and loss of the gag reflex) and that explains why glossopharyngeal neuralgia is so often caused by a PICA loop at the root entry zone. The proximity of the carotid bifurcation is also the reason the nerve's baroreceptor fibres are accessible to carotid-sinus massage and to stenting.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.findings: Paroxysmal, severe, lancinating pain in the posterior tongue, tonsil, pharynx, angle of the jaw or ear, triggered by swallowing, coughing, yawning or talking — and, in the vagal variant, accompanied by bradycardia, hypotension and syncope (because the vagal efferents are activated at the same time). The pain is in the nerve's own sensory distribution and the examination is normal between attacks.
before.vascular: A PICA or vertebral artery loop compressing the glossopharyngeal root entry zone; microvascular decompression is the treatment
before.note: The syncopal form is the dangerous one: the combination of throat pain and cardiac arrest localizes the lesion to the region shared by CN IX and CN X.

before.syndrome: Loss of the gag reflex and pharyngeal sensory loss (jugular-foramen lesion)
before.findings: A jugular-foramen lesion (glomus jugulare tumour, meningioma, metastasis, thrombosis) damages CN IX, X and XI together, producing loss of the gag reflex, a deviated uvula, hoarseness, dysphagia, and weakness and wasting of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius — the Vernet syndrome; adding CN XII through the hypoglossal canal gives the Collet-Sicard syndrome, and adding a Horner syndrome gives Villaret syndrome.
before.note: The gag reflex tests CN IX (afferent) and CN X (efferent) together, so its loss localizes to the pair, not to one nerve — the bedside version of the shared jugular foramen.

before.syndrome: Glossopharyngeal palsy with loss of parotid secretion and taste
before.findings: An isolated IX lesion is rare: it produces a dry mouth (loss of parotid secretomotor drive), loss of taste in the posterior third of the tongue, reduced pharyngeal sensation and a mild dysphagia, and it is usually part of a jugular-foramen or brainstem picture rather than a solitary nerve palsy. The taste loss is separable from that of CN VII because the two nerves serve different thirds of the tongue.
before.note: Taste is served by three nerves — CN VII (anterior two-thirds), CN IX (posterior third) and CN X (epiglottis) — so the pattern of taste loss is itself a localizing sign.

before.syndrome: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome with glossopharyngeal involvement
before.findings: The lateral medullary infarct destroys the nucleus ambiguus, the spinal trigeminal tract and the vestibular nuclei, producing vertigo, nystagmus, ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, hoarseness, dysphagia, a drooping palate and a reduced gag reflex with contralateral body sensory loss — a rostrocaudal gradient in which the glossopharyngeal fibres are the rostral end of the nerve output that fails here.
before.vascular: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery or vertebral artery occlusion
before.note: The glossopharyngeal and vagal deficits are efferent (ambiguus) and afferent (solitary and spinal trigeminal) at once, which is why the palatal and gag findings are asymmetric rather than absent.

after.findings: Posterior tongue/pharyngeal sensory or taste loss and impaired gag afference may occur. Gag responses vary normally and their absence alone does not establish a IX lesion. Combined IX/X lesions can impair swallowing.

Brief severe pain in throat, posterior tongue or ear may be triggered by swallowing or talking. Occasionally vagal cardioinhibitory reflexes accompany attacks; this is not the expected consequence of simply losing IX sensory input.
Mass, inflammation or vascular injury near the jugular foramen may combine IX/X/XI deficits. The pattern suggests a region but does not establish one cause.

afferent: Nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) — the branchial motor neurons for stylopharyngeus, shared with CN X and the cranial root of CN XI

Nucleus solitarius, caudal cardiorespiratory part (nuc-solitarius-caudal) — the central target of the carotid-body chemoreceptor and carotid-sinus baroreceptor afferents, the afferent limb of the reflexes that control breathing and blood pressure
Nucleus solitarius, rostral gustatory part (nuc-solitarius-rostral) — the central target of taste from the posterior third of the tongue

Spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal) — the general sensory afferents from the posterior tongue, tonsil, pharynx and middle ear, which is why a lateral medullary lesion reduces the gag reflex and the pain/temperature sense of the oropharynx
Inferior salivatory nucleus — the parasympathetic source for the parotid; no registry record exists for it, so it is named here in prose
efferent: Stylopharyngeus through the pharyngeal plexus — the only muscle this nerve supplies directly
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibres through the tympanic plexus, lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion to the parotid gland

Rootlets leave the postolivary sulcus at `surf-cn9-exit`, then the nerve passes through the pars nervosa of the jugular foramen (nrv-cn10-vagus and nrv-cn11-accessory share the same foramen and are therefore injured together by a jugular-foramen lesion)

The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (nuc-dmv) sends a small contingent of preganglionic fibres with this nerve to the pharyngeal and mucosal glands, which is why the ninth nerve contributes to vagal-phase secretion even though its own secretomotor output goes to the parotid
Carotid sinus nerve (of Hering) to the carotid body and sinus — the pathway whose interruption abolishes the baroreflex on that side

afferent: Superior/inferior sensory ganglion afferents: taste/visceral signals to solitary nucleus and general sensory signals to spinal trigeminal complex
efferent: Nucleus ambiguus motor fibers to stylopharyngeus
Inferior salivatory preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to otic ganglion and then parotid gland

contextNote.after: Authored schematic root/jugular course. The principal parasympathetic source is inferior salivatory nucleus; DMV is a vagal nucleus and is not substituted as IX secretomotor origin.

course.before: Three to five rootlets emerge from the postolivary sulcus of the rostral medulla, just above the vagal rootlets and dorsal to the inferior olive, at the landmark `surf-cn9-exit`, and run forward and laterally through the cerebellopontine cistern (the cisternal segment, where a PICA loop can compress the root) to the jugular foramen, where the nerve passes through its own compartment, the pars nervosa — the foramen this nerve uses at the skull base — with the inferior petrosal sinus. It then descends between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein, curves forward around the stylopharyngeus (which it supplies), passes between the internal and external carotid arteries, and distributes to the pharyngeal plexus, the tonsil, the posterior third of the tongue and the parotid gland through the otic ganglion, with the carotid sinus nerve (of Hering) descending to the carotid bifurcation.
course.after: Rootlets emerge from the postolivary sulcus of the medulla and exit the skull through the jugular foramen. Superior/inferior sensory ganglia lie near this exit. Branches reach the stylopharyngeus, pharynx/posterior tongue, carotid sinus/body and tympanic-otic parasympathetic route.

function.before: The nerve of the oropharynx and the carotid bifurcation. Its branchial motor fibres supply stylopharyngeus (which elevates the pharynx in swallowing); its parasympathetic fibres run from the inferior salivatory nucleus through the tympanic plexus and the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion and thence to the parotid gland; its general sensory fibres supply the posterior third of the tongue, the tonsil, the oropharynx and the middle ear, and carry the afferent limb of the GAG REFLEX; its special sensory fibres carry taste from the posterior third of the tongue to the rostral nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-rostral); and its visceral afferents carry chemoreceptor and baroreceptor information from the carotid body and carotid sinus to the caudal nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-caudal), which is the afferent limb of blood-pressure and oxygen-sensing reflexes. Its motor fibres arise from the nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) and its parasympathetic fibres from the inferior salivatory nucleus, which has no separate registry record and is therefore named in prose.
function.after: Supplies stylopharyngeus; conveys posterior-third tongue taste and pharyngeal general sensation; carries carotid sinus/body sensory input. Inferior salivatory axons reach the otic ganglion via tympanic and lesser petrosal routes, then the parotid through auriculotemporal nerve. CN IX commonly supplies a gag-reflex afferent limb, with vagal motor output.

modality.before: Mixed — branchial motor (stylopharyngeus), visceral motor (parasympathetic to the parotid), general sensory (posterior third of the tongue, oropharynx, tonsil, middle ear, Eustachian tube), special sensory (taste from the posterior third of the tongue) and visceral afferent (carotid body and sinus)
modality.after: Branchial motor, preganglionic parasympathetic, taste, visceral afferent and general sensory.

records.name: CN X Vagus nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal root is supplied by perforating branches of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery) and the vertebral artery (vasc-vertebral-artery); in the neck the nerve descends in the carotid sheath between the internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) and the internal jugular vein, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch while the right loops under the right subclavian artery. That asymmetry is directly load-bearing: an aortic-arch aneurysm, an enlarged left atrium or a mediastinal mass paralyses the left vocal fold through the left recurrent nerve, and the same vessel relationship is why the left nerve is the one injured in thoracic surgery. Within the thorax the vagus runs with the oesophagus, which is the reason oesophageal carcinoma invades it early.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.syndrome: Vagal (nuclear and infranuclear) palsy — palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal failure
before.findings: A unilateral lesion of the nucleus ambiguus or of the vagus droops the ipsilateral palate, deviates the uvula AWAY from the side of the lesion, paralyses the ipsilateral vocal fold with hoarseness and a bovine cough, and impairs swallowing with a risk of aspiration; bilateral lesions produce near-complete loss of pharyngeal and laryngeal function, and the loss of the afferent limb (nucleus solitarius) removes the protective cough. The side of the uvular deviation and the side of the vocal-fold palsy localize the lesion to the same side as the nerve.
before.vascular: PICA or vertebral artery for a nuclear/lateral medullary lesion; the neck and mediastinum for a peripheral one
before.note: The uvula deviates AWAY from the lesion because the intact contralateral palatal muscles pull it across — the opposite of the tongue's rule, and a classic bedside trap.

before.syndrome: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (an aortic-arch or mediastinal sign)
before.findings: Paralysis of the ipsilateral vocal fold with hoarseness, a weak cough and loss of the ability to raise pitch; the left nerve's long intrathoracic course under the aortic arch makes a left-sided palsy a classic presentation of an aortic-arch aneurysm, an enlarged left atrium (mitral stenosis), a mediastinal tumour or an apical lung carcinoma, while a right-sided palsy points below the right subclavian artery or at the thyroid.
before.vascular: Aortic arch (left recurrent nerve) or right subclavian artery (right recurrent nerve) — the vessel the nerve loops around is the vessel that names the level of the lesion
before.note: A patient with hoarseness and a normal larynx on examination needs a chest imaging study, because the nerve can be paralysed far from the larynx.

before.syndrome: Vagal dysautonomia, cough syncope and bradyarrhythmia
before.findings: Loss of vagal cardiac modulation removes beat-to-beat control of heart rate (producing a fixed tachycardia) while preserved sympathetic tone leaves the patient orthostatic; the opposite — vagal overactivity from irritation of the auricular branch in the external canal, from oesophageal distension or from a jugular-foramen lesion — causes cough syncope and sudden bradycardia or asystole. Gastroparesis and impaired intestinal motility follow loss of the gut's vagal drive.
before.vascular: Not primarily vascular; the neural-crest and brainstem lesions that cause dysautonomia are degenerative, surgical or traumatic
before.note: Vagal and sympathetic failure must be separated: vagal failure causes tachycardia and gut stasis, sympathetic failure causes orthostatic hypotension and a Horner syndrome.

before.syndrome: Jugular-foramen and Collet-Sicard syndromes (CN IX, X, XI, XII)
before.findings: A lesion at the jugular foramen takes CN IX, X and XI together (Vernet syndrome) and, when it extends to the hypoglossal canal, adds CN XII (Collet-Sicard syndrome), producing loss of the gag reflex, palatal and vocal-fold palsy, dysphagia, and weakness of the sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and tongue on one side — the combination that names the skull base as the site rather than the brainstem, because the brainstem syndromes produce crossed findings and a partial pattern.
before.vascular: Glomus jugulare tumour, meningioma, metastasis or internal jugular vein thrombosis
before.note: The one-sided, multiple-nerve, non-crossed pattern is what makes this a skull-base syndrome: at the foramen the nerves are physically together, and no brainstem lesion takes exactly this set without adding long-tract signs.

after.findings: Unilateral palatal and vocal-fold weakness can cause hoarseness, dysphagia and aspiration; the palate may sag ipsilaterally and uvula deviate away from the weak side. Severity and gag responses vary.

Recurrent laryngeal injury can impair vocal-fold movement. External superior laryngeal/cricothyroid injury particularly impairs pitch modulation. Surgery or lesions along neck/chest courses can affect these branches.

Vagal network injury can disturb cardiovascular and gastrointestinal regulation. Bradycardia from increased vagal activity is not equivalent to loss of parasympathetic neurons, which should not be presented as causing inevitable bradycardia/asystole.

afferent: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (nuc-dmv) — the preganglionic parasympathetic source, the largest visceral efferent column of the brainstem
Nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) — the branchial motor source for the pharynx and larynx, shared with CN IX and the cranial root of CN XI

Nucleus solitarius, caudal cardiorespiratory part (nuc-solitarius-caudal) — the central target of the aortic arch baroreceptor and chemoreceptor, pulmonary, cardiac and gastrointestinal afferents; the afferent limb of the baroreflex, the cough reflex and the vomiting reflex
Nucleus solitarius, rostral gustatory part (nuc-solitarius-rostral) — taste from the epiglottis and the pharynx
efferent: Pharyngeal plexus and the superior laryngeal nerve to the pharyngeal and cricothyroid muscles
Recurrent laryngeal nerve to all the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles (the reason a recurrent laryngeal palsy causes hoarseness and a weak cough)

Parasympathetic fibres to the cardiac plexus (slowing the heart), the pulmonary plexus (bronchoconstriction and secretion) and the enteric nervous system (motility and secretion as far as the splenic flexure)

Rootlets leave the postolivary sulcus at `surf-cn10-exit` and the nerve passes through the jugular foramen with CN IX and CN XI — a shared foramen that makes a jugular-foramen lesion a three-nerve syndrome
The auricular branch (Alderman's nerve) to the external ear, which shares its sensory field with CN VII and the upper cervical nerves

afferent: Superior/inferior vagal sensory ganglia: visceral/taste inputs to solitary nucleus and general sensory input to spinal trigeminal complex
efferent: Ambiguus branchiomotor neurons to palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles
Preganglionic cardiac vagal neurons including ambiguus region
DMV and other vagal parasympathetic outflow to ganglia near thoracoabdominal viscera
