course.before: Eight to ten rootlets emerge from the postolivary sulcus of the medulla, below the glossopharyngeal rootlets, dorsal to the inferior olive, at the landmark `surf-cn10-exit`, and run laterally through the cerebellopontine cistern (the cisternal segment, where a PICA loop can compress it) to the jugular foramen, where it passes through the pars vascularis with the internal jugular vein — the foramen this nerve uses at the skull base. In the foramen it forms the superior (jugular) ganglion, and just below it the inferior (nodose) ganglion; it then descends in the carotid sheath between the internal carotid artery (or the common carotid below the bifurcation) and the internal jugular vein, gives off the pharyngeal branches, the superior laryngeal nerve, and — on the right side looping under the subclavian artery, on the left under the aortic arch — the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and continues as the posterior and anterior vagal trunks through the oesophageal hiatus into the thorax and abdomen. The recurrent laryngeal nerve's different courses on the two sides are the anatomical reason a left-sided aortic arch lesion paralyses the left vocal fold.
course.after: Postolivary medullary rootlets leave through the jugular foramen with superior/inferior sensory ganglia. The vagus descends in the carotid sheath and gives pharyngeal, superior laryngeal, recurrent laryngeal, cardiac and thoracoabdominal branches. Right recurrent laryngeal loops under right subclavian artery; left loops under the aortic arch.

function.before: The longest cranial nerve and the principal parasympathetic outflow of the body: its preganglionic fibres from the dorsal motor nucleus (nuc-dmv) slow the heart, constrict the bronchi, and drive secretomotor and motor function throughout the gut as far as the splenic flexure; its branchial motor fibres from the nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) innervate the muscles of the soft palate (except tensor veli palatini), the pharynx (except stylopharyngeus) and, through the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves, all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx — so this nerve is what makes voice, cough, swallow and airway protection possible. Its visceral afferents from the aortic arch baroreceptors, the aortic bodies, the lungs, the heart and the gut ascend to the caudal nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-caudal), which closes the reflex loops for heart rate, respiration and vomiting; its general sensory and taste fibres (from the epiglottis) reach the spinal trigeminal and rostral solitary nuclei; and its auricular branch (of Alderman) supplies a small zone of the external ear, which is why stimulation of the ear canal can cause cough or syncope.
function.after: Motor supply to palate except tensor veli palatini, pharynx except stylopharyngeus, and larynx; external superior laryngeal supplies cricothyroid while recurrent laryngeal supplies other intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Visceral afferents reach solitary nucleus and parasympathetic axons regulate thoracoabdominal organs. Cardiac vagal neurons include an important ambiguus source; DMV contributes particularly to abdominal visceral control. The auricular sensory branch is Arnold nerve.

modality.before: Mixed — branchial motor (pharynx and larynx through the pharyngeal plexus and the recurrent laryngeal nerve), visceral motor (parasympathetic to the heart, airways and gut), general sensory (pharynx, larynx, external ear), special sensory (taste from the epiglottis) and visceral afferent (aortic arch, lungs, heart, gut)
modality.after: Branchial motor, preganglionic parasympathetic, visceral afferent, taste and small general sensory components.

records.name: CN XI Accessory nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal and foraminal portions are supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery) and the vertebral artery (vasc-vertebral-artery), whose V3 segment loops behind the atlas immediately lateral to the upper cervical accessory rootlets — the anatomical reason the nerve can be injured by a vertebral-artery dissection or by C1-C2 surgery. In the posterior triangle of the neck the spinal root runs superficially over the levator scapulae, supplied by small branches of the transverse cervical and occipital arteries; its superficial course, with no bony protection, is why it is injured by lymph-node biopsy, carotid surgery and penetrating neck trauma.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.syndrome: Accessory-nerve palsy — drooping shoulder with weak shrugging
before.findings: Weakness and wasting of the trapezius produce a dropped shoulder, an inability to shrug against resistance, winging of the scapula with the arm abducted, and weakness of head extension; sternocleidomastoid weakness makes it difficult to turn the head to the OPPOSITE side and to flex the neck against resistance. The winging is different from that of long thoracic-nerve palsy: the accessory's is most obvious with the arm abducted rather than elevated forward. The pattern localizes to the accessory nerve's external branch or to its spinal root, and the missing sensory loss is what separates it from a cervical radiculopathy.
before.vascular: Not primarily vascular; the commonest causes are surgical (neck dissection, lymph-node biopsy, carotid endarterectomy, internal jugular cannulation) and traumatic
before.note: The palsy is a double sign: the same nerve supplies two muscles with different actions, so the examination must test head rotation and shoulder elevation separately.

before.syndrome: Jugular-foramen syndrome and Vernet syndrome with accessory involvement
before.findings: A jugular-foramen lesion takes CN IX, X and XI: loss of the gag reflex, palatal and vocal-fold palsy with hoarseness and dysphagia, plus a dropped shoulder and weak head rotation. The accessory palsy is the finding that identifies a skull-base lesion rather than a medullary one, because a medullary lesion that destroys the nucleus or rootlets almost always adds long-tract or crossed sensory findings, and an isolated nuclear lesion would not affect the trapezius on the same side as the tongue or palate.
before.vascular: Glomus jugulare tumour, meningioma, metastasis, or jugular-vein thrombosis
before.note: The three-nerve, one-sided, non-crossed pattern is the skull-base signature; the accessory component is its most conspicuous motor sign.

before.syndrome: Foramen-magnum and high-cervical lesions of the spinal root
before.findings: The spinal root ascends through the foramen magnum, so a Chiari malformation, a foramen-magnum meningioma, a vertebral-artery dissection or a C1-C2 fracture can produce an accessory palsy with or without a myelopathy; the palsy may be the first sign of a foramen-magnum tumour, and it is typically accompanied by the sensory and long-tract signs of the level.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery (vasc-vertebral-artery) dissection or compression at the foramen magnum
before.note: A patient with a dropped shoulder and a normal neck examination still needs imaging of the foramen magnum, because the spinal root's intracranial ascent is the one part of this nerve that shares the posterior fossa.

before.findings: The external branch runs subcutaneously across the posterior triangle, where it is at risk during radical neck dissection, cervical lymph-node biopsy, internal jugular vein cannulation and carotid endarterectomy; the injury produces immediate shoulder drop and pain, with a characteristic compensatory elevation of the affected shoulder and a reduced ability to carry weight on that side.
before.vascular: Iatrogenic; the transverse cervical artery's branches mark the plane in which the nerve runs
before.note: The clinical value of the anatomy here is preventive: identification of the nerve at the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid is the step that prevents the palsy.

after.findings: Trapezius weakness can cause shoulder droop, impaired shrug and scapular dysfunction; sternocleidomastoid weakness impairs turning the head away from the weak muscle side. Deficits depend on lesion position. Posterior-triangle surgery/trauma is a recognized cause.
Combined IX/X/XI deficits suggest a skull-base region; isolated trapezius weakness can occur farther along the spinal accessory course. No single vascular cause is implied by the pattern.

afferent: Nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) — the branchial motor source of the cranial root, shared with CN IX and CN X; the rootlets emerge with the vagal rootlets at `surf-cn11-exit`

Accessory nucleus of the upper cervical spinal cord (segments C1–C5/6) — the somatic motor source of the spinal root; no registry record exists for it, because the taxonomy covers the brainstem and diencephalon and the spinal cord is out of its region set, so it is named here in prose

Corticospinal fibres descending from the motor cortex (ctx-m1) drive the accessory nucleus for voluntary head rotation and shoulder movement, and the corticobulbar fibres reach the cranial root's ambiguus neurons
No sensory component: the nerve carries no afferent fibres of its own, so all proprioceptive information from the two muscles travels with the cervical spinal nerves
efferent: Cranial root: through the vagus to the pharyngeal plexus and the recurrent laryngeal nerve, to the muscles of the larynx
Spinal root: the external branch to the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius — tested clinically by shrugging the shoulders against resistance and by turning the head against the examiner's hand

The spinal rootlets enter the skull through the foramen magnum, so a Chiari malformation, a foramen-magnum meningioma or a vertebral-artery dissection can damage the nerve before it reaches the jugular foramen

The common trunk traverses the jugular foramen (nrv-cn9-glossopharyngeal and nrv-cn10-vagus share the foramen), which is why the three nerves fail together in Vernet syndrome and why the accessory palsy is the sign that distinguishes a jugular-foramen lesion from a purely medullary one

afferent: Spinal accessory motor nucleus in upper cervical cord, with descending motor control
efferent: Ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; cervical plexus contributes additional fibers/proprioception

course.before: The cranial root arises from the caudal part of the nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) in the medulla and leaves the postolivary sulcus as a few rootlets with the vagal rootlets at the landmark `surf-cn11-exit`; the spinal root arises from the accessory nucleus in the anterior horn of the upper five or six cervical segments, ascends inside the spinal canal as a chain of rootlets, and enters the posterior cranial fossa through the foramen magnum — the foramen THIS ROOT uses — before joining the cranial rootlets. The united trunk's cisternal course then crosses the cerebellopontine and jugular (pars vascularis) cisterns to the jugular foramen (pars vascularis) — the foramen the common trunk uses — where the two roots separate: the cranial root joins the vagus and is distributed through its pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches to the larynx, while the spinal root descends as the external branch to supply the sternocleidomastoid and then the trapezius. The spinal root's subcutaneous course across the posterior triangle of the neck is long and superficial, which is why it is the nerve most often injured in neck surgery — a functional rather than an anatomical distinction from the other eleven.
course.after: Spinal accessory rootlets arise from upper cervical spinal cord segments, approximately C1-C5/6. They ascend through the foramen magnum and leave through the jugular foramen, then supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Medullary rootlets historically termed cranial XI are functionally part of the vagus.

function.before: Two nerves in one sheath. The cranial root is a branchiomotor nerve that supplies the intrinsic muscles of the larynx through the vagus's recurrent laryngeal nerve, so a lesion of the cranial root contributes to hoarseness and to laryngeal airway control. The spinal root is the somatic motor nerve of the sternocleidomastoid (head rotation to the opposite side and head flexion) and the trapezius (shoulder elevation, scapular rotation and head extension), so its failure produces the dropped shoulder and the inability to shrug, together with weakness of head rotation away from the affected side and, in long-standing disease, winging of the scapula. The accessory nucleus receives corticospinal input, so the muscle is under voluntary cortical control — but it is also driven by the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts for postural tone, which is why the shoulder droop is often more prominent than the weakness on formal testing.
function.after: Supports head turning through sternocleidomastoid and shoulder elevation/scapular movement through trapezius. The spinal nerve is distinct from vagal branchiomotor supply to palate/pharynx/larynx.

modality.before: Motor only, with two roots of different origin: branchial motor (cranial root, to the larynx through the recurrent laryngeal nerve) and somatic motor (spinal root, to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius). No sensory, no parasympathetic component
modality.after: Motor to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (spinal accessory component).

records.name: CN XII Hypoglossal nerve

bloodSupply.before: The cisternal rootlets and the canal segment are supplied by small branches of the vertebral artery (vasc-vertebral-artery) and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery); in the neck the nerve is supplied by the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries, whose branches it also crosses on its way to the tongue. The vertebral artery's relationship to the hypoglossal canal is the key vascular fact: the artery loops medially around the canal in most people, so a dolichoectatic or dissecting vertebral artery compresses the nerve against the canal's wall and produces an isolated hypoglossal palsy with tongue wasting — the classic vascular cause of a twelfth-nerve palsy, and the reason a hypoglossal palsy with neck pain or a headache must be investigated urgently for dissection.
bloodSupply.after: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

before.syndrome: Hypoglossal (lower motor neuron) palsy — tongue deviates TOWARD the lesion
before.findings: The tongue is weak, wasted and fasciculating on the affected side and deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion on protrusion, because the intact contralateral genioglossus pushes the tip across the midline; speech becomes dysarthric (lingual consonants), chewing and swallowing are impaired, and in long-standing cases the tongue is visibly atrophic with a wrinkled mucosa. The side of the deviation therefore names the side of the lesion — the opposite of the supranuclear rule below.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery compression at the hypoglossal canal, or a medullary infarct (medial medullary syndrome); in the neck, carotid dissection, tumour or surgical injury
before.note: An isolated twelfth-nerve palsy demands imaging of the canal and the skull base: the nerve can be compressed by an aberrant vertebral artery, a meningioma, a chordoma or a metastasis at the occipital condyle.

before.syndrome: Supranuclear (corticobulbar) palsy — tongue deviates AWAY from the lesion
before.findings: A lesion above the nucleus (motor cortex, corona radiata, internal capsule) weakens the tongue contralaterally, and because genioglossus has predominantly contralateral cortical input the tongue deviates AWAY from the side of the hemispheric lesion; there is no wasting and no fasciculation, and the tongue retains its automatic movements in swallowing. A capsular lesion adds a contralateral hemiparesis, which is the localizing combination.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery territory or the internal capsule (vasc-middle-cerebral-artery; lenticulostriate perforators, vasc-lenticulostriate-arteries)
before.note: Tongue TOWARD the lesion = nuclear or nerve (lower motor neuron, with wasting); tongue AWAY = supranuclear. The presence of wasting and fasciculation settles it before any imaging.

before.syndrome: Medial medullary syndrome with hypoglossal involvement (Dejerine syndrome)
before.findings: An infarct of the medial medulla destroys the hypoglossal nerve's rootlets or nucleus together with the pyramid and the medial lemniscus: ipsilateral tongue weakness and wasting that deviates toward the lesion, contralateral hemiparesis, and contralateral loss of position and vibration sense — the three-way crossed pattern that names the level.
before.vascular: Anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery paramedian branches (vasc-vertebral-artery)
before.note: The hypoglossal palsy is the ipsilateral element; the crossed weakness and sensory loss are what separate a medullary lesion from an isolated nerve palsy.

before.syndrome: Bilateral hypoglossal palsy with tongue atrophy and obstructive sleep apnoea
before.findings: Bilateral involvement — motor neuron disease, syringobulbia, Chiari malformation, a foramen-magnum lesion or bilateral carotid dissection — produces a small, wrinkled, fasciculating tongue with severe dysarthria and dysphagia, and, because the genioglossus is the muscle that holds the airway open, obstructive sleep apnoea and respiratory failure in sleep; it is one of the bulbar presentations of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
before.note: The tongue is a muscle like any other, so bilateral lower-motor-neuron disease shows the full picture of atrophy, fasciculation and weakness — and the airway consequence is the immediate danger.

after.findings: Nuclear, fascicular or nerve injury can weaken the ipsilateral tongue, which tends to deviate toward the weak side on protrusion. Atrophy and fasciculations may develop with lower motor neuron disease or chronic denervation.

A unilateral supranuclear lesion often weakens the contralateral tongue, with protrusion toward the weak side. Medial medullary lesions can combine ipsilateral XII weakness and contralateral limb weakness/sensory deficits. Neck/skull-base causes require localization along the nerve rather than one assumed artery.

afferent: Hypoglossal nucleus (nuc-hypoglossal) — the somatic motor neurons, a paramedian column under the hypoglossal trigone of the fourth-ventricle floor; the rootlets leave the preolivary sulcus at `surf-cn12-exit`
Corticobulbar fibres from the motor cortex (ctx-m1) — predominantly contralateral for genioglossus, which is the anatomical reason a supranuclear lesion deviates the tongue away from the lesion

Reticular and solitary-nucleus inputs (nuc-solitarius-caudal, nuc-medullary-reticular) drive the tongue's automatic movements in swallowing and chewing, which is why the tongue can still swallow after a cortical lesion that has weakened voluntary protrusion
No sensory component: the tongue's sensation and taste travel with CN V (general sensation), CN VII, CN IX and CN X (taste)
efferent: Intrinsic muscles of the tongue (longitudinal, transverse and vertical) — shape and precision movements
Extrinsic muscles except palatoglossus: genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus and chondroglossus
The C1 fibres that travel with the nerve to the geniohyoid and thyrohyoid after leaving it in the neck — the anatomical reason this nerve is not purely 'cranial'

The nerve traverses the hypoglossal canal with the vertebral artery looping around the canal's outside (vasc-vertebral-artery), which is why an aberrant vertebral artery or a dissection produces an isolated twelfth-nerve palsy

afferent: Hypoglossal somatic motor neurons; corticobulbar/reticular control terminates centrally.
efferent: Ipsilateral tongue musculature except palatoglossus
C1 accompanying fibers to geniohyoid/thyrohyoid and ansa cervicalis, distinguished from true XII fibers

course.before: The preolivary sulcus of the medulla, between the pyramid and the inferior olive, gives rise to a linear series of 10–15 fine filaments at the landmark `surf-cn12-exit`; their short cisternal course — the rootlets run through the cerebellomedullary (lateral medullary) cistern, which is the segment a vertebral or PICA aneurysm can compress — converges laterally and anteriorly into two bundles that pierce the dura and pass through the hypoglossal canal of the occipital bone — the foramen this nerve uses — with a meningeal branch and the venous plexus, where the vertebral artery's course around the canal is the clinically load-bearing relationship (an aberrant or dolichoectatic vertebral artery, or a dissection, compresses the nerve inside the canal). Outside the skull the nerve descends between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein, loops forward around the occipital artery and the sternocleidomastoid branch, crosses the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery, and runs forward above the hyoid and deep to the mylohyoid and the posterior digastric to distribute to the tongue, carrying with it the C1 fibres that supply the geniohyoid and the thyrohyoid. Its long, looped course means it is injured in the neck as well as in the canal.
course.after: Motor neurons in the hypoglossal nucleus send fascicles ventrally through the medulla, emerging in the preolivary sulcus between pyramid and olive. The nerve exits through the hypoglossal canal and courses toward the tongue. C1 spinal fibers briefly join its extracranial course.

function.before: The motor nerve of the tongue: it innervates all the intrinsic muscles (which change the tongue's shape) and all the extrinsic muscles except palatoglossus — genioglossus (which protrudes the tongue), hyoglossus (which depresses it), styloglossus (which retracts and elevates it) and the rest — so it is the nerve of articulation, mastication, swallowing and airway protection. The genioglossus is the key muscle clinically: it pulls the tongue forward and is the muscle that keeps the airway open in sleep, which is why hypoglossal dysfunction causes obstructive sleep apnoea and why bilateral genioglossus paralysis obstructs the airway. Corticobulbar input to the hypoglossal nucleus is predominantly CONTRALATERAL for genioglossus, so a supranuclear lesion deviates the tongue away from the lesion, while a nuclear or nerve lesion deviates it TOWARD the lesion and adds wasting and fasciculations — the single most useful distinction this nerve offers at the bedside.
function.after: Supplies intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (vagus). C1 fibers traveling with XII reach geniohyoid and thyrohyoid and contribute to ansa cervicalis; these are spinal fibers, not axons arising from the hypoglossal nucleus.

modality.before: Motor (somatic motor to all the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus); no sensory, no parasympathetic component

records.name: Pineal gland

Habenula and stria medullaris thalami fibers
efferent: Melatonin released into the systemic circulation and CSF (no blood-brain barrier)

afferent: Circadian autonomic pathway: SCN/hypothalamic networks to spinal sympathetic neurons and superior cervical ganglion; postganglionic sympathetic fibers to the pineal gland
efferent: Melatonin released into circulation and CSF

function.before: Neuroendocrine circumventricular organ converting SCN-driven, sympathetic (superior cervical ganglion) noradrenergic signaling into nightly melatonin secretion — the hormonal signal of darkness that entrains circadian physiology; it calcifies after puberty and serves as the radiographic midline landmark.
function.after: Midline epithalamic endocrine organ secreting melatonin with a daily rhythm under multisynaptic SCN/autonomic control. Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion mediate an important neural input. Pineal calcification is variable and can serve as an imaging landmark.

records.name: Habenular nuclei

before.findings: Lateral habenula hyperactivity is a robust correlate of major depression and helplessness in humans and animal models; habenula/fasciculus-retroflexus stimulation is an experimental treatment for refractory depression.
before.note: translational research syndrome

before.findings: Tumors or infarcts at the dorsal midline interrupting the habenulo-interpeduncular pathway contribute to reward-processing disturbance and sleep-wake dysregulation.

after.findings: Habenular circuits are studied in reward prediction, aversion and psychiatric disease. Depression is not a diagnosis of isolated habenular hyperactivity, and stimulation remains a research context rather than an established atlas lesion syndrome.

afferent: Stria medullaris thalami (septal nuclei, preoptic area, lateral hypothalamus)
Lateral pallidum (pallidohabenular fibers) and basal ganglia
Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis
efferent: Ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra pars compacta (inhibitory, lateral habenula)
Dorsal and median raphe nuclei
Interpeduncular nucleus via the fasciculus retroflexus (medial habenula)

afferent: Limbic/basal-forebrain afferents through the stria medullaris thalami
Hypothalamic and basal-ganglia-related inputs
efferent: Fasciculus retroflexus toward the interpeduncular nucleus and midbrain circuits
Lateral habenular outputs influence dopamine/serotonin systems through direct and indirect circuits, rather than being uniformly direct inhibitory projections

function.before: Limbic 'anti-reward' interface: the lateral habenula integrates stria-medullaris input from septum, hypothalamus and basal ganglia and suppresses dopaminergic (VTA/SNc) and serotonergic (raphe) activity — encoding negative reward prediction, aversion and pain expectation; the medial habenula relays to the interpeduncular nucleus for aversive behavioral control.
function.after: Paired medial and lateral habenular nuclei at the posterior dorsomedial thalamic border. They receive limbic/basal-forebrain inputs through the stria medullaris and project through the fasciculus retroflexus toward interpeduncular and other midbrain targets. Reward/aversion roles are supported particularly by experimental and translational studies; they are not a single anti-reward center.

before.findings: Compression of the posterior commissure/pretectal region by pineal tumors or hydrocephalus abolishes coordinated upgaze and convergence and yields light-near dissociation; see the syndrome browser entry.

records.name: Subthalamic nucleus

before.findings: Contralateral wild, flinging movements of the proximal arm and leg after STN infarction or hemorrhage; typically worst at onset and improving over weeks, with dopamine-receptor blockers or tetrabenazine for severe cases; see the syndrome browser entry.
High-frequency STN stimulation is standard therapy for advanced Parkinson motor fluctuations; current spread into limbic/associative STN territory can induce impulsivity, hypomania or dyskinesia.
before.note: therapeutic

after.findings: Contralateral STN-region injury is a classic cause of flinging/choreic movements, but lesions elsewhere in basal-ganglia networks also cause them. Hyperglycemia-associated cases often involve striatum. Evolution and additional signs vary.

STN stimulation is a clinical target for selected patients with Parkinson disease. Benefits and adverse effects depend on patient selection, stimulated circuitry and treatment settings; this schematic is not a targeting guide.

records.name: Zona incerta

before.findings: ZI stimulation suppresses tremor comparably to VIM thalamotomy and is used as a DBS target; lesions or current spread can rarely provoke transient hemiballismus-like movements.
before.note: therapeutic

before.findings: Subthalamic-region infarcts involving the zona incerta combine hemisensory loss, ataxia and involuntary movements (choreoathetosis or ballism).

after.findings: The posterior subthalamic area, including caudal ZI and adjacent cerebellothalamic fibers, has been investigated as a tremor-stimulation target. Benefit and adverse effects cannot be attributed to ZI alone or assumed equivalent to another procedure.
Larger regional lesions can combine motor, sensory and coordination findings according to adjacent pathways; these are not specific isolated-ZI syndromes.

function.before: A rostrocaudal GABAergic sheet between the thalamus and the subthalamic nucleus, continuous with the thalamic reticular nucleus: it gates viscerosensory, cerebellar and basal-ganglia traffic — influencing saccades, arousal, blood pressure and tremor networks — and is traversed by the H1/H2 fasciculi.
function.after: Thin subthalamic gray-matter sheet dorsal to the subthalamic nucleus and ventral to thalamus, adjacent to thalamic and lenticular fasciculi. It has broad sensory, motor and brainstem connections; its subregional functions are not fully represented by this atlas. H1 lies mainly dorsal and H2 ventral to the zona incerta, rather than both simply traversing it.

records.name: Fields of Forel (H1/H2)

before.findings: Hemorrhage or stereotactic lesions across the H fields mimic pallidotomy — reduced contralateral rigidity with a risk of choreoballismic movements.
Targeted H1/H2 interruption was used historically for tremor and rigidity and remains a named landmark concept in functional-neurosurgery planning.
before.note: historic/therapeutic

after.findings: Damage can interrupt basal-ganglia or cerebellar output toward motor thalamus. Consequences depend on the involved fibers; lesion effects should not be assumed to reproduce pallidotomy or a specific movement disorder.
Forel-field procedures have historical use in movement-disorder surgery. The atlas schematic is not a patient-specific target or treatment plan.

contextNote.before: Context record for the H1 (thalamic fasciculus) and H2 (lenticular fasciculus) white-matter zones medial to the zona incerta; the third field of Forel (H3, the prerubral field into which the ansa lenticularis turns before joining H1) is named but not drawn; drawn on plate-thalamus-mid and plate-coronal-midbrain. See also nuc-subthalamic and nuc-zona-incerta.
contextNote.after: Schematic context record for the H1/H2 white-matter regions around zona incerta. The source textbook labels the convergence area prerubral field H; numerical variants such as H3 are not used here. This silhouette is not a validated stereotactic target.

function.before: Fiber-field complex of the subthalamus: field H2 (lenticular fasciculus) carries pallidal output looping through the internal capsule, and field H1 (thalamic fasciculus) delivers it to the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei — the final common route of basal-ganglia output to the motor thalamus, shared with cerebellothalamic fibers.
function.after: Subthalamic white-matter fields associated with pallidal and cerebellar output. H2 (lenticular fasciculus) penetrates the internal capsule and runs dorsal to STN/ventral to ZI. Pallidal fibers from H2 and the ansa lenticularis converge in the prerubral field H, then enter the motor thalamus through H1 (thalamic fasciculus), which also includes cerebellothalamic fibers.

records.name: Cerebral aqueduct

bloodSupply.before: Paramedian and circumferential perforating branches of the PCA/SCA to the surrounding periaqueductal gray (no intrinsic choroid).
bloodSupply.after: The CSF lumen is not perfused tissue. Surrounding midbrain tissue receives variable PCA, SCA and basilar perforator contributions.

before.findings: Aqueduct obstruction (tectal glioma, post-hemorrhagic web, congenital stenosis) dilates the third and lateral ventricles with a normal fourth — headache, Parinaud signs and gait ataxia.
before.note: CSF-flow obstruction

before.findings: Lesions of the surrounding PAG (hemorrhage, demyelination) disturb pain modulation and the vertical-gaze centers flanking the duct.

after.findings: Aqueductal stenosis or external compression can enlarge the upstream third and lateral ventricles. Headache, vomiting or other raised-pressure signs may occur. Gaze palsy or ataxia depends on associated midbrain/cerebellar involvement and is not an obligatory sign of aqueduct obstruction.

function.before: The roughly 1.5 cm CSF conduit through the midbrain periaqueductal gray linking the third to the fourth ventricle beneath the colliculi; it is the narrowest CSF channel and the classic site of obstruction by tectal tumors, post-hemorrhagic webs or aqueductal stenosis.
function.after: Narrow CSF channel through the midbrain connecting third and fourth ventricles, surrounded by periaqueductal gray and lacking choroid plexus. Stenosis or compression can cause upstream obstructive hydrocephalus.

records.name: Corpus callosum (context)

before.findings: Surgical callosal section isolates the hemispheres — the left hand acts independently and cannot name objects seen by the right hemisphere; callosal thinning also appears in ALS and developmental disorders.
before.note: context syndrome

before.findings: Congenital absence elevates the third ventricle roof on sagittal imaging and may accompany hypothalamic dysregulation syndromes (e.g., episodic hypothermia).
before.note: developmental

after.findings: Callosal injury or surgical section can impair transfer of information between hemispheres. In a typical left-language-dominant patient, an object presented only to the left visual field or explored by the left hand may not be named verbally despite recognition by the right hemisphere. Alien-hand phenomena are possible but not obligatory.
Callosal agenesis has variable clinical expression and may be associated with other malformations. It does not by itself establish hypothalamic dysfunction.

function.before: The fan-shaped white-matter plane carrying all thalamocortical and corticofugal traffic — anterior limb (frontopontine), genu (corticobulbar), posterior limb (corticospinal and somatosensory thalamocortical), retrolenticular (optic radiations) — framing the thalamus laterally on the thalamic-level plates; the thalamic reticular nucleus hugs its inner surface.
function.after: Compact deep white-matter structure between caudate/thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. Its anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolenticular and sublenticular parts carry different thalamocortical and descending projections, including motor, sensory, visual and auditory routes. It does not carry every corticofugal or thalamocortical connection.

records.name: Lentiform nucleus (context silhouette)

before.findings: Small deep infarcts or hemorrhages here produce pure motor or sensorimotor hemiparesis; larger putaminal bleeds cause gaze deviation and reduced consciousness.

records.name: Preoptic area

before.findings: Anterior preoptic lesions abolish heat dissipation, producing hyperthermia unresponsive to antipyretics; larger lesions cause poikilothermia, with body temperature tracking the environment.
Ventrolateral preoptic damage produces profound sleep-onset failure with autonomic activation, as after anterior hypothalamic trauma, prion disease or encephalitis.
before.note: sleep-circuit lesion syndrome

after.findings: Anterior hypothalamic/preoptic injury can cause hyperthermia or insomnia, with severity depending on the affected circuits. Fatal familial insomnia is predominantly a thalamic prion disorder and should not be used as a specific preoptic lesion example.

function.before: Anterior hypothalamic zone rostral to the optic chiasm containing the median preoptic, ventrolateral preoptic and sexually dimorphic nuclei: warm-sensitive neurons trigger heat-defense (vasodilation, sweating), GABAergic ventrolateral preoptic neurons actively promote sleep, and the GnRH neurons of the preoptic/mediobasal hypothalamus provide the output of the reproductive hormone pulse, which is generated by the arcuate KNDy (kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin) network.
function.after: Rostral hypothalamic/preoptic region containing multiple medial and lateral cell groups. It participates in heat dissipation, reproductive neuroendocrine control and sleep promotion; GABAergic/galaninergic ventrolateral preoptic neurons inhibit arousal systems. This whole-area record combines paired and midline components rather than one discrete midline nucleus.

records.name: Suprachiasmatic nucleus

before.findings: SCN damage or de-timing (suprasellar tumors, blindness, shift work) desynchronizes sleep phase, melatonin and temperature rhythms, producing insomnia or free-running sleep.
before.note: bright light and timed melatonin are the chronotherapeutic levers

before.syndrome: Loss of endocrine rhythms after suprasellar lesions
before.findings: Chiasmal/hypothalamic tumors or their treatment abolish circadian melatonin and cortisol cycling, with inverted or arrhythmic sleep and altered symptom timing.
before.note: mass effect or treatment injury

after.findings: SCN-region injury can disrupt daily timing of sleep and endocrine rhythms. Blindness may reduce photic entrainment when nonvisual retinal input is lost; shift work causes circadian misalignment without implying anatomical SCN damage.

afferent: Retinal ganglion cells via the retinohypothalamic tract (fibers crossing in the optic chiasm)
Intergeniculate leaflet of the thalamus (photic and nonphotic entrainment)
Feedback from the pineal (melatonin, via the pars tuberalis axis)
efferent: Paraventricular nucleus, then intermediolateral column and superior cervical ganglion to the pineal (melatonin rhythm)
Dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus and preoptic sleep-wake systems (behavioral rhythms)

afferent: Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells through the retinohypothalamic tract
Additional modulatory retinal/thalamic/brainstem inputs
efferent: Hypothalamic circadian networks
Multisynaptic autonomic pathway through paraventricular region, spinal sympathetic neurons and superior cervical ganglion to pineal gland

function.before: The master circadian pacemaker: retinohypothalamic glutamatergic (with PACAP co-transmitter) input from melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells entrains an intrinsic ~24-hour transcriptional clock (BMAL1/CLOCK) that synchronizes pineal melatonin secretion, cortisol rhythm, and sleep timing through the paraventricular and dorsomedial nuclei.
function.after: Paired circadian timing nuclei immediately above the optic chiasm. Specialized melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells provide retinohypothalamic input that entrains daily rhythms; SCN output coordinates hypothalamic and autonomic pathways influencing sleep timing and pineal melatonin.

records.name: Supraoptic nucleus

before.findings: Destruction of supraoptic/paraventricular magnocellular neurons or their stalk axons (trauma, surgery, infiltrative disease) produces polyuria, polydipsia and hypernatremia that respond to desmopressin.
before.vascular: Anterior communicating/superior hypophyseal perforators or stalk transection

before.findings: Excess, unregulated ADH release — hypothalamic dysregulation, drugs or ectopic tumor production — causes euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine; the mirror failure of water balance to central DI.
before.note: contrasting water-balance failure of the same magnocellular system

after.findings: Sufficient injury to the hypothalamic-neurohypophyseal system can cause central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency), with dilute polyuria and thirst. Hypernatremia develops particularly when water intake cannot match losses, rather than occurring in every patient.
SIADH has many neurologic and nonneurologic causes and is not a diagnosis of isolated supraoptic nuclear damage.

records.name: Paraventricular nucleus (hypothalamus)

before.findings: Loss of magnocellular PVN (with supraoptic) neurons or their axons causes ADH deficiency — polyuria, polydipsia, hypernatremia.

before.vascular: Hypothalamic perforators (anterior communicating and paramedian PCA)

before.findings: Injury to parvocellular TRH/CRH neurons (craniopharyngioma, surgery, infiltrates) produces secondary hypothyroidism and hypocortisolism with fatigue and hypotension.

records.name: Arcuate nucleus (hypothalamus)

before.findings: Arcuate/ventromedial damage (craniopharyngioma surgery, infiltrative disease) abolishes satiety signaling, causing hyperphagia and treatment-refractory weight gain.
before.note: mass or surgical lesion

before.findings: Infundibular or tuberal compression interrupts tuberoinfundibular dopamine, releasing the pituitary lactotrophs from inhibition and moderately raising prolactin.
before.vascular: Sellar/suprasellar mass effect on the stalk and tuberal perforators

after.findings: Medial hypothalamic injury can contribute to obesity through altered appetite, energy expenditure and endocrine/autonomic mechanisms. The human syndrome cannot be assigned solely to a single arcuate or ventromedial nucleus.
Interruption of hypothalamic dopamine delivery to the anterior pituitary can raise prolactin. The effect reflects the delivery pathway and is not proof of selective arcuate nuclear loss.

function.before: Tuberal energy-balance and endocrine control center: NPY/AgRP (hunger) and POMC/CART (satiety) neurons sense leptin, ghrelin and insulin to drive feeding; GHRH and tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons regulate growth-hormone and prolactin secretion through the median eminence.
function.after: Tuberal hypothalamic nucleus adjacent to the median eminence. Multiple neuronal populations contribute to energy balance and hypothalamic endocrine regulation, including dopamine inhibition of prolactin and growth-hormone/reproductive regulation. Hunger- and satiety-related populations coexist, so an orexigenic center is not a synonym for the entire nucleus.

records.name: Ventromedial nucleus (hypothalamus)

before.findings: Bilateral ventromedial destruction yields voracious appetite, obesity and endocrine dysregulation — the classical 'hypothalamic obesity' lesion of the satiety center.
before.note: classical lesion syndrome (human and experimental)

before.findings: Ventromedial/perifornical lesions release defensive aggression with autonomic discharge (piloerection, mydriasis, hypertension).
before.note: rare; tumors, encephalitis, trauma

before.findings: Episodic hypertension, tachycardia, sweating and hyperthermia after ventromedial/diencephalic injury — the pattern of post-traumatic paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity.

after.findings: Lesions of medial hypothalamic networks may cause obesity, endocrine and autonomic changes. Experimental VMH lesion/stimulation findings do not establish a fixed human syndrome of voracious appetite, rage or autonomic storms from selective VMH injury.

function.before: Satiety and defensive-behavior center: leptin/insulin-responsive neurons terminate feeding and regulate glucose metabolism (destruction yields hyperphagia and obesity), while stimulation triggers defensive rage and sympathetically mediated stress responses via the periaqueductal gray.
function.after: Medial tuberal hypothalamic nucleus involved in energy balance, glucose regulation and behavioral/autonomic responses. Classical lesion/stimulation studies, mainly in animals, link it to feeding and defensive behavior; human hypothalamic obesity and aggression are distributed circuit phenomena.

records.name: Posterior hypothalamic nucleus

before.findings: Posterior hypothalamic infarcts or tumors impair heat conservation — core temperature falls with ambient cooling; combined anterior-plus-posterior damage causes full poikilothermia.

Posterior hypothalamic (histaminergic/orexin-adjacent) dysfunction underlies recurrent episodes of hypersomnia with behavioral change; the posterior hypothalamus also modulates narcolepsy-cataplexy circuits.
before.note: functional/imaging correlate

before.findings: Recurrent spontaneous hypothermia with corpus callosum agenesis maps to posterior hypothalamic thermoregulatory failure.
before.note: rare dysautonomic syndrome

after.findings: Bilateral posterior hypothalamic injury may impair thermoregulation and cause hypersomnia. Kleine-Levin syndrome and episodic hypothermia have uncertain/distributed mechanisms; they do not prove selective posterior-nuclear failure.

function.before: Caudal hypothalamic zone — with the tuberomammillary histaminergic neurons — that defends core temperature by conserving heat (cutaneous vasoconstriction, shivering) and maintains wakefulness through histaminergic and orexin-linked arousal output.
function.after: Posterior hypothalamic region participating in heat conservation and arousal. Nearby tuberomammillary histamine and lateral hypothalamic orexin systems contribute to wakefulness but are anatomically distinct populations rather than synonyms for the posterior hypothalamic nucleus.

records.name: Mammillary body

before.findings: Thiamine deficiency causes petechial hemorrhages of the mammillary bodies — confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia; prompt thiamine replacement prevents the Korsakoff state.
before.note: metabolic-toxic (thiamine deficiency)

before.findings: Mammillary body and anterior thalamic damage yields dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation; mammillary atrophy is the imaging signature.
before.note: sequela of untreated Wernicke encephalopathy

before.findings: Infarction isolating the mammillothalamic tract and anterior thalamus reproduces a Papez-circuit amnesia without thiamine deficiency.

after.findings: Wernicke/Korsakoff disease can involve mammillary, medial thalamic and additional periventricular/frontal networks. The classic acute triad, later confabulation or mammillary atrophy is not obligatory. Injury to mammillothalamic/anterior thalamic pathways can also impair memory without thiamine deficiency.

function.before: Paired round nuclei at the caudal-ventral hypothalamus forming the relay of the Papez memory circuit: they receive the hippocampal fornix and project via the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamus, consolidating episodic memory; the medial mammillary neurons are among the first structures to fail in thiamine deficiency.
function.after: Paired ventral posterior hypothalamic mammillary bodies participate in episodic/spatial memory networks. They receive postcommissural fornical input and project to anterior thalamus through the mammillothalamic tract, with tegmental connections as well. They are vulnerable in thiamine-deficiency disease, but are not a universally proven first site of failure.

records.name: Optic chiasm

function.before: The X-shaped crossing of the optic nerves on the hypothalamic floor: nasal retinal fibers decussate while temporal fibers continue ipsilaterally, so lesions here classically produce bitemporal hemianopia; it marks the rostral-ventral pole of the hypothalamus (supraoptic and arcuate nuclei flank it).
function.after: Optic pathway crossing on the ventral anterior diencephalon near the suprasellar region. Nasal retinal fibers cross while temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral. It lies beneath the anterior hypothalamus and anterior/superior to the pituitary stalk; central compression can produce bitemporal visual field loss.

records.name: Infundibulum (pituitary stalk)

bloodSupply.before: Superior hypophyseal artery (internal carotid/ACA origin) for the portal plexus; inferior hypophyseal artery supplies the posterior lobe.
bloodSupply.after: Superior hypophyseal branches, usually from internal carotid/posterior communicating region, supply median eminence and portal-system structures; inferior hypophyseal branches supply the posterior pituitary.

before.findings: Stalk compression or transection removes tonic dopamine inhibition (moderate hyperprolactinemia); complete section additionally causes permanent central diabetes insipidus and pituitary hormone failure.
before.vascular: Superior hypophyseal branches; surgical or mass injury

before.findings: Shearing of the stalk at the tuber cinereum causes the classic triphasic response: initial DI, then transient SIADH from released stored ADH, then permanent DI.
before.note: head trauma or pituitary surgery

after.findings: Compression or injury can interrupt dopamine delivery (hyperprolactinemia), hypothalamic-releasing hormone delivery, or vasopressin axons. DI and anterior-pituitary deficits depend on injury site and extent.
After pituitary-region surgery or trauma, some patients develop initial DI, transient antidiuresis, then recurrent DI. The sequence and permanent DI are not inevitable.

records.name: Anterior thalamic nucleus

bloodSupply.before: PCA — tuberothalamic (anterior thalamoperforating) artery, arising from the P1 segment or the posterior communicating artery.
bloodSupply.after: Tuberothalamic (polar) artery, usually arising from the posterior communicating artery; paramedian PCA supply may substitute when this vessel is absent.

afferent: Mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract (tract of Vicq d'Azyr)
Indirect hippocampal input through the mammillary bodies (mammillothalamic tract); a minor direct subicular projection to the anterior nuclei is described experimentally but is not the defining route
Prefrontal and retrosplenial cortical feedback
efferent: Cingulate gyrus (Brodmann areas 23, 24, 32) via the anterior limb of the internal capsule
Reciprocal projections to the mammillary bodies and prefrontal cortex

afferent: Mammillary bodies through the mammillothalamic tract
Hippocampal/subicular pathways through the fornix
Cingulate/retrosplenial cortical feedback
efferent: Cingulate and retrosplenial limbic cortex

function.before: Limbic relay of the Papez circuit: it receives hippocampal information via the mammillary bodies (mammillothalamic tract) and projects to the cingulate gyrus, gating episodic memory encoding and spatial navigation. Damage disconnects the Papez loop and reproduces a dense amnestic state.
function.after: Anterior thalamic nuclear group participating in hippocampal-diencephalic memory circuits. It receives mammillary input through the mammillothalamic tract, direct hippocampal/subicular inputs through the fornix, and cortical feedback; outputs reach cingulate/retrosplenial limbic cortex.

records.name: Ventral anterior nucleus (VA)

before.findings: Infarction involving VA disconnects pallidal output from the motor thalamus, adding motor-programming and initiation deficits (abulia, loss of spontaneous action) to the amnestic-apathic syndrome.
Acute inability to stand after rostral thalamic (VA-involving) lesions, with active pushing and falls but no weakness or cerebellar signs to explain them.

after.findings: VA-region lesions may contribute to disturbed movement initiation and executive behavior when neighboring thalamofrontal networks are involved. Thalamic astasia and active pusher behavior are different clinical phenomena and do not localize uniquely to VA.

records.name: Ventral lateral nucleus (VL)

bloodSupply.before: Thalamogeniculate artery (caudal VL) and tuberothalamic artery (rostral VL), branches of the PCA.
bloodSupply.after: Inferolateral (thalamogeniculate) PCA branches and variable tuberothalamic/posterior-communicating contributions rostrally.

function.before: Cerebellar and pallidal relay to the primary motor cortex: the oral posterior (cerebellar) division receives the crossed dentatothalamic fibers of the superior cerebellar peduncle and calibrates the timing and amplitude of voluntary movement. The ventral intermediate (VIM) zone is the stereotactic target for tremor suppression.
function.after: Motor thalamic relay for cerebellar and basal-ganglia inputs. Cerebellar output mainly reaches posterior VL (VLp/VL pars caudalis), while pallidal inputs preferentially reach more anterior motor-thalamic territories; nomenclature differs across atlases. The VIM region is a functional-neurosurgical tremor target.

records.name: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL)

before.findings: After a thalamogeniculate infarct, initial contralateral hemisensory loss evolves weeks to months later into severe burning pain with allodynia and hyperpathia; see the syndrome browser entry.
A lacune confined to VPL/VPM causes contralateral face-arm-leg hemianesthesia without weakness; proprioceptive loss may add sensory ataxia and transient choreoathetosis.

after.findings: VPL injury can cause contralateral body sensory loss, sometimes with sensory ataxia. VPM extension may add facial involvement.
Some lesions involving somatosensory pathways develop delayed neuropathic pain, allodynia or hyperpathia. This is not the inevitable evolution of a thalamic sensory infarct.

function.before: Obligatory thalamic relay of body somatosensation: medial-lemniscal (touch, vibration, joint-position) and spinothalamic (pain, temperature) fibers terminate in a somatotopic map — leg lateral, arm medial — and project to primary somatosensory cortex. Small-hole lesions here cause contralateral hemianesthesia and are the classic substrate of central post-stroke pain.
function.after: Major thalamic relay for contralateral body somatosensation, including medial-lemniscal vibration/position/discriminative-touch inputs and anterolateral inputs. It projects mainly to somatosensory cortex with broad leg-lateral/arm-more-medial topography. Pain processing also uses other thalamic and cortical routes, so VPL is not an obligatory relay for every aspect of body sensation.

records.name: Ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM)

bloodSupply.before: PCA — thalamogeniculate artery; paramedian (artery of Percheron) perforators contribute medially.
bloodSupply.after: Inferolateral (thalamogeniculate) PCA perforators to the ventral posterior complex, with variable overlap from neighboring thalamic territories.

before.findings: Pain and hypesthesia restricted to the contralateral corner of the mouth and the hand from small VPM/VPL-border infarcts — the somatotopic lips-beside-hand representation of the ventrobasal complex.
VPM lesions give hemifacial loss of touch, pain and temperature with a preserved corneal reflex arc; taste is lost when VPMpc is involved.

after.findings: VPM injury can impair contralateral facial sensation; small ventral-posterior lesions near the VPM/VPL border may cause contralateral perioral and hand numbness. Corneal blink circuitry lies in the brainstem and can be preserved. Taste dysfunction may occur when gustatory relay regions are involved.

records.name: Pulvinar

bloodSupply.before: PCA — thalamogeniculate artery and lateral posterior choroidal artery; the whole pulvinar is PCA territory (the middle cerebral artery never supplies the thalamus; the anterior choroidal artery is the only non-PCA contributor to the thalamus).
bloodSupply.after: Posterior choroidal and variable inferolateral branches of the PCA. Thalamic blood supply also includes the tuberothalamic artery from the posterior communicating artery and anterior choroidal contributions elsewhere; it is not uniformly a PCA-only system.

before.findings: Pulvinar and posterior-group involvement in thalamogeniculate infarcts contributes to central post-stroke pain and proprioceptive ataxia; see the syndrome browser entry.

before.syndrome: Homonymous visual attention and field deficits
before.findings: Pulvinar lesions give incongruous homonymous field loss or visual inattention; bilateral damage can produce Balint-like simultanagnosia with preserved acuity.
before.vascular: PCA — posterior choroidal or thalamogeniculate branches

after.findings: Pulvinar-region lesions can contribute to contralateral visual inattention or neglect. Visual field loss may reflect adjacent geniculate or visual pathway involvement rather than pulvinar injury alone.

afferent: Superior colliculus via the brachium of the superior colliculus
Extrastriate visual association cortex (areas 18/19)
Spinothalamic nociceptive fibers (posterior nuclear group)
efferent: Extrastriate visual and inferotemporal association cortex
Superior parietal lobule, prefrontal and cingulate cortex

afferent: Superior-collicular/tectal pathways
Parietotemporo-occipital association cortex
efferent: Parietotemporo-occipital association cortex and additional association networks

function.before: Largest thalamic nucleus and a hub of visual attention: it connects extrastriate, inferotemporal and parietal association cortex with the superior colliculus, assigning behavioral salience to stimuli and coordinating eye-hand orienting; its posterior (limbic) nuclei also forward spinothalamic nociceptive traffic.
function.after: Large posterior thalamic association complex with reciprocal parietal, temporal and occipital cortical connections and tectal input. It participates in visual attention and orienting toward relevant stimuli. It is distinct from the ventral posterior primary somatosensory relay and from smaller posterior nociceptive nuclei.

records.name: Mediodorsal nucleus (MD)

before.findings: Bilateral MD and midline infarction produces abrupt hypersomnia, vertical gaze palsy, dense anterograde amnesia and apathy; see the syndrome browser entry.
Thiamine-deficiency injury to the mediodorsal nuclei (with the mammillary bodies) underlies the confabulatory amnestic state.
before.note: metabolic-toxic (thiamine deficiency), not vascular

before.findings: MD lesions disconnect prefrontal cortex and mimic frontal syndromes: abulia with loss of spontaneous speech (medial/lateral MD) or disinhibition with orbitofrontal-pole involvement.

after.findings: MD/associated thalamic injury may affect memory, motivation, executive control and behavior. Bilateral paramedian lesions can also affect arousal or gaze circuitry; the full Percheron triad is not attributable solely to MD. Korsakoff memory impairment reflects a broader diencephalic/frontal network.

records.name: Centromedian-parafascicular nuclei

before.findings: Bilateral CM-PF and MD injury causes hypersomnia or coma at onset with subsequent inattention, memory disturbance and vertical gaze palsy.
Parafascicular and posterior-group involvement contributes to burning dysesthetic pain after deep thalamic strokes.
before.note: centromedian DBS is used experimentally for refractory epilepsy and disorders of consciousness

after.findings: Bilateral paramedian thalamic injury can affect arousal, attention and memory. Those effects involve a broader rostral intralaminar/midline/mediodorsal network and should not be attributed solely to CM-PF.
Intralaminar targets have been studied for epilepsy and disorders of consciousness; such target studies do not establish a specific isolated human lesion syndrome.

afferent: Globus pallidus and substantia nigra (centromedian)
Spinothalamic and spinoreticular nociceptive fibers (parafascicular)
Brainstem reticular formation: cholinergic (PPT/LDT) and monoaminergic arousal systems
efferent: Striatum (putamen and caudate) plus motor and premotor cortex (centromedian)
Widespread cortex, limbic system and brainstem arousal targets (parafascicular and midline projection system)

afferent: Basal-ganglia, brainstem reticular and sensory inputs
efferent: Striatum and cortical targets; exact projections differ by subdivision

function.before: Intralaminar system embedded in the internal medullary lamina: centromedian closes striatal-motor loops (pallidal input, striatal and motor-cortical output), while parafascicular — with the midline nuclei — forms the thalamic arm of the ascending reticular activating system; the rostral intralaminar group (central lateral, paracentral, central medial) is not covered by this record and relays the medial (arousal-affective) pain system.
function.after: Caudal intralaminar centromedian-parafascicular nuclear complex within the internal medullary lamina. It has major basal-ganglia/striatal connections and receives reticular and sensory inputs. Rostral intralaminar nuclei (central lateral, paracentral, central medial), which are distinct from this CM-PF record, have particularly important ascending-arousal connections.

records.name: Midline (paraventricular) thalamic nuclei

before.findings: Midline nuclear involvement in Percheron-territory infarcts contributes to hypersomnia, apathy, memory deficits and autonomic instability.

before.syndrome: Disorders of consciousness from bilateral paramedian thalamic damage
before.findings: The midline and intralaminar nuclei form the thalamic arm of the ascending arousal system, so bilateral injury — Percheron-territory infarction, thalamic haemorrhage or Wernicke encephalopathy — can leave coma, hypersomnia, akinetic mutism or a 'thalamic dementia' with severe anterograde amnesia and apathy, while the EEG shows diffuse slowing and the cortex looks structurally intact on imaging.
before.vascular: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches, including a shared artery of Percheron
before.note: One Percheron trunk can supply both medial thalami, so a single small-vessel occlusion produces bilateral disease — the reason the thalamus must be inspected in any undiagnosed coma or hypersomnia.

after.findings: Midline, rostral intralaminar and mediodorsal network injury can affect arousal, memory and behavior. Severity varies from sleepiness to severe consciousness impairment; a given EEG or structurally normal cortex is not a required signature.

records.name: Thalamic reticular nucleus

before.findings: Prion degeneration targeting the anteroventral and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei (with the inferior olive) abolishes sleep spindles and normal sleep architecture, producing progressive insomnia with dysautonomia.
before.note: neurodegenerative (PRNP) — the canonical human TRN/anterior-thalamus syndrome

before.findings: TRN burst firing through T-type calcium channels paces thalamocortical oscillations; ethosuximide blocks these channels and suppresses absence seizures.
before.note: physiological correlate of TRN rhythm generation

after.findings: Reticular and relay neurons participate in sleep spindles and thalamocortical rhythms, including circuitry relevant to absence epilepsy. These phenomena arise from distributed networks rather than an isolated TRN lesion. Fatal familial insomnia predominantly involves other thalamic nuclei and is not a canonical selective TRN lesion syndrome.

function.before: A thin GABAergic shell wrapping the lateral thalamus: the reticular nucleus receives collaterals of every corticothalamic and thalamocortical axon and returns inhibition to the relay nuclei, gating sensory traffic, generating sleep spindles and slow-wave rhythms, and implementing attentional filtering.
function.after: Thin GABAergic sheet between the dorsal thalamus and internal capsule. It receives thalamocortical/corticothalamic collaterals and modulatory inputs and returns inhibition to thalamic nuclei, participating in sensory gating, attention and sleep oscillations. Unlike dorsal-thalamic relay nuclei, it has no direct cortical output.

records.name: Lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)

before.findings: Anterior choroidal infarction of the LGN hilum gives a homonymous horizontal wedge sectoranopia; lateral posterior choroidal infarcts give the complementary horizontal sectoranopia — the dual blood supply produces mutually exclusive field patterns.

records.name: Medial geniculate nucleus (MGN)

records.name: Internal medullary lamina

before.findings: Deep thalamic hemorrhages arise from perforators along the lamina and often rupture into the third ventricle; contralateral sensory loss with 'wrong-way' eye deviation is typical.
Lesions crossing the lamina injure several nuclear groups at once, explaining the combined sensory loss, arousal failure and amnesia of deep thalamic strokes.

after.findings: Lesions extending across the internal medullary lamina may affect several thalamic nuclear groups and combine sensory, motor, memory or arousal deficits. Hemorrhage and intraventricular extension depend on the involved vessels and lesion extent.

function.before: Y-shaped sheet of myelinated fibers that partitions the thalamus into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear masses; the centromedian and parafascicular nuclei are embedded within its laminae, and its perforating vessels are a favored site of hypertensive thalamic hemorrhage.
function.after: Y-shaped intrathalamic white-matter sheet partitioning anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups, with intralaminar nuclei embedded in it. It is an anatomical partition rather than an independent neuronal relay or a uniquely established source of hypertensive hemorrhage.

records.name: Pyramid

bloodSupply.before: Anterior spinal artery (paramedian medullary branches)
bloodSupply.after: Paramedian vertebral branches, especially rostrally, and anterior spinal artery branches, especially caudally; territories overlap.

before.findings: Unilateral pyramidal infarction (medial medullary syndrome) weakens the opposite body below the face; because decussation lies caudal to the medulla, deficits are contralateral and the face is typically spared.

before.syndrome: Crossed hemiparesis — the brainstem signature of a pre-decussation lesion
before.findings: Above the decussation every corticospinal lesion is crossed relative to the accompanying cranial-nerve deficit, which is what generates the brainstem syndrome families: ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (Weber), ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsies with contralateral hemiparesis (Millard-Gubler), and ipsilateral tongue weakness with contralateral hemiparesis (Déjerine). The pyramid is the last station at which the bundle is still uncrossed, and therefore the level at which the pattern reverses.
before.vascular: Anterior spinal artery / basilar paramedian perforators
before.note: The face is spared by a pyramid lesion because corticobulbar fibres cross separately — a useful discriminator from a capsular stroke, in which face and limbs weaken together.

after.findings: A unilateral lesion of the pyramid above the motor decussation can cause contralateral arm and leg weakness, usually sparing the face. Associated ipsilateral tongue weakness suggests extension to hypoglossal fascicles in medial medullary syndrome.

Corticospinal weakness contralateral to a brainstem lesion can accompany an ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit when both pathways are involved. The pattern depends on lesion extent and is not required in every brainstem lesion.

records.name: Pyramidal decussation

before.findings: Lesions at the decussation (Chiari malformation, foramen magnum tumors) produce a characteristic cruciate paralysis: arm-predominant weakness from damage to the crossing fibers of the hand area, which decussate most caudally.

records.name: Internal arcuate fibers

before.syndrome: Side-of-deficit flip at the sensory decussation
before.findings: Because the internal arcuate fibers cross here, the laterality of a dorsal-column lesion flips at exactly this point: injury of the fasciculus or of the gracile/cuneate nucleus at or below the decussation (foramen magnum tumor, Chiari malformation, high cervical fracture-dislocation) removes vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch on the SAME side as the lesion, whereas damage to the medial lemniscus just above it produces the contralateral loss of the medial medullary syndrome. Midline involvement of the crossing sheet gives bilateral loss with sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis and a positive Romberg sign.
before.vascular: Anterior spinal artery and vertebral perforators
before.note: The most examinable fact about this structure: the side of the sensory deficit tells you whether the lesion sits in the dorsal columns, in the decussation itself, or in the medial lemniscus above it.

after.findings: Dorsal-column or gracile/cuneate nuclear injury before the crossing causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense; medial lemniscal injury after the crossing causes contralateral loss. Lesions involving the crossing fibers may affect both sides.

records.name: Fasciculus cuneatus

before.syndrome: Ipsilateral upper-limb sensory loss below the decussation
before.findings: The cuneate fasciculus carries uncrossed fibres from the arm and hand, so a lesion beneath the sensory decussation — a high cervical fracture-dislocation, a foramen magnum tumour or a Chiari malformation pressing on the dorsal medulla — removes vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch from the ipsilateral arm and hand, with pseudoathetosis of the fingers and a positive Romberg sign. Because the cuneate bundle lies lateral to the gracilis, a partial lesion spares the leg.
before.note: The bundle exists only above about T6: below that level the upper-limb fibres have not yet entered the cord, so the same lesion cannot produce this pattern.

after.findings: Pre-crossing pathway injury can impair ipsilateral upper-limb/upper-trunk vibration, position and discriminative touch. A restricted lesion may spare lower-body pathways; pseudoathetosis and a positive Romberg sign are possible rather than required.

records.name: Nucleus cuneatus

before.syndrome: Ipsilateral limb ataxia without conscious sensory loss (cuneocerebellar relay)
before.findings: The rostral accessory (external cuneate) part of the nucleus relays unconscious upper-limb proprioception to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, so its involvement in a dorsolateral medullary lesion adds ipsilateral dysmetria and past-pointing of the arm. Destruction of the principal part instead removes conscious vibration and joint-position sense from the ipsilateral arm and hand, because the internal arcuate fibres have not yet crossed.

before.note: A hyperintense dorsal medullary signal on MRI (subacute combined degeneration of the cord) or an enlarged cuneate tubercle is the imaging correlate of this nucleus failing.

after.findings: Principal cuneate nuclear lesions can impair ipsilateral upper-limb vibration, position sense and discriminative touch before the sensory decussation. Accessory cuneate injury can instead affect unconscious proprioceptive input to the cerebellum.

It lies lateral to the gracile nucleus in the dorsal caudal medulla, and its axons cross as internal arcuate fibers to form the contralateral medial lemniscus. The adjacent accessory (external) cuneate nucleus is a distinct nucleus that supplies the cuneocerebellar pathway.

records.name: Principal inferior olivary nucleus

function.before: The elegantly folded gray lamella that bulges as the olive on the ventrolateral medulla: source of all olivocerebellar climbing fibers, which cross the midline, ascend in the inferior cerebellar peduncle and wrap Purkinje cell dendrites with powerful complex spikes — the teaching (error and timing) signal that drives cerebellar motor learning. Actively regulated by the dentato-rubro-olivary loop via the central tegmental tract.
function.after: Folded gray lamella of the inferior olivary complex forming the ventrolateral medullary olive. Along with the accessory olivary nuclei, it provides crossed olivocerebellar climbing fibers through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to Purkinje cells and participates in timing and motor learning. The principal olive receives rubro-olivary input through the central tegmental tract.

records.name: Medial accessory olivary nucleus

before.syndrome: Palatal tremor from hypertrophic olivary degeneration (Guillain-Mollaret triangle)
before.findings: When the triangle is interrupted — by a lesion of the central tegmental tract, the dentate nucleus or the superior cerebellar peduncle — the medial accessory olive loses its rubro-olivary input and undergoes trans-synaptic hypertrophy, while its climbing-fibre output to the vermis fails, producing rhythmic 1-3 Hz palatal tremor that persists during sleep, often with synchronous ocular (pendular) and laryngeal movement. The tremor appears weeks to months after the causative stroke.
before.note: The olive is disinhibited and hypertrophied rather than destroyed, so MRI shows a swollen, T2-hyperintense inferior olive — the imaging signature of the triangle's interruption.

after.findings: Inferior olivary lesions or deafferentation can disrupt cerebellar function. Hypertrophic olivary degeneration and symptomatic palatal tremor are associated with disruption of dentato-rubro-olivary circuitry; those findings should not be localized specifically to this accessory subdivision from this atlas.

records.name: Medial lemniscus

bloodSupply.before: Anterior spinal artery in the medulla; paramedian basilar perforators in the pons
bloodSupply.after: Paramedian vertebral/anterior spinal branches in the medulla, basilar perforators in the pons, and proximal PCA/basilar-apex branches in the midbrain.

before.findings: Paramedian medullary infarcts (medial medullary syndrome) abolish contralateral vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch of the body, with sensory ataxia and positive Romberg; the face is spared because trigeminal modalities travel separately.

before.syndrome: Ataxic hemiparesis from a paramedian pontine lacune
before.findings: A small lacunar infarct in the paramedian basis pontis or internal capsule can catch the medial lemniscus together with the corticospinal fibres, giving weakness with disproportionate limb ataxia (ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand); the mild loss of joint-position sense is easily missed unless vibration and finger-nose testing are performed carefully.
before.note: Because the lemniscus hugs the midline throughout the brainstem it is involved in most paramedian brainstem strokes — medullary (Déjerine), pontine and midbrain variants differ only in the accompanying cranial-nerve signs.

after.findings: Damage after the sensory decussation can reduce contralateral vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch; sensory ataxia may occur. Brainstem level is determined by associated cranial nerve and long-tract findings, not this deficit alone.

A lesion affecting both the medial lemniscus and neighboring descending motor or cerebellar pathways may combine contralateral sensory loss, weakness and ataxia. Ataxic hemiparesis has several possible anatomical substrates.

function.before: The great ascending band of conscious mechanosensation: formed at the sensory decussation by crossed internal arcuate fibers and ascending alongside the midline to the ventral posterolateral thalamus. In the medulla its fibers are stacked with the leg lateral and the arm medial; the bundle gradually swings laterally and ventrally as it climbs through pons toward its midbrain position.
function.after: Ascending second-order dorsal-column pathway formed by crossed internal arcuate fibers, carrying vibration, proprioception and discriminative touch from the contralateral body to VPL. In the medulla the upright ribbon has lower-body fibers ventrally and upper-body fibers dorsally; with ascent into the pons it rotates so that lower-body fibers lie more laterally. Its position changes across brainstem levels.

records.name: Spinal trigeminal tract

before.findings: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarcts abolish pain and temperature over the ipsilateral face with a characteristic onion-skin gradient, dissociated from facial touch (principal sensory nucleus, rostral pons) and from contralateral body pain loss (spinothalamic tract).

before.syndrome: Dissociated facial sensory loss (tract vs principal nucleus)
before.findings: The descending tract and its nucleus subserve only pain and temperature, so an incomplete lateral medullary infarct can remove those modalities from the face while light touch and trigeminal motor function stay intact; the same dissociated pattern is produced deliberately by a tractotomy at the obex for intractable facial pain, and the preserved touch is the signature that separates a spinal-tract lesion from a lesion of the principal sensory nucleus in the mid-pons.
before.note: Afferents of CN V, VII, IX and X all run here, so lesions can also numb the external ear canal and the posterior tongue and pharynx.

after.findings: Lateral medullary or pontine lesions can cause ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss, sometimes with relative preservation of discriminative touch. The distribution depends on which fibers and nuclear subdivisions are affected; an onion-skin pattern is possible but not obligatory.

afferent: Pain-temperature primary afferents of CN V, VII, IX, X from the trigeminal, geniculate and superior-petrosal/inferior ganglia
efferent: Spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal)

afferent: Primary sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, with general sensory contributions from peripheral ganglia of CN VII, IX and X
efferent: Spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal)

function.before: Dorsolaterally descending bundle of CN V pain-temperature afferents (with contributions from CN VII, IX and X for the ear, pharynx and posterior tongue) running from the principal sensory nucleus to the upper cervical cord alongside the spinal trigeminal nucleus; fibers are somatotopically laminated so that V1 sits most ventral/rostral and V3 most dorsal/caudal — the substrate of the onion-skin pattern.
function.after: Descending primary sensory fibers entering with CN V at the lateral pons and traveling beside the spinal trigeminal nucleus into the medulla and upper cervical cord. They carry facial pain, temperature and some crude touch, with small general sensory contributions from CN VII, IX and X. V1, V2 and V3 have ventral-to-dorsal organization, distinct from the rostral-to-caudal concentric facial representation.

records.name: Spinal trigeminal nucleus

before.syndrome: Afferent limb loss of the corneal reflex
before.findings: Involvement of the nucleus/tract blunts ipsilateral facial nociception and the blink response to corneal stimulation; combined with ambiguus lesions it also removes the gag afferent-efferent arc components.

before.syndrome: Onion-skin facial sensory gradient (subnucleus caudalis topography)
before.findings: Subnucleus caudalis is laminated like the dorsal horn, with perioral fibres ending most rostrally, so a lesion of its caudal and dorsal laminae numbs the outer face, ear and scalp while sparing the nose and mouth — the onion-skin pattern of lateral medullary infarction. Because the tract and the nucleus are functionally coupled, a lesion of either is clinically indistinguishable.
before.note: The blink (corneal) and gag reflexes are relayed through the rostral subnuclei, which is why a lateral medullary lesion can blunt the corneal reflex as well as pain-temperature sensation.

after.syndrome: Ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss and impaired corneal reflex
after.findings: Damage can reduce ipsilateral facial nociception and the afferent component of the corneal blink reflex. Concentric facial sensory loss may occur because perioral regions are represented more rostrally and peripheral facial regions more caudally. The gag reflex is primarily a CN IX-X circuit and is not a specific test of this nucleus.
