records.name: Nucleus solitarius (cardiorespiratory part)

before.findings: Bilateral NTS or its afferent-nerve damage abolishes baroreceptor buffering, yielding volatile hypertension-tachycardia crises alternating with hypotension; unilateral lateral medullary infarcts acutely raise blood pressure and impair chemoreceptor (hypoxic) drive.
Loss of pharyngolaryngeal afferent processing contributes to post-stroke dysphagia and aspiration in lateral medullary strokes, together with ambiguus efferent failure.

after.findings: NTS-region injury can impair visceral afferent processing, baroreflex control and swallowing/airway protection. Medullary strokes may produce blood-pressure or respiratory instability, especially with neighboring autonomic circuitry involved; the direction and severity are not fixed by an isolated nucleus label.

records.name: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (CN X)

before.syndrome: Vagal dysregulation after lateral medullary stroke
before.findings: Involvement contributes to dysphagia, gastric stasis, bradyarrhythmias and impaired vagal reflexes in Wallenberg infarcts; bilateral dorsal medullary damage threatens vagal control of viscera.

Vagal preganglionic neurons here slow the heart, drive bronchial secretion and run the enteric motor programme, so dorsal medullary lesions — syringobulbia, Chiari malformation, posterior-fossa surgery, or paramedian extension of a lateral medullary infarct — remove beat-to-beat cardiac modulation, producing bradycardia or asystole, delayed gastric emptying and vomiting; bilateral involvement is needed for the full picture.
before.note: Cough syncope and swallowing-induced bradycardia appearing after posterior-fossa surgery are the practical warning signs of dorsal vagal nuclear injury.

after.findings: Dorsal vagal complex injury can disturb gastrointestinal motility and visceral reflexes. Swallowing and vocal-fold weakness in medullary syndromes primarily reflect ambiguus branchiomotor involvement; bradycardia or asystole is not the predictable result of simply losing DMV parasympathetic neurons.

function.before: Preganglionic parasympathetic column lying under the vagal trigone of the fourth-ventricle floor: its fibers ride the vagus to terminal ganglia of the heart (slowing rate), airways and the enteric wall, driving visceral smooth-muscle motility, secretion and vagal cardiovascular reflexes; baroreceptor information reaches it from the solitary nucleus.
function.after: Preganglionic parasympathetic nucleus beneath the vagal trigone in the dorsomedial medulla. Its axons travel in CN X to ganglia near thoracic and abdominal viscera, particularly controlling gastrointestinal motility and secretion. Cardiac vagal control also has an important source in the nucleus ambiguus and should not be assigned solely to the DMV.

records.name: Nucleus ambiguus

before.findings: Unilateral ambiguus failure droops the ipsilateral palate, paralyzes the ipsilateral vocal fold and destroys effective swallowing — the clinical core of the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome; aspiration pneumonia is the principal risk.

before.syndrome: Progressive bulbar palsy (bulbar-onset motor neuron disease)
before.findings: Selective degeneration of the branchiomotor neurons of the nucleus ambiguus — together with the hypoglossal and facial nuclei — produces progressive flaccid dysarthria, nasal regurgitation, choking on liquids and tongue wasting with fasciculations, whereas the pseudobulbar variant instead gives spastic dysarthria with emotional lability. Swallowing failure and aspiration are the leading causes of death in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
before.note: The nucleus sits deep in the lateral tegmentum, so bilateral involvement — motor neuron disease, a brainstem glioma or vascular disease on both sides — is needed for complete laryngeal paralysis.

after.findings: Unilateral nucleus/fascicle injury can produce ipsilateral palatal and vocal-fold weakness, hoarseness and dysphagia, with aspiration risk. Severity varies with lesion extent and compensating pathways.

Degeneration of ambiguus, hypoglossal and other bulbar motor neurons can cause progressive dysarthria and dysphagia. Bilateral corticobulbar disease causes a different, supranuclear pattern, often with spastic speech and emotional lability.

function.before: Branchiomotor column deep in the reticular formation sending LMNs through CN IX, CN X and the cranial root of CN XI to the striated muscles of the soft palate, pharynx and larynx — palatal elevation, pharyngeal constriction, vocal-fold abduction for airway protection and phonation. Solitarius afferents complete the swallow and gag reflex arcs through it.
function.after: Medullary branchiomotor neurons supplying stylopharyngeus through CN IX and palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles through CN X. Fibers historically called the cranial root of CN XI are functionally part of vagal outflow. The ambiguus region also contains cardiac parasympathetic neurons; its branchiomotor connections support swallowing, phonation and airway protection.

records.name: Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII)

bloodSupply.before: Anterior spinal artery (paramedian branches of the vertebral artery)
bloodSupply.after: Paramedian vertebral and anterior spinal artery branches, with regional overlap.

before.findings: Nuclear or rootlet destruction wastes the ipsilateral tongue, which fasciculates and deviates TOWARD the lesion on protrusion (the intact contralateral genioglossus pushes the tip across) — a feature of medial medullary syndrome.
before.note: UMN lesions deviate the tongue away from the cerebral lesion (toward the weak side) without wasting or fasciculations.

before.syndrome: Bilateral hypoglossal palsy — immobile, wasted tongue
before.findings: Bilateral nuclear or rootlet lesions — motor neuron disease, syringobulbia, a midline medullary lesion or bilateral medial medullary infarcts — leave a tongue that can neither be protruded nor moved side to side, with severe dysarthria, pooling of saliva and inability to propel a food bolus; wasting and fasciculations separate it from the spastic, non-wasted tongue of pseudobulbar palsy.
before.note: The nucleus bulges into the fourth-ventricle floor as the hypoglossal trigone, the surface landmark used to find it on the medullary plate.

after.findings: Nuclear/fascicular injury can cause ipsilateral tongue weakness and deviation toward the weak side on protrusion. Atrophy/fasciculations depend on denervation and time. Bilateral injury may severely impair speech and oral bolus movement; complete immobility is not obligatory.

before.findings: Irritation or infarction of the area postrema (PICA territory) produces severe vertigo with violent vomiting and hiccups, often mimicking vestibular neuritis or gastritis and delaying stroke diagnosis.

records.name: Inferior cerebellar peduncle

before.findings: Lateral medullary infarcts involving the restiform body yield ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor and past-pointing together with vertigo from the adjoining vestibular nuclei.

before.syndrome: Partial lateral medullary syndrome — isolated vertigo and ataxia
before.findings: A small PICA or vertebral branch infarct confined to the dorsolateral medulla can involve the restiform body and the adjacent vestibular nuclei alone, so the patient presents with acute vertigo, nausea, nystagmus and ipsilateral limb-trunk ataxia that mimics vestibular neuritis. The discriminators are the ipsilateral dysmetria and past-pointing plus lateropulsion, which a peripheral lesion does not produce; HINTS bedside testing (normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation) identifies the central cause.
before.note: This 'vestibular pseudo-neuritis' presentation is one of the commonest reasons a posterior-circulation stroke is missed in the emergency department.

after.findings: Restiform-body injury can cause ipsilateral limb dysmetria and gait ataxia. Adjacent vestibular involvement adds vertigo and nystagmus; a small lateral medullary stroke may initially resemble a peripheral vestibular disorder. Clinical findings alone in this schematic do not exclude stroke.

records.name: Arcuate nucleus (medulla)

before.syndrome: Central hypoventilation from ventral medullary chemoreceptor damage
before.findings: The superficial arcuate (chemo-sensitive) region on the ventral medullary surface detects CO2 and pH, so damage over it — surgery for a foramen magnum or vertebral lesion, subarachnoid haemorrhage, or a ventral medullary infarct — flattens the CO2 ventilatory response: the patient hypoventilates and sleeps apnoeically with a normal chest examination. Congenital loss of these neurons underlies central congenital hypoventilation (Ondine's curse).
before.note: The arcuate nucleus is the medullary homologue of the pontine nuclei: its crossed ventral external arcuate fibres carry cortical copies of movement to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

after.findings: Ventral medullary injury may affect multiple motor and respiratory pathways. An isolated arcuate-nucleus lesion is not an established explanation for congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, which is associated with pathogenic PHOX2B variants and impaired autonomic development.

function.before: Superficial paramedian cell groups astride the pyramids, homologous to the pontine nuclei: they receive descending cortical fibers and relay to the cerebellum through ventral external arcuate fibers that cross and join the inferior cerebellar peduncle; also described as a chemosensitive (CO2/pH) region of the ventral medullary surface.
function.after: Small cell groups on the ventral medullary surface near the pyramids. They are associated with external arcuate projections toward the cerebellum; proposed respiratory chemosensory roles are not established sufficiently to infer a specific human lesion syndrome from this nucleus alone.

records.name: Medullary reticular formation

before.findings: Bilateral damage of the ventrolateral medullary respiratory columns (syringobulbia, lateral medullary extension, high cervical-medullary surgery) removes automatic breathing — patients breathe only when awake (Ondine curse), with apnea and hypercapnia during sleep.
Lateral medullary strokes that irritate the rostral ventrolateral pressor area acutely elevate blood pressure and mimic hypertensive emergencies at presentation.
Involvement of the descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers coursing through the lateral reticular tegmentum yields ipsilateral ptosis and miosis as part of Wallenberg syndrome.

after.findings: Medullary reticular/ventrolateral respiratory and vasomotor network injury can disturb automatic breathing and cardiovascular regulation. The manifestations depend on which neuronal groups and descending pathways are affected.
Injury to descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral medullary tegmentum can produce ipsilateral mild ptosis, miosis and variable anhidrosis.

records.name: Fourth ventricle

bloodSupply.after: The ventricular lumen is not perfused tissue. Surrounding brainstem/cerebellar tissue and fourth-ventricular choroid plexus have separate variable vertebrobasilar/PICA/AICA/SCA supplies.

function.before: Tent-shaped midline CSF cavity between the dorsal pons and medulla in front and the cerebellum behind, continuous rostrally with the cerebral aqueduct and caudally with the central canal at the obex; CSF leaves it through the lateral foramina of Luschka and the midline foramen of Magendie into the subarachnoid space. function.after: CSF cavity between dorsal pons/open medulla and cerebellum, with its floor in the rhomboid fossa. CSF enters from the cerebral aqueduct and exits through the median aperture (Magendie) and paired lateral apertures (Luschka) into the subarachnoid space; the central canal continues caudally.

records.name: Accessory nerve (CN XI) exit

function.before: Cranial rootlets from the caudal ambiguus leave the postolivary sulcus and are joined by spinal rootlets ascending through the foramen magnum from C1-C5; the combined nerve exits the jugular foramen to innervate sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (with the cranial portion hitching onto the vagus for laryngeal adduction).
function.after: Spinal accessory rootlets arise from the upper cervical cord and ascend through the foramen magnum before leaving through the jugular foramen to supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Nearby caudal medullary rootlets historically termed the cranial root of XI travel with the vagus and are best understood functionally as CN X, rather than the source of shoulder motor fibers.

records.name: Obex

before.findings: Tonsillar herniation (Chiari I) is measured against the obex-foramen magnum line; lesions around the obex (syringobulbia, tumors) affect the area postrema and NTS with emesis and autonomic instability.
before.note: Open-medulla plates key the ventricle apex to the obex (lvl-olivary).

after.findings: The obex is a dorsal medullary landmark relevant to lesions near the fourth-ventricle floor. Cerebellar tonsillar descent in Chiari assessment is measured relative to the basion-opisthion (McRae) line of the foramen magnum, not an obex-foramen-magnum line.

function.before: The caudal apex of the fourth ventricle where its roof narrows into the central canal; flanked by the area postrema and gracile tubercles, it marks the cervicomedullary transition on the dorsal surface and is the key surgical and radiologic landmark of the posterior fossa outlet.
function.after: Caudal apex of the fourth ventricle at its transition to the central canal, adjacent to the area postrema. It marks the transition between open and closed medulla, rather than the spinal cord-medulla junction.

records.name: Cerebellar hemispheres and vermis (context)

before.findings: Hemisphere lesions produce ipsilateral dysmetria, intention (terminal) tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, hypotonia and rebound; gait is broad-based and veers toward the lesion.
Midline (vermal) involvement produces falling and staggering with relatively preserved limb coordination on the bed — typical of midline tumors and alcohol-related vermal atrophy.

after.findings: Hemispheric injury may cause ipsilateral appendicular dysmetria, intention tremor or impaired rapid alternating movements. Midline/vestibular injury may predominantly affect gait, trunk and eye movements. Lesion extent and connected pathways determine the actual combination.

efferent: Superior cerebellar peduncle (tract-scp) — dentate/interposed/fastigial output to contralateral thalamus, red nucleus and reticular formation

afferent: Crossed pontocerebellar fibers through the middle cerebellar peduncle (tract-mcp)

efferent: Dentate/interposed output mainly through the superior cerebellar peduncle to contralateral thalamus and red nucleus

function.before: Envelope of the cerebellum — two lateral hemispheres joined by the midline vermis dorsal to the pons and medulla. The lateral (neocerebellar) hemispheres plan skilled limb movements through the dentato-thalamo-cortical loop, the intermediate zone corrects ongoing limb trajectories via the interposed nuclei, and the vermis and flocculonodular lobe govern axial posture, gait and balance-eye coordination. Cerebellar output acts ipsilateral to the body because its efferents cross twice.
function.after: Cerebellar hemispheres joined by the midline vermis lie dorsal to pons and medulla. Lateral cortex participates in planning and coordination through dentate output; intermediate cortex connects to interposed nuclei; vermal and vestibular regions influence axial posture, gait, balance and eye movements. Lateral limb-control loops cross cerebellar output and later descending motor pathways, giving a predominantly ipsilateral relation to body coordination; medial outputs also have bilateral targets.

records.name: Dentate nucleus

before.findings: SCA infarcts or lesions of the dentate/SCP system produce ipsilateral intention tremor, dysmetria and decomposition of movement; bilateral dentate disease (neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, metronidazole or radiation toxicity) disturbs movement timing.
Dentate or SCP lesions interrupt the dentato-rubro-olivary triangle and secondarily degenerate the inferior olive, causing palatal myoclonus.
before.note: Links the dentate to the medullary olive via the contralateral red nucleus.

after.findings: Dentate injury can produce ipsilateral limb dysmetria and intention tremor. Output lesions above the SCP decussation instead affect the contralateral body; delayed tremor and other movement disorders vary by pathway extent.
Dentate or pre-crossing SCP injury can deafferent the contralateral inferior olive through dentato-rubro-olivary circuitry. Olivary MRI changes and palatal tremor are possible, not inevitable.

records.name: Interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose)

bloodSupply.before: Superior cerebellar artery (SCA)
bloodSupply.after: Deep cerebellar branches, often SCA-associated, with territorial variation.

before.syndrome: Ipsilateral limb dysmetria from interposed-nucleus loss
before.findings: The interposed (emboliform and globose) nuclei are the output of the intermediate spinocerebellum, so their destruction removes the on-line correction of ongoing limb movement: the ipsilateral arm overshoots and oscillates on finger-to-nose testing, with dysdiadochokinesia, hypotonia and a coarse intention tremor, while trunk control and gait are comparatively spared because the vermis and fastigial loop are intact.
before.note: Signs are ipsilateral because cerebellar outflow crosses twice (SCP decussation, then the cortical projection); the interposed output reaches the magnocellular red nucleus through the superior cerebellar peduncle.

after.findings: Interposed-nuclear injury can cause ipsilateral limb dysmetria and coordination difficulty. Tremor/tone/gait effects vary; preserved trunk or gait function cannot be assumed from an isolated label.

function.before: Medialmost deep nucleus of the vermis and vestibulocerebellum: receives vermal Purkinje output and drives axial posture and eye-position control through fibers that leave via the inferior cerebellar peduncle to vestibular and reticular nuclei and via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral VL and central tegmental tract — calibration of balance, gait and the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
function.after: Most medial deep cerebellar nucleus, receiving inhibitory Purkinje input mainly from the vermis. It influences balance, axial posture and eye-head coordination through bilateral vestibular and reticular targets, primarily along uncinate and juxtarestiform pathways; some output reaches the thalamus and tectum. The flocculonodular lobe also projects directly to vestibular nuclei.

records.name: Pretectal area

before.findings: Pretectal destruction abolishes the pupillary light reflex while sparing accommodation, producing large pupils that 'accommodate but do not react' together with vertical gaze palsy and convergence-retraction nystagmus.
before.vascular: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA; pineal region mass effect

before.findings: Selective pretectal-to-EW light-reflex interruption (classically neurosyphilis) yields small, irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light.
before.note: Contrast with Adie pupil, which is a lesion of the ciliary ganglion beyond the EW neurons.

after.syndrome: Light-near dissociation in dorsal midbrain disease
after.findings: Pretectal/posterior-commissural injury can impair the pupillary light response while sparing the near response, often with other dorsal-midbrain findings. The historical Argyll Robertson pupil is a clinical association with neurosyphilis, not a precisely established isolated pretectal lesion locator.

function.before: Pretectal interneurons receive retinal input and bilaterally drive the Edinger-Westphal nuclei to constrict both pupils in the light reflex; they coordinate the pupillary component of the near response and interface with the vertical gaze centers of the rostral midbrain.
function.after: Pretectal region rostral to the superior colliculi. The olivary pretectal light-reflex relay receives retinal input and projects bilaterally to preganglionic parasympathetic oculomotor neurons, partly through the posterior commissure. Nearby rostral-midbrain gaze circuitry is distinct from this pupillary relay.

records.name: Oculomotor nucleus (CN III)

before.findings: Fascicular CN III palsy (ipsilateral ptosis, mydriasis, 'down and out' eye) combined with contralateral hemiplegia of face, arm, and leg from crus cerebri involvement.
before.vascular: Paramedian branches of the PCA (posterior thalamoperforating)

before.findings: Compressive lesions (classically posterior communicating artery aneurysm) at the fascicle or nerve produce mydriasis with ptosis and ophthalmoparesis; parasympathetic fibers run peripherally in the nerve, so pupillary involvement signals compression and demands emergency imaging.
before.vascular: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm; PCA/SCA interval infarct (pupil-sparing, microvascular)

after.findings: Nuclear injury can cause bilateral or asymmetric ocular motor deficits. Fascicular injury may give ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral weakness or ataxia according to neighboring pathways.
A new CN III palsy can reflect compressive, ischemic or other disease. Pupil involvement raises concern for aneurysmal compression, but pupil sparing does not exclude a dangerous compressive cause.

function.before: Somatic motor complex innervating the medial, superior, and inferior rectus, the inferior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris via CN III; arranged as paired subnuclei plus a single midline central caudal (levator) column. Each subnucleus supplies contralateral target muscles except the superior rectus, so nuclear lesions can produce bilateral ptosis with asymmetric ophthalmoparesis.
function.after: Somatic motor nuclear complex in the rostral midbrain at the superior-collicular level. Medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique subnuclei mainly supply ipsilateral muscles; the superior-rectus subnucleus supplies the contralateral muscle, and a midline central caudal subnucleus supplies both levators. Nuclear injury may therefore produce bilateral ptosis or superior-rectus deficits rather than a simple unilateral nerve pattern.

records.name: Edinger-Westphal preganglionic neurons

before.findings: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) and severe diabetic/autonomic lesions interrupt the pretectal input to the EW nucleus so the pupil accommodates but does not constrict to light.
before.vascular: Paramedian PCA perforators; also seen with large-fiber diabetic autonomic neuropathy (afferent/efferent pupillary fibers)

before.findings: Fascicular or peripheral CN III lesions that sweep the EW-derived parasympathetic fibers produce a dilated, poorly reactive pupil with ptosis and diplopia.

after.findings: EWpg or outgoing parasympathetic-fiber injury can impair pupil constriction and accommodation. Light-near dissociation reflects differential pathway disruption; a peripheral autonomic lesion does not automatically establish pretectal-to-EW interruption.

function.before: Parasympathetic preganglionic (visceral oculomotor) nucleus dorsal to the oculomotor complex: its preganglionic fibers travel with CN III to the ciliary ganglion, where postganglionic fibers excite the sphincter pupillae (miosis) and the ciliary muscle (accommodation).
function.after: Preganglionic parasympathetic neurons associated with the oculomotor complex whose axons travel in CN III to the ciliary ganglion. Postganglionic neurons then supply sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. These EWpg neurons must be distinguished from centrally projecting Edinger-Westphal (EWcp) neurons, which have different functions and are not the pupillary motor relay.

records.name: Trochlear nucleus (CN IV)

before.findings: Vertical diplopia worst on contralateral gaze and ipsilateral head tilt (Bielschowsky head-tilt test); patients tilt the head away from the paretic side. Common causes: closed head trauma at the dorsal exit/decussation and microvascular ischemia.
before.vascular: Paramedian perforators; long subarachnoid course makes the nerve vulnerable to tentorial-edge trauma

before.findings: Bilateral dorsal exit/decussation injury produces a 'V-pattern' esotropia with large excyclotorsion — a classic sequela of severe closed head injury.
before.vascular: Collicular/SCA branches at the dorsal midbrain

after.findings: A trochlear nuclear or pre-crossing fascicular lesion affects the contralateral superior oblique; a post-crossing nerve lesion affects the ipsilateral muscle. Superior-oblique weakness causes vertical/torsional diplopia, often worse in downgaze and contralateral gaze relative to the weak eye, with hypertropia increased by head tilt toward that eye.
Dorsal crossing or nerve injury may affect both superior obliques after trauma. Bilateral findings are variable and do not prove the precise exit-zone site.

records.name: Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus

before.findings: Because the mesencephalic nucleus provides the afferent limb, bilateral corticobulbar (pseudobulbar) disease releases the jaw-jerk reflex, which becomes brisk — a sign of upper motor neuron involvement above the trigeminal motor nucleus.

records.name: Red nucleus

before.findings: Ventral tegmental lesion of CN III fascicles plus the red nucleus: ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral tremor, choreoathetosis, or ataxia.
More dorsal tegmental lesion combining CN III palsy with contralateral ataxia from red nucleus and dentatorubrothalamic (SCP) fiber involvement.
Lesions of the red nucleus or its dentatorubral input produce a low-frequency (2-4.5 Hz) rest-and-postural tremor, sometimes appearing weeks to months after the injury.

after.findings: CN III fascicular injury with neighboring cerebellothalamic pathway injury can combine ipsilateral ophthalmoparesis with contralateral ataxia or tremor (Claude/Benedikt patterns). Historical eponym boundaries vary.
Delayed low-frequency rest, postural and action tremor can follow lesions of distributed cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal networks. It should not be localized exclusively to the red nucleus.

records.name: Substantia nigra, pars compacta

before.findings: Loss of more than half of SNc dopaminergic neurons with striatal dopamine depletion produces the cardinal tetrad: resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability.
Infarcts or hemorrhages involving the substantia nigra cause contralateral parkinsonism or hemiparkinsonism, and acute nigral lesions may add hemiballistic or dystonic movements.
before.vascular: PCA paramedian perforators; anterior choroidal artery

after.findings: Degeneration of SNc dopaminergic neurons contributes to bradykinesia, rigidity and often rest tremor. Nonmotor symptoms may precede motor diagnosis; postural instability is often later. A fixed cell-loss threshold or mandatory symptom tetrad should not be used as a diagnostic rule.
Rare focal nigral lesions can produce parkinsonism. More typical vascular parkinsonism involves broader subcortical vascular disease, and the phenotype depends on affected networks.

function.before: Melanin-pigmented dopaminergic nucleus forming the dorsal band of the substantia nigra: its nigrostriatal projection to the caudate and putamen facilitates the direct (movement-facilitating) basal ganglia pathway, while mesocortical and mesolimbic projections modulate cognition and reward. Progressive degeneration of SNc neurons with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies, depleting striatal dopamine, produces Parkinson's disease.
function.after: Neuromelanin-containing dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta. Nigrostriatal projections to caudate and putamen modulate direct and indirect basal-ganglia pathways. Mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine projections arise mainly from the neighboring ventral tegmental area, rather than being defining SNc outputs.

records.name: Substantia nigra, pars reticulata

before.findings: SNr infarcts or hemorrhages disinhibit thalamic and collicular targets, producing contralateral dystonia, chorea, or hemiballism-like involuntary movements.
before.vascular: PCA paramedian perforators; anterior choroidal artery

before.findings: SNr neurons fire tonically and hold the superior colliculus under GABAergic inhibition, so loss of nigral output removes the brake on reflexive visually guided saccades: patients make unwanted, short-latency saccades towards novel stimuli and are visually distractible, a pattern also described in progressive supranuclear palsy, in which SNr cell loss is a pathological hallmark.
before.vascular: PCA paramedian perforators; anterior choroidal artery
before.note: The mirror image of Parkinson's disease: here the dopaminergic pars compacta is spared while the GABAergic output nucleus fails, so the picture is hyperkinetic and saccade-happy rather than bradykinetic.

after.findings: SNr is a tonic inhibitory basal-ganglia output nucleus with thalamic, collicular and brainstem targets. Injury or network dysfunction can disturb movement and eye-movement control, but an isolated human lesion does not define a predictable hyperkinetic or visually distractible syndrome.

records.name: Crus cerebri

function.before: Ventral midbrain fiber bundle (basis pedunculi) carrying all descending corticofugal fibers with strict medial-to-lateral somatotopy: frontopontine fibers most medial, then corticobulbar fibers, then corticospinal fibers, and temporoparietooccipitopontine fibers most lateral. Rostrally continuous with the internal capsule; caudally it disperses into the longitudinal fasciculi of the basis pontis and re-forms as the medullary pyramids.
function.after: Ventral midbrain descending fiber compartment (basis pedunculi). Medial fibers are predominantly frontopontine, the middle part carries corticospinal/corticobulbar fibers, and lateral fibers include temporoparieto-occipitopontine projections. This is a broad topographic scheme, not a strictly separated fiber map. Corticospinal fibers continue through the pons to the medullary pyramids.

records.name: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussation

before.findings: Paramedian lesions of the decussation interrupt cerebellar outflow producing limb ataxia and intention tremor; involvement of the adjacent oculomotor complex and MLF adds diplopia and gaze palsies.

after.findings: A lesion centered on the SCP crossing can interrupt output from both cerebellar hemispheres and cause bilateral ataxia. Deficits above or below the crossing depend on which fibers are affected; nearby trochlear/MLF involvement may add ocular motor findings.

function.before: Ventral midline crossing of the superior cerebellar peduncles in the caudal midbrain tegmentum: virtually all dentatothalamocortical cerebellar output decussates here, so each cerebellar hemisphere ultimately coordinates the contralateral body through the red nucleus, VL/VA thalamus, and motor cortex.
function.after: Crossing of the major dentate/interposed cerebellar efferents in the caudal midbrain near the inferior-collicular level. Crossed fibers reach contralateral red-nuclear and thalamic targets; after the additional crossing in descending motor pathways, each cerebellar hemisphere has a net influence on the ipsilateral body.

records.name: Superior cerebellar peduncle

before.findings: SCP or dentate outflow lesions produce ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor, and limb ataxia; SCA-territory infarcts classically combine these with vertigo and nystagmus.
before.note: Adult-onset lesions may later develop contralateral (double-crossed) dystonia or choreoathetosis.

before.findings: Damage to the dentato-rubro-thalamic route at or above the peduncular decussation — the midbrain tegmentum, the red nucleus or the thalamic VL — leaves a coarse, slow (2-5 Hz) tremor of the contralateral limbs that is present at rest, worsens with posture and explodes on goal-directed movement, often with mild accompanying ataxia.
before.vascular: Superior cerebellar artery / paramedian basilar tip perforators
before.note: The delay of weeks to months between the stroke and the tremor, its contralateral side, and its partial response to levodopa or to VIM/subthalamic deep-brain stimulation separate it from acute cerebellar ataxia.

after.findings: The side of ataxia depends on crossing: ipsilateral below the caudal-midbrain SCP decussation, contralateral above it, and potentially bilateral at the crossing.
Delayed Holmes-type tremor can follow cerebellothalamic network injury, often with additional nigrostriatal dysfunction. Side, latency and treatment response vary.

function.before: Principal efferent peduncle of the cerebellum: dentate and interposed nucleus fibers sweep rostrally through the dorsolateral pons and caudal midbrain, decussate completely in the ventral midbrain tegmentum, and reach the contralateral red nucleus and VL/VA thalamus (dentatorubrothalamic system). Because cerebellar output double-crosses, lesions here cause ipsilateral limb ataxia; chronic lesions may add contralateral dystonia.
function.after: Major cerebellar output route from dentate and interposed nuclei through the rostral pons to the caudal-midbrain decussation, then toward contralateral thalamus and red nucleus. It also carries anterior spinocerebellar afferents. Pre-crossing output injury causes mainly ipsilateral limb ataxia; post-crossing cerebellothalamic injury causes contralateral ataxia.

records.name: Dorsal raphe nucleus

before.findings: Dorsal raphe serotonergic neurons are the principal pharmacological target of SSRIs; midbrain raphe involvement is associated with mood disturbance, sleep-wake disruption, and altered pain thresholds in brainstem disease.
before.note: Serotonergic dysfunction is documented pharmacologically and functionally rather than as a focal stroke syndrome.

after.findings: Dorsal raphe neurons participate in distributed serotonergic circuits influencing sleep and affect. SSRIs act on serotonin transporters throughout serotonergic projections, not exclusively on this nucleus; a focal dorsal-raphe lesion is not a specific diagnostic mood syndrome.

function.before: Largest of the rostral serotonergic (5-HT) raphe nuclei, lying midline between the MLFs ventral to the periaqueductal gray: it projects diffusely to the forebrain, diencephalon, and spinal cord, modulating sleep-wake cycling, mood, and nociception, and partners with the PAG in descending antinociception.
function.after: Predominantly serotonergic cell group in the midline periaqueductal region of the midbrain and rostral pons, with major ascending projections to forebrain structures. It modulates arousal, affect and other behaviors. Caudal medullary raphe groups provide important descending spinal serotonergic pain modulation; they should not be conflated with the dorsal raphe.

records.name: Cuneiform nucleus

before.syndrome: Gait ignition failure / freezing of gait
before.findings: The cuneiform-pedunculopontine mesencephalic locomotor region drives gait initiation; its degeneration or disconnection in parkinsonism contributes to freezing of gait and akinesia, and it is an investigational deep-brain-stimulation target.

after.findings: Mesencephalic locomotor circuitry is studied in gait initiation/freezing and neuromodulation. Freezing of gait has distributed mechanisms and does not uniquely diagnose cuneiform nuclear degeneration.

function.before: Mesencephalic reticular formation of the dorsolateral tegmentum (with the adjacent pedunculopontine region forming the mesencephalic locomotor region): initiates and modulates gait and postural tone through descending reticulospinal systems, contributes to arousal via ascending projections to the intralaminar thalamus, and participates in pain modulation and startle.
function.after: Dorsolateral mesencephalic reticular nucleus included with neighboring pedunculopontine circuitry in descriptions of the mesencephalic locomotor region. Experimental and translational studies link this region to locomotion and arousal; precise selective human nuclear lesion functions are not established by this atlas.

records.name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) exit

before.findings: Ventral midbrain lesion at the exit zone: ipsilateral CN III palsy (ptosis, mydriasis, down-and-out eye) with contralateral hemiplegia.

after.findings: CN III palsy may involve ptosis, extraocular weakness and variable pupil dysfunction. Midbrain fascicular extension can add contralateral weakness/ataxia. Acute aneurysmal or herniation-related compression is possible; pupil sparing does not exclude compression.

records.name: Pontine nuclei

before.findings: Basis pontis infarction (including the pontine relay gray) abolishes nearly all voluntary movement except vertical eye movements and blinking, while the dorsal tegmentum and consciousness are spared.
Osmotic stress demyelinates the central basis pontis, damaging the pontine gray and the fiber systems threading through it, and producing spastic quadriparesis with pseudobulbar palsy.
before.note: Classically follows over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia.

after.findings: Pontine nuclei relay cortical information to the contralateral cerebellum; their injury may contribute to ataxia. Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral corticospinal/corticobulbar disconnection with preserved consciousness, rather than isolated pontine gray injury.

Central pontine myelinolysis primarily affects myelin in the central pons, often after osmotic stress associated with correction of chronic hyponatremia. It may cause dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis; it is not primarily destruction of pontine neuronal gray matter.

records.name: Longitudinal and transverse pontine fibers

before.findings: Interruption of the longitudinal fibers in the ventral pons disconnects the motor cortex from all spinal and cranial motor nuclei below, sparing only the oculomotor pathways in the tegmentum.

A small paramedian lacunar infarct confined to the basis pontis destroys descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres together with the transverse pontocerebellar fibres, so the patient shows a clumsy, slow hand with mild weakness of the same limbs and dysarthria — plus gait ataxia disproportionate to the weakness. Larger lesions produce the full locked-in picture.
before.note: The transverse fibres decussate here and gather as the middle cerebellar peduncle, so a unilateral basis lesion also de-afferents the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere and can add crossed cerebellar ataxia.

after.findings: Bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar injury in the basis pontis can produce locked-in syndrome when arousal systems remain intact. Small unilateral lesions may cause contralateral weakness, dysarthria and clumsy-hand or ataxic-hemiparesis patterns; not every larger pontine lesion produces locked-in syndrome.

records.name: Trigeminal motor nucleus (CN V)

before.findings: Wasting and weakness of the ipsilateral masticatory muscles; on opening, the jaw deviates toward the weak side (unopposed lateral pterygoid of the normal side), and the jaw jerk is abolished.
before.vascular: Short circumferential branches of the basilar artery (superior cerebellar artery branches at the rostral pole)
before.note: In striking contrast, UMN (corticobulbar) lesions weaken the jaw only slightly because the nucleus is bilaterally innervated.

after.findings: Lower motor neuron injury can weaken ipsilateral mastication and produce jaw deviation toward the weak side on opening. Atrophy or reduced jaw reflex depends on extent and chronicity. Bilateral cortical input often limits weakness after unilateral supranuclear injury.

records.name: Facial nucleus (CN VII)

before.findings: Paralysis of the entire ipsilateral hemiface including the forehead: the eye will not close, tears pool, food collects in the buccal vestibule and the smile flattens; hyperacusis may appear if stapedius fibers are involved. Nuclear or fascicular lesions combine this with other pontine deficits (Millard-Gubler).
Contralateral weakness confined to the lower face with forehead sparing, produced by lesions of the corticobulbar fibers above the nucleus (cortex, internal capsule, cerebral peduncle).
before.note: Forehead sparing reflects the bilateral cortical innervation of the upper-division motoneurons.

after.findings: Nuclear/fascicular injury may weaken the entire ipsilateral face, including forehead and eye closure. Other pontine findings depend on lesion extent.
Unilateral cortical/corticobulbar injury often predominantly weakens contralateral lower face with relative upper-face preservation. Forehead sparing is a useful pattern rather than an absolute rule.

before.syndrome: Ipsilateral dry eye and reduced salivation
before.findings: Pontine or proximal CN VII lesions involving the nucleus or nervus intermedius reduce lacrimation and submandibular-sublingual salivation; the same fibers are affected in Bell palsy, explaining dry eye and altered taste together.

records.name: Nucleus solitarius (rostral gustatory part)

bloodSupply.before: Basilar short circumferential branches; AICA at the pontomedullary junction
bloodSupply.after: Vertebral/PICA regional medullary branches, with variable overlap near the pontomedullary junction; precise gustatory subnuclear perfusion is not independently mapped.

before.findings: Rare in isolated form; loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior two-thirds of the tongue accompanies pontine lesions of the solitary complex or its central tegmental output.

after.findings: Solitary-nucleus or ascending gustatory injury can impair taste. Side and distribution vary with lesion extent; central loss is not limited to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

afferent: Taste-bud primary afferents via CN VII, CN IX and CN X
efferent: Central tegmental tract (tract-central-tegmental) to parabrachial nuclei and VPM
Hypothalamic and amygdaloid viscerosensory projections

afferent: Taste primary afferents through CN VII, IX and X
efferent: Ascending gustatory fibers toward VPM through the central tegmental region

function.before: Rostral (gustatory) pole of the solitary nuclear complex reaching the caudal pons: the first central synapse for taste afferents of CN VII (chorda tympani, greater petrosal), CN IX and CN X. Output rises in the central tegmental tract to the parabrachial nuclei and, via thalamic relay in VPM, to the insular gustatory cortex.
function.after: Rostral gustatory part of the solitary nucleus in the rostral medulla. It receives taste afferents from CN VII, IX and X; in humans the ascending gustatory pathway reaches VPM and then insular/frontal-opercular cortex. Rodent parabrachial-relay organization should not be imposed as an obligatory human relay.

geometryNote.after: Rostral gustatory NTS is in rostral medulla. Legacy numeric placement is conceptual and not registered to serial sections; exact coordinates and boundary remain unvalidated.

records.name: Superior vestibular nucleus

before.findings: Unilateral involvement produces vertigo with nystagmus and past-pointing as part of AICA or lateral pontine syndromes.

before.syndrome: Skew deviation and the ocular tilt reaction (otolith pathway)
before.findings: Utricular signals relayed through the superior vestibular nucleus are distributed by the MLF to the ocular motor nuclei and to the interstitial nucleus of Cajal; when they become asymmetric — a superior vestibular nerve or nucleus lesion, or a brainstem tegmental lesion — the brain misjudges 'down' and produces an ocular tilt reaction of head tilt, skew deviation (one eye higher than the other) and conjugate ocular torsion. The direction of the tilt indicates the side of the imbalanced utricular input.
before.note: Skew deviation is a graviceptive (otolith) sign, not a nerve palsy: ductions and versions are full, and the vertical diplopia is commonly dissociated from the degree of vertigo.

after.findings: Injury in the superior vestibular region can cause vertigo, nystagmus and abnormalities of vestibulo-ocular control. Skew deviation and ocular tilt reaction reflect imbalance of distributed otolith pathways and are not specific to this nucleus.

records.name: Medial vestibular nucleus

before.findings: Lesions impair the vestibulo-ocular reflex, producing oscillopsia, gaze-evoked nystagmus and impaired smooth pursuit-vestibular cooperation in lateral pontomedullary strokes.

before.syndrome: Lateropulsion (ipsilateral trunk push) in lateral medullary and vestibular lesions
before.findings: The medial vestibular nucleus is the source of the medial vestibulospinal tract and of the MLF vestibulo-ocular fibres, so its involvement — classically in a Wallenberg infarct — produces lateropulsion: the patient actively pushes the trunk and falls toward the side of the lesion, with the head and eyes deviated the same way, and the symptom may outlast the vertigo and nystagmus by weeks.
before.vascular: PICA / vertebral (dorsolateral medulla); AICA at the pontine level
before.note: Distinguishing lateropulsion (vestibulospinal, toward the lesion) from cerebellar past-pointing (limb, ipsilateral, with dysmetria) is a classic bedside discriminator.

after.findings: Medial vestibular injury can disturb the VOR, gaze stability and head-neck posture. Lateropulsion may accompany lateral medullary injury but involves distributed vestibular and spinocerebellar pathways; it is not proof of isolated medial vestibular nuclear injury or synonymous with active pusher behavior.

records.name: Lateral vestibular nucleus

before.findings: Acute unilateral involvement contributes to ipsilateral past-pointing and postural instability (falling toward the lesion); decerebrate extensor rigidity reflects release of the lateral vestibulospinal system from cerebellar control.

after.findings: Injury can disturb vestibulospinal regulation and balance. Direction/severity of falling and limb signs depend on the wider vestibular/cerebellar lesion; decerebrate posturing involves distributed brainstem motor-control imbalance.

function.before: Deiters nucleus: gives origin to the ipsilateral lateral vestibulospinal tract, which facilitates extensor (antigravity) muscle tone of the limbs and trunk for postural support; governed by inhibitory Purkinje input from the vestibulocerebellar vermis, so loss of cerebellar restraint yields excessive extensor tone.
function.after: Lateral (Deiters) vestibular nucleus contributes importantly to the predominantly uncrossed lateral vestibulospinal tract, influencing extensor tone and posture. It integrates vestibular, cerebellar and other inputs. Postural effects reflect a network rather than one cerebellar-release mechanism.

records.name: Inferior vestibular nucleus

before.findings: The inferior (descending) vestibular nucleus processes vertical-canal and otolith signals and is the caudalmost link between the vestibular nerve and the vestibulocerebellum; lesions at the caudal medulla or craniocervical junction — a dorsal PICA-territory infarct, a small cerebellar haemorrhage or a Chiari malformation — are associated with vertical (typically downbeat) or direction-changing positional nystagmus, postural instability with falls, and dysequilibrium that outlasts the acute vertigo.
before.note: Hearing is usually preserved: the cochlear nuclei and nerve root lie rostral to this nucleus, which is why a 'vestibular' medullary infarct can present exactly like vestibular neuritis.

after.findings: Injury can contribute to vertigo, nystagmus and disequilibrium in medullary or cerebellar disease. Downbeat nystagmus has multiple cerebellar and brainstem substrates and should not be presented as the defining isolated syndrome of this nucleus.

function.before: Caudalmost, longitudinally oriented vestibular nucleus descending toward the upper cervical cord: integrates vestibular input with spinocerebellar afferents and projects through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the vestibulocerebellum and to the reticular formation for vestibulo-spinal tuning.
function.after: Caudal/descending vestibular nucleus in the dorsolateral medulla, integrating vestibular signals with cerebellar and spinal inputs. It connects to the cerebellum, other vestibular nuclei and reticular systems involved in posture. It is not a nucleus extending into the upper cervical cord.

records.name: Ventral cochlear nucleus

bloodSupply.before: AICA (labyrinthine/internal auditory arcade branches)
bloodSupply.after: AICA and nearby vertebrobasilar branches to the pontomedullary cochlear nuclear region; the labyrinthine artery supplies the inner ear and intrameatal CN VIII rather than being synonymous with the cochlear nuclear arterial supply.

before.findings: Destruction of the cochlear nuclei or the entering CN VIII fibers abolishes ipsilateral hearing (there is no bilateral backup at this first relay); classically produced by AICA infarction or cerebellopontine-angle tumors.
before.vascular: Short circumferential branches of the basilar artery (AICA territory for the caudal part of the nucleus)
before.note: Beyond the cochlear nuclei, auditory information is bilaterally represented, so central lesions cause only subtle hearing loss.

after.findings: Damage to the entering cochlear nerve or sufficiently extensive cochlear nuclear complex can cause ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Auditory signals become bilaterally represented above the cochlear nuclei; complete deafness cannot be inferred from a small lesion of this one subdivision.

records.name: Dorsal cochlear nucleus

before.syndrome: Ipsilateral sensorineural deafness with tinnitus (cerebellopontine angle lesion)
before.findings: Compression or infarction of the dorsal cochlear nucleus at the cerebellopontine angle — the usual site of a vestibular schwannoma, an AICA-territory infarct or an epidermoid — removes hearing and adds tinnitus on that side, usually with vertigo and facial numbness from the neighbouring structures. Because the auditory pathway decussates at the trapezoid body and is bilateral from the cochlear nuclei onwards, lesions above this level never cause unilateral deafness.
before.note: Its surface bulge is the acoustic tubercle over the inferior cerebellar peduncle; the nucleus is also a site of somatosensory-auditory convergence implicated in tinnitus generation.

after.findings: The dorsal cochlear nucleus contributes to auditory processing; cochlear-complex or CN VIII injury at the pontomedullary junction can impair ipsilateral hearing. Complete ipsilateral deafness is not an obligatory consequence of an isolated dorsal subdivision lesion. Tinnitus has multiple peripheral and central substrates.

records.name: Superior olivary complex

before.syndrome: Loss of binaural sound localization (impaired interaural processing)
before.findings: The complex is the brain's first binaural comparator, so a lesion that removes it — typically a small basilar or AICA-territory pontine infarct — leaves pure-tone thresholds relatively preserved while destroying the ability to judge which side a sound comes from and degrading speech understanding against background noise; the deficit is easily missed because routine audiometry is normal.
before.note: The same complex gives rise to the medial olivocochlear bundle, so its damage also removes efferent control of the cochlea (protection from loud sound and the 'anti-masking' reflex).

after.findings: Superior olivary circuitry compares timing and level signals from both ears. Lesions can impair sound localization and hearing in noise despite relatively preserved pure-tone thresholds; the degree is variable and is not a unique diagnostic pattern.

records.name: Trapezoid body

before.syndrome: Bilateral representation of each ear (auditory decussation)
before.findings: The trapezoid body is the first decussation of the auditory system: section of it, or of the ventral cochlear nucleus output that feeds it, removes the crossed contribution of one ear to the opposite lateral lemniscus. Clinically this is expressed as part of a ventral caudal pontine infarct, where the auditory finding is muffled hearing and impaired sound localization rather than an isolated deafness, because the uncrossed projection from each cochlear nucleus survives.
before.vascular: Basilar paramedian and short circumferential perforators
before.note: This decussation is why each inferior colliculus and each auditory cortex is driven by both ears — and why a brainstem lesion almost never causes unilateral deafness.

after.findings: Crossed cochlear output contributes to bilateral auditory representation. Injury may impair binaural processing, but the clinical effects vary with extent and adjacent auditory structures. Unilateral hearing loss remains possible with more peripheral or cochlear-complex involvement.

records.name: Lateral lemniscus

before.syndrome: Auditory component of the lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome
before.findings: The lateral lemniscus lies in the subpial lateral tegmentum beside the middle cerebellar peduncle, exactly where an AICA infarct lands: patients then report tinnitus and reduced hearing on that side, although the damage that produces the deafness is at the cochlear nuclei and nerve root rather than in the lemniscus itself. An isolated lemniscal lesion barely changes pure-tone thresholds because each lemniscus already carries information from both ears (the ventral cochlear nuclei project bilaterally through the trapezoid body); the typical residual is difficulty localizing sound and understanding speech in noise.
before.note: Teaching point for localization: unilateral deafness is never central — it points to the cochlea, the auditory nerve or the cochlear nuclei, not to this bundle.

after.findings: An isolated unilateral lateral lemniscus lesion usually causes subtler auditory-processing or localization deficits because inputs represent both ears. Hearing loss in a lateral pontine stroke can reflect additional cochlear nucleus, CN VIII or labyrinthine injury.

records.name: Middle cerebellar peduncle

before.findings: Unilateral MCP damage (infarct, demyelination, pontine tumors) produces severe ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia with dysmetria, because the peduncle feeds the ipsilateral (already double-crossed) cerebellar hemisphere.
T2 hyperintensity and atrophy of the MCP is a classic MRI sign in spinocerebellar ataxias, fragile-X tremor-ataxia syndrome and Wilson disease.
before.note: The sign localizes to degeneration of pontocerebellar fibers rather than to a vascular event.

after.findings: MCP injury can cause ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia by disrupting input to the cerebellum on the same side.

MCP T2 signal abnormality is seen in several conditions, including fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome and pontocerebellar degeneration. It is nonspecific and may also occur after ischemic or other injury.

records.name: Locus coeruleus

function.before: The principal noradrenergic nucleus of the brain: about half of all brain norepinephrine arises here, and its axons ramify through virtually the entire neuraxis (neocortex, hippocampus, thalamus, cerebellum and spinal cord). Phasic LC firing sharpens attention to salient stimuli and gates cortical plasticity; tonic firing sets global arousal and helps orchestrate the sleep-wake cycle, stress responses and descending pain modulation. Neuromelanin pigment gives the fresh nucleus its characteristic blue-black color.
function.after: Paired noradrenergic cell groups in the dorsolateral rostral pons near the fourth ventricle. Their widespread ascending and descending projections modulate arousal, attention, stress responsiveness, learning and pain processing. Neuromelanin gives the adult human nucleus its characteristic dark pigmentation.

records.name: Pontine reticular formation (oral and caudal nuclei)

before.findings: Bilateral paramedian damage of the upper brainstem reticular core (basilar tip occlusion) abolishes arousal while the cortex itself is structurally spared — the classic brainstem (ascending reticular activating system) basis of coma.
Lesions of the pontine reticulospinal output bias antigravity tone; combined with PPRF damage this underlies the gaze-posture findings of dorsal pontine syndromes (Foville).

after.findings: Extensive bilateral upper brainstem reticular injury may impair consciousness; a broad pontine record does not establish coma from every bilateral lesion. Reticulospinal/postural effects depend on the affected networks and are not a defining mechanism of every Foville pattern.

records.name: Paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)

before.findings: A unilateral PPRF lesion abolishes rapid conjugate gaze toward the lesion; the eyes rest deviated away, and the intact contralateral PPRF drives gaze in the opposite direction. Conjugacy is preserved, so diplopia is absent.
before.note: Doll's-eye (oculocephalic) or cold-caloric testing may still move the eyes because the vestibulo-ocular reflex reaches the abducens nucleus directly, bypassing the PPRF.

before.findings: Combined PPRF/abducens and ipsilateral MLF lesions leave only one residual eye movement — contralateral abduction — producing the one-and-a-half syndrome of the dorsal pons.

after.findings: PPRF injury can impair conjugate saccades toward the lesion. With a sufficiently isolated PPRF lesion the VOR may be preserved because vestibular inputs also reach the abducens nucleus directly. Resting eye deviation and absence of diplopia are not obligatory.
Combined ipsilateral PPRF or abducens nuclear injury and ipsilateral MLF injury can leave contralateral abduction as the only horizontal version movement.

function.before: The horizontal conjugate gaze center: excitatory burst neurons here command ipsilateral saccades by driving the immediately adjacent abducens nucleus, whose motor neurons turn the ipsilateral eye out and whose internuclear neurons (crossing via the MLF) turn the contralateral eye in. Omnipause neurons within the PPRF gate burst onset; the frontal eye field and superior colliculus trigger it.
function.after: Pontine premotor region containing burst neurons important for horizontal saccades toward the ipsilateral side. It drives the ipsilateral abducens nucleus, whose internuclear neurons cross into the opposite MLF to activate medial-rectus motoneurons. Nearby omnipause neurons regulate saccades; the PPRF is not the final common pathway for every horizontal eye movement.

records.name: Trigeminal nerve (CN V) exit

before.findings: Root-zone lesions (CPA tumors, AICA aneurysms, demyelination) combine ipsilateral facial sensory loss with masseter weakness; vascular root compression at the entry zone underlies classic trigeminal neuralgia.
before.note: The root entry zone is the lateral benchmark of the midpontine level (lvl-pons-middle).

after.findings: A root-region lesion may impair ipsilateral facial sensation and/or mastication. Neurovascular compression can contribute to classical trigeminal neuralgia, but root dysfunction is not a fixed AICA infarct territory and examination patterns do not prove a single cause.

function.before: The large sensory root (portio major) and the smaller medial motor root of CN V emerge together from the mid-lateral pons, crossing the prepontine cistern to the trigeminal (gasserian) ganglion in Meckel cave; the root carries all facial and cranial somatosensory afferents and, in its motor root, the fibers to the muscles of mastication.
function.after: Large sensory and smaller motor CN V roots attach at the mid-lateral pons. The sensory root connects to trigeminal ganglion in Meckel cave; motor fibers bypass the ganglion to join V3. Much facial/cranial general sensation uses V, with additional small contributions from other cranial nerves.

records.name: Abducens nerve (CN VI) exit

before.findings: Horizontal diplopia worst at distance with failure of ipsilateral abduction; because of the long cisternal course, CN VI palsy is the classic false-localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure (stretching against the petrous ridge).

after.findings: Impaired ipsilateral abduction can cause horizontal diplopia. Raised intracranial pressure may affect the long intracranial nerve course as a false-localizing sign; other causes occur, and neighboring nucleus/PPRF injury instead affects conjugate gaze.

function.before: CN VI rootlets emerge ventromedially at the pontomedullary junction, between the pyramid and the middle cerebellar peduncle, then run the longest cisternal subarachnoid course in the posterior fossa, up the clival dura to Dorello's canal before entering the cavernous sinus and orbit.
function.after: CN VI rootlets emerge near the midline at the pontomedullary junction and ascend along the clivus toward Dorello canal, cavernous sinus and superior orbital fissure.

records.name: Facial nerve (CN VII) exit

before.findings: CPA masses (vestibular schwannoma, meningioma) or AICA infarcts compress/infarct CN VII at the exit zone, producing complete ipsilateral LMN facial weakness often with hearing loss and diminished corneal reflex.

after.findings: Mass, vascular or other regional disease may affect VII motor fibers and produce ipsilateral facial weakness. Hearing/balance changes or impaired blink can accompany neighboring nerve/brainstem involvement; the full combination and complete facial paralysis are not required.

records.name: Facial colliculus

function.before: The rounded bulge in the floor of the fourth ventricle over the abducens nucleus, produced by the internal genu of CN VII fibers sweeping dorsomedially around the nucleus before turning ventrally to exit; a landmark of the caudal pontine floor together with the neighboring median eminence and striae medullares.

records.name: Caudate nucleus, head

bloodSupply.before: Recurrent artery of Heubner (a medial lenticulostriate branch of the ACA) supplies the head and its adjacent anterior limb of the internal capsule; lateral lenticulostriate branches of the MCA supply the lateral part of the head. The venule-rich anterior perforated substance is the surgical landmark.
bloodSupply.after: Recurrent artery of Heubner/other ACA perforators and MCA lenticulostriate branches, with variable territories.

before.findings: Apathy, loss of spontaneous speech and movement, disinhibition and contralateral neglect, often mistaken for a frontal-lobe lesion; the head is supplied by Heubner's artery, so this accompanies ACA territory infarction.
before.vascular: Recurrent artery of Heubner (anterior cerebral artery)

before.findings: Selective loss of striatal medium spiny neurons begins in the caudate head and body, giving chorea, executive decline and psychiatric change with the characteristic boxcar appearance of the frontal horns on imaging.
before.note: Neurodegenerative (CAG repeat in HTT), not vascular

after.findings: Can produce abulia, executive/behavioral changes or language/attention deficits according to side and associated injury; a motor deficit often reflects adjacent capsule involvement.
Striatal degeneration, including caudate and putamen, contributes to motor, cognitive and psychiatric manifestations; caudate atrophy can enlarge the frontal horns.
after.note: Degenerative, not a focal vascular syndrome.

function.before: The anterior, bulging third of the C-shaped striatum, forming the lateral wall of the frontal horn and lying against the anterior limb of the internal capsule. It is the associative and limbic striatum: prefrontal, cingulate and orbitofrontal projections converge here before the striatopallidal loops select behaviour, and its dopaminergic input comes from the substantia nigra pars compacta.
function.after: The enlarged anterior caudate forms a bulge along the lateral wall of the frontal horn, medial to the anterior limb of the internal capsule. It participates in associative, oculomotor and motivational corticostriatal loops; functional territories overlap rather than dividing cleanly at the head/body boundary.

bloodSupply.before: Lateral lenticulostriate branches of the MCA, with additional supply from the anterior choroidal artery posteriorly; the subependymal and thalamostriate veins drain it into the internal cerebral vein.

function.before: The thin arched middle segment of the caudate, lying in the floor of the lateral ventricle body with the thalamostriate vein and stria terminalis along its medial edge and the internal capsule below. bloodSupply.before: Anterior choroidal artery (from the internal carotid) for the tail and the adjacent temporal horn choroid plexus; posteriorly the tail borders the thalamogeniculate branches of the PCA.

before.findings: Contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia — the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic radiation and the tail region fall together in the anterior choroidal territory; the tail lesion adds little clinically to the capsular deficit.

function.before: The thinnest, most posterior segment of the striatum, which arcs downward behind the thalamus into the roof of the temporal horn, ending at the amygdaloid complex. Because it carries the limbic-striatal transition, its tail provides a continuous anatomical bridge between the dorsal (sensorimotor) and ventral (limbic) striatum.

Temporal/visual association inputs contribute to caudate-tail networks; anatomical proximity to amygdala does not make it a continuous bridge to ventral striatum.

records.name: Putamen

bloodSupply.before: Lateral lenticulostriate branches of the MCA (the perforators that make the putamen the commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage); the inferior and posterior parts also receive anterior choroidal branches. The lateral lenticulostriate arteries pass through the putamen to reach the internal capsule.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly MCA lenticulostriate branches, with variable anterior choroidal/ACA contributions.

before.findings: Sudden contralateral hemiplegia and hemisensory loss with gaze deviation toward the lesion and, when large, depressed consciousness and transtentorial herniation — the classic deep hypertensive bleed from lenticulostriate rupture.
Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine depletes putamenal input, producing bradykinesia and rigidity; chronic dopamine replacement drives maladaptive putamenal plasticity and dyskinesias.
before.note: Neurodegenerative — the putamen is the imaging and surgical target (putaminal DBS/grafts)

before.findings: Small putamenal lenticulostriate infarcts or microhaemorrhages commonly involve the adjacent posterior limb of the internal capsule, giving a pure motor or sensorimotor lacunar syndrome.

after.findings: May cause contralateral weakness/sensory loss through adjacent capsule injury, with gaze or consciousness changes when extensive.
Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine alters striatal and wider basal-ganglia activity; the primary degenerating population is in SNc.
after.note: Common DBS targets are STN or GPi; this record is not a treatment recommendation.

function.before: The sensorimotor striatum — the large, somatotopically organized lateral division of the lentiform nucleus, separated from the caudate by the internal capsule and from the insula by the external capsule and claustrum. It receives topographic input from the primary motor and somatosensory cortices and, with the centromedian intralaminar nucleus, sets the gain of the direct and indirect pathways that release wanted and suppress unwanted movement.
function.after: The putamen is the lateral component of the lentiform nucleus and a major sensorimotor striatal input region. It lies lateral to pallidum, separated from the insula by external capsule, claustrum and extreme capsule. Its motor, associative and limbic territories overlap within corticostriatal networks.

records.name: Globus pallidus, external segment

bloodSupply.before: Lenticulostriate branches of the MCA for the upper two-thirds; anterior choroidal artery for the inferior and posterior part (the same territory that supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the optic radiation).
bloodSupply.after: MCA lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal supply, with variability.

before.findings: Focal or segmental dystonia after GPe/indirect-pathway lesions (stroke, anoxia, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation), reflecting loss of the STN brake and excess GPi output.

Carbon monoxide poisoning, manganese exposure, methanol and heroin pyrolysis selectively injure the globus pallidus, producing parkinsonism, dystonia and, in carbon monoxide cases, delayed encephalopathy after a lucid interval.
before.note: Toxic/metabolic rather than vascular

after.findings: Focal or bilateral pallidal damage can accompany movement disorders, but dystonia is not predicted reliably by a simple GPe-STN firing-rate chain.
Carbon monoxide and other hypoxic/toxic exposures can involve both pallidal segments and wider brain networks; patterns vary.
after.note: Avoid treating all toxins as selective GPe lesions.

function.before: The relay of the indirect pathway: it receives GABAergic striatal input and projects a tonic GABAergic brake onto the subthalamic nucleus, so it controls how strongly the STN excites the output nuclei. Loss of GPe output therefore disinhibits the STN and raises GPi firing — the mechanism by which pallidal lesions generate dystonia and by which the indirect pathway modulates movement.
function.after: GPe is the lateral pallidal segment, between putamen and GPi, separated by medullary laminae. It provides inhibitory projections to STN and other basal-ganglia targets and receives substantial excitatory STN input. The indirect-pathway teaching model captures only part of its recurrent circuitry.

before.findings: Lesioning or high-frequency stimulation of GPi relieves levodopa-induced dyskinesia and generalized dystonia and reduces rigidity and tremor, because silencing the output nucleus releases the motor thalamus — the clinical proof of the rate model of basal-ganglia output.

function.before: One of the two output nuclei of the basal ganglia and a tonically active inhibitor of the motor thalamus: because GPi neurons fire continuously, movement is produced by a phasic withdrawal of inhibition through the direct pathway and a phasic increase through the indirect pathway. Its axons leave as the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus (H2) to reach VA/VL through the thalamic fasciculus (H1), and the intralaminar centromedian nucleus is its second major target.
function.after: GPi is the medial pallidal segment next to the internal capsule and is a major GABAergic basal-ganglia output nucleus alongside SNr. Pallidothalamic axons travel via ansa lenticularis/lenticular fasciculus into the thalamic fasciculus; outputs also reach brainstem targets. Firing patterns and network timing are as relevant as mean rate.

bloodSupply.before: Anterior perforated substance: the recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) and the medial lenticulostriate branches of the MCA at the junction of the anterior and middle cerebral territories; venous drainage through the anterior cerebral and striate veins.

function.before: The limbic striatum at the junction of the caudate head, putamen and septal area (nucleus accumbens and fundus striati): it is where motivation becomes movement, receiving convergent prefrontal, hippocampal and amygdalar input and dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area. Its shell and core subdivisions serve reward prediction, incentive salience and the invigoration of goal-directed behaviour.
function.after: The ventral striatum includes nucleus accumbens and ventromedial caudate/putamen territories near the basal forebrain. It integrates cortical and limbic information with dopaminergic modulation in motivation, reinforcement learning and action selection. It overlaps the accumbens record rather than representing a separate encapsulated nucleus.

records.name: Nucleus accumbens

bloodSupply.before: The anterior perforated substance: the recurrent artery of Heubner (anterior cerebral artery) and the medial lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery meet here, which makes the accumbens the watershed of the two anterior territories. Venous drainage runs through the anterior cerebral and striate veins to the basal vein and the cavernous sinus.
bloodSupply.after: Variable ACA/Heubner and MCA basal perforator contributions; this schematic record is not an arterial boundary map.

before.findings: Repeated exposure to drugs of abuse produces lasting changes in accumbens dopamine transmission and medium spiny neuron plasticity that transform a hedonic 'liking' signal into pathological 'wanting' (incentive salience) and cue-driven relapse; the region is the shared anatomical target of opioids, psychostimulants, nicotine and alcohol.
before.note: Circuit-level (functional and preclinical literature), not a focal lesion syndrome

before.syndrome: Accumbens deep brain stimulation for refractory depression and OCD
before.findings: Chronic high-frequency stimulation of the nucleus accumbens/ventral capsule improves treatment-resistant depression and obsessive-compulsive symptoms in selected patients, evidence that the limbic striatum gates mood and compulsion as well as reward.
before.note: Investigational/selected therapy, not a spontaneous syndrome

before.findings: Small infarcts supply disinhibition, apathy or obsessive-compulsive behaviour and can unmask mania; they usually accompany an anterior cerebral artery infarct of the caudate head.
before.vascular: Recurrent artery of Heubner (anterior cerebral artery) or medial lenticulostriate arteries

after.findings: Human imaging and experimental work implicate accumbens-centered networks in reinforcement and incentive motivation; dopamine does not simply convert pleasure into craving.
Accumbens/ventral-capsule stimulation has been studied for refractory psychiatric disorders; indication, efficacy and approval differ by condition and jurisdiction.
after.note: Research/selected clinical context, not a general treatment claim.

function.before: The best-defined subregion of the ventral (limbic) striatum, sitting at the junction of the caudate head, putamen and septal area beneath the anterior limb of the internal capsule: its shell (medial, infralimbic) mediates the unconditioned, motivational response to reward through the extended amygdala, while its core (lateral, prelimbic) mediates cue-conditioned, goal-directed approach and the instrumental invigoration of behaviour. It is the anatomical convergence point where motivation becomes movement — the ventral counterpart of the dorsal striatum's direct/indirect pathway architecture, with the same medium spiny neuron composition and the same reliance on dopamine, but receiving limbic rather than sensorimotor cortex.
function.after: Nucleus accumbens occupies the ventral junction of caudate and putamen and is part of ventral striatum. Core/shell subdivisions participate in overlapping reward, motivational and learning circuits. Detailed rodent infralimbic/prelimbic terminology should not be treated as a one-to-one human cortical map.

records.name: Ventral pallidum

bloodSupply.before: The anterior perforated substance and the region of the anterior commissure: the recurrent artery of Heubner (anterior cerebral artery) and medial lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery, with the anterior choroidal artery reaching the region of the substantia innominata from behind. Venous drainage into the basal vein of Rosenthal.
bloodSupply.after: Variable basal perforating arteries from ACA/MCA and adjacent carotid-system branches; subregional territory is not independently mapped here.

before.syndrome: Hedonic deficit and blunted reward (ventral pallidum lesion)
before.findings: Lesions of the ventral pallidum abolish the normal orofacial 'liking' reactions to sweet taste without changing the ability to detect it, and produce a profound loss of goal-directed drive — the strongest causal evidence that the ventral pallidum carries the hedonic component of reward.
before.note: Lesion and animal literature; in humans the region is affected by stroke of the anterior perforated substance and by neurodegeneration

before.findings: Infarcts here form part of the Heubner/medial lenticulostriate territory and cause apathy, disinhibition or obsessive-compulsive behaviour, adding a motivational deficit to the motor findings of an anterior cerebral artery stroke.
before.vascular: Recurrent artery of Heubner or medial lenticulostriate arteries

before.syndrome: Ventral pallidum in the extended amygdala and addiction circuitry
before.findings: The ventral pallidum is a relay of the extended amygdala, so its plasticity contributes to withdrawal-related negative affect and to cue-induced relapse after abstinence.
before.note: Circuit-level observation rather than a focal syndrome

after.findings: Injury involving this region may contribute to reduced motivation or behavioral change, but a unique human ventral-pallidal lesion syndrome is not established.
Animal manipulations support reward/hedonic functions; they do not establish that a focal human lesion abolishes all pleasure.
after.note: Species and experimental manipulation must be distinguished from clinical evidence.

function.before: The limbic counterpart of the dorsal pallidal segments, lying in the substantia innominata beneath the anterior commissure and continuous with the subcommissural part of the globus pallidus: it is the principal output nucleus of the ventral striatopallidal system, receiving GABAergic input from the accumbens shell and core and relaying it — through a thalamic route to the mediodorsal nucleus and cortex, and through a descending route to the lateral hypothalamus and brainstem — into motivated behaviour. Its neurons encode hedonic 'liking' reactions (the taste-reactivity substrate) and, with the mediodorsal thalamus, the reward-prediction signal that keeps behaviour directed at a goal.
function.after: The ventral pallidum is a basal-forebrain pallidal region below the anterior commissure, continuous with ventral pallidal territories. It receives ventral-striatal input and participates in reward, motivation and action through thalamic, hypothalamic and midbrain connections. Findings about taste-reactivity hotspots largely derive from animal experiments.
