records.name: Claustrum

bloodSupply.before: Insular (M2) branches of the middle cerebral artery and the lateral lenticulostriate arteries reach the claustrum and the adjacent external/extreme capsules; the region is a common site of involvement in MCA insular infarction and in lenticulostriate haemorrhage.
bloodSupply.after: Predominantly MCA insular/deep cortical branches; precise subregional supply varies.

before.syndrome: Claustrum and the loss of consciousness (case report literature)
before.findings: A small bilateral claustral lesion following status epilepticus and a small unilateral lesion in a patient who abruptly lost consciousness have been reported as evidence that the claustrum coordinates the cortical networks required for conscious awareness — a provocative but single-case observation.
before.note: Case-report level evidence; not a vascular syndrome

before.findings: The insula and claustrum are infarcted in the majority of MCA occlusions because the M2 branches arise first; the result is usually a large MCA syndrome with autonomic instability rather than an isolated claustral deficit.
Seizures arising in the operculo-insular/claustral region cause unpleasant throat and chest sensations, dyspnoea, laryngeal constriction and autonomic signs, often misdiagnosed as panic attacks.
before.note: Epileptic rather than vascular; the claustrum is part of the ictal network

after.findings: Infarction, inflammatory injury or seizure-associated changes may involve claustrum with adjacent insula/capsules. There is no unique, validated claustrum-only consciousness syndrome.
Throat/visceral symptoms can occur in operculo-insular networks; they should not be attributed uniquely to claustrum.

efferent: Reciprocal, topographically organized claustrocortical projections returning to the same cortical areas (the substrate of the proposed binding function)

function.before: A thin, sheet-like band of deep gray matter between the putamen medially and the insular cortex laterally, separated from the putamen by the external capsule and from the insula by the extreme capsule. Although classically grouped with the basal ganglia, it is a cortico-cortical hub: it receives an exceptionally broad projection from almost every cortical area and returns a topographically organized one, and its neurons respond to the conjunction of stimuli across modalities. Current views assign it a role in the binding and salience of multimodal information and in the coordination of cortical networks (including the slow-wave oscillation between claustrum and cortex), which is why minute bilateral lesions have been reported to disrupt consciousness.
function.after: The claustrum is a thin gray-matter sheet between external capsule medially and extreme capsule laterally, deep to insular cortex. It has extensive reciprocal cortical connections and is anatomically adjacent to, but not a standard component of, the motor basal-ganglia circuit. Its precise contribution to attention, integration and consciousness remains under investigation.

records.name: Cerebral cortex (context envelope)

bloodSupply.before: Three territories meet on the cortex: ACA (medial surface, callosomarginal branch), MCA (lateral convexity and insula) and PCA (medial occipital and inferior temporal). The ACA/MCA border runs along the superior convexity and the MCA/PCA border along the lateral occipital surface — both are watershed strips that infarct with systemic hypotension.
bloodSupply.after: ACA supplies much of medial frontal/anterior parietal cortex, MCA most lateral convexity and insula, and PCA medial occipital/inferomedial temporal cortex. Borders and collateral flow vary.

before.findings: Bilateral, roughly symmetric weakness or sensory loss of the proximal limb with relative sparing of the hand and face, after a hypotensive episode; the lesion straddles the ACA/MCA border on the convexity or the MCA/PCA border posteriorly.
before.vascular: ACA/MCA or MCA/PCA border zone (internal watershed along the corona radiata is the deep variant)

before.findings: Global hypoxic-ischaemic injury destroys the metabolically most demanding middle cortical layers, giving T1-hyperintense ribbon-like cortical signal with laminar (pseudolaminar) necrosis on MRI.
before.note: Hypoxic-ischaemic (cardiac arrest, prolonged hypotension) rather than territorial infarction

before.findings: Cortical/subcortical bleeding (cerebral amyloid angiopathy in the elderly, arteriovenous malformation in the young) causes focal cortical deficits with headache and, often, seizure — the counterpart of the deep hypertensive haemorrhage of the basal ganglia.
before.note: Amyloid angiopathy spares the deep perforator territories, which is why lobar bleeds favour the cortex

after.findings: Deficits depend on region and network involvement; aphasia, neglect, field loss, seizures or discriminative sensory deficits may occur.
ACA-MCA or MCA-PCA border-zone injury can follow impaired perfusion; symptoms vary with location and extent.

function.before: The 2.5–4 mm laminated gray-matter ribbon folded over the cerebral white matter — the substrate of conscious perception, voluntary action, language, memory and social behaviour. Its six layers segregate the input (granular layer IV), the local processing (II/III) and the output (V/VI) of every cortical area. In this atlas the ribbon is a context envelope, not a nucleus: the six lobes and the named gyri carry the functional detail.
function.after: The folded gray matter of the cerebral hemispheres supports perception, action, language, cognition and memory in interacting networks. Most is six-layered neocortex; hippocampal and olfactory allocortex have different lamination. Cortical thickness and areal boundaries vary across regions and individuals.

records.name: Frontal lobe

bloodSupply.before: MCA (superior division) supplies the lateral convexity, including Broca's area and most of the motor strip; ACA (pericallosal and callosomarginal branches) supplies the medial surface, the supplementary motor area and the leg representation at the vertex; the recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) and the medial lenticulostriate branches supply the adjoining caudate head and anterior limb of the internal capsule.
bloodSupply.after: MCA supplies most lateral frontal cortex; ACA supplies much of the medial frontal surface and a superior strip. Territories vary.

before.findings: Contralateral face-and-arm-predominant weakness with gaze deviation toward the lesion, and (dominant hemisphere) non-fluent Broca aphasia with preserved comprehension; the leg is spared because the ACA territory supplies the medial motor strip.
Contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss with abulia, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex and mutism when the supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate are involved.
Dorsolateral lesions cause apathy, abulia and executive failure with perseveration; orbitomedial lesions cause disinhibition, inappropriate jocularity and impaired social judgement.
before.note: Degenerative (frontotemporal dementia), traumatic or tumour-related rather than vascular in most cases

after.findings: May cause contralateral face/arm-predominant weakness and dominant-hemisphere nonfluent aphasia; leg involvement varies with lesion extent.
May cause reduced initiation or abulia; involvement of paracentral/SMA regions can add leg-predominant weakness or reduced speech.
Executive, motivational or behavioral changes depend on lesion site and interacting networks; no single frontal-lobe syndrome is obligatory.

Posterior association cortex through the superior longitudinal fasciculus and the uncinate fasciculus
Dopaminergic VTA/SNc and noradrenergic/cholinergic ascending systems
efferent: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres from the precentral gyrus, through the corona radiata, genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule
Frontopontine fibres of the corticopontine tract (medial third of the crus cerebri)

function.before: The largest lobe, and the one that turns intention into action: the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) and the premotor/supplementary motor areas programme movement, the frontal eye fields direct gaze, Broca's area generates speech, and the dorsolateral, orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortices hold working memory, inhibit impulses and evaluate reward. It also contains the anterior portion of the lateral ventricle and the frontopontine fibres on their way to the cerebellum.
function.after: The frontal lobe lies anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Motor/premotor regions support action and gaze, while prefrontal and cingulate networks contribute to executive control, motivation, social judgment and language in the dominant hemisphere.

records.name: Parietal lobe

bloodSupply.before: MCA inferior division supplies the angular and supramarginal gyri and the posterior temporal-parietal junction; MCA superior division supplies the postcentral gyrus and superior parietal lobule; PCA (parieto-occipital and splenial branches) supplies the precuneus and the medial parietal surface.
bloodSupply.after: MCA supplies most lateral parietal cortex; ACA supplies anterior medial parietal/paracentral cortex and PCA more posterior medial areas. The precuneus may span ACA/PCA territories.

before.findings: Fluent (Wernicke-type) aphasia with poor comprehension and repetition, alexia and acalculia on the left; hemispatial neglect, anosognosia and dressing apraxia on the right.
Contralateral hemisensory loss with preserved crude touch but lost graphaesthesia, stereognosis and two-point discrimination; sensory ataxia of the hand without weakness.
before.vascular: MCA superior division (or a small cortical branch infarct)

before.findings: Dominant angular gyrus lesion: finger agnosia, agraphia, acalculia and right-left disorientation — a disconnection syndrome of the dominant parietal lobe.

after.findings: Right-predominant attention-network injury can produce left neglect; dominant parietal injury can impair praxis, calculation, writing or language, depending on extent.
Can impair contralateral discriminative touch, proprioception and cortical sensory tasks; crude sensation is not invariably preserved.
after.vascular: MCA lateral or ACA medial sensorimotor branches

after.findings: Acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation may occur with dominant parietal network injury; an isolated angular-gyrus lesion is not the only explanation.

afferent: VPL/VPM thalamocortical radiations to the postcentral gyrus (somatotopic: leg medial over the hemisphere, face lateral)
Pulvinar and lateral posterior nucleus (visuospatial and associative input)
Corticocortical input from visual, auditory and premotor areas via the superior longitudinal fasciculus
efferent: Corticospinal and corticopontine fibres from the postcentral and superior parietal cortex through the corona radiata
Superior longitudinal fasciculus to the frontal lobe; cingulum to the posterior cingulate

afferent: VPL/VPM somatosensory thalamocortical input to postcentral cortex
Visual, auditory, frontal and association thalamic inputs to parietal networks
efferent: Reciprocal frontal/temporal/occipital and callosal connections

function.before: The sensory-associative lobe: the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) maps the contralateral body surface, the superior parietal lobule and precuneus build the body schema and guide visually directed reaching, and the supramarginal and angular gyri at the temporoparietal junction support spatial attention, praxis and (on the left) language comprehension. It is the principal cortical bridge between what is sensed and what is done.
function.after: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, above the lateral temporal region and anterior to the occipital boundary. Postcentral cortex processes somatic input, while superior/inferior parietal and medial parietal networks contribute to body representation, attention, praxis and language-related functions.

records.name: Temporal lobe

bloodSupply.before: MCA inferior division supplies the lateral temporal convexity (superior and middle temporal gyri); PCA (temporal and hippocampal branches) supplies the medial temporal lobe, inferior temporal gyrus and posterior hippocampus; the anterior choroidal artery (from the internal carotid) supplies the amygdala, hippocampal head and temporal horn choroid plexus.
bloodSupply.after: MCA supplies most lateral temporal cortex; PCA supplies much inferomedial temporal cortex/hippocampal formation. Anterior choroidal contributions to anterior medial structures are variable.

before.syndrome: MCA inferior-division infarct with temporal involvement
before.findings: Wernicke aphasia (dominant hemisphere) with contralateral superior quadrantanopia from Meyer-loop damage, plus a dense sensory deficit if the parietal territory is included.

before.syndrome: PCA territory infarct of the medial temporal lobe
before.findings: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with memory impairment; bilateral PCA infarcts produce cortical blindness and a severe amnestic state (the hippocampus is in the PCA territory).
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (temporal and hippocampal branches)

before.findings: Hippocampal sclerosis produces stereotyped auras (déjà vu, epigastric rising sensation, fear), automatisms and impaired awareness; the temporal lobe is the commonest site of focal epilepsy in adults.
before.note: Sclerosis rather than stroke — but the same medial temporal structures are involved and the temporal horn dilates

after.findings: May cause fluent aphasia; injury to temporal optic radiations may add contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
Memory impairment depends on laterality, bilaterality and network extent; a visual field defect requires involvement of visual pathways.
after.vascular: PCA/anterior choroidal territories or nonvascular causes

after.findings: May produce experiential or autonomic auras, automatisms and impaired awareness; these features are not specific to one nucleus.

afferent: MGN via the auditory radiations to Heschl's gyrus
Perirhinal/entorhinal cortex fed by unimodal and polymodal association areas; amygdala input from the thalamus and brainstem
LGN via the optic radiation (Meyer loop) to the inferior visual field representation
efferent: Hippocampus to the fornix; amygdala to the stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway
Wernicke's area to the inferior frontal lobe via the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus; uncinate fasciculus to the orbitofrontal cortex
Corticopontine (temporopontine) fibres through the lateral third of the crus cerebri

afferent: MGN auditory radiation to primary auditory cortex
Association-cortical inputs to temporal visual, language and medial temporal networks
efferent: Association pathways to frontal/parietal/occipital regions
Hippocampal outputs through fornix/entorhinal routes and amygdalar outputs to cortical/subcortical targets

function.before: Hearing, language comprehension, memory and emotion in one lobe: primary auditory cortex on the superior temporal plane (Heschl's gyrus and planum temporale), Wernicke's area posteriorly, the fusiform and inferior temporal cortex for visual object and face recognition, and the medial temporal allocortex (hippocampus, amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus) for memory encoding and threat evaluation. Its white matter carries Meyer's loop of the optic radiation into the temporal pole.
function.after: The temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus. Superior temporal cortex participates in hearing and language networks, ventral occipitotemporal cortex in object/face recognition, and medial temporal structures in memory and emotion. Temporal optic-radiation fibres, including Meyer's loop, convey contralateral superior visual-field information.

records.name: Occipital lobe

bloodSupply.before: PCA — calcarine and parieto-occipital branches supply the medial occipital surface and the visual cortex; the occipital pole usually has a dual supply, receiving a variable contribution from the MCA as well, which is why macular vision is often spared in PCA infarction.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly PCA calcarine/parieto-occipital branches, with variable MCA contributions to lateral/polar cortex and collateral flow.

before.findings: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (dual blood supply of the occipital pole); left-sided lesions that also involve the splenium give alexia without agraphia, and involvement of the pulvinar or thalamus adds hemi-sensory loss.
Bilateral occipital infarction causes blindness that the patient denies, with confabulated visual descriptions — damage to the visual cortex with preserved association cortex.
before.vascular: Bilateral posterior cerebral arteries (or basilar tip embolism)

before.syndrome: Visual field defect from optic-radiation lesions
before.findings: Incongruous quadrantanopia from a retrolenticular/temporal lesion versus a congruent hemianopia from a complete radiation or occipital lesion — a distinction that locates the damage anterior or posterior in the geniculostriate pathway.
before.vascular: Anterior choroidal artery (retrolenticular) or MCA/PCA branches along the radiation

after.findings: Unilateral visual-cortex injury may cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia or a smaller homonymous defect; macular sparing is possible, not obligatory.
May cause cortical blindness with preserved pupillary light responses. Some patients have denial/confabulation (Anton syndrome), but this is not universal.
A classic pattern follows dominant (usually left) occipital plus splenial injury, disconnecting visual input from language networks.

afferent: LGN via the optic radiations (dorsal bundle through the parietal lobe, Meyer loop through the temporal lobe)
Pulvinar and lateral posterior nucleus (visual association feedback)
Callosal fibres connecting the two occipital poles along the vertical meridian representation
efferent: Dorsal stream to the parietal lobe (where/how) and ventral stream to the temporal lobe (what), through the superior and inferior longitudinal fasciculi
Corticopontine (occipitopontine) fibres; corticothalamic feedback to the LGN and pulvinar

afferent: LGN via optic radiation to V1
Reciprocal extrastriate, pulvinar and callosal connections
efferent: Interconnected dorsal parietal and ventral temporal visual networks
Corticothalamic and other descending visual projections

function.before: The visual cortex: primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex) is wrapped around the calcarine fissure with a precise retinotopic map in which the macula occupies a disproportionate posterior share, and the surrounding extrastriate areas (V2–V5) extract form, colour, motion and depth. It is the cortical terminus of the geniculostriate pathway and the target of the optic radiations.
function.after: The occipital lobe contains primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus and multiple extrastriate areas. V1 maps the contralateral visual hemifield; interconnected visual association regions process form, color, motion and spatial relationships.

records.name: Insula

bloodSupply.before: MCA — insular (M2) branches of both the superior and inferior divisions course over its surface; the lateral lenticulostriate arteries arise at the level of the insular apex before turning into the basal ganglia, so insular infarction and deep lacunar infarction share a source.
bloodSupply.after: MCA insular (M2) branches. Deep lenticulostriate branches usually arise from proximal MCA and supply different deep territories; insular and basal-ganglia supply should not be equated.

before.findings: The insula is infarcted in nearly every MCA occlusion because its branches arise first; lesions of the right insula are associated with autonomic instability, arrhythmia and sudden death, and insular strokes impair taste and interoceptive awareness.
Damage to the insula disrupts the conscious urge to smoke and can abolish addiction in some patients; the same region is activated by visceral and emotional stimuli.
before.note: Lesion-observation and functional-imaging literature, not a vascular syndrome

after.findings: May affect taste, somatic/visceral awareness, speech or autonomic regulation. Isolated deficits and laterality effects are variable.
Can include throat discomfort, somatic sensations or autonomic symptoms; clinical semiology alone does not prove insular onset.

afferent: Thalamic relay nuclei (VPMpc for taste; VMpo and posterior thalamus for interoception and pain affect)
Amygdala, orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex (salience and emotional input)
Brainstem and hypothalamic autonomic afferents via the parabrachial nucleus
efferent: Autonomic effector columns: insular efferents to the lateral hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, nucleus of the solitary tract and the vagal/dorsal motor nuclei
Cortical efferents to the anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal cortex and frontal operculum

afferent: Thalamic somatosensory/gustatory and association inputs
Reciprocal anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal, temporal and amygdalar connections
efferent: Cortical salience/interoceptive networks
Connections with hypothalamic and brainstem autonomic systems

function.before: The buried fifth lobe in the floor of the sylvian fissure: the posterior granular insula is primary interoceptive cortex (visceral sensation, temperature, pain affect), while the anterior agranular insula is a salience hub linking autonomic state, taste, emotion and decision-making. It sits directly over the putamen and is the surface across which the MCA's insular branches and the lenticulostriate arteries run.
function.after: The insula is buried in the lateral sulcus and covered by frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. Its long/short gyri and anterior-posterior cytoarchitectural gradient participate in taste, somatic/visceral sensation, salience, emotion and autonomic regulation within wider networks.

records.name: Limbic lobe

bloodSupply.before: ACA (pericallosal/callosomarginal) supplies the subcallosal and anterior cingulate cortex; PCA (splenial, posterior pericallosal, temporal and hippocampal branches) supplies the posterior cingulate, retrosplenial, parahippocampal and hippocampal cortices; the anterior choroidal artery supplies the uncal and amygdalar end.
bloodSupply.after: ACA supplies much anterior cingulate/subcallosal cortex; PCA contributes posterior cingulate/retrosplenial and inferomedial temporal supply. Anterior medial temporal supply varies.

before.findings: Subacute short-term memory loss, temporal-lobe seizures, behavioural change and medial temporal FLAIR signal — the limbic ring is inflamed, most often autoimmunologically (anti-LGI1, anti-NMDAR) or as a paraneoplastic syndrome.
before.note: Autoimmune/paraneoplastic — the imaging target is the limbic lobe itself

before.syndrome: PCA infarct involving the posterior limbic ring
before.findings: Infarction of the posterior cingulate, retrosplenial and parahippocampal cortex adds memory loss to the hemianopia of PCA occlusion.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (splenial and temporal branches)

before.findings: Bilateral temporal-limbic destruction (herpes encephalitis, trauma, frontotemporal dementia) produces hyperorality, hypersexuality, visual agnosia and emotional blunting — the classic proof that the limbic ring gates affect and object recognition.
before.note: Structural/infectious rather than vascular

after.findings: Can cause subacute memory disturbance, seizures and behavioral changes, often with medial temporal involvement; MRI findings and antibody associations vary.
Posterior medial or medial temporal lesions may impair memory or orientation depending on extent.

afferent: Anterior and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei (cingulate cortex); entorhinal cortex from unimodal and polymodal association areas
Amygdala and septal nuclei via the stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway
efferent: Cingulum and fornix: cingulate/parahippocampal cortex interconnects the septal area, entorhinal cortex and hippocampal formation, and the fornix carries hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies and septal region
Cingulate projections to the striatum and to the pontine nuclei (limbic-motor interface)

afferent: Association cortex and anterior/MD thalamic inputs, varying by subregion
Amygdalar and hippocampal/parahippocampal network connections
efferent: Cingulum and other association connections between medial cortical regions
Hippocampal output via fornix and cortical routes; cortical/subcortical motivational connections

function.before: Broca's grand lobe limbique: the ring of allocortical and paralimbic cortex — subcallosal area, cingulate and parahippocampal gyri and the hippocampal formation — that encircles the corpus callosum and the diencephalon. It is defined morphologically as a rim rather than a function, and it is the cortical component of the circuit (Papez) that links emotion, olfaction and memory to the hypothalamus.
function.after: The traditional limbic lobe is a morphological grouping of medial cortical regions including cingulate and parahippocampal cortex. These areas participate in distributed memory, motivational and affective networks; the term does not define a single isolated emotion system.

records.name: Cingulate gyrus

bloodSupply.before: ACA — pericallosal and callosomarginal branches supply the anterior and mid cingulate gyrus; PCA — splenial and posterior pericallosal branches supply the posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex. This ACA/PCA junction on the cingulate is a classic watershed zone in the sagittal plane.
bloodSupply.after: ACA branches supply much anterior/midcingulate cortex; PCA supplies posterior cingulate/retrosplenial regions, with variable overlap.

before.findings: Akinetic mutism or abulia with urinary incontinence, grasp reflex and mutism when the supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate are infarcted bilaterally; unilateral lesions cause contralateral leg weakness with apathy.
Amnesia and topographical disorientation; the retrosplenial cortex is an early metabolic casualty in Alzheimer disease and a target of limbic encephalitis.

before.syndrome: Cingulotomy for intractable pain or OCD
before.findings: Stereotactic lesions of the anterior cingulate relieve the affective distress of chronic pain and improve refractory obsessive-compulsive symptoms, with apathy and disinhibition as the main adverse effects.
before.note: Lesion therapy — the clinical proof that the cingulate encodes the suffering component of pain

after.findings: Can contribute to abulia; extensive bilateral damage may produce akinetic mutism. Limb weakness requires involvement of motor pathways.
May impair episodic memory or topographical orientation.

afferent: Anterior thalamic nucleus (mammillothalamic relay) to the anterior cingulate; mediodorsal and midline thalamic nuclei
Amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex, insula and posterior cingulate via the cingulum
efferent: Cingulum to the hippocampal formation and parahippocampal/entorhinal cortex
Corticostriate projections to the ventral striatum and caudate; corticospinal-adjacent projections to the pontine nuclei (limbic-motor interface)
Autonomic projections to the periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus and brainstem nuclei

afferent: Anterior and association thalamic inputs
Frontal, parietal, medial temporal, insular and amygdalar connections
efferent: Cingulum/association projections to frontal, medial parietal and parahippocampal regions
Subcortical motivational, motor and autonomic network projections, varying by subregion

function.before: The arch of cortex above the corpus callosum, divided into an anterior (affective, rostral/ventral) and a mid-posterior (cognitive, dorsal) subdivision: the dorsal midcingulate monitors conflict and errors and drives response selection, while the rostral anterior cingulate regulates emotion, pain affect and autonomic tone. It is the cortical hub of the Papez circuit and carries the cingulum bundle in its white matter.
function.after: The cingulate gyrus arches above the corpus callosum and continues posteriorly toward the parahippocampal region. Anterior/midcingulate regions contribute to motivation, control, pain affect and action; posterior cingulate/retrosplenial regions participate in memory and spatial/contextual processing.

records.name: Parahippocampal gyrus

bloodSupply.before: PCA — hippocampal and temporal branches of the posterior cerebral artery supply the parahippocampal gyrus and the posterior hippocampal formation; the anterior (uncal) end is supplied by the anterior choroidal artery from the internal carotid.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly PCA temporal branches, with variable anterior choroidal and other anterior contributions.

before.syndrome: PCA infarct of the medial temporal lobe
before.findings: Amnesia (entorhinal/hippocampal damage) with contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia from Meyer-loop involvement; bilateral infarcts cause a persistent amnestic syndrome.
Bilateral but asymmetric necrosis of the medial temporal and inferior frontal cortex with fever, headache, seizures and profound amnesia — the classic infectious lesion of the limbic ring.
before.note: Infectious (HSV-1 via the olfactory route); treated with aciclovir

before.findings: Neurofibrillary pathology begins in the entorhinal cortex and spreads through the hippocampal circuit to the posterior cingulate and neocortex — the anatomical reason episodic memory fails first.
before.note: Neurodegenerative staging (Braak), not vascular

after.findings: May impair memory or scene/context recognition; associated field loss requires visual-pathway involvement.
Medial temporal injury can cause memory impairment and seizures; infection and autoimmunity are among the possible causes.

afferent: Perirhinal and postrhinal cortex from unimodal and polymodal association areas of all four lobes
Amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex; posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex via the cingulum
efferent: Perforant path from the entorhinal cortex to the dentate gyrus and hippocampal CA fields (the first leg of the trisynaptic circuit)
Cingulum to the posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex; reciprocal projections back to the association cortices

afferent: Perirhinal and multimodal association-cortical inputs
Posterior cingulate/retrosplenial, entorhinal and amygdalar connections
efferent: Entorhinal pathways to hippocampal formation and reciprocal cortical return
Cingulum/association connections to medial and lateral association cortex

contextNote.after: A broad cortical surface/concept label on the derived hemisphere ribbon; the displayed surface does not independently trace this lobe/gyrus boundary or establish a cytoarchitectural parcel. Named level membership is teaching/navigation metadata and has not been validated as a literal intersection of every displayed transverse section. function.before: The medial temporal gateway to the hippocampal formation: its anterior part is the entorhinal cortex (Brodmann 28/34), which receives the convergent output of every association area and funnels it through the perforant path into the dentate gyrus, while the posterior part (with the perirhinal and postrhinal cortex) encodes scenes, contexts and object familiarity. It is the cortical interface between neocortex and hippocampus — and therefore the epicentre of early Alzheimer pathology.
function.after: This medial temporal gyrus lies medial to the collateral/rhinal sulcus and is continuous with the cingulate isthmus posteriorly. Its anterior entorhinal/perirhinal regions and posterior parahippocampal cortex link association cortex with hippocampal memory networks; the boundaries of these cortical areas do not coincide with the whole gyrus.

records.name: Planum temporale

bloodSupply.before: MCA inferior division — the posterior temporal and angular branches supply the superior temporal plane; the posterior extremity borders the PCA territory, and the deep plane territory is reached by the temporo-occipital branches.
bloodSupply.after: Predominantly MCA temporal/insular branches; arterial patterns vary.

before.findings: Destruction of the posterior superior temporal plane and adjacent superior temporal gyrus produces fluent but empty speech with impaired comprehension and repetition, with anosognosia for the deficit — the classic receptive aphasia.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, inferior (posterior temporal) division

before.findings: Loss or reversal of the normal leftward planum temporale asymmetry has been reported in developmental dyslexia and in some language-impaired populations.
before.note: Developmental structural association — controversial and not a lesion syndrome

before.findings: Bilateral planum temporale lesions disconnect Heschl's gyri from Wernicke's area: hearing is intact but spoken words cannot be recognized.
before.note: Disconnection syndrome of the superior temporal plane

after.findings: Can impair recognition or analysis of speech or other sounds; bilateral and dominant-hemisphere lesions may produce different patterns.
Aphasia depends on dominant temporal/parietal network involvement; the planum temporale is not identical to Wernicke's area.

afferent: Heschl's gyrus and the MGN via the auditory radiations (tonotopic input)
Corticocortical input from the adjacent superior temporal gyrus and the inferior parietal lobule
efferent: Arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus to the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area) and to the inferior parietal lobule
Corticothalamic feedback to the MGN and brachium of the inferior colliculus

afferent: Primary and surrounding auditory cortex
Temporal/parietal association and interhemispheric connections
efferent: Reciprocal superior temporal/inferior parietal and frontal auditory-language networks
Descending corticothalamic auditory modulation

contextNote.after: A broad cortical surface/concept label on the derived hemisphere ribbon; the displayed surface does not independently trace this lobe/gyrus boundary or establish a cytoarchitectural parcel. function.before: The triangular expanse of superior temporal plane cortex posterior to Heschl's gyrus — the core auditory association area that computes spectrotemporal patterns and, on the left, the anatomical substrate of Wernicke's area. Its leftward size asymmetry is one of the best-documented structural asymmetries of the human brain and the classic anatomical correlate of language lateralization.
function.after: The planum temporale is the superior temporal surface posterior to Heschl's gyri. It participates in auditory association and auditory-motor/language networks. Population-level asymmetry does not establish an individual's language dominance or diagnose dyslexia.

records.name: Primary visual cortex (V1)

bloodSupply.before: Posterior cerebral artery — the calcarine branch (with a parieto-occipital contribution to the cuneus). The occipital pole usually has a dual supply from PCA and MCA collaterals, which is why PCA occlusion spares macular vision; bilateral PCA infarction destroys the calcarine cortex on both sides and produces cortical blindness.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly PCA calcarine branches; occipital-pole collateral supply from MCA/PCA varies. Macular sparing is neither obligatory nor unique to cortical lesions.

before.syndrome: PCA infarct with homonymous hemianopia and macular sparing
before.findings: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia that spares central (macular) vision because the occipital pole has a dual PCA/MCA supply, whereas the anterior calcarine cortex — carrying the monocular temporal crescent — is infarcted only by PCA occlusion.
Bilateral V1 destruction causes total loss of vision with denial of blindness and confabulated visual descriptions; the pupils and optokinetic responses remain normal, proving the lesion is cortical.
before.vascular: Bilateral posterior cerebral arteries or basilar-tip embolism

before.syndrome: Cortical visual impairment of the preterm infant
before.findings: Periventricular leukomalacia involving the optic radiations and striate cortex produces visual impairment out of proportion to the ocular examination, with preserved pupillary responses.
before.note: Ischaemic white-matter injury of prematurity rather than territorial infarction

after.findings: Unilateral V1 injury can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, quadrantanopia or scotoma according to extent; central vision may be spared.

Bilateral primary visual-cortex injury may cause cortical blindness with preserved pupillary light reflexes. Denial/confabulation can occur; optokinetic nystagmus may be absent or impaired, and normal pupils alone do not prove the lesion location.

Corticocortical feedback from V2, V3, V4/MT and the pulvinar/lateral posterior nucleus
Callosal fibres along the vertical meridian representation, connecting the two occipital poles
efferent: V2 and V3 (the dorsal and ventral streams begin here: MT/parietal 'where' versus V4/temporal 'what')

function.before: Primary visual cortex — the striate cortex of Brodmann area 17, wrapped around the banks of the calcarine fissure on the medial occipital surface and reaching the occipital pole with the macular representation. It receives the geniculostriate projection from the lateral geniculate nucleus as a precise retinotopic map (the macula occupies a disproportionate posterior share, the monocular temporal crescent the anterior-most part), and it is the first cortical stage of form, orientation and spatial-frequency analysis — layer IVc receives the magno/parvo input, and the stripe of Gennari marks the line of Baillarger that gives the cortex its name.
function.after: V1 (striate cortex, approximately Brodmann area 17) lies along the banks of the calcarine sulcus. It receives LGN input and represents the contralateral visual hemifield, with central vision disproportionately represented near the occipital pole. Upper-bank cortex represents lower visual field and lower-bank cortex upper visual field.

records.name: Secondary visual cortex (V2)

bloodSupply.before: Posterior cerebral artery — parieto-occipital and calcarine branches supply the medial prestriate cortex; the lateral occipital branches reach the lateral prestriate surface, and the MCA/PCA border zone runs along the lateral occipital convexity (a watershed strip).
bloodSupply.after: Mainly PCA occipital branches, with variable MCA/PCA border territory laterally.

before.syndrome: PCA infarct with preserved V1 but damaged prestriate cortex
before.findings: Lesions that spare the calcarine cortex but involve prestriate cortex leave elementary vision (acuity, fields) relatively intact while producing visual agnosia for form, colour or motion — the dissociation that defines the association cortices.

Bilateral ventral occipitotemporal lesions abolish colour perception while luminance vision is preserved — a striking demonstration that colour is computed after V1, downstream of the V2 thin stripes.
before.vascular: Bilateral posterior cerebral artery (ventral occipitotemporal branches)

before.findings: Bilateral lesions of the human MT/V5 complex cause the loss of visual motion perception — moving objects appear to jump — while static vision is retained.
before.note: Rare focal lesion or bilateral PCA infarction; the dorsal-stream counterpart of achromatopsia

after.findings: Occipital/occipitotemporal association injury can impair recognition, color or motion analysis, depending on the network; a particular syndrome is not specific to V2 alone.

function.before: The first visual association area, wrapped around V1 on the medial and lateral occipital surface (Brodmann 18). It is the site of the thick-pale-thin cytochrome-oxidase stripe system: the thick stripes project to MT/V5 for motion, the thin stripes to V4 for colour, and the pale interstripes carry form and depth — the anatomical reason the dorsal 'where/how' and ventral 'what' streams separate so early. V2 also completes the representation of the vertical meridian and the far periphery that V1 leaves incomplete, and it is the cortical source of the visual filling-in that makes a physiological blind spot imperceptible.
function.after: V2 is an extrastriate visual area adjoining V1 and is often associated with parts of Brodmann area 18; this is an approximate correspondence, not an exact parcellation. It contributes to processing contours, binocular relationships, form, color and motion through interconnected visual networks.

records.name: Primary auditory cortex (A1)

bloodSupply.before: Middle cerebral artery, inferior (temporopolar/posterior temporal) division — the superior temporal plane is reached by the temporopolar and anterior temporal branches, and the posterior part borders the PCA territory. Embolic MCA occlusion is therefore the usual cause of a cortical auditory lesion.
bloodSupply.after: Predominantly MCA branches supplying the superior temporal plane; exact branches vary.

before.findings: Bilateral lesions of the primary auditory cortex produce apparent deafness with intact brainstem auditory evoked potentials: the ear hears but the cortex cannot decode. Unilateral A1 lesions cause only subtle deficits (impaired localization and temporal discrimination) because the pathway is bilateral from the cochlear nuclei onward.
before.vascular: Bilateral middle cerebral artery infarction (or bilateral temporal injury of any cause)

before.findings: Bilateral lesions of A1 and the surrounding belt, or disconnection of both Heschl's gyri from Wernicke's area, leave spontaneous speech, reading and writing intact while spoken words cannot be understood or repeated.

before.syndrome: Auditory hallucinations and tinnitus of cortical origin
before.findings: Irritative lesions and epileptic discharges of the temporal plane produce formed auditory hallucinations; A1 hyperexcitability is implicated in the cortical component of tinnitus.
before.note: Epileptic/functional rather than vascular

after.findings: Unilateral injury may impair sound localization or complex auditory processing; bilateral auditory cortical/radiation injury can cause cortical deafness.
after.vascular: MCA temporal territories or nonvascular causes

after.findings: Impaired understanding of spoken words with relatively preserved reading and spontaneous language can follow bilateral or dominant central auditory-network injury; it is not simply synonymous with deafness.

function.before: Primary auditory cortex, buried on the superior temporal plane in the transverse temporal gyri of Heschl at the floor of the sylvian fissure. It receives the auditory radiation from the medial geniculate nucleus as a tonotopic map (low frequencies anterolateral, high frequencies posteromedial) and performs the first cortical analysis of frequency, intensity and temporal structure; because the projection from the cochlear nuclei onward is bilateral, a unilateral A1 lesion does not cause deafness. Its core is surrounded by the belt and parabelt fields that feed A2 and Wernicke's area.
function.after: Primary auditory cortex lies predominantly on Heschl's transverse temporal gyri within the lateral sulcus, approximately area 41. Tonotopic core regions receive MGN input. Because each ear has bilateral central projections, a unilateral cortical lesion usually does not cause complete deafness in one ear.

records.name: Auditory association cortex (A2)

bloodSupply.before: Middle cerebral artery, inferior (posterior temporal) division — the posterior temporal and angular branches supply the superior temporal plane; the posterior extremity borders the PCA territory through the temporo-occipital branches.

before.note: Developmental structural association — not a lesion syndrome

after.vascular: MCA temporal territory or nonvascular causes

function.before: Auditory association cortex on the planum temporale behind Heschl's gyrus: the belt and parabelt fields that compute what the primary area has already encoded — spectrotemporal patterns, pitch sequences, voice identity and the phonemic categories of speech. It sits at the posterior end of the superior temporal plane and, on the left, is the anatomical core of Wernicke's area; the leftward planum temporale asymmetry is one of the best-documented structural asymmetries of the human brain and the classic correlate of language lateralization.
function.after: This record summarizes nonprimary auditory association cortex surrounding auditory core fields on the superior temporal plane and adjacent temporal cortex. The label A2 is a teaching shorthand and is not coextensive with the planum temporale or all language-comprehension cortex. These regions analyze complex sounds within bilateral and lateralized networks.

records.name: Wernicke's area

bloodSupply.before: Middle cerebral artery, inferior (posterior temporal/parietal) division — the posterior temporal branches supply the superior temporal gyrus and the angular branch the temporoparietal junction. This is the classic embolic MCA territory infarct of the dominant hemisphere.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly dominant-hemisphere MCA posterior temporal/inferior-division branches, with variable boundaries.

before.findings: Fluent, prosodically normal but empty speech with impaired comprehension and impaired repetition, plentiful phonemic and semantic paraphasias, neologisms and anosognosia: the patient is unaware that the output is incomprehensible. Reading and writing are usually comparably impaired.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, inferior division (posterior temporal branches)

before.findings: Fluent speech with intact comprehension but strikingly impaired repetition, with frequent self-corrections — the disconnection syndrome between Wernicke's and Broca's areas.
before.vascular: MCA territory infarct involving the supramarginal gyrus and the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus

before.findings: Impaired comprehension with preserved repetition (the perisylvian language core is intact but disconnected from meaning): a watershed lesion between MCA and PCA territories around the temporoparietal junction.

after.findings: Dominant posterior language-network injury may cause fluent paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension and repetition; awareness and individual features vary.
Disproportionately impaired repetition with relatively preserved comprehension can follow dorsal language-network cortical or white-matter injury; it is not confined to a severed arcuate fasciculus.

function.before: The receptive language area of the posterior superior temporal gyrus (with the planum temporale and the supramarginal gyrus of the temporoparietal junction): it maps sound onto meaning, storing the phonological and lexical representations that allow a heard or read word to be recognised. Left-hemisphere dominant in ~95% of right-handers, it is the second node of the classic language circuit — input arrives from A1/A2 through the auditory association cortex, and output leaves through the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus to Broca's area and through the extreme capsule and uncinate fasciculus to semantic regions of the temporal pole and orbitofrontal cortex.
function.after: Wernicke's area is a historical label for dominant posterior temporal/perisylvian language cortex, often centered on posterior superior temporal gyrus with variably included adjacent regions. Comprehension, lexical and phonological processing depend on a distributed temporal, parietal and frontal network. Language dominance is usually left-sided but varies between individuals.

records.name: Broca's area

bloodSupply.before: Middle cerebral artery, superior (frontal) division — the ascending frontal/opercular branches reach the inferior frontal gyrus; the adjacent insular M2 branches and the recurrent artery of Heubner supply the underlying caudate head and anterior limb of the internal capsule. Dominant-hemisphere MCA superior-division infarction is the usual cause of the syndrome.
bloodSupply.after: MCA superior-division frontal/opercular branches, with individual variation.

before.findings: Effortful, telegraphic, agrammatic speech with relatively preserved comprehension, intact awareness of the deficit and, when the adjacent precentral cortex is involved, a contralateral face-and-arm weakness: the classic inferior (frontal) division MCA infarct of the dominant hemisphere.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, superior division (ascending frontal branches)

before.findings: A small opercular lesion can abolish articulate speech while writing, comprehension and even singing are preserved — proof that Broca's area runs the articulatory programme rather than language itself.
before.vascular: Small cortical branch infarct of the precentral/opercular region

before.findings: Progressive atrophy of the left inferior frontal and insular cortex produces effortful, agrammatic speech with preserved single-word comprehension — the neurodegenerative analogue of Broca aphasia.
before.note: Neurodegenerative (frontotemporal lobar degeneration), not vascular

after.findings: Usually nonfluent, effortful, agrammatic speech with impaired repetition; comprehension may be relatively better yet is often impaired for complex syntax. Persistent classic aphasia commonly involves a larger network than areas 44/45 alone.
Apraxia of speech or dysarthria can occur with adjacent speech-motor network injury and must be distinguished from aphasia.

function.before: The motor speech area of the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis and triangularis, Brodmann 44/45): it retrieves and sequences the articulatory programmes for words and assembles them into grammatical utterances. It is the output node of the dorsal language stream, receiving the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus from Wernicke's area, and it also serves non-speech functions including action observation, imitation and the syntactic component of comprehension; the adjacent precentral cortex supplies the face and tongue motor representation that actually executes the movement.
function.after: Broca's area conventionally includes pars opercularis/triangularis of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus (approximately areas 44/45). It contributes to language production, syntax and speech-related control in a distributed network; neighboring premotor, insular and motor regions also contribute to articulation.

records.name: Primary motor cortex (M1)

bloodSupply.before: MCA superior division supplies the lateral convexity (hand, face and arm); ACA callosomarginal/pericallosal branches supply the medial surface and the vertex (foot, leg and bladder representation). The MCA/ACA border runs along the superior convexity, which is why proximal limb weakness with a spared hand and face suggests a watershed infarct rather than a territorial one.
bloodSupply.after: MCA supplies most lateral sensorimotor cortex; ACA supplies medial paracentral regions, with variable border territories.

before.syndrome: MCA superior-division infarct with contralateral hemiparesis
before.findings: Face-and-arm-predominant contralateral weakness with gaze deviation toward the lesion and (dominant hemisphere) Broca aphasia; the leg is relatively spared because the medial motor strip is ACA territory.

before.syndrome: ACA territory infarct with leg-predominant weakness
before.findings: Contralateral foot and leg weakness with abulia, urinary incontinence and grasp reflex when the medial motor strip, supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate are all infarcted.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal and callosomarginal branches)

before.findings: An irritative M1 lesion (tumour, arteriovenous malformation, epileptogenic focus) produces a focal motor seizure that marches along the homunculus, and the post-ictal state leaves a transient contralateral paresis (Todd paralysis) that mimics a stroke.
before.note: Structural/epileptic; the march follows the somatotopic map described above

after.findings: Can cause contralateral weakness distributed according to affected motor regions; cortical/subcortical extent influences face-arm-leg pattern.
after.vascular: MCA lateral or ACA medial branches

after.findings: Motor-cortical network activation can produce focal movements and sometimes a Jacksonian march; spread does not have to follow each displayed homuncular segment.

function.before: Primary motor cortex on the precentral gyrus (Brodmann 4): the giant Betz cells of layer V issue the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres that produce voluntary movement, and the somatotopic map of the motor homunculus runs from the medial surface (foot and leg, in the ACA territory) over the vertex (trunk, arm, hand) to the lateral convexity (face, tongue and larynx, in the MCA territory) — the anatomical reason a proximal limb deficit with a spared leg localizes to the convexity. Its activity reflects the coding of force and direction of movement, with the hand and face representations disproportionately large.
function.after: M1 lies mainly in precentral gyrus/anterior paracentral lobule (approximately area 4). Layer V pyramidal neurons contribute to corticospinal/corticobulbar output; Betz cells are a minority of corticospinal neurons. The teaching homunculus summarizes broad contralateral effector organization, while actual representations overlap and participate in wider action networks.

records.name: Primary somatosensory cortex (S1)

bloodSupply.before: MCA superior division supplies the lateral postcentral gyrus (hand, face and arm); ACA supplies the medial paracentral surface (foot and leg). before.findings: Contralateral loss of discriminative sensation with crude touch preserved: graphaesthesia, stereognosis, two-point discrimination and vibration are lost, and the patient has sensory ataxia of the hand without weakness (the 'cortical sensory' pattern).

before.findings: Lesions of the postcentral cortex and underlying white matter produce spontaneous burning pain and hyperpathia on the contralateral side, sometimes with a raised threshold — the cortical counterpart of the Déjérine-Roussy thalamic syndrome.

before.syndrome: Sensory Jacksonian seizure and Todd sensory deficit

function.before: Primary somatosensory cortex on the postcentral gyrus: area 3b receives the dense thalamocortical projection from VPL/VPM and constructs the somatotopic map of discriminative touch, while areas 3a (muscle spindle and joint proprioception), 1 and 2 elaborate texture, shape, vibration and limb position. The hand, lips and tongue occupy a disproportionate share of the strip (the sensory homunculus mirrors the motor one), and this cortex is the necessary substrate for stereognosis, graphaesthesia and two-point discrimination — the functions whose loss defines a cortical rather than a peripheral sensory deficit.
function.after: S1 comprises areas 3a, 3b, 1 and 2 in and around the postcentral gyrus/posterior paracentral lobule. It processes somatic input from the contralateral body and face with overlapping somatotopic representations. Discriminative sensation and object recognition require S1 plus wider parietal networks.

bloodSupply.before: Middle cerebral artery, superior (frontal) division — the ascending frontal branches and the precentral (rolandic) branch supply the premotor convexity; the MCA/ACA border zone runs along the superior convexity just above it.
bloodSupply.after: Predominantly MCA frontal branches; superior portions approach ACA/MCA border territory.

before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, superior division (precentral branches)

before.findings: Loss of the ability to perform learned gestures to command (with preserved ability to perform them spontaneously) after dominant-hemisphere premotor and parietal lesions.

function.before: The lateral part of Brodmann area 6, immediately anterior to M1 on the lateral convexity: it selects and prepares movements in response to sensory (especially visual) cues, programmes the posture and proximal limb orientation that a reach requires, and contains the dorsal and ventral premotor fields with their mirror-neuron populations for action observation and imitation. Unlike M1 it works through movement sets and sequences rather than single muscles, and its output is largely routed through M1 and the corticospinal system.
function.after: Lateral premotor cortex lies anterior to M1 and is conventionally associated with lateral area 6. It contributes to preparation, selection and sensory guidance of actions through dorsal/ventral premotor and wider parietofrontal networks. It has both corticocortical and direct descending motor projections.

records.name: Supplementary motor area (SMA)

bloodSupply.before: Anterior cerebral artery — the callosomarginal and pericallosal branches at the medial surface, with the venous drainage into the superior sagittal sinus. The SMA lies in the ACA territory, adjacent to the ACA/MCA border zone on the convexity.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly ACA medial frontal branches.

before.findings: Contralateral leg weakness plus transient mutism or severely reduced spontaneous speech with preserved repetition and comprehension, and contralateral grasp reflex or alien-limb behaviour; the mutism characteristically recovers over days to weeks.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery (callosomarginal/pericallosal branches), sometimes from vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage

before.findings: Lesions of the SMA and its callosal connections (including the anterior cerebral artery territory and the callosal variant) release limb behaviour that the patient does not own: the hand performs apparently purposeful movements that are attributed to someone else.
before.vascular: ACA territory infarction, including the callosal disconnection variant

before.syndrome: Akinetic mutism and abulia with bilateral lesions
before.findings: Bilateral SMA/anterior cingulate damage produces a profound loss of spontaneous movement and speech, with eyes open and sleep-wake cycles preserved — the extreme of the apathy-abulia spectrum.
before.vascular: Bilateral ACA infarction (often a single ACA from a hypoplastic A1, or vasospasm of both A2 segments)

after.findings: Injury or resection may cause reduced initiation, contralateral akinesia/weakness and, in dominant networks, reduced speech. Recovery and residual deficits vary.
Can cause severe abulia or akinetic mutism when cingulate and related initiation networks are involved; SMA injury alone is not a mandatory explanation.

function.before: The medial part of Brodmann area 6 on the dorsomedial surface of the hemisphere, in front of the medial M1 foot representation: it plans and internally sequences complex, self-initiated (rather than stimulus-triggered) movement, holds bimanual coordination and postural set, and links motivation to action through its dense connections with the cingulate motor areas and the basal-ganglia loop. The pre-SMA anteriorly is involved in the selection and switching of action sets; activity here precedes movement onset, which is why it is regarded as the cortical origin of the readiness potential.
function.after: SMA occupies medial superior frontal cortex anterior to medial M1, within the conventional area 6 region. SMA/pre-SMA contribute to movement initiation, sequencing, action selection and bimanual coordination through wider motor and cognitive networks. Readiness potentials are distributed signals rather than proof of one cortical origin.

records.name: Entorhinal cortex

bloodSupply.before: Posterior cerebral artery — the hippocampal and anterior temporal branches (with the anterior choroidal artery from the internal carotid supplying the uncal end, and the PCA temporal branches posteriorly). The territory is the reason PCA infarction impairs memory as well as vision.
bloodSupply.after: PCA temporal/hippocampal branches with variable anterior contributions.

before.syndrome: Alzheimer disease (Braak stages I–II begin here)
before.findings: Neurofibrillary tangles appear first in the entorhinal cortex and then spread through the hippocampal circuit to the posterior cingulate and neocortex, which is the anatomical reason episodic memory fails before other cognitive domains.
before.note: Neurodegenerative staging (Braak), not vascular

before.findings: Bilateral (usually asymmetric) necrotizing infection of the medial temporal lobes including the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus produces fever, headache, seizures and profound anterograde amnesia; it is the classic infectious cause of a dense amnestic syndrome.
before.note: Infectious (HSV-1 via the olfactory route); contrast-enhancing medial temporal lesions are the imaging signature

before.findings: Infarction of the entorhinal and hippocampal territory adds memory loss to the contralateral homonymous hemianopia of PCA occlusion; bilateral involvement causes a persistent amnestic state.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (hippocampal and anterior temporal branches)

after.findings: Entorhinal/hippocampal network injury can impair new declarative memory; deficit depends on laterality and extent.
Transentorhinal/entorhinal regions are early sites in typical tau staging, but clinical presentations and pathological spread vary.
after.note: Staging association, not a rule that all disease begins in one area.

Amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate; cholinergic and noradrenergic input from the basal forebrain and locus coeruleus
Cingulum (tract-cingulum) from the posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex

efferent: Predominantly layer-II input to dentate/CA3 and mainly layer-III input to CA1/subiculum, with contributions from other layers and parallel hippocampal pathways

function.before: The gateway cortex of the hippocampal formation: the anterior part of the parahippocampal gyrus (Brodmann 28 laterally, 34 medially) receives the convergent, highly processed output of every association area through the perirhinal and postrhinal cortices and funnels it into the hippocampus along the perforant path. It carries the head-direction signal, grid cells and spatial-context representations, and it is the anatomical reason episodic memory depends on the medial temporal lobe; its layers II and III are the origin of the perforant path and its layer V is the hippocampal output route back to the neocortex.
function.after: Entorhinal cortex occupies part of the anterior parahippocampal region and links association cortex with hippocampal formation. Layers II/III provide major dentate/CA inputs, including perforant and direct routes; hippocampal/subicular return reaches deep entorhinal layers and wider cortex. This is an interconnected memory system, not a single feedforward funnel.

records.name: Frontal eye fields

bloodSupply.before: Middle cerebral artery, superior (frontal) division — the precentral and ascending frontal branches; the frontal eye field lies at the anterior edge of the MCA territory, immediately behind the ACA/MCA border on the convexity.
bloodSupply.after: Predominantly MCA frontal branches, with variation.

before.syndrome: Destructive frontal lesion with ipsilateral gaze deviation
before.findings: An acute destructive lesion of the frontal eye field (MCA infarct) leaves both eyes looking toward the side of the lesion and away from the hemiparesis, because the unopposed contralateral FEF drives gaze across; the deviation is transient and can be overcome by the oculocephalic manoeuvre.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, superior division (frontal branches)

before.findings: An irritative FEF lesion drives the eyes away from the lesion — the mirror image of the destructive deficit — often as the first manifestation of a frontal-lobe seizure, followed by head version and a Jacksonian march.
before.note: Epileptic rather than vascular; the direction of deviation is the localizing sign

before.syndrome: Saccadic palsy of the horizontal gaze centres
before.findings: Lesions that disconnect the FEF from the PPRF (including the PPRF itself in the dorsal pons) abolish voluntary saccades to the contralateral side while reflex (vestibular) eye movements are preserved.
before.vascular: Basilar paramedian perforators (PPRF infarct) or MCA territory infarction of the FEF

after.findings: Acute injury may reduce contralateral saccades and produce gaze preference toward the lesion; exceptions occur, and the sign is not specific to a small FEF lesion.
Seizure activity may drive contralateral eye/head deviation, but timing and propagation limit lateralization from this sign alone.

afferent: Posterior parietal cortex (area 7, lateral intraparietal area) and the middle temporal visual area for target selection
Prefrontal (dorsolateral) cortex for task rules and the supplementary eye field for sequence learning
Thalamic input from MD and the pulvinar/lateral posterior nucleus
efferent: Contralateral PPRF (nuc-pprf) and the superior colliculus (nuc-superior-colliculus) via the corticotectal and frontopontine routes — the final common path for horizontal saccades
Caudate nucleus (the oculomotor striatal territory) and the pontine nuclei; corticothalamic feedback

afferent: Posterior parietal/visual association and prefrontal inputs

efferent: Superior colliculus and brainstem saccadic networks, including contralateral horizontal gaze circuitry

function.before: The cortical centre for voluntary, purposeful saccades, in the posterior middle frontal gyrus at the junction of the precentral and superior frontal sulci (Brodmann 8). It transforms the intention to look — a remembered location, a target chosen from a visual scene, or a planned scan — into a command that reaches the contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) and the superior colliculus, and it also carries a smooth-pursuit and a visual-attention signal. Its descending pathway crosses in the midbrain to reach the contralateral horizontal gaze centre, which is why a destructive frontal lesion deviates the eyes toward the side of the lesion.
function.after: Human frontal eye fields lie around the junction of the precentral and superior frontal sulci, often overlapping area 6; the historical area 8 label is approximate. They contribute to voluntary saccades and attention through superior-collicular, brainstem, thalamic and cortical networks, with a strong contralateral saccadic bias.

bloodSupply.before: The olfactory bulb and tract are supplied by the olfactory branches of the anterior cerebral artery (vasc-anterior-cerebral-artery), with contributions from the anterior ethmoidal branches of the ophthalmic artery in the olfactory fossa; the convergence of these small vessels on the anterior perforated substance places the nerve next to the anterior communicating artery (vasc-anterior-communicating-artery), which is why the nerve is at risk during anterior-communicating-aneurysm surgery and why subarachnoid blood from that aneurysm can leave anosmia. The olfactory epithelium itself is supplied by the anterior ethmoidal artery, and venous drainage runs through the ethmoidal veins, whose proximity to the subarachnoid space is why a fracture here leaks CSF.
bloodSupply.after: Nasal mucosa is supplied by ethmoidal and other nasal arteries; bulb/tract receive small ACA/carotid-system branches. Segment-specific territory is not mapped here.

before.findings: Loss of smell must be split into a conductive type (the odorant never reaches the epithelium or the cribriform foramina are blocked — rhinosinusitis, nasal polyposis, allergic rhinitis, a deviated septum) and a sensorineural type (the fila, bulb or tract are damaged). The distinction localizes the lesion, and only the sensorineural type is a neurological sign: a persistently unilateral anosmia in a patient with no nasal disease is a structural lesion until proven otherwise.
before.note: The clinically load-bearing test is unilateral testing of each nostril with a familiar odour; bilateral anosmia is often unnoticed by the patient and reported as loss of taste, because retronasal olfaction carries most of the flavour of food while the tongue's taste buds (CN VII, IX, X) remain normal.

before.findings: Head injury, particularly occipital impact with contre-coup against the anterior cranial fossa, avulses the fila olfactoria as they pass through the cribriform plate; the bulb and tract may also be contused against the orbital roof. The deficit is typically unilateral or asymmetric, is often unnoticed until the patient cannot smell smoke or gas, and is a recognized cause of permanent disability after apparently minor trauma.
before.note: Because the fila are the torn element, recovery is possible (they regenerate and re-synapse) but is usually incomplete — the anatomical reason recovery after traumatic anosmia is partial at best, unlike the recovery after a conductive cause is treated.

before.findings: A meningioma of the olfactory groove compresses the nerve and bulb on one side, producing ipsilateral anosmia and ipsilateral optic atrophy from direct compression of the optic nerve, while raised intracranial pressure produces papilloedema in the other eye; anosmia may precede visual symptoms by years, and a frontal-lobe syndrome with abulia, anosmia and gait disturbance can be the presenting picture.
before.vascular: Not vascular — the artery that matters is the anterior cerebral artery displaced by the tumour

before.syndrome: Anosmia after subarachnoid haemorrhage and in neurodegenerative disease
before.findings: Blood in the subarachnoid space (most often from an anterior communicating artery aneurysm, which lies immediately behind the olfactory tract) damages the nerve and produces anosmia distinct from the headache and meningism; a slowly progressive anosmia with no nasal disease is an early non-motor feature of Parkinson disease and of dementia with Lewy bodies, and it also precedes the memory loss of Alzheimer disease.
before.vascular: Anterior communicating artery / anterior cerebral artery territory

after.findings: May follow nasal obstruction/inflammation, viral injury, trauma, intracranial disease or neurodegeneration; reduced smell alone does not establish one neurological diagnosis.
Shearing of fila at the cribriform plate or injury of bulb/tract can impair smell; degree of recovery varies.
A large anterior cranial-fossa lesion can cause ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema, sometimes with anosmia; the full pattern is uncommon.

afferent: Olfactory receptor neurons of the olfactory epithelium (bipolar cells whose cilia carry the odorant receptors) — the true first-order neurons; their axons are the fila olfactoria and they regenerate throughout life, which is why post-viral anosmia can recover

Central modulation of the bulb through the medial olfactory stria (from the anterior olfactory nucleus, the diagonal band and the contralateral bulb via the anterior commissure), which sharpens and gates the incoming odour signal

Note on the registry: no `nuc-` record exists for the olfactory bulb or its mitral/tufted cells, so the first relay of this nerve is named here in prose rather than linked; the nucleus-level records this record can link are the cortical targets listed under efferent
efferent: Primary olfactory (piriform) cortex of the uncus and anterior parahippocampal gyrus — the main cortical target, with no thalamic relay
Amygdala (nuc-amygdala) and the periamygdaloid cortex — the substrate of odour-driven emotion and of the visceral responses to smell
Entorhinal cortex (ctx-entorhinal) and thence the hippocampus (nuc-hippocampus) — the route by which an odour becomes a memory, severed early in Alzheimer disease
Thalamus (nuc-md, mediodorsal nucleus) and the orbitofrontal cortex — the secondary pathway that makes odour a conscious, nameable percept; this is the relay that a frontal lesion interrupts
The bulb and tract also project back into the epithelium through centrifugal fibres from the horizontal limb of the diagonal band, the anatomical reason attention modulates odour detection

afferent: Bipolar olfactory receptor neurons in the superior nasal neuroepithelium
efferent: First synapse in olfactory-bulb glomeruli on mitral/tufted cells
Bulb output continues in olfactory tract to piriform/periamygdaloid and other olfactory regions; higher processing includes orbitofrontal/MD pathways

course.before: From the olfactory epithelium of the superior nasal cavity (bipolar receptor neurons) the unmyelinated axons (fila olfactoria, about 20 bundles per side) pierce the cribriform plate of the ethmoid — the foramen this nerve uses — and enter the olfactory bulb of the anterior cranial fossa; from the bulb the olfactory tract runs posteriorly in the olfactory sulcus on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe, at the limen insulae dividing into the medial and lateral olfactory striae that reach the anterior perforated substance and the piriform cortex. There is no true cisternal segment: the intracranial part of CN I is the bulb and tract, which lie on the orbital surface rather than in the subarachnoid cisterns, and the nerve owns no subarachnoid course of the kind CN III delivers to the interpeduncular cistern. The bulb and tract are therefore included in this one record, because the fila, bulb and tract are the same first-order pathway and the clinical lesions (trauma, frontal tumour) damage them together.
course.after: Receptor-neuron axon bundles pass through cribriform foramina to the olfactory bulb in the anterior cranial fossa. The bulb and tract are CNS structures along the orbital frontal surface; their axons continue through olfactory striae to central olfactory targets. The depicted course is schematic and does not resolve individual fila.

function.before: The only cranial nerve that reaches the brain without a thalamic relay: its first-order axons synapse directly on the mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb, which are the output neurons of a three-layered cortical structure. The bulb performs the first stage of odour processing (glomerular convergence and lateral inhibition through periglomerular and granule cells) and sends the result along the tract to the primary olfactory cortex — the piriform cortex, the periamygdaloid cortex and the anterior cortical nucleus of the amygdala, with a smaller projection to the rostral entorhinal cortex (ctx-entorhinal). This is why smell has a uniquely direct route to the limbic system (odours are recognised, remembered and emotionally tagged before any conscious analysis), and why the tract's projections are the anatomical basis of odour-triggered memory and of the uncinate-fit phenomenon. The nerve also carries the afferent limb of retronasal olfaction, so it is the dominant contributor to what patients call taste.
function.after: CN I consists of primary olfactory receptor-neuron axons (olfactory fila) from the superior nasal neuroepithelium to the bulb. Mitral/tufted cells then project in the CNS olfactory tract to primary olfactory regions without a compulsory initial thalamic relay. Olfaction contributes to flavor and emotional/memory networks, but it is distinct from gustatory taste.

modality.before: Special sensory — smell (olfaction); also a special visceral afferent carried from the nasal epithelium, and the afferent limb of the smell-taste flavour system
modality.after: Special sensory: olfaction; often classified as special visceral afferent in traditional cranial-nerve schemes
