records.name: CN II Optic nerve

bloodSupply.before: The intraorbital and intracanalicular nerve is supplied by the ophthalmic artery (branches of the internal carotid artery, vasc-internal-carotid-artery): the central retinal artery runs inside the nerve's substance and the short posterior ciliary arteries supply its anterior portion, which is why occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries produces anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. The intracranial segment is supplied by the superior hypophyseal arteries and small branches of the internal carotid — a rich anastomotic supply that lets the nerve tolerate gradual compression from a sellar mass, and the same vessels that surgeons must preserve when the chiasm is approached from below. Compression of this cisternal segment by the internal carotid or by a suprasellar tumour is the anatomical reason a junctional scotoma localizes the lesion to the nerve-chiasm junction.
bloodSupply.after: Optic-nerve head: mainly short posterior ciliary branches; orbital/canalicular nerve: ophthalmic/pial circulation; intracranial nerve: small carotid/ACA-related branches. Central retinal artery principally supplies inner retina.

before.findings: Subacute painful monocular visual loss with reduced colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect and a central scotoma, typically in a young adult woman and often the first symptom of multiple sclerosis; the nerve enhances on MRI and vision usually recovers over weeks. Pain on eye movement localizes the inflammation to the intraorbital and intracanalicular nerve, where the meninges are mobile.
before.note: Inflammatory/demyelinating (anti-AQP4 or MOG antibody disease in atypical or bilateral cases), not vascular

before.findings: Because the optic-nerve sheath is continuous with the subarachnoid space, raised intracranial pressure is transmitted along the cisternal segment and produces bilateral disc swelling, transient visual obscurations and enlarged blind spots; prolonged compression produces optic atrophy. The raised pressure also produces the false localizing abducens palsy (nrv-cn6-abducens) and, in a chronic picture, an empty sella.
before.vascular: Not vascular — CSF pressure transmitted through the sheath; the sheath's continuity with the subarachnoid space is the anatomical fact

before.syndrome: Compressive optic neuropathy (sellar, suprasellar and orbital)
before.findings: A pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, tuberculum-sellae or optic-sheath meningioma compressing the cisternal or canalicular nerve causes progressive monocular visual loss with a central scotoma, a junctional scotoma when the nerve-chiasm junction is involved, or optic atrophy; a mass in the orbital apex adds proptosis and ophthalmoplegia from the neighbouring CN III, IV, V1 and VI.
before.note: Compressive rather than vascular; the pattern of the field defect — not the acuity — localizes the level

before.syndrome: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy and central retinal artery occlusion
before.findings: Infarction of the anterior nerve from occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries gives sudden painless monocular loss with an altitudinal field defect and a swollen disc (arteritic in giant-cell arteritis; non-arteritic otherwise), while central retinal artery occlusion gives sudden painless loss with a cherry-red spot and a markedly attenuated arterial tree. Both are diseases of the nerve's own blood supply rather than of the nerve as a conductor.
before.vascular: Short posterior ciliary arteries and the central retinal artery (ophthalmic artery); the arteritic form accompanies giant-cell arteritis

before.findings: The nerve is fixed at the optic canal, so a deceleration injury tears it or shears its vessels at the canal while the globe is displaced; the deficit is immediate and irreversible. The same fixed point is why the nerve is at risk in endoscopic sinus surgery and during orbital decompression, and why the clinical priority in suspected injury is a documented pupillary examination before any imaging.
before.note: Mechanical; the optic canal is the anatomical choke point, and the nerve's fixation there is the reason for the injury pattern

after.findings: Inflammatory, ischemic, compressive or traumatic injury can cause monocular visual loss, color/field abnormalities and asymmetric afferent pupillary responses; prognosis and pain vary.
Raised intracranial pressure can produce optic-disc swelling through the meningeal sheath; not every swollen disc is papilledema.
Central retinal artery occlusion primarily injures inner retina; posterior ciliary ischemia can injure optic-nerve head. These are distinct anterior visual-pathway sites.

afferent: Retinal ganglion cells of the ipsilateral retina — the first-order afferents, whose receptive-field organization is already computed in the retina before the axons reach this nerve

The optic nerve is afferent-only in the classical sense; its efferent partner is the olivary pretectal projection to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (nuc-edinger-westphal), which is what makes the pupillary light reflex a two-nerve loop rather than a one-nerve arc
efferent: Optic chiasm (ctx-optic-chiasm) — the crossing point where the nasal fibres of each nerve pass to the contralateral tract
Optic tract (tract-optic-tract) — the continuation carrying the contralateral visual half-field
Lateral geniculate nucleus (nuc-lgn) — the thalamic relay for conscious vision
Pretectal area (nuc-pretectal) — the pupillary light reflex, reached by fibres that leave the tract before the geniculate body
Suprachiasmatic nucleus (nuc-suprachiasmatic) — the retinohypothalamic tract for circadian photoentrainment
Superior colliculus (nuc-superior-colliculus) — the small collicular projection that supports orienting to a visual target

afferent: Retinal ganglion-cell axons from the ipsilateral eye; retinal circuitry has already processed the input
efferent: Continuation through chiasm into optic tracts
Retinal axons ultimately reach LGN, pretectal, collicular and hypothalamic targets; these are not separate synapses within the nerve

course.before: From the optic disc (where about one million retinal ganglion-cell axons converge) the nerve runs through the orbit in the cone of extraocular muscles, pierces the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery — the foramen this nerve uses — and enters the middle cranial fossa. Its intracranial (cisternal) segment, about 10 mm long, runs posteromedially and superiorly through the suprasellar cistern, bathed in CSF and wrapped in meninges, to join the contralateral nerve at the optic chiasm. The nasal fibres cross at the chiasm and the temporal fibres stay ipsilateral, so the chiasm is the end of this nerve and the beginning of the optic tract (tract-optic-tract). Because the nerve is a CNS tract rather than a peripheral nerve it is myelinated by oligodendrocytes, is enclosed in all three meninges, and is the reason it is the only cranial nerve that swells in papilloedema.
course.after: From optic disc through intraorbital and canalicular segments, the nerve passes the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery, then continues in the suprasellar region to the chiasm. Posterior nerve is oligodendrocyte-myelinated and surrounded by meninges with a continuous subarachnoid sheath. The displayed course does not establish patient-specific canal or orbital anatomy.

function.before: Carries the entire visual signal from the photoreceptors to the brain: the retina's three-neuron chain (photoreceptor to bipolar cell to ganglion cell) converges on the axons of this nerve, which are organized retinotopically. The macula — about 5 degrees of central vision — occupies roughly two-thirds of the axons and the far nasal periphery the remainder, so the fibre arrangement inside the nerve explains the field pattern of a partial lesion (central scotoma for a macular-fibre lesion, an arcuate defect for a nerve-fibre-bundle lesion, an altitudinal defect for an ischaemic anterior lesion). The nerve also carries the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex: its fibres leave the tract before the lateral geniculate nucleus (nuc-lgn) to reach the pretectal area (nuc-pretectal), and a minority leave near the chiasm for the suprachiasmatic nucleus (nuc-suprachiasmatic) to entrain circadian rhythm. Its relationship to this record's sibling, `tract-optic-nerve`, is the split between the v8 optic-pathway record (the whole nerve as a tract of the visual pathway, with real baked meshes) and this cranial-nerve record (the nerve as CN II, classified with the other eleven and carrying the foramen, nerve-sheath and clinic of a cranial nerve). Both are registered on purpose: the registry holds one answer for the nerve's region and one for its kind, and the two records carry different content.
function.after: CN II conveys retinal ganglion-cell output from one eye through the optic canal to the chiasm. The optic nerve is a CNS tract by development and myelination, conventionally named a cranial nerve. Its retinal axons contribute to visual, pupillary and circadian pathways after their central continuation.

modality.before: Special sensory — vision (special somatic afferent); retinal ganglion-cell axons carrying the retinotopic map of the contralateral visual field half, plus the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex
modality.after: Special somatic afferent: vision/reflex retinal output from the ipsilateral eye before partial chiasmal crossing

records.name: Subiculum

bloodSupply.before: Posterior cerebral artery — the posterior hippocampal and temporal branches supply the subiculum along the hippocampal body; the anterior (uncal) portion, adjacent to the amygdala, is supplied by the anterior choroidal artery from the internal carotid. The transition between the two territories lies near the hippocampal head.
bloodSupply.after: Shares mainly PCA hippocampal/temporal supply with variable anterior choroidal contribution.

before.findings: The subiculum and CA1 are the fields most consistently atrophic and gliotic in hippocampal sclerosis, and the subiculum also shows the mossy-fibre sprouting and interneuron loss that make the sclerotic hippocampus epileptogenic; it is often the seizure-onset zone, and its resection (with the rest of the mesial temporal block) is the standard surgical treatment of refractory temporal-lobe epilepsy.
before.vascular: Not primarily vascular — sclerosis follows prolonged febrile seizures, hypoxia or repeated seizures

before.findings: Neurofibrillary pathology spreads from the entorhinal cortex into the subiculum and CA1, which is why the subiculum shows atrophy on volumetric MRI before the neocortex does; subicular atrophy correlates with episodic memory failure.
before.note: Neurodegenerative staging (Braak), not vascular

before.findings: Infarction of the posterior hippocampal formation produces anterograde amnesia as part of the PCA syndrome, together with a contralateral homonymous hemianopia and, with thalamic involvement, sensory loss.

after.findings: Can disrupt hippocampal output and memory, but an isolated subicular clinical syndrome cannot be inferred from a schematic marker.
Subicular/hippocampal circuits may participate in epileptic activity; onset must be established clinically and electrophysiologically.

afferent: CA1 pyramidal cells (nuc-ca1) through the Schaffer collateral-commissural system — the direct intrahippocampal projection
Entorhinal cortex (ctx-entorhinal) layer III through the temporoammonic (alvear) path, which reaches CA1 and the subiculum directly, bypassing the trisynaptic loop
Septal (medial septal nucleus and diagonal band) cholinergic and GABAergic input through the fimbria-fornix
efferent: Entorhinal cortex (ctx-entorhinal) layer V — the return route of the memory trace to the neocortical association areas
Fornix (tract-fornix) to the mammillary body (nuc-mammillary-body) and the anterior thalamic nucleus for the Papez circuit; precommissural fibres to the septal region
Presubiculum and parasubiculum, then the retrosplenial and posterior cingulate cortex through the cingulum

afferent: CA1 and entorhinal cortical inputs
Other medial temporal and septal modulatory inputs
efferent: Entorhinal/association cortical return
Fornix projections to mammillary, septal and anterior thalamic targets; other limbic outputs

contextNote.before: Authored structure — schematic placement: the subiculum is a cytoarchitectural field (the transitional cortex between CA1 and the entorhinal cortex) with no separate baked mesh. The record is anchored on the medial-concave surface of the baked hippocampal cast at x ≈ 20.7, y ≈ 11.8, z ≈ 0.6 (probed from ctx-hippocampus-l by the v8 content-authoring run); the pickable volume stays `nuc-hippocampus`, and the placement is schematic rather than a boundary-accurate subfield reconstruction.
contextNote.after: A microscopic laminated hippocampal-field concept represented by an authored marker. The shape/coordinate does not establish CA/dentate/subicular boundaries; a host hippocampal mesh cannot independently validate a subfield segmentation. Named level membership is teaching/navigation metadata and has not been validated as a literal intersection of every displayed transverse section. The clinical text describes possible associations, not diagnostic rules.

function.before: The principal output structure of the hippocampal formation: a three-layered transitional cortex between CA1 (with which it is cytoarchitecturally continuous) and the entorhinal cortex, whose large pyramidal cells receive the CA1 projection and send the hippocampal output back to the entorhinal cortex, the presubiculum and the septal region. It is the last leg of the intrahippocampal circuit and the anatomical origin of the fornix's postcommissural fibres to the mammillary body, so it converts a stored hippocampal representation into a signal the rest of the brain can read; the dorsal (posterior) subiculum carries spatial and contextual information, the ventral (anterior) part is preferentially connected with the amygdala and the stress axis.
function.after: The subiculum is transitional cortex between CA1 and the parahippocampal/entorhinal region. It receives hippocampal input and is a major source of output to entorhinal cortex, fornix and other cortical/subcortical memory networks. It is a laminated cortical field rather than a discrete spherical nucleus.

records.name: CA1 (Sommer sector)

bloodSupply.before: Posterior cerebral artery — the posterior hippocampal branches (with the anterior choroidal artery supplying the uncal/head portion from the internal carotid). CA1 lies in the border zone between the hippocampal branches and the adjacent territories, which is why it sustains selective necrosis after global ischaemia.
bloodSupply.after: Hippocampal PCA branches with variable anterior choroidal contribution; selective cellular vulnerability is not proof of a macroscopic border-zone location.

before.findings: Global cerebral ischaemia from cardiac arrest or profound hypotension selectively destroys the CA1 pyramidal cells (together with the neocortical layers III/V/VI and the Purkinje cells): the patient survives with a dense anterograde amnesia while remote memories are relatively spared. This selective vulnerability is known as the Sommer sector lesion.
before.vascular: Global hypoperfusion/hypoxia rather than a single-territory infarct

before.syndrome: Mesial temporal sclerosis and CA1 seizure onset
before.findings: CA1 is the hippocampal field with the most severe cell loss in mesial temporal sclerosis, and the CA1/subiculum border is the most common seizure-onset zone recorded with depth electrodes — the rationale for mesial temporal resection in drug-resistant epilepsy.
before.note: Epileptogenic remodelling following early-life insult

before.syndrome: Alzheimer disease (CA1 atrophy precedes neocortical involvement)
before.findings: The perforant-path-entorhinal-CA1 axis is the earliest affected circuit; CA1 atrophy on high-resolution MRI predicts progression from mild cognitive impairment to dementia.
before.note: Neurodegenerative, not vascular

after.findings: CA1 injury can contribute to new-memory impairment; global injury may also affect other hippocampal fields, cortex and cerebellum.
CA1 cell loss/gliosis is prominent in common patterns, but sclerosis subtypes differ and MRI does not resolve every histological boundary.

afferent: CA3 (nuc-ca2-ca3) through the Schaffer collateral-commissural system onto the apical dendrites of the stratum radiatum
Entorhinal cortex (ctx-entorhinal) layer III through the temporoammonic path onto the distal apical dendrites (the direct, trisynaptic-bypassing input)
Septal cholinergic and GABAergic input, and local interneuron networks that generate the theta rhythm

Fornix (tract-fornix) — the caudal CA1/CA3 output field joins the fimbria and carries hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies and septum
A small projection to the contralateral hippocampus through the ventral hippocampal commissure

Direct entorhinal and septal/modulatory input
efferent: Subiculum and entorhinal cortical return

The record is anchored on the dorsal-lateral surface of the baked hippocampal body at x ≈ 24.8, y ≈ 13.8, z ≈ −0.9 (probed from ctx-hippocampus-l by the v8 content-authoring run); the pickable volume stays `nuc-hippocampus`.

function.before: The largest and best-understood field of the hippocampus proper: a single layer of pyramidal cells that integrates two inputs — the Schaffer collaterals from CA3 (the third leg of the trisynaptic circuit, carrying the pattern-completed memory code) and the direct temporoammonic path from entorhinal layer III (carrying the raw sensory-context signal) — and whose output goes to the subiculum and back to the entorhinal cortex. It performs the comparison between a stored prediction and the current input that underlies novelty detection and memory encoding, and its place fields remap with context; because it sits at a vascular and metabolic watershed it is also the most vulnerable hippocampal field to hypoxia and ischaemia.
function.after: CA1 is a pyramidal-cell field between CA2 and subiculum. It receives CA3 Schaffer-collateral input and direct entorhinal input and relays to subiculum/entorhinal output networks. Its neurons are particularly vulnerable in some global ischemic and hippocampal-sclerosis patterns, for reasons not reducible to a fixed arterial watershed.

records.name: CA2 and CA3 fields

bloodSupply.before: Posterior cerebral artery — the posterior hippocampal branches, with anterior choroidal supply to the uncal head end. CA2 lies between the ischaemia-vulnerable CA1 and the more resistant CA3, and its relative sparing (the 'resistant sector') is a classic pathological marker of hypoxic injury.
bloodSupply.after: Shared hippocampal arterial territory, mainly PCA with variable anterior contribution.

before.findings: After cardiac arrest the Sommer sector (CA1) and the hilus are destroyed while CA2 is relatively spared — the 'resistant sector' that makes the pattern of hippocampal damage characteristic rather than uniform, and the reason histological staging of hypoxic injury examines CA1/CA2/CA3 side by side.

In mesial temporal sclerosis the mossy fibres of dentate granule cells sprout back into the dentate inner molecular layer and form recurrent excitatory synapses on granule cells, creating the self-sustaining circuit that generates spontaneous seizures; CA3 is the downstream amplifier of this activity.
before.note: Epileptogenic plasticity, not vascular

before.syndrome: CA2 and social memory (rodent and human evidence)
before.findings: Selective manipulation of CA2 impairs social recognition memory and alters aggression in rodents, and CA2 involvement has been proposed in human social-cognitive disorders; it is a striking exception to the idea that the hippocampus is only about episodic memory.
before.note: Preclinical/circuit-level evidence

after.findings: CA2/CA3 involvement varies; relative CA2 sparing is common in some patterns but is not guaranteed.
Selective CA2 manipulations affect social recognition in mice; direct extension to human psychiatric diagnoses remains uncertain.

afferent: Dentate gyrus (nuc-dentate-gyrus) granule cells through the mossy fibres — large, powerful synapses on CA3 proximal dendrites
Recurrent collaterals of other CA3 pyramidal cells (the auto-associative matrix) and the septal cholinergic/GABAergic input

Entorhinal cortex layer II perforant-path fibres to the distal dendrites, and hilar mossy cells; CA2 additionally receives dense supramammillary and hypothalamic (vasopressin) input, which is its defining afferent
efferent: CA1 (nuc-ca1) and the subiculum (nuc-subiculum) through the Schaffer collateral-commissural system
Commissural fibres to the contralateral CA3/CA1 through the ventral hippocampal commissure, and the longitudinal association path within the hippocampus
Fimbria/fornix output from the caudal fields to the septal area and mammillary bodies

afferent: CA3: dentate mossy fibres, entorhinal and recurrent CA3 projections
CA2: entorhinal and other hippocampal/hypothalamic inputs; not equivalent to the CA3 mossy-fibre relay
efferent: CA3 Schaffer-collateral projections to CA1 and other hippocampal outputs
CA2 projections to CA1 and other hippocampal targets

function.before: CA3 is the auto-associative network of the hippocampus: its pyramidal cells receive the dentate mossy fibres on their proximal dendrites and extensive recurrent collaterals from each other, so they can complete a stored pattern from a partial cue — the cellular basis of memory recall. CA2, a narrow field between CA3 and CA1, is the 'resistant sector' that is relatively spared by ischaemia and by mesial temporal sclerosis; it is marked by a distinct molecular profile and has been linked to social memory and to the hippocampal control of aggression, and it also holds the densest innervation by hypothalamic vasopressin fibres.
function.after: This atlas groups two distinct cytoarchitectural fields for display convenience. CA3 receives dentate mossy fibres and has recurrent excitatory circuitry; CA2 lies between CA3 and CA1 with distinct inputs and physiology. Experimental CA2 social-memory findings largely come from animal work and do not define a validated human lesion syndrome.

records.name: CA4 (hilar field)

bloodSupply.before: Posterior cerebral artery — hippocampal branches; the hilus lies within the dentate/hippocampal territory and shares the anterior choroidal supply at the uncal end. Hilar cells are highly vulnerable to hypoxia, and hilar sclerosis is one of the earliest changes after status epilepticus.
bloodSupply.after: Shared hippocampal arterial supply, mainly PCA branches with variable anterior contribution.

before.syndrome: Hilar cell loss and mesial temporal sclerosis
before.findings: Loss of hilar mossy cells and interneurons with subsequent granule-cell dispersion and mossy-fibre sprouting is the core lesion of mesial temporal sclerosis: the dentate gate fails, granule cells become hyperexcitable and the hippocampus generates spontaneous seizures.
before.note: Epileptogenic remodelling following early-life febrile seizures, hypoxia or repeated seizures

before.findings: Prolonged seizures cause acute necrosis of hilar and CA1/CA3 neurons, setting up the chronic epileptic state — the reason status epilepticus is treated as a time-critical emergency, and the rationale for the experimental latency period between an initial insult and the emergence of spontaneous seizures.
before.note: Excitotoxic injury, not a vascular territory syndrome

before.findings: Because the hilus gates the first hippocampal relay, its damage degrades the encoding of new episodic memories while sparing previously consolidated ones.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (hippocampal branches) or hypoxic-ischaemic injury

after.findings: Hilar/CA4 cell loss occurs in recognized sclerosis patterns, including CA4-predominant type; severity and clinical consequences vary.
Prolonged seizure activity may injure hippocampal cells, but hilar injury/sprouting is not a sufficient explanation for every subsequent epilepsy syndrome.

afferent: Dentate gyrus (nuc-dentate-gyrus) granule cells through the mossy fibres, which traverse the hilus on their way to CA3
Entorhinal cortex (ctx-entorhinal) through the perforant path, which innervates hilar interneurons directly
Commissural fibres from the contralateral dentate gyrus and hilar mossy cells
efferent: Associational and commissural projections of mossy cells back onto granule-cell dendrites (the dentate feedback loop)
Local GABAergic inhibition of granule cells and of CA3 pyramidal cells (basket and hilar interneurons)
Fimbria/fornix output with the rest of the hippocampal formation

afferent: Dentate granule-cell mossy-fibre collaterals and local hippocampal inputs
efferent: Local hilar/dentate/CA3 circuits, depending on cell type

contextNote.before: Authored structure — schematic placement: CA4 is the polymorphic cell layer in the hilus of the dentate gyrus, wedged between the granule-cell blades, and is not a dissectable volume. The record is anchored in the core of the baked hippocampal body at x ≈ 25.1, y ≈ 12.7, z ≈ −1.2 (probed from ctx-hippocampus-l by the v8 content-authoring run); the pickable volume stays `nuc-hippocampus`.

Named level membership is teaching/navigation metadata and has not been validated as a literal intersection of every displayed transverse section. The clinical text describes possible associations, not diagnostic rules.

function.before: The polymorphic layer enclosed by the dentate gyrus blades — the hilus, historically labelled CA4 because the mossy fibres cross it and its cells resemble CA3 pyramids. It contains the hilar mossy cells and a rich population of inhibitory interneurons, and it is the integration and gate-keeping station of the dentate: mossy cells project back to the granule cells of the same and the contralateral dentate (an associational/commissural feedback loop), while the hilar interneurons provide the feed-forward inhibition that keeps granule-cell activity sparse. This excitatory-inhibitory balance is what makes pattern separation reliable, and its failure — hilar cell loss with mossy-fibre sprouting — is the cellular hallmark of temporal-lobe epilepsy.
function.after: CA4 is a historical cytoarchitectural label used for cells within the dentate hilus; the hilus also contains mossy cells and inhibitory interneurons, so the terms are not exact synonyms in every nomenclature. Local dentate/hilar circuits regulate excitation and sparse coding. This is a microscopic field, not a validated separate volume in the current atlas.

records.name: Hippocampus

bloodSupply.before: PCA — hippocampal branches of the posterior cerebral artery for the body, tail and most of the head; the anterior choroidal artery (internal carotid) supplies the uncus, amygdala and anterior hippocampal head, and the posterior choroidal arteries supply the adjoining choroid plexus.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly PCA hippocampal branches with variable anterior choroidal contribution, especially anteriorly.

before.syndrome: Bilateral hippocampal infarction (PCA or global hypoxia)
before.findings: Dense anterograde amnesia with preserved remote memory and procedural learning (patient H.M. after bilateral temporal lobectomy; CA1 Sommer sector is the most vulnerable zone to hypoxia).
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (hippocampal branches) or hypoxic-ischaemic injury

before.syndrome: Mesial temporal sclerosis and temporal-lobe epilepsy
before.findings: Hippocampal atrophy with T2 hyperintensity and loss of internal architecture produces drug-resistant focal seizures with déjà vu, epigastric aura and automatisms; anterior temporal lobectomy is curative in selected patients.
before.note: Sclerotic rather than vascular — but the surgical anatomy is the hippocampal segment shown here

before.findings: Entorhinal and hippocampal neurofibrillary degeneration explains the earliest and most disabling symptom, episodic memory failure, with hippocampal atrophy on coronal MRI.
before.note: Neurodegenerative (Braak staging)

before.findings: Abrupt, self-limited anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning and preserved identity, associated with punctate hippocampal diffusion restriction in some patients.
before.note: Mechanism debated (venous congestion, migraine, seizure); the hippocampus is the common final pathway

after.findings: Bilateral injury can cause severe impairment of new declarative learning; remote, working and procedural memory may be relatively preserved but outcomes vary. H.M. had bilateral medial temporal resections, not a selective hippocampal infarct.
Atrophy and signal changes may accompany mesial temporal epilepsy; sclerosis is not present in every case and does not by itself establish seizure onset.
Transient anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning may show delayed punctate hippocampal DWI lesions; this clinical syndrome is not synonymous with stroke or epilepsy.

afferent: Perforant path from the entorhinal cortex (layer II) to the dentate gyrus and CA3; temporoammonic path (layer III) to CA1
Septal (medial septal/diagonal band) cholinergic and GABAergic input; supramammillary and hypothalamic afferents
Noradrenergic locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe and dopaminergic ventral tegmental input
efferent: Fornix: subicular and CA1/CA3 axons leave as the fimbria and fornix to the mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus (indirectly, via the mammillothalamic tract) and septal nuclei
Subiculum to the entorhinal cortex, amygdala and prefrontal cortex
Commissural fibres through the hippocampal commissure (dorsal and ventral hippocampal commissures) to the contralateral hippocampus

afferent: Entorhinal/perirhinal/parahippocampal cortical pathways
Septal inputs through fornix and brainstem neuromodulation
efferent: Subicular/hippocampal output to entorhinal and wider association cortex
Fornix output to septal, mammillary and anterior thalamic targets

contextNote.after: Gross structure/pathway teaching representation. Retained coordinates, dimensions, subdivisions and waypoints are custom renderer metadata; no independently registered patient/standard-atlas comparison validates their numerical extent here. Named level membership is teaching/navigation metadata and has not been validated as a literal intersection of every displayed transverse section. The clinical text describes possible associations, not diagnostic rules.

function.before: The allocortical engine of declarative memory: the cornu ammonis (CA1–CA3) and dentate gyrus form the trisynaptic circuit that converts a single experience into a distributed cortical memory trace, and place cells and grid-like codes in this circuit build the cognitive map of space. It is the classic site of long-term potentiation, the cellular model of learning.
function.after: The hippocampal formation curves along the medial floor of the temporal horn and includes hippocampus proper, dentate gyrus and subiculum in common usage. It participates in formation of new declarative memories and spatial/contextual representations through intrinsic circuits and distributed cortical/diencephalic networks. The whole structure is not a single nucleus.

records.name: Dentate gyrus

bloodSupply.before: PCA — hippocampal branches of the posterior cerebral artery (the dentate lies within the hippocampal formation territory); the anterior (uncal) end also receives anterior choroidal branches.
bloodSupply.after: Shares hippocampal arterial territory, mainly PCA branches with variable anterior contribution.

before.findings: The dentate gyrus shows granule-cell dispersion and aberrant mossy-fibre sprouting in sclerotic hippocampi, creating recurrent excitatory circuits that sustain focal seizures.
before.note: Epileptogenic remodelling rather than vascular injury

before.findings: Because it is inseparable from the hippocampal formation in the PCA territory, dentate infarction always presents as part of a medial temporal infarct: anterograde amnesia with hemianopia, never as an isolated syndrome.

Reduced dentate neurogenesis is reported in chronic stress, depression and epilepsy models, and is stimulated by exercise and antidepressants — the anatomical basis of the dentate gyrus as a plasticity hub.
before.note: Preclinical and human-postmortem evidence

after.findings: Granule-cell dispersion and mossy-fibre sprouting can occur, but neither finding alone proves the cause of seizures.
Dentate injury may affect encoding/discrimination within the wider hippocampal network; hemianopia requires separate visual-pathway injury.

afferent: Perforant path from the entorhinal cortex (layer II) onto granule-cell dendrites
Hilar mossy cells and commissural fibres from the contralateral dentate gyrus via the hippocampal commissure
efferent: Mossy fibres to CA3 pyramidal cells (the second leg of the trisynaptic circuit)
Hilar projections to the septum and, through the fimbria, to the fornix

afferent: Predominantly entorhinal layer-II perforant input, with contributions from other layers
Local hilar/interneuron and septal modulatory inputs
efferent: Granule-cell mossy fibres to CA3 and local hilar circuits

The record is positioned on the medial concave edge of the baked hippocampal cast (x ≈ 16, y ≈ 14, z ≈ −2, the record's own origin3d, probed from ctx-hippocampus-l by the v8 content-authoring run), and the pickable volume stays `nuc-hippocampus`. Named level membership is teaching/navigation metadata and has not been validated as a literal intersection of every displayed transverse section. The clinical text describes possible associations, not diagnostic rules.

function.before: The thin, three-layered (allocortical) blade of cortex tucked between the hippocampus and the subiculum: it is the first relay of the trisynaptic circuit, receiving the perforant path and sending mossy fibres to CA3, and it is one of the very few sites of adult neurogenesis in the human brain. Its granule-cell layer acts as a pattern separator that converts similar experiences into distinguishable memory codes.
function.after: The dentate gyrus is a folded, three-layered component of hippocampal formation with a granule-cell layer bordering the hilus. Entorhinal input reaches granule cells, whose mossy fibres project primarily to CA3. Experimental and human data support sparse coding/pattern separation; adult human neurogenesis has supporting evidence, while measured abundance and functional consequences remain method-dependent.

records.name: Amygdala

bloodSupply.before: Anterior choroidal artery (internal carotid) for the amygdala and the anterior uncus, with a variable contribution from the MCA (temporal branches) and the posterior communicating/anterior temporal arteries; venous drainage through the basal vein of Rosenthal.
bloodSupply.after: Variable anterior choroidal, MCA temporal and PCA anterior temporal contributions.

before.findings: Contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia (internal capsule, posterior limb; thalamus; optic radiation) — the amygdala lies in the same territory, and its infarction is usually overshadowed by the capsular deficit.
Bilateral amygdalectomy (or herpes encephalitis, trauma, frontotemporal dementia) produces hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia and hypermetamorphosis.
before.note: Structural/infectious; experimentally reproduced in monkeys by bilateral temporal lobectomy

before.findings: Selective bilateral amygdala destruction abolishes the normal fear response to threat and impairs recognition of fear in faces while leaving declarative memory and intellect intact.
before.note: Genetic (ECM1 mutation) — the human lesion model of the amygdala

before.findings: The amygdala is part of the epileptogenic zone in temporal-lobe epilepsy, generating the fear aura and the autonomic features (epigastric rising, tachycardia) that precede impaired awareness.
before.note: Epileptogenic rather than vascular

after.findings: Can produce elements of Klüver-Bucy syndrome; the complete pattern usually involves broader temporal networks and is not obligatory after isolated amygdala damage.
Fear or autonomic auras can involve amygdala-centered networks, but these symptoms do not uniquely establish amygdala onset.
May impair recognition/learning of threat-related signals; preservation or loss of fear depends on stimulus and wider systems.

efferent: Stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway to the septum, hypothalamus, orbitofrontal cortex and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis

Projections to the ventral striatum and medial dorsal thalamus (emotional modulation of the limbic loop)

afferent: Association/sensory cortex and hippocampal/entorhinal input

function.before: The threat-detection and emotional-salience centre of the temporal lobe: the basolateral complex evaluates sensory and social signals, the central nucleus drives the autonomic and hormonal fear response through the hypothalamus and brainstem, and the corticomedial group handles olfactory and reproductive input. It also tags emotionally significant events so that the hippocampus and cortex store them preferentially.
function.after: The amygdala is a nuclear complex in the anterior medial temporal lobe, anterior/superior to the hippocampal head. Its basolateral, corticomedial and central groups participate in emotional salience, learning, motivation and autonomic responses through widespread networks. It is not a single fear center or the sole source of fear.

records.name: Fornix

bloodSupply.before: Supplied along its course by the choroidal arteries (anterior and posterior choroidal) and the pericallosal branches of the ACA near the body; the columns are supplied by small branches of the anterior communicating/anterior cerebral complex.
bloodSupply.after: Small variable ACA/anterior communicating and choroidal-system branches along its course; no single vessel supplies the entire fornix.

before.findings: Bilateral fornix damage (surgery, colloid cyst, infarction, penetrating trauma) reproduces the mammillary-body form of amnesia: dense anterograde episodic amnesia with relative preservation of recognition and procedural learning.
before.vascular: Pericallosal/anterior cerebral branches, or posterior choroidal artery for the body

before.syndrome: Colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro
before.findings: A cyst at the anterior third ventricle compresses both fornices and obstructs the interventricular foramina, causing positional headache, drop attacks and hydrocephalus — a classic cause of reversible amnesia and sudden death.

Thiamine deficiency damages the mammillary bodies and the fornix along with the anterior and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei, producing the diencephalic amnestic syndrome with confabulation and oculomotor signs.
before.note: Nutritional/toxic (thiamine deficiency, alcohol-related)

after.findings: Bilateral injury can impair episodic memory; severity, recognition and recovery vary with lesion extent and associated damage.
Surgery or lesions near the foramen of Monro can injure fornices and impair memory; obstructive hydrocephalus is a distinct mechanism.

efferent: Mammillary bodies (postcommissural column) → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus (Papez circuit)

function.before: The principal efferent bundle of the hippocampal formation: fibres leave the hippocampus as the fimbria, ascend as the crus, join beneath the corpus callosum as the body (with the commissure of the fornix between the two crura), and split anteriorly — the postcommissural column to the mammillary body (the Papez circuit) and the precommissural fibres to the septal area and hypothalamus. It is the anatomical substrate of hippocampal control over memory-related diencephalic and endocrine circuits.
function.after: The fornix is an arch-shaped hippocampal white-matter pathway formed from alveus/fimbria, crura, body and columns. Postcommissural fibres reach mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus; precommissural fibres reach septal/basal-forebrain targets. It also carries septohippocampal afferents, so it is not purely efferent.

before.findings: Lesions of the splenium and the underlying hippocampal commissure produce disconnection of the two hemispheres for visual and memory material: alexia without agraphia with a left occipital infarct, and interhemispheric memory dissociation.

function.before: The midline crossing of hippocampal fibres beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum (the dorsal hippocampal commissure plus the ventral commissure of the fornix): it interconnects the two hippocampal formations, synchronizing their activity and permitting the bilateral hippocampal coordination that supports spatial and contextual memory.
function.after: The hippocampal commissure lies between the fornical crura beneath the posterior corpus callosum and carries interhemispheric medial temporal connections. bloodSupply.before: Anterior choroidal artery (anterior part, in the temporal horn) and posterior cerebral artery hippocampal branches (posterior part), the same territories that supply the hippocampus itself.

function.before: The white-matter fringe on the medial-dorsal surface of the hippocampus, formed by the axons leaving the subiculum and CA fields; it runs posteriorly, thickens into the crus of the fornix and so constitutes the first segment of the hippocampal outflow. function.after: The fimbria is a white-matter fringe along the medial/superior hippocampal surface beside the choroidal fissure. Fibres from the alveus converge into it and continue posteriorly as the fornical crus. It carries hippocampal outputs and returning septal afferents.

records.name: Optic nerve

bloodSupply.after: Optic-nerve head: mainly short posterior ciliary circulation; posterior orbital/canalicular nerve: ophthalmic/pial branches; intracranial segment: small carotid/ACA-related branches. Supply is segment-specific.

before.findings: Subacute painful monocular visual loss with reduced colour vision, an afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) and a central scotoma; the commonest presentation of demyelinating disease and the classic first symptom of multiple sclerosis, with the nerve enhancing on MRI and vision recovering over weeks.
before.note: Inflammatory/demyelinating (anti-AQP4 or MOG antibody disease in atypical cases), not vascular

before.syndrome: Papilloedema and optic atrophy from raised intracranial pressure
before.findings: Raised intracranial pressure is transmitted along the optic-nerve sheath, causing bilateral disc swelling, transient visual obscurations and enlarged blind spots; prolonged compression produces optic atrophy and permanent visual loss — the reason fundoscopy is mandatory in every headache assessment.
before.vascular: Not vascular — CSF pressure transmitted through the optic-nerve sheath (the sheath is continuous with the subarachnoid space)

before.findings: Infarction of the anterior optic nerve from occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries produces sudden painless monocular loss with an altitudinal field defect and a swollen disc (arteritic, giant-cell arteritis, in the elderly; non-arteritic otherwise).
before.vascular: Short posterior ciliary arteries (ophthalmic artery); the arteritic form accompanies giant-cell arteritis

before.syndrome: Optic-nerve compression by a sellar or suprasellar lesion
before.findings: A pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma or meningioma compressing the intracranial optic nerve causes monocular visual loss with a central or junctional scotoma, often before any endocrine symptom.
before.note: Compressive; the junctional scotoma (ipsilateral central plus contralateral temporal defect) localizes the lesion to the nerve-chiasm junction

after.findings: Can cause monocular acuity/color/field loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect when asymmetric. Patterns depend on inflammatory, ischemic, compressive or other causes.
Raised intracranial pressure can cause optic-disc swelling through the continuous nerve-sheath subarachnoid space; disc swelling also has other causes.

afferent: Retinal ganglion-cell axons from the ipsilateral eye
efferent: Continuation through optic chiasm into optic tracts, with retinal projections ultimately reaching LGN and extrageniculate targets

decussation.before: Not in the nerve itself: within each optic nerve all fibres are ipsilateral. The nasal half of each retina (52–55 % of the fibres) crosses in the optic chiasm immediately distal to the nerve, so the two optic nerves become the two optic tracts at that point.
decussation.after: No crossing within the optic nerve. Nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasm; temporal retinal fibres remain ipsilateral.

function.before: The second cranial nerve is not a peripheral nerve but a central white-matter tract evaginated from the diencephalon, wrapped in meninges and bathed in CSF along its intracranial segment — which is why it swells in papilloedema and is compressed by suprasellar masses. It carries the axons of roughly one million retinal ganglion cells from each eye and conveys the entire visual signal from photoreceptors to the brain, with the macula occupying about two-thirds of the fibres and the temporal crescent the far nasal periphery. Its fibres are organized retinotopically, so the pattern of a partial lesion (altitudinal, arcuate, central scotoma) localizes the damage along the visual pathway.
function.after: The optic nerve contains retinal ganglion-cell axons from one eye before the chiasm. It is developmentally a CNS pathway, with oligodendrocyte myelin posterior to the lamina cribrosa and a meningeal sheath. It conveys retinal output for vision and reflex/circadian pathways; it does not yet encode one contralateral binocular hemifield.

modality.before: Special sensory — vision; retinal ganglion-cell axons carrying the retinotopic map of the contralateral visual field half
modality.after: Special somatic sensory: retinal output from the ipsilateral eye before chiasmal partial crossing

origin.before: Retinal ganglion cells (the innermost retinal layer, whose axons converge at the optic disc, having relayed photoreceptor and bipolar-cell signals through the retina)
origin.after: Retinal ganglion cells of the ipsilateral eye

records.name: Optic chiasm (chiasmatic crossing)

bloodSupply.before: The superior hypophyseal arteries (branches of the internal carotid) and the prechiasmal branches of the ophthalmic and anterior cerebral arteries form a rich anastomotic supply, which is why the chiasm tolerates gradual compression before failing; sudden compression or surgical devascularization causes acute bitemporal loss. The chiasm lies immediately above the diaphragma sellae between the two internal carotid arteries.
bloodSupply.after: Small branches of carotid/superior hypophyseal and ACA/anterior communicating systems; contributions vary.

before.findings: Compression of the crossing nasal fibres produces loss of the temporal (peripheral) field of both eyes, beginning superiorly and progressing to a complete bitemporal hemianopia; the patient bumps into objects on both sides and may not notice until it is advanced. The classic cause is a pituitary adenoma growing out of the sella, followed by craniopharyngioma, meningioma of the tuberculum sellae and a suprasellar/parasellar aneurysm.
before.note: Compressive rather than vascular — a chiasmal lesion is diagnosed by the pattern of the field defect (bitemporal, respecting the vertical midline, chiasmal compression from below starts superiorly)

before.findings: A lesion at the junction of one optic nerve and the chiasm damages the ipsilateral optic nerve and the crossing fibres of the contralateral inferior nasal retina (Wilbrand's knee): a central scotoma in one eye with a superior temporal defect in the other localizes the lesion precisely, and is almost pathognomonic of a suprasellar mass.
before.note: Compressive; the pattern, not the field loss alone, is the localizing sign

before.findings: Sudden haemorrhagic infarction of a pituitary adenoma expands into the chiasm within minutes, producing acute bitemporal visual loss with severe headache, meningism, ophthalmoplegia and, in the catastrophic form, adrenal crisis — a neurosurgical emergency.
before.vascular: Pituitary apoplexy (haemorrhagic infarction of an adenoma); the chiasm is compressed rather than infarcted

after.findings: Can cause bitemporal field loss with variable asymmetry; compression from below often affects superior temporal fields first, but other patterns occur.
Optic-nerve loss in one eye plus a temporal defect in the other suggests nerve/chiasm involvement; it does not require a normal Wilbrand knee or prove one specific mass.

afferent: Optic nerves (tract-optic-nerve) from both eyes — nasal fibres crossing and temporal fibres passing through uncrossed
No other afferent: the chiasm is a pure crossing point, and its blood supply comes from the superior hypophyseal arteries and the internal carotid branches above the sella
efferent: Optic tracts (tract-optic-tract) — each tract now carries the contralateral visual half-field: temporal retina ipsilaterally, nasal retina contralaterally
Fibres of the retinohypothalamic tract leave the chiasm region to reach the suprachiasmatic nucleus for circadian photoentrainment

afferent: Retinal ganglion-cell axons via both optic nerves
efferent: Optic tracts; retinal fibres to hypothalamic circadian targets also leave the anterior visual pathway

The two records are deliberately distinct: the surface landmark marks the structure on the plates, this context record carries the fibre-crossing semantics and the clinical territory of the chiasm. BP3D's optic-chiasm mesh (FMA 90717, BP5710) is registered by the v8 geometry tasks.

function.before: The X-shaped midline crossing where the two optic nerves exchange their nasal retinal fibres: about 53 % of the axons (the nasal retina of each eye, which subserves the temporal visual field of that eye) cross to the contralateral side, while the temporal retinal fibres stay ipsilateral. The result is the fundamental reorganization of the visual pathway — from that point onward every structure carries the contralateral half-field rather than the contralateral eye. The crossing is topographically ordered (the macular fibres occupy the central and posterior part, the inferior nasal fibres loop forward into the contralateral nerve — Wilbrand's knee — and the dorsal fibres pass posteriorly), and the chiasm sits directly above the pituitary sella between the internal carotid arteries, which is why sellar masses compress it from below and in front.
function.after: The optic chiasm is a flattened midline partial crossing above the pituitary/sella and below the hypothalamus. Nasal retinal fibres cross while temporal retinal fibres remain ipsilateral, reorganizing each optic tract to represent the contralateral binocular visual hemifield. There is no synaptic relay here; Wilbrand's knee should not be taught as a verified normal human fibre loop.

records.name: Optic tract

bloodSupply.after: Variable anterior choroidal and proximal carotid/PCA-related branches.

before.findings: A complete or partial optic-tract lesion produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopia that is characteristically incongruous (the two eyes' defects differ in size and shape, because the crossing and non-crossing fibres are not yet perfectly aligned for corresponding retinal points) — the field defect that distinguishes a tract lesion from a cortical one, where the defects are congruent.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (thalamogeniculate/anterior temporal branches) or anterior choroidal artery (which supplies the tract's lateral part and the adjacent internal capsule and optic radiation)

before.syndrome: Riddoch phenomenon and the tract's asymmetric pupillary defect
before.findings: Because a minority of tract fibres carry the pupillary light reflex afferents to the pretectum, an optic-tract lesion can produce a subtle contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect (the pupillary sign described by Bell) in addition to the hemianopia — absent in lesions behind the LGN.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery territory; the pupillary fibres leave the tract before the LGN

before.syndrome: Incipient or incomplete hemianopia with macular sparing patterns
before.findings: Slowly growing sellar/suprasellar or temporal-lobe lesions produce a partial hemianopia that is often misinterpreted as chiasmal or retinal disease; because the macular fibres occupy a large central portion of the tract and the LGN is organized with the macula posterolaterally, careful perimetry is required to localize the level.
before.note: Compressive (tumour) rather than vascular; the pattern of field loss is the localizing tool

after.findings: Can cause contralateral homonymous field loss, often incongruous, but congruity alone does not reliably locate every lesion.
An asymmetric optic-tract lesion may cause a contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect. This is distinct from the Riddoch phenomenon, which concerns residual motion perception.

efferent: LGN for geniculostriate vision; pretectal and superior-collicular targets for reflex/orienting pathways

decussation.before: Complete by this point: the tract itself does not cross. Each optic tract carries the whole contralateral visual half-field, and its fibres are rearranged inside the lateral geniculate nucleus, where the laminae segregate the crossed and uncrossed inputs for the same point in visual space.
decussation.after: No crossing in the optic tract; partial retinal crossing has occurred at the chiasm.

function.before: The postchiasmatic segment of the visual pathway: it sweeps from the chiasm around the cerebral peduncle beneath the temporal lobe, hugging the diencephalon, and delivers a retinotopically ordered fibre bundle to the lateral geniculate nucleus. The tract carries the entire contralateral half-field, and its fibres are sorted into the laminated structure of the LGN (layers 1, 4, 6 from the contralateral eye and 2, 3, 5 from the ipsilateral eye) before the geniculostriate relay to V1. Its close relation to the uncus and the medial temporal lobe explains the congruity of the visual defects of temporal-lobe surgery, and its course alongside the internal capsule and the third nerve explains the classic syndromes of the region.
function.after: Each optic tract continues posterolaterally from the chiasm around the diencephalic/cerebral-peduncular region and carries the contralateral visual hemifield from both eyes. Most fibres reach the LGN; others serve pretectal and collicular functions. The retinohypothalamic circadian projection is a separate retinal pathway, not an obligatory tract-to-SCN relay.

modality.before: Special sensory — vision; the contralateral visual half-field, with the nasal retinal fibres crossed at the chiasm and the temporal fibres uncrossed
modality.after: Special somatic sensory: contralateral binocular visual hemifield and retinal reflex/orienting projections

origin.before: Optic chiasm (each tract is the continuation of the ipsilateral temporal and contralateral nasal fibres)
origin.after: Optic chiasm: ipsilateral temporal plus contralateral nasal retinal fibres

records.name: Primary motor cortex (M1) — toe representation

bloodSupply.before: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal and callosomarginal branches) — the medial surface above the cingulate sulcus.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly ACA medial sensorimotor branches, with variation.

before.syndrome: Focal motor deficit of the toe — cortical (M1) localisation
before.findings: Contralateral foot/leg weakness with a relatively spared hand and face; the medial position of this segment makes an anterior cerebral artery territorial infarct the leading explanation, and the deficit may be accompanied by abulia and urinary incontinence when the adjacent SMA and anterior cingulate are involved.

before.syndrome: Jacksonian march starting in this segment
before.findings: An irritative lesion of the toe representation produces a focal motor seizure that marches to the neighbouring segment in somatotopic order (the next more lateral body part), followed by a transient Todd paresis of the same distribution.
before.note: Structural/epileptic; the march follows the order in `anchors.somatotopicOrder`

after.findings: An injury of the corresponding motor network may impair the represented movement; isolated body-part symptoms also have peripheral and subcortical causes.

afferent: Thalamocortical input from the ventral lateral (VL) and ventral anterior (VA) nuclei (nuc-vl, nuc-va) — the cerebellothalamocortical and pallidothalamocortical motor loops, in the same somatotopic order as the strip

efferent: Corticospinal fibres for the toe through the corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, crus cerebri, basis pontis and pyramid (tract-corticospinal-lateral), keeping the same somatotopic order in the pyramid

afferent: Motor thalamic and premotor/SMA network input

contextNote.before: Authored v9 record for the toe segment of the somatotopic map. PLACEMENT IS SCHEMATIC ON THE DERIVED ctx-hemisphere-l RIBBON, not a gyral or cytoarchitectonic boundary: the centre is the ribbon vertex nearest to an authored landmark on the precentral bank, measured with nearest-vertex projection by .dsh-scratch/somatotopy-probe7b.mjs (residual 0.04 au = 0.05 mm to the nearest surface vertex; mean triangle edge 1.31 au = 1.57 mm; 1 au = 1.2 mm). The patch reads its outward normal (-0.759, 0.633, 0.15) from that vertex and its half-sizes [3.8, 3.0, 3.0] au from the measured spacing between neighbouring segments; the ordering coordinate is the arc length along the fitted strip (s = 0.00 au at this segment), strictly increasing from toe to larynx on both strips. Why the number matters: nearest-vertex residuals came down from a first-pass min 0.56 / median 2.60 / max 3.93 au (probe4) to min 0.01 / median 0.04 / max 0.16 au on M1 and min 0.29 / median 0.78 / max 2.29 au on S1, so the two S1 segments that snap to a different fold (foot/toe 1.00 au, leg 2.29 au, larynx 2.20 au) are the least certain placements in the table. The two strips are NOT a cytoarchitectonic segmentation (no Brodmann 4/3a/3b/1/2 map exists in this atlas) and the atlas' derived ribbon does not carry central-sulcus geometry, so the Primary motor cortex (M1) attribution is a position along the fitted medial-paracentral -> lateral-opercular strip, not a sulcus traced on the mesh. contextNote.after: Schematic toe teaching patch on a derived hemisphere ribbon. The authored coordinate, patch size, surface normal and displayed order are renderer metadata, not subject-specific fMRI, a traced central sulcus, or a cytoarchitectural segmentation. A small distance to the host mesh does not validate functional location. Bilateral mirrored display does not imply identical functional maps. The eight-segment homunculus simplifies overlapping/interleaved motor and sensory representations; laryngeal/orofacial placements are especially uncertain.

function.before: The most medial part of the motor strip, tucked into the paracentral lobule on the medial surface of the hemisphere: it drives the intrinsic foot and toe muscles through the most medial (and longest-running) corticospinal fibres. Its medial position is why a foot-predominant weakness points at an anterior cerebral artery territory lesion rather than at the convexity, and why the foot and bladder representations are described together on the medial surface.
function.after: Teaching marker for the toe component of the motor homunculus in precentral/anterior paracentral cortex, broadly associated with the medial paracentral foot/toe region. Representations overlap; voluntary control is predominantly contralateral for distal limbs, while axial and orofacial control has substantial bilateral network contributions. This patch is a schematic teaching aid, not a measured functional boundary.

before.syndrome: Cortical (S1) sensory loss of the toe

before.syndrome: Thalamic pain syndrome after a lesion of the ascending relay

before.note: The cortical segment itself is not the lesion, but it is the end of the pathway whose loss is described

after.findings: Somatosensory cortical injury can impair relevant contralateral sensory discrimination, but deficits do not verify an exact patch boundary.

records.name: Body of the lateral ventricle

bloodSupply.before: Anterior choroidal artery (internal carotid) and the lateral posterior choroidal artery (posterior cerebral artery) supply the choroid plexus and the subependymal tissue of the body through the choroidal fissure; the adjacent thalamus is supplied by the posterior choroidal and thalamogeniculate branches, and the adjacent caudate body by the lenticulostriate arteries. Venous drainage is through the thalamostriate vein into the internal cerebral vein.
bloodSupply.after: The CSF cavity is not an arterial tissue territory. Body plexus receives mainly lateral posterior choroidal supply with choroidal anastomoses; adjacent caudate/thalamus/callosal tissue receives its own striate, thalamic or callosal arterial supply.

before.syndrome: Central neurocytoma (foramen of Monro/body of the lateral ventricle)
before.findings: A calcified, enhancing intraventricular mass attached to the septum pellucidum at the level of the foramen of Monro in a young adult causes intermittent obstructive hydrocephalus and headache; it is the classic tumour of the ventricular body in this age group.
before.vascular: Choroidal feeders (anterior/posterior choroidal arteries) at surgery

before.syndrome: Thalamostriate vein displacement as a mass sign
before.findings: On coronal imaging the thalamostriate vein and the internal cerebral vein form the venous angle at the foramen of Monro; their displacement distinguishes an intraventricular mass (displacing the vein laterally) from a thalamic mass (displacing it medially).
before.note: Imaging localizing sign rather than a disease

before.findings: Tumour cells and infection spread along the ependyma of the body and the subependymal plate, producing linear enhancement; the same subependymal germinal matrix is the origin of periventricular nodular heterotopia and the site of germinal-matrix haemorrhage at the caudothalamic groove.
before.note: Neoplastic/infectious, or developmental for heterotopia

before.findings: Because the body is bounded above by the corpus callosum and below by the thalamus, its disproportionate enlargement with an upgoing third ventricle on sagittal MRI is the hallmark of aqueductal stenosis, and it produces the 'Mickey Mouse' appearance of the frontal horns on axial imaging.
before.note: CSF dynamics and imaging interpretation

after.findings: Central neurocytoma often attaches near the septum pellucidum/foramen region and may obstruct CSF. Calcification and enhancement can support a differential diagnosis but histopathology establishes tumor type.

Tumor or infection can involve the ependymal/subependymal region; abnormal enhancement is nonspecific. Developmental heterotopia and premature-infant germinal-matrix haemorrhage have different mechanisms and should not be treated as the same disorder.
Can accompany upstream CSF obstruction or tissue-volume loss. Aqueductal stenosis typically enlarges lateral/third ventricles; no body shape alone is a specific diagnostic hallmark.

afferent: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle (vent-choroid-plexus-lateral), which occupies the floor of the body
Frontal horn (vent-lateral-ventricle-frontal-horn) anteriorly
efferent: Interventricular foramen of Monro (vent-interventricular-foramen) anteriorly → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle; the atrium and temporal horn posteriorly are terminal recesses, not a route to the aqueduct
Venous drainage of the ependymal surface through the thalamostriate and internal cerebral veins, which converge at the venous angle behind the foramen of Monro

afferent: Frontal-horn and atrial CSF communication
CSF secretion from choroid plexus
efferent: Foramen of Monro → third ventricle; horns/atrium are communicating recesses

contextNote.before: Authored at a documented plane: the body is the segment of the lateral-ventricle cast that the v8 bake splits between the frontal horn and the atrium — the boundaries are the plane z = +28 (foramen/body boundary — the anterior limit of this segment on the baked cast) and the plane z = −6 (atrium boundary), which reproduce the segment's measured extent y 40.1…59.3, z −6…27.9 (the frontal horn's documented extent, z 25.2…37.5, overlaps this segment across the boundary because both numbers describe one continuous cast, not a cut mesh), centroid (5.5, 50.2, 10.7) probed from tel-lateral-ventricle-l by the v8 content-authoring run. The plane anchors are recorded so the split is documented rather than implicit (docs/NEUROATLAS_V8_PLAN.md §1c, §4.5).
contextNote.after: Schematic segment of the committed lateral-ventricular model. The origin and dimensions are display anchors in the atlas frame; segment cut planes and mesh-centroid measurements do not validate boundaries or dimensions in an individual brain. Refer to the complete cast and surrounding anatomical relationships.

function.before: The central part of the lateral ventricle — the long horizontal segment between the frontal horn (at the interventricular foramen) and the atrium, roofed by the body of the corpus callosum and floored by the thalamus medially and the caudate nucleus laterally, with the choroid plexus running along its floor through the choroidal fissure. It is the segment that defines the thalamostriate groove: the thalamostriate vein and the stria terminalis mark the caudothalamic junction along its floor, the vein of Galen's tributaries (internal cerebral veins) run in the tela choroidea above the thalamus, and the subependymal venous angle at the foramen of Monro is the surgical landmark for the anterior third ventricle. Its width and the height of the corpus callosum above it are the standard measures of ventricular enlargement.
function.after: Central portion posterior to the foramen of Monro and anterior to the atrium, roofed by the corpus callosum. Floor relations include caudate body laterally and thalamus more medially, separated by the stria terminalis/thalamostriate region; fornix and septum pellucidum contribute medially. Choroid plexus lies along the choroidal fissure. This describes gross relationships, not precise boundaries in every specimen.

records.name: Lateral ventricle

bloodSupply.before: The ependymal surface itself is avascular and nourished by CSF; the adjoining walls are supplied by the anterior choroidal artery (temporal horn and atrium region), the lateral and medial posterior choroidal arteries (body and trigone) and lenticulostriate branches (adjacent basal ganglia). Subependymal veins (thalamostriate and internal cerebral veins) drain the region.
bloodSupply.after: The ventricle is a fluid space, not an arterial tissue territory. Adjacent neural walls have region-specific arterial supply; its choroid plexus is supplied mainly by anterior and lateral posterior choroidal arteries. Subependymal/deep veins drain surrounding tissue, not the CSF cavity.

before.findings: Blockage at or below the interventricular foramen dilates the lateral ventricles disproportionately, with transependymal CSF seepage, headache, papilloedema and, in infants, macrocephaly with a sun-setting sign.
before.vascular: Not vascular — mechanical obstruction (colloid cyst, tumour, aqueductal stenosis, intraventricular haemorrhage)

before.findings: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy with a normal opening pressure presents as the triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and dementia — the one reversible dementia of CSF dynamics.
before.note: CSF dynamics; ventricular size alone does not distinguish it from ex vacuo dilatation

before.findings: Germinal-matrix bleeding in the caudothalamic groove ruptures into the lateral ventricle, and the resulting blood and ependymal injury cause post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus — the commonest cause of acquired hydrocephalus in newborns.

Mild asymmetry and an asymmetric occipital horn are common normal variants; a disproportionately large temporal horn is an early sign of true hydrocephalus, whereas uniform ventricular enlargement with cortical atrophy indicates ex vacuo dilatation.
before.note: Imaging interpretation rather than a syndrome

after.findings: Blockage at a foramen of Monro can enlarge one or both lateral ventricles; aqueductal blockage usually enlarges both lateral and third ventricles with a relatively normal fourth. Symptoms and transependymal flow depend on pressure and time course.

A clinical syndrome with gait impairment, cognitive difficulty and urinary symptoms associated with ventriculomegaly. The full triad is not required and one normal pressure measurement is not diagnostic; ventricular size alone cannot distinguish it from atrophy.

In premature infants, fragile germinal-matrix vessels near the caudothalamic groove can bleed into the ventricle. Subsequent CSF obstruction and impaired absorption may cause post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation.
Mild asymmetry can be a normal variant. Interpretation requires surrounding tissue, obstruction and clinical context, rather than a horn-size rule alone.

afferent: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle (vent-choroid-plexus-lateral), which produces most of the CSF this space contains
efferent: Interventricular foramen of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle; the subarachnoid space is reached through the fourth-ventricle foramina
Venous drainage of its walls through subependymal veins (thalamostriate, septal, caudate) into the internal cerebral vein and the great cerebral vein

afferent: CSF secretion mainly from its choroid plexus
efferent: Interventricular foramen → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → Magendie/Luschka apertures → subarachnoid space

function.before: The paired C-shaped CSF space of the cerebral hemisphere: its body lies under the corpus callosum with the caudate above the thalamus, and its frontal, temporal and occipital horns extend into the three lobes around the thalamus. It hosts the choroid plexus that produces most of the CSF it contains and drains through the interventricular foramen of Monro into the third ventricle, and thence through the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle — the atrium and the temporal and occipital horns are terminal recesses of the same compartment, so its shape is a direct readout of the deep hemispheric anatomy.
function.after: Paired C-shaped CSF cavities within the cerebral hemispheres. The frontal horn lies anterior to the foramen of Monro, the body continues posteriorly under the corpus callosum, and the atrium joins body with occipital and temporal horns. Each lateral ventricle communicates with the third ventricle through its own interventricular foramen. Plexus is present in the body, atrium and temporal horn, not the frontal or occipital horn.

records.name: Frontal horn of the lateral ventricle

bloodSupply.before: Recurrent artery of Heubner and medial lenticulostriate branches of the ACA supply the caudate head forming its lateral wall; the anterior choroidal artery and the septal veins drain and supply the medio-inferior adjacent tissue. The ependyma is sustained by CSF.
bloodSupply.after: No arterial supply to the CSF space itself. Caudate/septal/callosal walls receive their own variable ACA/MCA/deep perforator supply; venous drainage concerns the wall tissue.

before.findings: Frontal-horn widening is quantified by the Evans index (maximal frontal horn width divided by maximal inner skull width); a ratio above 0.3 defines ventriculomegaly and is the standard criterion on CT.

before.syndrome: Colloid cyst obstruction at the foramen
before.findings: A colloid cyst at the anterior third ventricle plugs one or both interventricular foramina, dilating the frontal horns abruptly and causing positional headache, drop attacks, papilloedema and sudden death.
before.note: Mechanical obstruction; the frontal horns are the first to dilate

before.findings: In preterm infants, bleeding in the caudothalamic groove at the junction of the frontal horn and body ruptures through the ependyma; graded I-IV by the extent of ventricular and parenchymal blood.

after.findings: Frontal-horn width can be used in the Evans index (maximum frontal horn width / maximum internal skull width). A value around or above 0.30 is commonly used as a ventriculomegaly screening threshold, but it does not establish hydrocephalus or its cause.
A colloid cyst or other lesion near Monro may obstruct one or both lateral ventricles. Enlargement is upstream, not proven to start exclusively in the frontal horns.
Premature-infant caudothalamic germinal-matrix haemorrhage can extend into the frontal horn/body. Periventricular haemorrhagic infarction is not simply an extension grade of intraventricular blood.

afferent: None — the frontal horn is a blind anterior recess with no choroid plexus of its own
efferent: Continuous posteriorly with the body; CSF leaves through the interventricular foramen of Monro in the posterior floor of the horn, into the third ventricle

afferent: CSF communication with the ventricular body; no local plexus
efferent: Body/interventricular foramen region → third ventricle

records.name: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle

bloodSupply.before: Anterior choroidal artery (internal carotid) supplies the choroid plexus of the temporal horn and the adjacent hippocampus/amygdala; the posterior cerebral artery (hippocampal and posterior choroidal branches) supplies the posterior part. The basal vein of Rosenthal drains the region.
bloodSupply.after: The cavity has no intrinsic arterial supply. Temporal-horn choroid plexus receives anterior choroidal and lateral posterior choroidal contributions; adjacent hippocampal/amygdalar tissue has variable PCA, anterior choroidal and other regional supply.

before.findings: A widened temporal horn is one of the earliest reliable signs of true (as opposed to ex vacuo) ventricular enlargement, because the temporal horn is the first part of the lateral ventricle to dilate.
Hippocampal atrophy with loss of the normal internal architecture narrows the temporal horn on the affected side and is accompanied by T2 hyperintensity and secondary temporal-lobe volume loss.
before.note: Epilepsy-related; the temporal horn is the imaging window onto the hippocampus

before.findings: The temporal horn choroid plexus and the hippocampus/amygdala fall in the anterior choroidal territory, so temporal-horn infarction accompanies the capsular triad of hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia.

after.findings: May be an early sign of hydrocephalus, but may also result from hippocampal or temporal tissue atrophy, a trapped horn or normal asymmetry. It does not by itself distinguish obstruction from ex-vacuo enlargement.
after.vascular: CSF obstruction or regional volume loss

after.findings: Hippocampal atrophy with altered internal architecture and increased T2/FLAIR signal may be accompanied by ipsilateral temporal-horn and choroidal-fissure enlargement, not narrowing. These secondary signs are not sufficient alone for diagnosis.
Neural tissue or plexus near the horn may infarct; the CSF cavity itself does not infarct. Capsular/visual findings depend on the additional affected structures.
after.vascular: Anterior choroidal and overlapping regional branches

records.name: Occipital horn of the lateral ventricle

bloodSupply.before: Lateral posterior choroidal artery branches (from the PCA) supply the adjoining plexus and walls of the trigone; the calcarine (PCA) branches and the splenial vessels supply the medial wall, with venous drainage through the internal cerebral vein and the basal vein.
bloodSupply.after: No arterial supply to the CSF space. Adjacent occipital and callosal tissue has PCA and variable collateral supply; choroidal arteries supply nearby atrial plexus, not plexus within this horn.

before.findings: One occipital horn is commonly larger than the other or absent (especially on the left); recognising this as a normal variant avoids misdiagnosing atrophy or hydrocephalus.
before.note: Normal anatomical variation

before.findings: Posterior periventricular white-matter injury (prematurity, ischaemia) enlarges the occipital horns disproportionately, producing the characteristic colpocephaly pattern.

The tapetum forming the roof of the occipital horn is part of the splenium's outflow; lesions of the splenium that spare the optic radiations can produce interhemispheric visual disconnection without a field defect.

after.findings: Size and asymmetry vary substantially, and a horn may be very small or absent. A fixed side preference is not established by this model.

Can accompany white-matter volume loss, developmental abnormalities or hydrocephalus. Colpocephaly describes disproportionate occipital-horn enlargement and is not uniquely synonymous with periventricular leukomalacia.

efferent: None — blind posterior recess: CSF returns to the atrium and leaves the ventricle only through the interventricular foramen of Monro

function.before: The posterior extension of the lateral ventricle into the occipital lobe: its roof is formed by the tapetum (splenial fibres of the corpus callosum), its medial wall carries the calcar avis (the bulge of the calcarine fissure) and the bulb of the posterior horn, and its lateral wall carries the collateral trigone. function.after: Variable posterior recess extending from the atrium into the occipital lobe. Tapetum forms much of its roof and lateral wall; the medial wall can show a bulb related to forceps major and the calcar avis related to the calcarine sulcus. No choroid plexus extends into the occipital horn proper.
