records.name: Atrium of the lateral ventricle

bloodSupply.before: Lateral posterior choroidal artery (posterior cerebral artery) supplies the glomus and the atrial plexus, with contributions from the anterior choroidal artery anteriorly and the medial posterior choroidal artery medially; venous drainage via the internal cerebral and basal veins.
bloodSupply.after: No arterial supply to the cavity. Atrial glomus/plexus is supplied chiefly by lateral posterior choroidal branches with anterior choroidal contributions; neighbouring white matter and wall tissue have their own supply.

before.findings: The glomus at the atrial trigone is the commonest site of choroid plexus xanthogranuloma and of asymptomatic plexus cysts; both are usually incidental but can obstruct CSF flow when large.

The trigone is the classic site of intraventricular meningioma, presenting with headache, papilloedema and contralateral homonymous field loss (adjacent optic radiation) rather than with focal weakness.

before.syndrome: Atrial enlargement as an early hydrocephalus sign
before.findings: The atrium and temporal horn dilate before the frontal horns in early hydrocephalus because they have the least surrounding white-matter bulk to compress them.
before.note: CSF dynamics and imaging interpretation

after.findings: Meningioma and other intraventricular masses may arise here, causing headache or obstruction. Adjacent optic-radiation injury or surgical corridor injury may cause a homonymous field defect.
Calcification and small choroid plexus cysts may be incidental. Imaging appearance and context distinguish these from tumor or obstruction.
Can be part of hydrocephalus or regional tissue loss; a universal atrium-before-frontal-horn sequence or least-white-matter explanation is not established.

afferent: Body of the lateral ventricle and the occipital horn converge here; the choroid plexus fills the trigone from the choroidal fissure
efferent: CSF leaves through the body and the interventricular foramen of Monro; the temporal and occipital horns are terminal recesses. The plexus at the glomus absorbs and produces CSF and is the landmark for atrial surgery

afferent: Body, temporal horn and occipital horn communicate here; local plexus secretes CSF
efferent: Through body to the foramen of Monro; temporal/occipital horns are recesses, not separate routes to the aqueduct

records.name: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle

bloodSupply.before: Anterior choroidal artery (from the internal carotid) supplies the plexus in the temporal horn and inferior body; the lateral posterior choroidal artery (from the PCA) supplies the body, trigone and glomus; the medial posterior choroidal artery supplies the plexus near the foramen and the third ventricle. These arteries are the feeders of choroid plexus tumours.
bloodSupply.after: Main lateral-ventricular plexus inflow from anterior choroidal and lateral posterior choroidal arteries, with variable anastomotic contributions. Medial posterior choroidal branches primarily supply third-ventricular plexus. Choroidal veins drain into the deep venous system.

before.findings: A villous neoplasm (usually in the lateral ventricle of a child or the fourth ventricle of an adult) overproduces CSF, causing communicating hydrocephalus with enlarged plexus and, when malignant, drop metastases through the CSF pathways.
before.vascular: Anterior and posterior choroidal arteries (the vessels to be embolized or controlled at surgery)

before.findings: Physiological calcification of the atrial glomus is common after the fourth decade and must be distinguished from a calcified tumour or from subependymal spread of a germinoma.
before.note: Normal ageing finding

before.findings: Bacterial or cryptococcal ventriculitis enhances the plexus avidly on MRI and causes loculated hydrocephalus, which is why plexus enhancement in a febrile patient is treated urgently.
before.note: Infectious

before.findings: Small cysts at the glomus are common and almost always incidental in adults; in fetuses they are a soft marker that resolves in most cases.
before.note: Incidental finding

after.findings: A plexus tumor may cause hydrocephalus through obstruction, CSF overproduction and/or impaired absorption after bleeding. Lateral-ventricular tumors are commoner in children and fourth-ventricular tumors in adults; location alone does not establish tumor type.
Atrial glomus calcification can be a normal age-related finding; age, symmetry, mass and enhancement determine whether further evaluation is needed.
Normal choroid plexus enhances because its capillaries are fenestrated. Abnormal enhancement may occur with inflammation or tumor, but enhancement alone does not diagnose infection.

afferent: Anterior choroidal artery (internal carotid) to the temporal horn and the inferior body; lateral and medial posterior choroidal arteries (posterior cerebral) to the body, trigone and glomus
Choroidal fissure attachments through the tela choroidea, along which it enters each ventricle
efferent: CSF secreted into the lateral ventricles flows through the interventricular foramen to the third ventricle — the atrium and temporal horn are the plexus-bearing terminal segments of that same lateral-ventricle compartment
Venous drainage through choroidal veins into the internal cerebral, basal and great cerebral veins

afferent: Arterial blood through anterior/lateral posterior choroidal branches

efferent: CSF secretion into the lateral ventricle

function.before: The villous, fenestrated capillary-CSF interface that secretes the great majority of the cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood-CSF barrier: it extends from the interventricular foramen along the body and atrium into the temporal horn, but is absent from the frontal and occipital horns. Its epithelial tight junctions, carbonic anhydrase activity and aquaporin-1 expression make CSF production a regulated, energy-dependent process — and the target of acetazolamide.
function.after: Vascular villous tissue projecting into the ventricular body, atrium and temporal horn, absent from the frontal and occipital horns. Choroid epithelium actively secretes much of the CSF and its tight junctions form the blood-CSF barrier; the capillaries themselves are fenestrated. It connects with the third-ventricular plexus near the interventricular foramen.

records.name: Interventricular foramen

bloodSupply.before: Supplied at its margins by the anterior choroidal artery, the medial posterior choroidal artery and small branches of the anterior cerebral/anterior communicating complex; the foramen lies adjacent to the thalamostriate and internal cerebral veins.
bloodSupply.after: The opening itself is not perfused tissue. Nearby thalamic/forniceal and plexal tissue has variable deep/choroidal arterial supply; deep veins are adjacent landmarks.

before.syndrome: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
before.findings: A cyst impacted at the foramen of Monro causes intermittent positional headache, drop attacks and acute hydrocephalus with dilated lateral ventricles and a normal-sized third ventricle, and is a recognized cause of sudden death.

before.findings: Obstruction of one foramen (tumour, cyst, ventriculitis, shunt malfunction) dilates only that lateral ventricle, shifting the septum pellucidum across the midline.

before.findings: A enhancing mass at the foramen of Monro in a patient with tuberous sclerosis obstructs CSF flow and is one of the major diagnostic criteria for the disease.
before.note: Genetic/hamartomatous; the location makes it symptomatic

after.findings: A lesion near Monro can obstruct one or both lateral ventricles, sometimes causing intermittent or acute hydrocephalus. Sudden deterioration is possible but not the usual course of every small cyst.
One blocked foramen can produce predominantly ipsilateral lateral-ventricular enlargement; ventricular asymmetry alone does not prove obstruction.
A subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis or another intraventricular mass may obstruct CSF flow. Imaging and disease context are needed for diagnosis.

records.name: Body of the corpus callosum

bloodSupply.before: ACA — pericallosal and callosomarginal branches supply the anterior body; PCA — splenial and posterior pericallosal branches supply the posterior body; the callosal arteries run in the pericallosal cistern above the body.
bloodSupply.after: Mainly ACA pericallosal branches; posterior callosal territory may overlap PCA supply.

before.findings: Infarction of the callosal body accompanies anterior cerebral artery stroke and adds interhemispheric disconnection to the leg-predominant hemiparesis: the left hand acts against the patient's intent (alien hand), and bimanual tasks decompose.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal branches); posterior body also receives posterior cerebral (splenial) branches

before.findings: Sectioning the callosal body prevents secondary generalization of seizures and reveals the disconnection syndrome: the left hand behaves independently, and objects palpated by the left hand cannot be named.
before.note: Therapeutic lesion — the classical experimental model of disconnection

before.findings: Necrosis of the callosal body (and genu/splenium) in chronic severe alcohol use causes acute confusion, dysarthria, apraxia and interhemispheric disconnection with T2-hyperintense callosal lesions.

before.findings: Callosal atrophy with regional specificity (anterior in frontotemporal dementia, posterior in Alzheimer disease, focal in ALS) is a marker of the cortical regions whose commissural fibres have degenerated.

after.findings: Lesions can impair bimanual tasks or interhemispheric motor/sensory transfer; signs depend on portion and associated cortical damage.

function.before: The long arched trunk of the commissure that forms the roof of the lateral ventricles, carrying the great majority of the ~200 million callosal axons between the sensorimotor, parietal and temporal association cortices. Its topographical organization mirrors the cortical map: the anterior body connects motor and premotor areas, the posterior body connects parietal and auditory regions, and the ventricular-facing fibres are the thinnest and most recently evolved.
function.after: The callosal body is the arch-shaped trunk above the lateral ventricles. It carries interhemispheric fibres, including sensorimotor and parietal connections, with overlapping topography and variable individual organization.

bloodSupply.before: PCA — splenial branches (from the posterior cerebral artery) and the posterior pericallosal artery; the splenium is at the junction of the ACA and PCA pericallosal territories.

before.findings: A left occipital infarct that also destroys the splenium isolates the intact right visual cortex from the left language areas: the patient can write but cannot read what they have written, and can copy letters without comprehension.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (left calcarine and splenial branches)

before.findings: Selective splenial lesions impair interhemispheric transfer of visual and memory information (for example matching across the midline) while visual fields remain full — a pure transfer defect.

function.before: The thick, rounded posterior end of the corpus callosum: its fibres form the forceps major (interconnecting the occipital and posterior parietal cortices, arching as the tapetum over the occipital and temporal horns) and the dorsal hippocampal commissure lies immediately beneath it. It is the decisive interhemispheric link for visual material, so its destruction disconnects the seeing right hemisphere from the speaking left one.
function.after: The splenium is the thick posterior corpus callosum and carries posterior interhemispheric visual/association connections. Forceps major extends into occipital white matter, while tapetal fibres line parts of the lateral ventricle. The adjacent hippocampal commissure is anatomically distinct.

records.name: Internal capsule, anterior limb

bloodSupply.before: Recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) and the medial lenticulostriate branches of the MCA supply its anterior half; the lateral lenticulostriate arteries supply its posterior half, and the anterior choroidal artery reaches its posterior-inferior edge.
bloodSupply.after: ACA/Heubner and MCA lenticulostriate branches with variable overlap.

before.findings: Small perforator infarcts here produce subtle frontal-executive slowing, apathy or a mild contralateral hemiparesis rather than a dense stroke; they are frequently mistaken for lacunes of the caudate head.
before.vascular: Medial lenticulostriate arteries (middle cerebral artery) / recurrent artery of Heubner

before.syndrome: Frontopontine fibre involvement in capsular stroke
before.findings: Damage to the anterior limb interrupts corticopontine traffic to the contralateral cerebellum (via the double crossing of the pontocerebellar system), which is why capsular strokes may leave mild ipsilateral cerebellar-type ataxia alongside the hemiparesis.

after.findings: May disrupt frontal-thalamic networks and produce executive, motivational or behavioral changes; weakness depends on associated motor-fibre injury.
Capsular/corona-radiata injury can combine contralateral weakness and ataxia on the same affected body side; ataxia is not ipsilateral to the cerebral lesion.

efferent: Frontopontine fibres from the frontal cortex to the pontine nuclei; cortico-amygdalar and corticostriate fibres crossing its bed

function.before: The front half of the internal capsule, lying between the head of the caudate medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally: it carries the anterior thalamic radiation (MD and anterior nuclei to the prefrontal and cingulate cortex) in its anterior part and the frontopontine fibres descending from the frontal lobe posteriorly. function.after: The anterior limb lies between caudate head medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. It carries anterior thalamic radiation, reciprocal frontal-thalamic fibres and frontopontine projections. It is a projection-fibre corridor, not an independent relay nucleus.

before.findings: Corticobulbar fibre damage yields contralateral lower facial and tongue weakness with relatively preserved limb power; bilateral involvement of the genu produces pseudobulbar palsy with emotional incontinence.

after.findings: Can cause contralateral lower facial or tongue weakness and dysarthria; bilateral pathway injury can produce pseudobulbar syndrome.

efferent: Corticobulbar fibres from the lower precentral gyrus and frontal operculum to the motor nuclei of CN V, VII, IX/X and XII; corticoreticular fibres to the brainstem reticular formation

function.before: The apex of the internal capsule, where the fibre plane turns from the anterior to the posterior limb between the caudate head and the thalamus: it contains the corticobulbar (corticonuclear) fibres bound for the cranial-nerve motor nuclei, with the face and tongue representations lying immediately adjacent in the posterior limb. function.after: The genu is the bend between anterior and posterior limbs, near the caudate-thalamus transition. Corticobulbar projections are conventionally localized to genu/anterior posterior-limb regions, but their precise distribution is not a rigid single compartment.

records.name: Internal capsule, posterior limb

bloodSupply.before: Lateral lenticulostriate branches of the MCA (the classic territory of hypertensive lacunar infarction and of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm rupture) with the anterior choroidal artery supplying the retrolenticular/inferior posterior part.
bloodSupply.after: MCA lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal branches; superior/inferior and anterior/posterior territories vary.

before.findings: A small posterior-limb lacune produces dense, proportional contralateral face-arm-leg weakness without sensory loss, aphasia or hemianopia — the archetypal lacunar syndrome, and the commonest stroke presentation from lenticulostriate disease.

Repeated stereotyped episodes of hemiparesis, dysarthria or hemisensory loss over hours to days (a stuttering lacunar onset) precede a permanent capsular infarct; the mechanism is perforator hypoperfusion or microembolism rather than large-vessel occlusion.
The complete syndrome is contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia: posterior limb of the internal capsule, thalamus/optic tract and optic radiation all fall in one territory.

before.syndrome: Ataxic hemiparesis from a capsular lesion
before.findings: Weakness with out-of-proportion ipsilateral limb ataxia from a small capsular or pontine lacune; the corticopontine fibres to the contralateral cerebellum explain the cerebellar-type component.

after.findings: Can cause contralateral face-arm-leg weakness, with sensory loss depending on lesion extent. Pure motor hemiparesis is a pattern, not proof of a single location.
Contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss may coexist when the relevant capsule/visual structures are injured; the full triad is not obligatory.
Weakness and disproportionate limb ataxia are on the body side contralateral to a hemispheric lesion; pontine and other sites can cause a similar pattern.

efferent: Corticospinal fibres from the precentral gyrus (somatotopic: arm anterior, leg posterior) to the crus cerebri, basis pontis and pyramid

function.before: The motor and sensory trunk of the capsule, between the thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally: the corticospinal fibres occupy its posterior third in a somatotopic order (face and arm anteriorly, leg posteriorly), the corticorubral and corticoreticular fibres lie anterior to them, and the somatosensory thalamocortical radiations travel with them. Its compactness is why a lesion the size of a pea can produce a complete contralateral hemiplegia.
function.after: The posterior limb lies between thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. Motor fibres are conventionally mapped more anteriorly and somatosensory thalamocortical fibres more posteriorly, with overlap and individual variability. Retrolenticular optic and sublenticular auditory radiations are adjacent distinct capsular subdivisions.

records.name: Corona radiata

bloodSupply.before: The internal watershed zone: deep medullary branches of the MCA (and the anterior choroidal/lenticulostriate system medially) meet the superficial MCA cortical branches here, so the corona radiata is the classic site of haemodynamic (low-flow) infarction, and it is also the territory of the long penetrating medullary arteries damaged by chronic hypertension and diabetes.
bloodSupply.after: Long medullary branches from cerebral cortical arteries and variable deep perforator overlap; some regions are vulnerable to internal border-zone ischemia.

before.findings: Hypoperfusion from carotid stenosis or systemic hypotension infarcts the Rosary-like chain of lesions along the corona radiata: contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss that is worse in the proximal limb and hand, with fluctuating or stepwise onset. It is the deep counterpart of the cortical watershed infarct.
before.vascular: Internal watershed between superficial MCA branches and the deep lenticulostriate/medullary arteries

before.syndrome: Small-vessel disease of the centrum semiovale
before.findings: Chronic hypertensive and diabetic arteriolopathy produces confluent periventricular and deep white-matter T2 hyperintensities (leukoaraiosis) and lacunes along the corona radiata, the anatomical substrate of vascular cognitive impairment and of gait apraxia.
before.vascular: Long penetrating medullary arteries (middle cerebral artery)

before.findings: Periventricular and juxtacortical demyelinating lesions characteristically involve the corona radiata and centrum semiovale, producing pyramidal weakness, sensory disturbance and ataxia that follow a relapsing or progressive course.
before.note: Autoimmune demyelination rather than vascular

before.syndrome: Corona radiata stroke with disproportionate deficit
before.findings: Because the motor and sensory projections are tightly packed, small infarcts here cause dense hemiparesis or hemianaesthesia with little cortical impairment — motor recovery is nonetheless often better than after capsular lesions because adjacent fibres can be recruited.
before.vascular: Medullary branches of the middle cerebral artery

after.findings: Can cause contralateral motor/sensory deficits or cognitive changes according to fibres involved.
May produce chains of deep white-matter infarcts with impaired perfusion; lesion pattern and clinical deficits require imaging correlation.
Can involve this region but are not diagnosed from one symptom or atlas location.

function.before: The fan of ascending and descending projection fibres between the internal capsule below and the cortical surface above — the centrum semiovale is simply the part of the corona radiata seen above the level of the lateral ventricles. Descending corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine fibres interdigitate with ascending thalamocortical radiations, so the corona radiata is the anatomical site where the motor and sensory projections to the entire hemisphere are packed into the space of a few centimetres.
function.after: The corona radiata is the fan of ascending and descending projection fibres above the internal capsule. The centrum semiovale also contains association and commissural fibres and is not simply synonymous with corona radiata. Fibre overlap complicates inference from a small displayed coordinate.

records.name: MCA insular segment (M2)

bloodSupply.before: The M2 branches lie in the Sylvian fissure, surrounded by CSF and covered by the opercula; their walls are the target of the vasospasm that follows subarachnoid haemorrhage, which is why an MCA aneurysm can infarct the insular and opercular territory without occluding the trunk.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: MCA M1 near the limen insulae. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Occlusion of one M2 branch produces a partial MCA syndrome: a face-and-arm-predominant hemiparesis with Broca aphasia when the superior division is involved, or a Wernicke aphasia / neglect with a superior quadrantanopia when the inferior division is involved. The leg is spared because its representation lies in the anterior cerebral territory at the vertex.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, M2 insular segment

after.findings: Deficits depend on the superior/inferior division and collateral supply; motor/language, sensory or neglect/visual findings can occur. Insular involvement does not establish infarction of the whole putamen or internal capsule.

efferent: The superior and inferior division trunks (M3/M4) that continue onto the opercular and cortical surfaces

function.before: The insular segment of the middle cerebral artery: after leaving the Sylvian cistern the M1 trunk divides at the limen insulae into two (sometimes three) trunks that run across the insula in the Sylvian fissure â€” the M2 segment â€” before turning at the circular sulcus onto the opercular surface as the M3 segments. The M2 branches are the intermediate vessels of the MCA tree: they give off the small insular perforators to the claustrum, external capsule and extreme capsule, and they are the vessels that must be preserved when the Sylvian fissure is split. Because they lie on the insula, an occlusion of a single M2 branch produces a partial MCA syndrome â€” a division infarct â€” rather than the complete territory deficit.
function.after: Insular segment of the MCA, usually comprising division trunks travelling over the insula before continuing into opercular M3 branches. Small insular branches supply insular cortex and portions of adjacent extreme/external capsule and claustral tissue; they are distinct from the major M1 lenticulostriate group.

before.syndrome: Superior division infarct (face and arm, with Broca aphasia)
before.findings: Contralateral face-and-arm-predominant weakness and sensory loss with the leg relatively spared. In the dominant hemisphere, Broca aphasia: non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension and the patient aware of the errors. In the non-dominant hemisphere, gaze deviation toward the lesion and contralateral neglect of the arm.

before.syndrome: Prefrontal branch infarct with frontal-lobe signs
before.findings: Infarction of the prefrontal (orbitofrontal and prefrontal) MCA branches produces apathy, disinhibition, perseveration and impaired planning with little or no weakness â€” a "silent" infarct on motor examination but not on bedside cognitive testing.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, superior division prefrontal branches

after.findings: Often produces contralateral face/arm-predominant weakness, sometimes sensory loss, and nonfluent aphasia with dominant frontal involvement. Deficits are variable and cannot be predicted from the rendered branch alone.

bloodSupply.before: Its branches run in the subarachnoid space of the temporal and parietal opercula; the posterior temporal and temporo-occipital branches form the leptomeningeal border zone with the PCA, which is why an MCA occlusion sometimes spares the occipital pole.

before.syndrome: Inferior division infarct (Wernicke aphasia or neglect)
before.findings: Contralateral superior quadrantanopia from Meyer's-loop involvement, with Wernicke aphasia in the dominant hemisphere (fluent but empty and paraphasic speech with poor comprehension, the patient unaware of the deficit) or hemispatial neglect and anosognosia in the non-dominant hemisphere; the motor deficit is milder than in a superior division infarct.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, inferior division (posterior temporal and angular branches)

before.vascular: MCA inferior division temporo-occipital branch with the PCA (border zone)

after.findings: Can cause fluent aphasia with dominant posterior temporal involvement or neglect with right temporoparietal injury, usually with little weakness. Homonymous field loss depends on the involved cortex/white matter and is not always a superior quadrantanopia.

function.before: The inferior (parietotemporal) division trunk of the middle cerebral artery: it crosses the insula below the superior trunk, leaves the Sylvian fissure and divides into the temporopolar, anterior/middle/posterior temporal, temporo-occipital and angular branches â€” the arteries of the temporal convexity, the posterior parietal association cortex and the lateral occipital region. function.after: Inferior MCA division supplies variable lateral temporal and posterior parietal territory. Temporal optic-radiation fibres (Meyer's loop) represent the contralateral superior visual field; parietal fibres represent the inferior field. The entire parietal-temporal course is not Meyer's loop.

records.name: MCA posterior temporal branch

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the subarachnoid space of the posterior temporal convexity; its border zone with the PCA is where a posterior temporal infarct can be produced by either circulation, and where leptomeningeal collateral flow is recruited.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually MCA inferior division. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

after.findings: May cause fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension or naming in the dominant hemisphere. Homonymous field loss can occur when underlying optic radiations are affected; a cortical branch label does not uniquely specify a quadrant.

records.name: MCA temporo-occipital branch

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the subarachnoid space of the temporo-occipital convexity; because its border zone with the PCA is the largest leptomeningeal anastomotic bed of the hemisphere, its patency is what allows a failing PCA to be rescued from the MCA side, and vice versa.

before.findings: A watershed infarct at the MCA/PCA junction produces a homonymous hemianopia or quadrantanopia with relatively preserved central vision, sometimes with a mild aphasia or visual agnosia; it is the pattern that follows a systemic hypotension in a patient with bilateral carotid and vertebrobasilar disease.
before.vascular: MCA temporo-occipital branch with the PCA (border zone)

after.findings: Can cause visual, language or higher visual processing deficits depending on lesion location. Border-zone injury can follow hypoperfusion or embolism and does not require simultaneous occlusion of both arteries.

bloodSupply.before: It lies in the subarachnoid space over the frontal operculum and inferior frontal gyrus; its occlusion is the anatomical basis of the "prefrontal" component of a superior division infarct.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually MCA superior division. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Infarction of the lateral prefrontal convexity produces apathy or disinhibition, perseveration, impaired set-shifting and reduced verbal fluency with minimal weakness. In the dominant hemisphere, an infarct that reaches the inferior frontal gyrus adds a transcortical-motor or Broca-type aphasia.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, prefrontal (M4) branch of the superior division

after.findings: May impair initiation, executive function or verbal fluency; aphasia can occur with dominant inferior frontal network injury. The clinical pattern depends on the actual cortical/white-matter lesion.

afferent: Middle cerebral artery superior division (M3/M4 transition at the opercular surface)
efferent: Inferior and middle frontal gyri, including Broca's area and the frontal eye field; anastomoses with the anterior cerebral artery orbitofrontal branches on the frontal convexity

function.before: A named M4 cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery superior division: it leaves the Sylvian fissure in front of the precentral artery and ascends over the inferior and middle frontal gyri to the frontal pole region. records.name: MCA M4 precentral branch

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the subarachnoid space of the precentral sulcus. Its territory borders the anterior cerebral artery at the vertex, which is why a proximal MCA occlusion spares the leg but a distal one may not.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually MCA superior division. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Occlusion of the precentral branch infarcts the hand-knob and face representations of the primary motor cortex: a dense contralateral hemiparesis of the face and arm with hypotonia and a Babinski sign, sparing the leg. Recovery is poorest for the hand, because the infarct destroys the cortical output rather than a tract segment.

before.syndrome: Isolated hand weakness from a cortical infarct
before.findings: A small embolus lodged in the precentral branch can infarct only the hand knob, producing a "pseudoperipheral" wrist and finger palsy that mimics a radial or ulnar lesion; the accompanying cortical signs (ideomotor apraxia, sensory extinction) are what identify it as cortical.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, precentral branch (hand knob territory)

after.findings: May cause contralateral face or upper-limb weakness. A small hand-knob lesion can mimic a peripheral nerve palsy and may occur without other obvious cortical signs; recovery cannot be ranked from vessel name alone.

afferent: Middle cerebral artery superior division, M3/M4 transition at the opercular surface
efferent: Primary motor cortex for the face, arm and hand, and the premotor cortex in front of it; anastomoses with the anterior cerebral artery at the parasagittal border zone (the leg area)

afferent: Usually MCA superior division
efferent: Lateral precentral and adjacent premotor cortex

It is the single most consequential cortical branch of the MCA: its occlusion produces the dense contralateral face-and-arm weakness that defines the middle cerebral syndrome, and it is the vessel the neurosurgeon maps with stimulation during awake craniotomy.

records.name: MCA M4 central (rolandic) branch

bloodSupply.before: It lies in the subarachnoid space of the central sulcus, between the two largest functional areas of the hemisphere; its occlusion therefore destroys both the motor and the sensory representation of the same body part, which is why the deficit is sensorimotor rather than purely motor.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually MCA superior division. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: A sensorimotor cortical infarct of the face and hand with impaired fine finger movement, asteognosis and impaired two-point discrimination on the contralateral side; the sensory loss is cortical in type (impaired discrimination with relatively preserved primary modalities) and the weakness is distal-predominant.

after.findings: Can cause contralateral sensorimotor deficits, including impaired fine movement and discriminative sensation. Deficit distribution depends on cortical somatotopy and the extent of white-matter involvement.

afferent: Middle cerebral artery superior division, M3/M4 transition
efferent: Primary motor and primary somatosensory cortex of the face and upper limb; the parasagittal border zone with the anterior cerebral artery lies immediately behind it

afferent: Usually MCA superior division
efferent: Lateral precentral/postcentral cortex

function.before: The M4 cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs in or beside the central sulcus, supplying both the motor cortex behind the precentral gyrus and the somatosensory cortex of the postcentral gyrus for the face, arm and hand. It is the vessel whose occlusion produces a sensorimotor cortical deficit rather than a pure motor one, and it is the cortical branch most often involved in the "hand knob plus postcentral" infarcts of embolic stroke.
function.after: Central or rolandic cortical branch travels in or near the central sulcus and supplies variable adjacent precentral motor and postcentral somatosensory cortex. Motor cortex is anterior to the central sulcus and sensory cortex posterior to it.

records.name: MCA M4 anterior parietal branch

bloodSupply.before: It lies in the subarachnoid space over the postcentral gyrus, in the border zone between the superior and inferior divisions of the MCA â€” which is why an anterior parietal infarct can show features of both division syndromes.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Variable MCA division branch. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: A cortical sensory deficit of the contralateral trunk and proximal limb with impaired graphaesthesia and stereognosis; in the dominant hemisphere, added acalculia and finger agnosia bring the picture toward the Gerstmann constellation without the full tetrad.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery, anterior parietal branch

after.findings: May cause contralateral cortical sensory impairment, such as reduced graphesthesia or stereognosis, with the affected body region determined by actual somatotopic location.

afferent: Middle cerebral artery superior division at the opercular surface
efferent: Postcentral gyrus (trunk and proximal limb), anterior inferior parietal lobule; the angular branch continues behind it into the posterior parietal cortex

afferent: Variable MCA division branch
efferent: Postcentral/anterior parietal cortex

function.before: The M4 cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs posterior to the central sulcus across the postcentral gyrus and the anterior inferior parietal lobule. It supplies the somatosensory cortex of the trunk and the proximal limb, and it is the branch whose occlusion adds a cortical sensory deficit and, in the dominant hemisphere, elements of the Gerstmann constellation to an inferior division infarct.
function.after: Variable cortical MCA branch to postcentral and adjacent anterior parietal cortex. The sensory body representation and boundary with neighbouring branches vary; Gerstmann syndrome is more closely associated with dominant inferior parietal network injury than with this branch name.

records.name: Pericallosal artery (A2–A3)

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the callosal cistern, above the corpus callosum and below the falx, where it is at risk from falcine meningiomas and from the retraction used in interhemispheric approaches; its distal branches anastomose with the posterior cerebral artery at the splenium.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Distal ACA beyond the ACoA region. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss with abulia, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex and, when the supplementary motor area is involved, mutism that recovers over days. The arm and face are relatively spared because their representation lies on the lateral convexity in the MCA territory.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery, pericallosal and callosomarginal branches

before.findings: Infarction of the anterior corpus callosum (a pericallosal branch territory) leaves an alien hand, agraphia of the left hand, apraxia to verbal command in the left hand and left-hand anomia â€” the modern disconnection syndrome, and the reason the pericallosal branches are named in the ACA clinical picture.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery, pericallosal branches to the corpus callosum

after.findings: Medial sensorimotor injury may cause contralateral leg-predominant weakness or sensory loss. Medial frontal/callosal injury can add abulia, impaired initiation or disconnection signs; none is obligatory.

afferent: Anterior cerebral artery A1 segment through the anterior communicating artery complex
efferent: Callosomarginal artery (its major branch), frontopolar and orbitofrontal branches proximally; the inferior internal parietal (precuneal) artery distally
Small callosal perforators that supply the corpus callosum itself â€” their occlusion is the anatomical basis of the callosal disconnection syndrome

afferent: Distal ACA beyond the ACoA region
efferent: Callosal and variable medial frontal/parietal branches

function.before: The continuation of the anterior cerebral artery beyond the anterior communicating artery: it curves around the genu of the corpus callosum (A2), runs backward in the callosal cistern on the dorsal surface of the corpus callosum (A3), and ends at the splenium as the inferior internal parietal (precuneal) artery. It supplies the medial frontal and parietal surfaces, the anterior corpus callosum, the cingulate gyrus, the supplementary motor area and the paracentral lobule â€” the cortical representation of the leg and foot. It is the artery of the ACA territory syndrome.
function.after: Distal ACA continuation that courses around the genu and along the dorsal corpus callosum. Variable branches supply portions of the callosum and medial frontal/parietal cortex; distal callosal supply overlaps PCA/splenial branches. Segment and terminal-branch nomenclature varies.

records.name: Callosomarginal artery (A3)

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the cingulate sulcus, between the cingulate gyrus and the medial frontal convexity; its branches are the ones retracted in interhemispheric surgery, and their occlusion is what produces the leg-predominant deficit of an ACA infarct.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Variable distal ACA/pericallosal origin. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.syndrome: Callosomarginal branch infarct (supplementary motor area syndrome)
before.findings: Infarction of the callosomarginal territory produces a contralateral leg-predominant weakness with a characteristic transient mutism and akinesia (the supplementary motor area syndrome) that recovers over days to weeks â€” a deficit that looks catastrophic on day one and is often nearly resolved by day ten.

before.syndrome: Anterior cerebral artery territory infarct with behavioural change
before.findings: When the callosomarginal and pericallosal territories infarct together, the leg weakness is joined by abulia, incontinence and grasp reflexes; the behavioural change is disproportionate to the motor deficit, which is the clinical signature of the medial frontal territory.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery, callosomarginal and pericallosal branches

after.findings: Can cause leg-predominant weakness, reduced initiation, speech disturbance or SMA-related motor planning deficits. Recovery varies; a fixed day-ten near-resolution prediction is unsupported.

afferent: Pericallosal artery (A2/A3) in the callosal cistern
efferent: Anterior, middle and posterior internal frontal arteries and the paracentral artery â€” the medial convexity above the cingulate sulcus, including the supplementary motor area and the leg representation

function.before: The largest cortical branch of the pericallosal artery: it arises in the callosal cistern, runs in or beside the cingulate sulcus, and gives off the anterior, middle and posterior internal frontal arteries and the paracentral artery, which supply the medial frontal convexity, the cingulate gyrus above the sulcus and the paracentral lobule. It is the vessel that carries the supplementary motor area and the medial leg representation â€” the anatomical reason an ACA infarct weakens the leg.

records.name: Frontopolar artery (A2)

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the anterior interhemispheric fissure, over the medial frontal pole; its occlusion produces the most anterior and least eloquent part of the ACA territory.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually distal ACA, variable origin. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Infarction of the frontal pole produces apathy, reduced initiative and impaired social judgement with no weakness or sensory loss â€” a "silent" infarct on the motor examination that shows on bedside frontal testing and on imaging.

after.findings: May affect initiative, executive or social-behavioural function. Small lesions can be subtle; absence of motor deficits does not establish a clinically silent lesion.

records.name: ACA orbitofrontal branch

bloodSupply.before: It runs beneath the frontal lobe in the subarachnoid space of the orbital cistern, where it is displaced by olfactory-groove meningiomas and is divided in the pterional approach to the anterior communicating complex.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Variable early distal ACA origin. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Infarction of the medial orbitofrontal cortex produces disinhibition, inappropriate jocularity, anosmia and impaired olfactory discrimination on the ipsilateral side; the deficit is behavioural rather than motor and is easily missed unless frontal and olfactory testing is performed.

after.findings: May affect behavioural regulation or decision-making. Anosmia would require involvement of relevant olfactory structures/pathways and is not an obligatory sign of an isolated orbitofrontal cortical infarct.

records.name: Parieto-occipital artery (P4)

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the subarachnoid space of the quadrigeminal cistern and then in the parieto-occipital sulcus, where it lies against the medial occipital cortex; it is the vessel most often involved when a PCA infarct extends above the calcarine fissure.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Distal PCA cortical branch. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Infarction above the calcarine fissure removes the upper quadrant of the contralateral visual field (a "pie in the sky" defect on the corresponding side) and adds visuospatial and constructional difficulty from precuneus involvement; macular vision is often preserved because the occipital pole has a dual PCA/MCA supply.

after.findings: Upper-bank striate cortex injury causes contralateral inferior quadrantanopia (a lower-field defect). Association-cortex injury can add visuospatial deficits. The branch territory and macular sparing vary.

afferent: Posterior cerebral artery P2/P3 segment in the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns
efferent: Precuneus, cuneus and medial superior parietal surface; the splenial artery and the calcarine artery run beside it, and the medial occipital branches anastomose with the MCA temporo-occipital branch laterally

afferent: Distal PCA cortical branch
efferent: Cuneus and variable medial parieto-occipital cortex

function.before: One of the two terminal cortical branches of the posterior cerebral artery: it leaves the quadrigeminal cistern, runs backward and upward in the parieto-occipital sulcus, and supplies the medial surface of the parietal and occipital lobes above the calcarine fissure â€” the precuneus, the cuneus and the medial surface of the superior parietal lobule. records.name: Calcarine artery (P4)

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the calcarine fissure, between the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below; the dual supply of the occipital pole from the MCA leptomeningeal anastomoses is what preserves central vision in a PCA occlusion.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Distal PCA cortical branch. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.syndrome: Calcarine branch infarct (homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing)
before.findings: Occlusion of the calcarine artery produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopia that respects the vertical meridian and typically spares central vision, because the occipital pole receives a dual PCA/MCA supply. The patient is usually aware of the deficit, unlike a hemineglect patient, and a lesion of the left calcarine plus the splenium gives alexia without agraphia.

Bilateral calcarine infarction â€” from an embolus at the basilar apex or from both PCAs â€” produces complete cortical blindness. When the patient denies the blindness and confabulates (Anton syndrome), the lesion involves the visual association cortex as well; the pupillary light reflex is preserved because the lesion is cortical.
before.vascular: Bilateral posterior cerebral arteries, calcarine branches (or the basilar apex)

after.findings: Can cause contralateral homonymous field loss. Macular sparing may occur through preserved cortex or collateral supply, but is not universal. Bilateral cortical injury can impair vision with preserved pupillary light responses.

afferent: Posterior cerebral artery P3 segment in the quadrigeminal cistern
efferent: Striate cortex (V1) and the peristriate cortex of the cuneus and lingual gyrus; the occipital pole, where it anastomoses with the MCA temporo-occipital branch â€” the anatomical reason for macular sparing

afferent: Distal PCA cortical branch
efferent: Striate cortex of cuneus/lingual gyrus and occipital pole

function.before: The principal cortical branch of the posterior cerebral artery and the artery of the primary visual cortex: it runs in the calcarine fissure from the quadrigeminal cistern to the occipital pole, supplying the striate cortex (V1) above and below the fissure, the posterior cingulate region adjacent to it and, through its cortical branches, the occipital pole itself. Its occlusion is the anatomical basis of the classic homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
function.after: Distal PCA cortical branch running in/along the calcarine sulcus, supplying primary visual cortex on both banks and variable adjacent cortex. Posterior cingulate cortex is not a standard core calcarine territory.

records.name: Posterior temporal branches of the PCA

bloodSupply.before: They arise from the P2 segment beside the oculomotor and trochlear nerves and then run in the ambient and parahippocampal cisterns; their occlusion is what makes a PCA infarct damage memory as well as vision, and their preservation is the goal of temporal-lobe epilepsy surgery.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Variable PCA P2/distal origin. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.syndrome: PCA temporal branch infarct with memory loss
before.findings: Infarction of the hippocampal and posterior temporal branches adds an anterograde amnesia to the visual field defect; because the posterior cerebral artery supplies both the medial temporal memory structures and the occipital cortex, a single PCA occlusion can produce hemianopia and amnesia together â€” and when both PCAs are involved the amnesia is severe and permanent.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery, posterior temporal (hippocampal) branches

after.findings: May affect visual recognition or memory according to cortical and hippocampal involvement. Amnesia does not follow every posterior temporal branch infarction.

records.name: Splenial artery

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the quadrigeminal and splenial cisterns, against the dorsal surface of the splenium; its anastomosis with the pericallosal artery is the anatomical basis of the collateral flow that can keep the splenium alive in either a PCA or an ACA occlusion.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Variable distal PCA branch. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.syndrome: Splenial infarct with alexia without agraphia
before.findings: A left PCA infarct that includes the splenial artery destroys the splenium together with the left occipital cortex and disconnects the intact right visual cortex from the left language areas: the patient cannot read (and cannot name colours) but can still write. It is the classic disconnection syndrome and the reason the splenial artery is worth naming separately.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery, splenial branch (with the left calcarine artery)

before.findings: Isolated splenial infarction without occipital involvement produces a milder disconnection: pure alexia for letters, impaired transfer of visual information between hemispheres, and difficulty naming objects presented in the left visual field.

after.findings: Dominant occipital injury combined with splenial disruption can cause alexia without agraphia. Isolated splenial injury has variable disconnection findings and does not by itself establish the classic syndrome.

records.name: Thalamogeniculate arteries

bloodSupply.before: They are end arteries a few hundred micrometres across, arising beside the oculomotor and trochlear nerves; their occlusion is the classic cause of central post-stroke pain and of the sensory stroke that follows a PCA infarct.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually PCA P2. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Infarction of the thalamogeniculate territory produces contralateral hemianaesthesia that evolves into spontaneous burning pain with hyperpathia and allodynia â€” the archetype of central post-stroke pain. There may be a mild transient hemiparesis and hemiataxia from capsular and cerebellar-thalamic involvement, and the pain often begins weeks after the stroke.

before.syndrome: Posterolateral thalamic infarct with sensory loss
before.findings: A smaller thalamogeniculate infarct gives an isolated, complete contralateral sensory loss for all modalities (a "pure sensory stroke" of thalamic type) with preserved strength; the deficit is often dense and persistent, in contrast with the lacunar pure sensory stroke of the capsule.

after.findings: Can cause contralateral sensory loss, ataxia and sometimes later central post-stroke pain. Full hemisensory loss or pain is not inevitable; territory varies.

records.name: Posteromedial central (thalamoperforating) branches

bloodSupply.before: They are the perforators whose individual anatomy is most variable: the artery of Percheron is a normal variant in which one paramedian branch serves both medial thalami, which is why a single small infarct can produce a bilateral thalamic syndrome.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually PCA P1; a Percheron variant has one shared origin. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: A single paramedian thalamic artery arising from one P1 supplies both medial thalami: bilateral infarction produces sudden coma or hypersomnia, a severe amnestic syndrome, vertical gaze palsy, skew deviation and marked apathy. It is the classic "top of the basilar" thalamic syndrome and it is easily missed because the CT is often normal.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery, P1 posteromedial central (thalamoperforating) branches â€” artery of Percheron

before.findings: A unilateral posteromedial central infarct produces a tuberothalamic-like picture on one side: apathy and abulia, disorientation, memory loss and, on the left, a transcortical-like aphasia with preserved repetition; the pupil may be small and the vertical gaze may be impaired if the midbrain is involved.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery, posteromedial central branches

after.findings: Bilateral paramedian thalamic injury can cause altered consciousness, memory impairment and vertical gaze abnormalities; midbrain involvement is variable. Other causes of bilateral thalamic lesions must be considered.

records.name: Pontine perforating arteries

bloodSupply.before: Each perforator is an end artery in the basis pontis, so an individual occlusion produces a lacune and a trunk occlusion produces a complete ventral pontine infarct; that single anatomical fact explains both the lacunar pontine syndromes and locked-in syndrome.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Basilar artery. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.syndrome: Locked-in syndrome (basilar occlusion with perforator loss)
before.findings: Occlusion of the basilar trunk removes all the paramedian perforators at once and infarcts the whole basis pontis while sparing the tegmentum: the patient is conscious, blinks and moves the eyes vertically but is otherwise quadriplegic and anarthric. It is the most devastating expression of a perforator territory and the reason the basilar is treated as an emergency.
before.vascular: Basilar artery and its pontine perforating arteries

before.findings: A single paramedian pontine perforator infarct produces a small lacune in the basis pontis: a pure motor hemiparesis contralateral to the lesion, without sensory loss, aphasia or visual field defect, and often with a dysarthriaâ€“clumsy hand picture when the lesion sits more rostrally. It is clinically indistinguishable from a capsular lacune, which is why imaging is required.

A slightly larger paramedian or short circumferential infarct reaches the facial nucleus or the abducens nucleus and PPRF, producing the alternating syndromes: ipsilateral facial weakness (or conjugate gaze palsy) with contralateral hemiparesis, and in the Foville form a contralateral sensory loss from medial lemniscus involvement.
before.vascular: Basilar artery pontine perforating arteries (paramedian and short circumferential)

after.findings: Can cause pure motor weakness, ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria-clumsy hand; tegmental extension adds gaze or cranial nerve signs. Bilateral ventral pontine injury can cause locked-in syndrome, but basilar occlusion does not invariably spare the tegmentum.

afferent: Basilar artery along its whole prepontine course, from the pontomedullary junction to the pontomesencephalic junction
efferent: Basis pontis (pontine nuclei and transverse fibres), corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, medial lemniscus, abducens nucleus, facial nucleus and the paramedian pontine reticular formation
Short circumferential branches reach the middle cerebellar peduncle; long circumferential branches belong to AICA and SCA rather than to the perforator group

records.name: Lateral branch of the superior cerebellar artery

bloodSupply.before: It runs in the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns, immediately below the trochlear nerve; its occlusion is the classic "cerebellar" infarct, and the swelling it produces is what compresses the fourth ventricle and the brainstem.

records.name: Labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery

bloodSupply.before: It is the artery of the internal auditory canal: it travels with the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, which is why an AICA infarct produces deafness, vertigo and facial weakness together, and why hearing is at risk in surgery of the cerebellopontine angle.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually AICA, sometimes basilar artery. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Occlusion of the AICA or of its labyrinthine branch produces the lateral pontine syndrome with the addition of sudden unilateral deafness and tinnitus: vertigo, nystagmus, ipsilateral facial weakness and sensory loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ataxia with contralateral pain-temperature loss. The deafness is the feature that separates it from a PICA (Wallenberg) infarct, which spares hearing.
before.vascular: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery and its labyrinthine branch

before.syndrome: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss of vascular origin
before.findings: An isolated labyrinthine artery occlusion produces sudden unilateral sensorineural deafness with vertigo and tinnitus, without brainstem signs; it is the vascular differential of idiopathic sudden hearing loss and the reason a posterior-circulation examination belongs in the workup of sudden deafness.

after.findings: Can cause sudden ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo and tinnitus without brainstem signs. A parent AICA infarct may add pontine/cerebellar findings; labyrinthine occlusion alone does not cause the full lateral pontine syndrome.

function.before: The third segment of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery: after its anterior medullary and lateral medullary segments, the PICA turns posterolaterally behind the inferior olive, climbs over the tonsil in the tonsillomedullary fissure, and forms the tonsillar loop â€” the caudal loop that is the lowest point of the artery and the landmark the neurosurgeon uses to identify it. function.after: Third PICA segment in a common five-segment scheme. It traverses the tonsillomedullary region and forms a variable caudal loop before the telovelotonsillar segment. bloodSupply.before: It runs in the telovelotonsillar fissure against the roof of the fourth ventricle, where it is the artery encountered in the telovelar approach to the fourth ventricle and the one whose injury produces a cerebellar mutism syndrome in children.

before.syndrome: Telovelotonsillar (PICA terminal) infarct with fourth-ventricular involvement

function.before: The fourth and terminal segment of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery: from the tonsillar loop the artery ascends in the telovelotonsillar fissure â€” between the tonsil and the inferior medullary velum â€” and forms the cranial loop before dividing into its vermian and hemispheric branches on the superior surface of the tonsil and the inferior vermis. records.name: Anterior spinal artery

bloodSupply.before: It is a single midline vessel in the anterior median fissure, smaller than the territory it serves; the cord depends on the radicular reinforcements, which is why aortic surgery and hypotension produce anterior spinal cord infarction rather than a medullary one.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Vertebral anterior spinal branches; spinal radiculomedullary contributors. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.findings: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or of a paramedian vertebral branch infarcts the ventral medulla: contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face (pyramid), contralateral loss of position and vibration sense (medial lemniscus) and ipsilateral tongue weakness (hypoglossal nerve) â€” the classic alternating syndrome, with the tongue pointing to the side of the lesion.
before.vascular: Anterior spinal artery or paramedian vertebral branches

before.syndrome: Anterior spinal artery syndrome (anterior cord infarction)
before.findings: Infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord spares the dorsal columns: a flaccid paraplegia that becomes spastic, with loss of pain and temperature below the level and preserved vibration and position sense, together with bladder and bowel dysfunction. It follows aortic surgery, dissection or prolonged hypotension, and the level of the lesion is set by which radicular arteries remain patent.
before.vascular: Anterior spinal artery with its radicular reinforcements

after.findings: Medial medullary lesions may combine contralateral weakness and vibration-position loss with ipsilateral tongue weakness. Spinal anterior-cord infarction may cause motor/autonomic and pain-temperature deficits with relative dorsal-column preservation; level, extent and initial spinal shock vary.

efferent: Ventral medulla (pyramids, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal fibres), the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord, and the ventral grey and white matter of the cord through the sulcal arteries

afferent: Vertebral anterior spinal branches; spinal radiculomedullary contributors

function.before: The anterior spinal artery: the paired ventral branches of the vertebral arteries that join in the midline at the level of the foramen magnum into a single vessel that descends in the anterior median fissure of the medulla and spinal cord. It supplies the ventral two-thirds of the cord and the paramedian ventral medulla â€” the pyramids, the medial lemniscus and the hypoglossal nerve fibres â€” and is reinforced below by the anterior radicular arteries, of which the artery of Adamkiewicz is the largest. It is the artery of the medial medullary syndrome and of anterior spinal cord infarction.
function.after: Usually formed by vertebral branches that converge onto the ventral medullary midline and continue into the spinal anterior median fissure. Medullary paramedian supply overlaps vertebral perforators; spinal sulcal branches supply much of the anterior two-thirds of the cord and receive radiculomedullary reinforcement.

records.name: Lateral lenticulostriate arteries

bloodSupply.before: These are end arteries: each supplies a territory with no significant anastomosis to its neighbours, which is the anatomical reason a lesion this small produces a complete, sharply bounded infarct rather than a penumbra.
bloodSupply.after: Arterial inflow: Usually MCA M1. Linked structures indicate partial supplied tissue; the exact territory is variable.

before.syndrome: Lacunar infarction of the internal capsule and basal ganglia
before.findings: Occlusion of one lateral lenticulostriate artery infarcts a small deep territory: pure motor stroke (posterior limb, corticospinal fibres), pure sensory stroke (thalamocapsular fibres), ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria–clumsy hand. There is no aphasia, no neglect, no hemianopia and no drowsiness — the cortex is untouched, which is the clinical signature of a deep perforator lesion. NOTE: this atlas has no dedicated lacunar-syndrome card in src/data/syndromes, so `supply` is empty by the honesty rule rather than by oversight; the clinical picture is documented here and in the four child records.
before.vascular: Lateral lenticulostriate arteries (middle cerebral artery M1 perforators)

before.findings: Rupture of a Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysm on a lenticulostriate artery fills the putamen and spreads along the internal capsule into the ventricle: sudden contralateral hemiplegia with conjugate gaze deviation, depressed consciousness and, with a large clot, transtentorial herniation. It is the commonest site of spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage.
before.vascular: Lateral lenticulostriate arteries (lenticulostriate microaneurysms of chronic hypertension)

before.findings: When several lenticulostriate arteries occlude at once — typically by an embolus lodging at the M1 bifurcation or by a carotid occlusion with poor collateral flow — the infarct becomes a large striatocapsular cavity with hemiplegia and, on the left, a cortical-like aphasia from the adjacent insular and opercular involvement. The clinical picture can imitate a complete MCA infarct; imaging separates them.
before.vascular: Lateral lenticulostriate arteries as a group (M1 occlusion)

after.findings: Small capsular infarcts can cause pure motor or sensorimotor deficits without cortical signs. Larger striatocapsular lesions can have more complex findings. Hypertension-related deep small-vessel injury can cause putaminal haemorrhage; the mechanism is not always a proved ruptured microaneurysm.

afferent: Middle cerebral artery M1 (sphenoidal) segment — the perforators arise from its superior and posterior wall along the first 10–20 mm, which is why an M1 occlusion infarcts both the cortex and the basal ganglia
efferent: Four authored chains (children `-1` to `-4`) fanning to the antero-superior, middle, postero-inferior and lateral putamen, with capsular branches continuing to the internal capsule and corona radiata
The lateral group is the classic source of lacunar infarction and of hypertensive putaminal haemorrhage (Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms)

afferent: Usually MCA M1

function.before: The lateral group of the lenticulostriate arteries: a spray of six to twelve hair-thin perforators that leave the superior wall of the proximal M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery, cross the anterior perforated substance and pass upward and laterally through the putamen to the internal capsule, the external capsule and the corona radiata. Each is an end artery roughly 0.2–0.8 mm across, which is why a single occlusion destroys a cylinder of tissue a few millimetres wide and produces one of the lacunar syndromes without any cortical sign. They also bear the Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of chronic hypertension, which is why hypertensive basal-ganglia haemorrhage begins in the putamen.
function.after: Variable group of proximal MCA perforators entering the anterior perforated substance to supply portions of caudate, putamen, pallidum and internal capsule/corona radiata. The four child tubes are illustrative routes, not a fixed human branch count or four reproducible subterritories. Limited collaterals make these vessels vulnerable to small-vessel infarction.

function.before: The medial group of the lenticulostriate arteries and its named member, the recurrent artery of Heubner: it arises from the proximal A2 (or the A1–A2 junction) of the anterior cerebral artery, turns sharply back and laterally, runs 15–30 mm through the subarachnoid space, enters the brain through the anterior perforated substance just lateral to the carotid bifurcation, and ends in the caudate head, the anterior putamen, the anterior limb of the internal capsule and the ventral pallidum. It is the artery that ties the anterior cerebral territory to the basal ganglia, and it is the perforator an anterior communicating aneurysm most often catches: its occlusion produces a caudate-head infarct whose syndrome is behavioural rather than motor.
function.after: Medial striate branches arise from ACA; the recurrent artery of Heubner usually arises near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2, less commonly A1, and returns toward the anterior perforated substance. Supplies variable caudate-head, anterior putaminal/pallidal and anterior capsular territory. Two child tubes illustrate routes and do not assert universal duplicated Heubner arteries.

records.name: Internal carotid artery

bloodSupply.before: Supplied by the vasa vasorum of its wall in the neck and by the caroticotympanic and capsular branches intracranially; the cavernous segment is surrounded by the cavernous sinus and its nerves, and the supraclinoid segment by the subarachnoid space, which is why aneurysms here bleed into the subarachnoid space or into the sinus.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow from the common carotid artery. Through its ACA, MCA, anterior choroidal and communicating branches it supplies variable cortical and deep territories; a fetal PCA configuration can extend the carotid territory into the occipital lobe.

before.findings: Occlusion of the internal carotid produces the largest infarcts of all — a combined ACA/MCA territory deficit with contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia, hemianopia, gaze deviation and (dominant hemisphere) global aphasia; embolism from an atherosclerotic plaque at the bifurcation is the usual mechanism, and the deficit may be stepwise rather than sudden.
before.vascular: Internal carotid artery (with middle cerebral artery territory dominance)

before.syndrome: Amaurosis fugax and ocular ischaemic syndrome
before.findings: Transient monocular blindness ('a curtain coming down') from emboli to the ophthalmic/retinal circulation, or chronic hypoperfusion of the eye with venous stasis retinopathy — a direct marker of ipsilateral carotid stenosis.
before.vascular: Ophthalmic artery (first branch of the internal carotid) from an internal carotid plaque

before.findings: A cavernous-carotid aneurysm or fistula compresses cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI within the sinus, producing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, facial sensory loss in the first two divisions, a pulsatile bruit and (with a fistula) proptosis and chemosis with arterialized conjunctival veins.
before.vascular: Internal carotid artery (cavernous segment) — the segment whose wall IS the sinus

before.findings: A tear in the cervical internal-carotid wall (spontaneous, traumatic or connective-tissue related) creates an intramural haematoma with ipsilateral neck/face pain, Horner syndrome, pulsatile tinnitus and a risk of embolism, especially in patients under 50.

after.findings: Clinical extent ranges from no deficit with effective collateral flow to retinal ischaemia, MCA-predominant infarction, watershed injury or a combined ACA/MCA infarction. Possible findings include contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss, with aphasia in a language-dominant hemisphere or neglect in the other hemisphere.
after.vascular: Internal carotid artery and its branches

after.findings: Transient monocular visual loss can result from ipsilateral carotid embolism or hypoperfusion of the retinal circulation; carotid disease is one of several possible causes.

after.syndrome: Cavernous ICA aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula
after.findings: Compression can affect ocular motor nerves and V1/V2 sensation. A fistula may cause proptosis, chemosis, pulsatile bruit and arterialized conjunctival veins. The cavernous ICA is extradural; haemorrhage patterns differ from intradural aneurysms.
May cause ipsilateral head or neck pain, partial Horner syndrome and cerebral or retinal ischaemia from thromboembolism or reduced flow.

afferent: Common carotid artery at the carotid bifurcation (the anterior circulation's inflow)

Collateral inflow through the circle of Willis: the anterior communicating artery from the contralateral side, and the posterior communicating artery from the posterior cerebral artery — the two routes that can rescue a failing carotid territory
efferent: Ophthalmic artery (orbit and retina — the origin of amaurosis fugax), posterior communicating artery (vasc-posterior-communicating-artery), anterior choroidal artery (vasc-anterior-choroidal-artery)

Terminal bifurcation into the anterior cerebral artery (vasc-anterior-cerebral-artery) and the middle cerebral artery (vasc-middle-cerebral-artery); the lateral lenticulostriate perforators arise from the proximal M1 middle cerebral artery and the medial group (including the recurrent artery of Heubner) from the proximal A1 anterior cerebral artery

afferent: Common carotid artery at the carotid bifurcation
Possible collateral flow through the anterior or posterior communicating arteries; adequacy depends on individual anatomy and haemodynamics
efferent: Ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries
Terminal ACA and MCA; lateral lenticulostriate arteries usually arise from M1, and the recurrent artery of Heubner usually arises near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2, less often A1

function.before: The anterior feeding trunk of the cerebral circulation: it enters the skull through the carotid canal, runs through the cavernous sinus (where it is related to cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI) and turns upward and backward through the dural ring to become the supraclinoid segment, giving off the ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries before dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries at the carotid bifurcation. Its four segments (cervical, petrous, cavernous, supraclinoid) each generate a distinct syndrome, and together with the vertebrobasilar system it completes the circle of Willis at the base of the brain.
function.after: Paired source of the anterior cerebral circulation. After cervical and petrous segments, the ICA passes through the cavernous sinus, then enters the subarachnoid space as the supraclinoid segment. CN VI and sympathetic fibres lie beside the cavernous ICA; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the sinus lateral wall. Major distal branches are the ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries, followed by the terminal ACA and MCA. These four segment names are a teaching simplification of more detailed segment classifications.

records.name: Vertebral artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is supplied by the vasa vasorum of the periosteal and dural sleeves along the cervical loop; the V4 segment lies in the subarachnoid space in front of the medulla, where it is adjacent to the hypoglossal rootlets, the vertebral venous plexus and the lower cranial nerves.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow from the subclavian artery; distal branches include medullary perforators, anterior/posterior spinal branches and usually PICA.

before.findings: Vertebral artery occlusion at the origin of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarcts the dorsolateral medulla: vertigo, nystagmus, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ataxia, loss of pain-temperature on the ipsilateral face and the contralateral body, dysphagia, hoarseness and diminished gag reflex with intact strength.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery at the PICA origin (or the PICA itself)

before.findings: Infarction of the paramedian medullary territory supplied by the anterior spinal/vertebral arteries produces contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid) sparing the face, contralateral loss of position and vibration sense (medial lemniscus) and ipsilateral tongue weakness (hypoglossal nerve) — the classic alternating brainstem syndrome.
before.vascular: Anterior spinal artery or paramedian vertebral branches

before.syndrome: Vertebral artery dissection and subarachnoid haemorrhage
before.findings: Cervical dissection causes posterior-circulation transient ischaemic attacks and stroke in young adults with neck pain and occipital headache; rupture of an intracranial vertebral aneurysm fills the subarachnoid space around the brainstem and can present with a devastating brainstem infarct.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery (cervical segment for dissection, V4 for aneurysm)

before.findings: Occlusion or compression of the contralateral vertebral artery with head rotation (a variant of the atlantoaxial anatomy) causes vertigo, diplopia and syncope on turning the head.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery (V2/V3 segment at the atlantoaxial level)

after.findings: A lateral medullary infarct can produce ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ipsilateral ataxia and Horner syndrome, vertigo, nystagmus, dysphagia and hoarseness. The full constellation is not required, and vertebral or PICA disease can be responsible.
Paramedian injury can combine contralateral weakness and vibration-position loss with ipsilateral hypoglossal weakness. The triad is often incomplete.
after.vascular: Paramedian vertebral branches rostrally and anterior spinal branches more caudally

after.findings: May produce head/neck pain and posterior circulation ischaemia. Intracranial dissections can also rupture into the subarachnoid space.

function.before: The paired feeding trunk of the posterior circulation: each artery ascends through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae (V1/V2), loops laterally behind the atlas and then pierces the dura to run upward and medially in front of the medulla (V4). Its branches supply the cervical cord, the lateral medulla and the inferior cerebellum, and the two vertebral arteries unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery — the union being the last point where the posterior circulation is still paired.
function.after: Paired arteries arising from the subclavian arteries. V1 runs to the transverse foramen, V2 usually ascends through C6-C2 transverse foramina, V3 curves around the atlas, and V4 passes through the dura and foramen magnum to the ventral medulla. The vertebral arteries usually unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. Medullary, spinal and PICA branches provide variable supply to the medulla, upper cord and inferior cerebellum.
