records.name: Basilar artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is supplied by small vasa vasorum from the pontine perforators; the artery lies within the prepontine cistern, surrounded by CSF, which is why aneurysms of its apex present with subarachnoid haemorrhage and a third-nerve palsy, and why the basilar apex is the classic target of endovascular thrombectomy in acute basilar occlusion.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow from both vertebral arteries; branches supply the pons and contribute to cerebellar, midbrain and posterior cerebral circulation. Communicating-artery collateral flow is variable.

before.findings: Occlusion of the basilar artery with infarction of the basis pontis but sparing of the tegmentum leaves the patient conscious with intact vertical eye movements and blinking but completely paralysed and anarthric — quadriplegia, aphonia and preserved awareness, often misdiagnosed as coma.
before.vascular: Basilar artery (paramedian pontine perforators, basis pontis)

before.findings: A dorsal pontine lesion involving the paramedian pontine reticular formation and the adjacent medial longitudinal fasciculus abolishes horizontal gaze to one side and adduction on the other, leaving abduction with nystagmus in the only surviving direction; brainstem infarction (basilar perforators or a small tegmental haemorrhage) is the commonest cause.
before.vascular: Basilar artery paramedian perforators (dorsal caudal pons)

before.findings: Ventral pontine infarction produces an alternating syndrome: ipsilateral facial weakness (facial nucleus/nerve) or conjugate gaze palsy (abducens nucleus/PPRF) with contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal tract) and, in the full Foville form, contralateral sensory loss (medial lemniscus).
before.vascular: Basilar artery paramedian perforators (caudal pons), sometimes the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

before.findings: Embolic occlusion of the basilar apex infarcts the midbrain, thalamus and occipital cortex together: somnolence, peduncular hallucinosis, vertical gaze palsy, pupillary abnormality, memory loss and cortical blindness with relative sparing of motor function.
before.vascular: Basilar artery apex (with posterior cerebral artery territory)

after.findings: Bilateral ventral pontine injury can cause quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved awareness; vertical eye movements and blinking are often retained in the classic form. Basilar occlusion can also cause impaired consciousness or other syndromes when the tegmentum is affected.

A unilateral dorsal pontine lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus plus the ipsilateral MLF causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia; the other eye can still abduct. Infarction is one possible cause.

Caudal pontine lesions can combine ipsilateral facial or abducens dysfunction with contralateral weakness; dorsal extension may add gaze palsy and sensory loss. Findings depend on the actual lesion rather than on an eponym alone.

Distal basilar disease can affect variable combinations of rostral midbrain, thalami, occipital and medial temporal regions, causing altered consciousness, eye movement abnormalities, memory impairment and visual deficits.

function.before: The single midline trunk of the posterior circulation, formed at the pontomedullary junction by the union of the two vertebral arteries and running in the prepontine cistern along the ventral surface of the pons to divide into the two posterior cerebral arteries at the interpeduncular fossa. It supplies the whole basis pontis through crowded paramedian and circumferential perforators, gives off the anterior inferior cerebellar arteries and the superior cerebellar arteries, and its paramedian branches feed the medial lemniscus, the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres, the abducens nucleus, the paramedian pontine reticular formation and the cranial-nerve nuclei of the pons — so its occlusion can destroy the entire ventral brainstem at once.
function.after: Single trunk formed by the vertebral arteries near the pontomedullary junction. It runs in the prepontine cistern along the ventral pons, gives paramedian and circumferential pontine branches, AICA and SCA, and usually divides into the PCAs. Different branches supply ventral pontine motor pathways and dorsal or lateral tegmental structures; the extent of injury from basilar disease depends on the occlusion site and collateral circulation.

records.name: Anterior cerebral artery

bloodSupply.before: The A1 segment is supplied by its own perforators and lies above the optic chiasm in the subarachnoid space; aneurysms of the anterior communicating complex are the commonest cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage and are the classic source of a visual or amnestic deficit from rupture (chiasmatic and hypothalamic compression).
bloodSupply.after: Inflow usually from the ipsilateral ICA through A1; the ACoA can provide cross-flow from the opposite A1. A1 asymmetry and distal ACA variants alter this pattern.

before.findings: Contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss with abulia, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex and, when the supplementary motor area is involved, mutism that recovers over days; the arm and face are relatively spared and consciousness is preserved.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal and callosomarginal branches)

before.findings: Infarction of the anterior corpus callosum (a branch territory of the pericallosal artery) leaves the patient with an alien hand, agraphia of the left hand, apraxia to verbal command in the left hand and left-hand anomia — the modern disconnection syndrome.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal branches to the corpus callosum)

before.findings: Rupture fills the interhemispheric and basal cisterns, producing sudden severe headache, meningism and, in about a third of survivors, an amnestic syndrome with personality change from hypothalamic and septal injury; visual loss is uncommon but recognized with large aneurysms compressing the chiasm.

A single ACA supplying both hemispheres (hypoplastic or absent contralateral A1) or vasospasm of both A2 segments infarcts both medial surfaces: profound abulia or akinetic mutism with bilateral leg weakness, incontinence and grasp reflexes.
before.vascular: Anterior cerebral artery (with a hypoplastic contralateral A1 as the anatomical predisposition)

after.findings: Usually causes contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss. Abulia, impaired initiation, grasp reflexes, incontinence, language disturbance or an alien hand can occur with medial frontal/callosal involvement. Large infarcts can affect the arm as well.

Injury may impair transfer of motor or language-related information between hemispheres, causing left-hand apraxia or agraphia in a typical left language-dominant brain; alien-hand phenomena can have frontal or callosal mechanisms.
after.vascular: ACA callosal and medial frontal branches

after.findings: Bilateral medial frontal infarction can cause severe abulia or akinetic mutism and bilateral leg weakness. An azygos/bihemispheric distal ACA or one dominant A1 feeding both sides can increase shared vulnerability, but variants are not equivalent.

afferent: Internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) at the carotid bifurcation (A1 segment)
Anterior communicating artery (vasc-anterior-communicating-artery) — the interhemispheric cross-link that allows one ACA to supply both hemispheres
efferent: Recurrent artery of Heubner (vasc-lenticulostriate-arteries family) and medial lenticulostriate perforators to the caudate head, accumbens and anterior limb of the internal capsule
Orbitofrontal, frontopolar, callosomarginal and pericallosal branches along the medial surface; the pericallosal artery continues to the splenium and the precuneus
Small medial striate and hypothalamic (anterior communicating) perforators to the optic chiasm, hypothalamus and septum

afferent: ICA A1 segment
ACoA collateral connection with the opposite ACA
efferent: Heubner artery near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2, occasionally A1; other ACA perforators
Pericallosal, callosomarginal and variable medial frontal/parietal cortical branches

function.before: The medial-surface artery of the cerebral hemisphere: it arises from the internal carotid, runs medially above the optic chiasm through the interhemispheric fissure, is joined to its fellow by the anterior communicating artery (completing the anterior part of the circle of Willis) and then continues as the pericallosal artery above the corpus callosum, giving the callosomarginal branch. It supplies the medial frontal and parietal surfaces, the foot and leg representation of the motor and sensory strips at the vertex, the supplementary motor area and the anterior corpus callosum — so its occlusion produces the leg-predominant, behaviourally distinctive syndrome rather than a hemiplegia.
function.after: ACA arises from the ICA and courses medially toward the anterior communicating artery. Distal branches curve around and above the corpus callosum to supply much of the medial frontal and anterior medial parietal cortex, including the paracentral leg/foot sensorimotor region, and portions of the corpus callosum. Deep ACA branches, including the recurrent artery of Heubner, supply parts of the anterior basal ganglia and internal capsule. Territory boundaries and branch patterns vary.

records.name: Anterior communicating artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is nourished by small perforator twigs and it lies in the subarachnoid space above the chiasm between the two A1 segments; the surrounding cistern is the site of the blood that produces the headache and meningism of its rupture.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow through the ACA A1 segments. Its direct perforators supply a limited basal forebrain/hypothalamic region; cortical ACA territory is a potential collateral destination, not its direct tissue territory.

before.syndrome: Anterior communicating aneurysm rupture with subarachnoid haemorrhage
before.findings: Sudden severe headache with meningism and loss of consciousness; the associated deficits are the ones of the territory it feeds — visual loss from chiasmal compression, an amnestic-Korsakoff-like state and personality change from hypothalamic and septal injury, and frontal-lobe signs from the interhemispheric haematoma.
before.vascular: Anterior communicating artery (the commonest site of ruptured intracranial aneurysm)

before.syndrome: Anterior communicating artery infarction with hypothalamic dysfunction
before.findings: Occlusion of the artery (surgically, or by embolus) removes the perforator supply to the anterior hypothalamus: memory loss, personality change, diabetes insipidus, thermoregulatory and autonomic instability.

before.syndrome: Collateral rescue of a failing carotid territory
before.findings: When one internal carotid occludes slowly, flow crosses through the anterior communicating artery and keeps both medial hemispheres perfused — often with no deficit at all, which is why the circle is described as a functional rather than an anatomical anastomosis.
before.vascular: Anterior communicating artery (the collateral channel, with both A1/A2 segments acting as the donor and recipient limbs)
before.note: Physiological collateral rather than a disease

after.findings: Rupture can cause sudden severe headache, meningism and altered consciousness. Basal forebrain injury or damage to adjacent perforators may add memory or behavioural dysfunction; sufficiently large aneurysms may compress the optic apparatus.
Injury to hypothalamic or basal forebrain perforators, including during aneurysm treatment, can cause memory, behavioural or autonomic/endocrine dysfunction depending on the territory involved.

afferent: Both anterior cerebral arteries (vasc-anterior-cerebral-artery) — normally flowing from the dominant A1 across the midline
efferent: Both A2 segments of the anterior cerebral artery, permitting collateral supply of the contralateral medial hemisphere
Small hypothalamic, septal and chiasmatic perforators to the anterior hypothalamus, septum pellucidum and optic chiasm region

afferent: ACA A1 segments, with flow direction determined by pressure and individual anatomy
efferent: ACA A2 segments as a communicating collateral route

function.before: The short midline cross-link between the two anterior cerebral arteries that closes the anterior part of the circle of Willis: it allows flow to be redistributed between the hemispheres, so that one carotid can perfuse both medial surfaces — the anatomical reason unilateral carotid occlusion is often neurologically silent. It is also the commonest site of intracranial saccular aneurysm (approximately 30–35 % of all ruptured aneurysms) because the vessel sits at a bifurcation where haemodynamic stress is maximal, and it gives rise to the small hypothalamic, septal and chiasmatic perforators that supply the anterior hypothalamus and the optic chiasm region.
function.after: Short connection between the two ACAs at the anterior circle of Willis. It can redistribute blood between the A1/A2 systems when pressure gradients permit, but a complete effective collateral route is not present in everyone. Small perforators supply parts of the anterior hypothalamic, septal/basal forebrain and optic-chiasm region. It is a common intracranial aneurysm site.

records.name: Middle cerebral artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall and the perforators arising from M1 are nourished by the surrounding subarachnoid CSF and small vasa vasorum; the MCA is the commonest site of embolic occlusion (the embolus travels the straightest path from the carotid), of MCA-territory thrombectomy, and of dissection-related and vasospasm-related infarction.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow from the ICA. Lenticulostriate branches supply parts of the basal ganglia and internal capsule; surface branches supply lateral cortex and subcortical white matter, with variable leptomeningeal collateral connections.

before.findings: Contralateral hemiplegia and hemianaesthesia with gaze deviation toward the lesion, homonymous hemianopia and (dominant hemisphere) global aphasia, or (non-dominant) anosognosia and hemispatial neglect; a large infarct also causes drowsiness from oedema and mass effect. The face and arm are more affected than the leg because the leg representation lies at the vertex in the ACA territory.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery (M1 occlusion, often embolic from the heart or the carotid)

before.findings: Contralateral face-and-arm-predominant weakness with Broca aphasia (dominant) or gaze deviation and neglect (non-dominant), with the leg spared — the classic 'inferior-to-the-sylvian-fissure-sparing' pattern.
Wernicke aphasia (dominant) or hemispatial neglect and anosognosia (non-dominant) with a contralateral superior quadrantanopia from Meyer-loop involvement, and a less severe motor deficit.

A large MCA infarct with space-occupying oedema between days 2 and 5 causes progressive drowsiness, pupillary dilation and herniation — the indication for decompressive hemicraniectomy, and the reason large infarcts are monitored rather than simply observed.
before.vascular: Middle cerebral artery (with mass effect rather than a new occlusion)

after.findings: Combined cortical and deep injury can produce contralateral hemiplegia, sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia and gaze preference toward the lesion, with global aphasia in a language-dominant hemisphere or neglect in the other hemisphere. Large infarcts may develop dangerous swelling.
after.vascular: MCA stem / combined divisions and perforators

after.findings: Often causes contralateral face/arm-predominant weakness and sometimes cortical sensory loss; dominant frontal involvement can cause nonfluent aphasia.

Can cause fluent aphasia in the dominant hemisphere or neglect in the other hemisphere, with a contralateral field deficit and relatively little weakness. The field pattern depends on involved cortex and white matter.
Capsular involvement can cause pure motor or sensorimotor deficits; a larger striatocapsular lesion may have more complex findings.

The record carries no `supply` entry: no syndrome card in this atlas attributes its lesion to the middle cerebral artery (the two entries an earlier revision carried — Parkinson's disease and lateral medullary syndrome — are a degenerative alpha-synucleinopathy and a PICA/vertebral territory respectively), so the MCA's named syndromes are documented in its own clinical array and in the territory structures it lists. Meshes: the sphenoid (M1) part `FJ1692`/`FJ1692M` (800 faces each), the insular (M2) parts (`FJ1660`/`FJ1660M`, `FJ1694`/`FJ1694M`), and the 34 terminal M2–M4 branch elements the inventory groups under this record (FMA 50080/50081/50365–50370); the generic MCA branch/zone elements (44 files) are listed as source-only support.

function.before: The largest and clinically most important cerebral artery: it runs laterally through the sylvian fissure (M1, giving off the lenticulostriate perforators), over the insula (M2 insular branches) and out onto the lateral convexity (M3/M4), supplying the entire lateral surface of the hemisphere — the motor and sensory strips for the face and arm, Broca's and Wernicke's areas, the insula, the temporal convexity and the lateral occipital cortex. It also gives the deep perforators that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule, so an MCA occlusion commonly produces both a cortical and a deep (capsular) infarct, which is the anatomical basis of the classic dense hemiplegia with aphasia or neglect.
function.after: Major ICA terminal artery. M1 travels laterally toward the Sylvian fissure and gives deep lenticulostriate perforators; insular M2, opercular M3 and cortical M4 branches supply most of the lateral frontal, parietal and temporal cortex and underlying white matter. ACA and PCA territories border this distribution, so the entire lateral surface is not uniformly MCA territory. Superior/inferior division anatomy is variable.

records.name: Posterior communicating artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is supplied by small vasa vasorum and it lies in the subarachnoid space below the optic tract and medial to the uncus; it is the second commonest site of saccular aneurysm, which characteristically presents with a painful third-nerve palsy because the oculomotor nerve runs immediately above it.
bloodSupply.after: Usually receives ICA inflow; cross-flow between the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems depends on vessel calibre and pressure. Fetal PCA anatomy carries dominant ICA-to-PCA flow.

before.syndrome: Posterior communicating aneurysm with third-nerve palsy
before.findings: An aneurysm at the carotid-posterior communicating junction compresses the oculomotor nerve where it passes beside the vessel: a painful, pupil-involving third-nerve palsy with ptosis, a divergent eye and diplopia — the classic 'posterior communicating' presentation, and one of the few genuinely urgent diplopias.
before.vascular: Posterior communicating artery (junction with the internal carotid)

before.findings: Occlusion of the premammillary perforators infarcts the anterior thalamic nuclei and gives the tuberothalamic syndrome: apathy and abulia, disorientation, memory loss and, on the left, a transcortical-like aphasia.

A small infarct of the subthalamic nucleus — classically from a perforator of the posterior communicating or anterior choroidal artery — releases the indirect-pathway brake and produces violent, involuntary, proximal flinging movements of the contralateral limbs.
before.vascular: Posterior communicating artery or anterior choroidal artery perforators to the subthalamic nucleus

before.syndrome: Fetal-type posterior communicating artery and posterior-circulation infarction
before.findings: In about 20 % of people the posterior cerebral artery is supplied predominantly by the internal carotid through a large posterior communicating artery; in that configuration carotid occlusion infarcts the occipital lobe and thalamus as well as the anterior territory — the reason the vascular anatomy must be established before any carotid intervention.
before.vascular: Posterior communicating artery (fetal-type configuration of the posterior cerebral artery)
before.note: Anatomical variant that changes the territory of a carotid occlusion

after.syndrome: ICA-PCoA aneurysm with CN III palsy
after.findings: An aneurysm can compress the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, producing ptosis, diplopia, impaired adduction/elevation/depression and often pupillary dilation. Pupil sparing does not by itself exclude compression.
Can cause disorientation, memory disturbance, abulia and sometimes dominant-hemisphere language impairment; territory varies with anterior thalamic arterial anatomy.
Injury to motor basal ganglia circuitry can cause contralateral hemichorea/hemiballismus; the responsible lesion need not be confined to the STN.
Carotid embolism may cause PCA cortical infarction because the carotid is the dominant inflow to that PCA. This is an anatomical variant, not itself a disease.

afferent: Internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery), supraclinoid segment
Retrograde flow from the posterior cerebral artery in the fetal-type configuration, and from the basilar in the adult configuration
efferent: Posterior cerebral artery (vasc-posterior-cerebral-artery) at the P1–P2 junction — the anastomosis that defines the circle

Premammillary (anterior thalamoperforating) and tuberothalamic perforators to the anterior and medial thalamus, the hypothalamus, the optic tract and the subthalamic nucleus; small branches to the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the oculomotor nerve

afferent: Supraclinoid ICA
Possible PCA-to-ICA collateral flow in an appropriate pressure gradient
efferent: PCA at the P1-P2 junction
Variable perforators, including the tuberothalamic/premammillary artery, to anterior thalamic and hypothalamic regions

function.before: The posterior limb of the circle of Willis: a short vessel running backward from the supraclinoid internal carotid to join the posterior cerebral artery at the P1–P2 junction, so that the anterior and posterior circulations can share flow. It is the single most important collateral in carotid occlusive disease — a large, fetal-type posterior communicating artery supplies the entire posterior cerebral territory when the basilar contribution is small — and it gives off the premammillary perforators that supply the anterior thalamus, the posterior hypothalamus, the optic tract, the subthalamic nucleus and the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
function.after: Connects the supraclinoid ICA to the PCA at the P1-P2 junction. Perforators supply variable hypothalamic, subthalamic, optic-tract and anterior thalamic regions; the tuberothalamic artery usually arises here. In a fetal PCA configuration, carotid inflow through a large PCoA is dominant and P1 is hypoplastic or absent. This changes occipital embolic supply, but not necessarily all thalamic perforator origins.

records.name: Posterior cerebral artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is supplied by small vasa vasorum; the P2 segment encircles the midbrain in the ambient cistern, adjacent to the oculomotor and trochlear nerves (the anatomical reason a PCA aneurysm or a PCA infarct with swelling causes a third- or fourth-nerve palsy), and its cortical branches are the target of occipital leptomeningeal collateral flow from the MCA.
bloodSupply.after: Usually basilar inflow through P1, with carotid communication through PCoA; ICA inflow dominates in a fetal PCA. Distal anastomoses may provide collateral flow.

before.findings: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (the occipital pole has a dual PCA/MCA supply), often with preserved awareness of the deficit unless both hemispheres are involved; involvement of the splenium adds alexia without agraphia on the left, and involvement of the pulvinar or thalamus adds hemisensory loss.

A single paramedian thalamic artery arising from one P1 supplies both medial thalami: bilateral infarction produces sudden coma or hypersomnia, a severe amnestic syndrome, vertical gaze palsy, skew deviation and, often, marked apathy — the classic 'top of the basilar' thalamic syndrome.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (P1 paramedian perforators, artery of Percheron)

before.findings: Infarction of the thalamogeniculate territory (VPL/VPM and the adjacent white matter) produces contralateral hemianaesthesia followed by spontaneous, burning, hyperpathic pain with allodynia — the archetype of central post-stroke pain.

before.syndrome: Bilateral PCA infarction with cortical blindness and amnesia
before.findings: Embolic occlusion of the basilar apex or both PCAs destroys both occipital cortices and the medial temporal lobes: cortical blindness (sometimes denied — Anton syndrome), a dense anterograde amnesia and, with midbrain involvement, vertical gaze palsy.
before.vascular: Bilateral posterior cerebral arteries (or the basilar apex)

after.findings: Often produces a contralateral homonymous field defect; macular sparing may occur but is not obligatory. Dominant occipital-splenial involvement can cause alexia without agraphia, and medial temporal involvement may affect memory.

A single P1-origin perforator variant supplies both paramedian thalami, sometimes with rostral midbrain. Occlusion can cause altered consciousness, memory dysfunction and vertical gaze abnormalities; this is one mechanism of bilateral thalamic injury.
Contralateral sensory loss may be followed by central post-stroke pain. Sensory deficits and pain vary and need not both occur.
May cause cortical visual impairment or blindness with preserved pupillary reflexes; medial temporal or association-cortex involvement can add memory or higher visual dysfunction.

function.before: The artery of the visual cortex and the posterior diencephalon: it arises from the basilar bifurcation, curves around the midbrain (P2) and divides into the calcarine, parieto-occipital and posterior temporal branches (P3) that supply the medial and inferior occipital lobe, the medial temporal lobe and the posterior thalamus, while its paramedian and thalamogeniculate perforators supply the midbrain tectum and tegmentum, the thalamus and the medial geniculate body. Its occlusion therefore produces the classic visual syndrome (contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing) together with the memory, thalamic and midbrain deficits of the structures it feeds along the way.
function.after: Usually the terminal basilar branch. P1 extends to the PCoA junction; P2 curves around the midbrain, and distal branches reach the medial/inferior temporal and occipital cortex. Separate perforator groups supply much of the thalamus and portions of the midbrain; posterior choroidal branches supply choroid plexus and adjacent tissue. Cortical and deep deficits depend on which branches are affected, and fetal PCA anatomy alters inflow.

records.name: Superior cerebellar artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is supplied by small vasa vasorum within the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns; the artery lies immediately below the trochlear nerve and above the trigeminal root, which is why aneurysms here present with a fourth-nerve palsy or with trigeminal neuralgia-like facial pain.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow usually from the distal basilar artery; origin and cerebellar branch distribution vary and overlap neighbouring cerebellar arteries.

before.syndrome: Superior cerebellar artery infarct with cerebellar syndrome
before.findings: Vertigo and vomiting, ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia, dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia with an intention tremor, and — because the dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle are involved — a marked cerebellar syndrome that may be accompanied by contralateral pain and thermal sensory loss from adjacent spinothalamic involvement.
before.vascular: Superior cerebellar artery (tract-scp and nuc-dentate territory)

before.syndrome: SCA territory infarct with brainstem compression
before.findings: A large SCA infarct with oedema can compress the fourth ventricle and the brainstem, producing hydrocephalus and progressive drowsiness — the cerebellar infarct that requires posterior fossa decompression.

Combined SCA and collicular PCA branch occlusion destroys the superior cerebellar peduncle and the tectum: ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia with a contralateral oculomotor palsy and impaired vertical gaze — a dorsal midbrain-plus-cerebellum syndrome.
before.vascular: Superior cerebellar artery and collicular branches of the posterior cerebral artery

after.findings: Usually produces ipsilateral limb/gait ataxia, dysmetria and dysarthria; associated brainstem signs depend on proximal branch involvement.

A large infarct in any major cerebellar artery territory may obstruct the fourth ventricle or compress the brainstem, causing deterioration. The need for an intervention depends on clinical and imaging findings.

afferent: Basilar artery (vasc-basilar-artery) just proximal to its bifurcation
efferent: Superior cerebellar and vermian cortical branches, and the deep branches to the dentate, interposed and fastigial nuclei and the superior cerebellar peduncle
Small perforating branches to the caudal midbrain tegmentum (the collicular/quadrigeminal territory shared with the PCA) and to the trochlear nerve

afferent: Distal basilar artery, usually just proximal to the PCA origin
efferent: Superior cerebellar hemispheric and vermian branches
Branches to deep cerebellar tissue, SCP and a variable small rostral pontine/caudal midbrain region

function.before: The artery of the superior cerebellar surface and the deep cerebellar nuclei: it arises from the upper basilar just below the bifurcation, encircles the midbrain below the oculomotor and trochlear nerves and supplies the superior vermis and hemisphere, the dentate and interposed nuclei, the superior cerebellar peduncle and — through its small perforators — the caudal midbrain tegmentum. Its intimate relation to the trochlear nerve and to the superior cerebellar peduncle explains why its occlusion produces a cerebellar syndrome with brainstem signs, and why it is the classic cause of the 'cerebellar' infarct that compresses the brainstem and requires decompression.
function.after: Usually arises from the distal basilar artery just before the PCA. It courses around the upper pons/caudal midbrain, normally below CN III, and supplies the superior cerebellar surface, superior vermis, much of the deep cerebellar white matter and nuclei, and parts of the superior cerebellar peduncle. Small brainstem branches have variable overlapping territory; the tectum/red nucleus are not assigned wholesale to the SCA.

records.name: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is supplied by vasa vasorum in the cerebellopontine angle cistern; because the artery loops into the internal auditory canal with the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, it is the vessel implicated in neurovascular compression syndromes and the one at risk during cerebellopontine-angle surgery.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow usually from the basilar artery. The AICA/PICA cerebellar border and labyrinthine branch origin vary.

before.findings: Sudden vertigo with vomiting, ipsilateral sensorineural deafness and tinnitus (labyrinthine branch), ipsilateral facial paralysis and loss of lacrimation (facial nucleus and superior salivatory fibres), ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss (spinal trigeminal) and ipsilateral limb ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle), with contralateral body pain-temperature loss and Horner syndrome — the full syndrome requires occlusion of the AICA at its origin.
before.vascular: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery, including its internal auditory branch

before.syndrome: AICA infarction with isolated audiovestibular loss
before.findings: A small AICA or labyrinthine branch occlusion can present as sudden deafness with vertigo and no other neurological sign, which is why sudden sensorineural hearing loss in a vascular patient is investigated as a posterior-circulation event.
before.vascular: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (internal auditory/labyrinthine branch)

before.findings: Vascular compression of the facial nerve root by an AICA loop causes involuntary synchronous contractions of the ipsilateral facial muscles; the same mechanism on the vestibulocochlear nerve causes brief spells of vertigo — both treated by microvascular decompression.
before.vascular: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (a looping branch compressing the facial or vestibulocochlear nerve at the brainstem root entry zone)
before.note: Neurovascular compression rather than arterial occlusion

after.findings: May combine ipsilateral facial weakness, hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia and facial pain-temperature loss with contralateral body pain-temperature loss. Individual findings depend on the involved branches, and the complete pattern is uncommon.
Can cause acute sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo, either in isolation or with pontine/cerebellar stroke. These symptoms have nonvascular causes as well.
An AICA or another vascular loop may contribute to facial or vestibular nerve compression syndromes. Mere contact on imaging does not establish symptomatic compression.

function.before: The artery of the cerebellopontine angle: it arises from the lower basilar artery, loops around the pontomedullary junction and supplies the middle cerebellar peduncle, the flocculus and the anteroinferior cerebellar surface, together with the labyrinth through its internal auditory (labyrinthine) branch. Its long cisternal course around the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves is what makes it both a common cause of a combined cochleovestibular and brainstem syndrome in stroke, and the vessel most often implicated in neurovascular compression of the facial nerve (hemifacial spasm) and the vestibulocochlear nerve (vestibular paroxysmia).
function.after: Usually arises from the lower basilar artery and courses toward the cerebellopontine angle. Supplies variable lateral caudal pontine territory, middle cerebellar peduncle, flocculus and anteroinferior cerebellum. The labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA but may arise directly from the basilar artery. Relationships to CN VII/VIII and cerebellar territories vary.

records.name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery

bloodSupply.before: Its wall is supplied by vasa vasorum within the cisterna magna; the artery's relationship to the tonsil and the fourth ventricle makes it the artery of the far-lateral approach and the vessel whose injury during foramen-magnum surgery causes a cerebellar infarct.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow usually from the vertebral artery; origins, loops and balance with AICA/SCA vary.

before.findings: Vertigo, nausea and nystagmus (vestibular nuclei), ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss (spinal trigeminal), contralateral body pain and temperature loss (spinothalamic tract), dysphagia, hoarseness and absent gag reflex (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral Horner syndrome (descending sympathetic fibres), ipsilateral limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle) and impaired taste (solitary nucleus) — with strength, vibration sense and consciousness spared.
before.vascular: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (or the vertebral artery at its origin)

before.syndrome: PICA territory cerebellar infarct with oedema
before.findings: A large cerebellar infarct can obstruct the fourth ventricle and compress the brainstem, producing hydrocephalus, impaired consciousness and brainstem signs — the indication for posterior fossa decompression, and the reason a 'benign' lateral medullary syndrome is monitored for deterioration.
before.vascular: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (with mass effect)

before.findings: Aneurysms of the vertebral-PICA junction present with sudden headache, meningism and, frequently, a lateral medullary deficit from mass effect or vasospasm.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery / posterior inferior cerebellar artery junction

after.findings: Can cause ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ataxia and Horner syndrome with vertigo, dysphagia and hoarseness. Strength is often preserved, but extensions and incomplete patterns occur. Vertebral disease is also an important cause.
Vertigo, nausea and gait/limb ataxia may occur. A large infarct can cause fourth-ventricular obstruction or brainstem compression as it swells.
A proximal or distal PICA aneurysm may rupture into the subarachnoid space, sometimes with intraventricular blood; associated deficits depend on haemorrhage and neighbouring tissue injury.

afferent: Vertebral artery (vasc-vertebral-artery) — the usual origin, at the level of the olive, with a caudal loop that descends to the foramen magnum before turning up

Anastomotic flow from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and the superior cerebellar artery along the cerebellar surface (the reason cerebellar infarcts can be smaller than the territory suggests)
efferent: Anterior medullary, lateral medullary, tonsillomedullary and telovelotonsillar segments (the standard five-segment scheme) with medullary branches to the dorsolateral medulla (vestibular nuclei, spinal trigeminal complex, nucleus ambiguus, solitary nucleus, inferior cerebellar peduncle, spinothalamic and hypothalamospinal tracts)
Cortical branches to the inferior vermis and the inferior cerebellar hemisphere

afferent: Usually vertebral artery, with variable PICA origin/course
efferent: Medullary perforators to variable lateral medullary territory
Distal inferior cerebellar, vermian and fourth-ventricular choroidal branches

function.before: The artery of the lateral medulla and the inferior cerebellar surface: it arises from the vertebral artery (occasionally from the basilar) and makes a characteristic caudal loop around the tonsil before supplying the inferior vermis, the inferior cerebellar hemisphere and the dorsolateral medulla. Because its medullary branches supply the vestibular nuclei, the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, the nucleus ambiguus, the solitary nucleus, the inferior cerebellar peduncle, the spinothalamic tract and the descending sympathetic fibres in one territory, its occlusion produces the single most famous brainstem stroke syndrome — and it is also the artery whose absence must be checked before vertebral sacrifice.
function.after: Usually arises from the vertebral artery. Its variable course wraps around the medulla and cerebellar tonsil to the inferior vermis and hemisphere. The commonly described five segments are anterior medullary, lateral medullary, tonsillomedullary, telovelotonsillar and cortical. Medullary perforators share lateral medullary supply with vertebral branches; distal branches also supply fourth-ventricular choroid plexus.

records.name: Lenticulostriate arteries

bloodSupply.before: Supplied by their parent trunks; the perforators traverse the anterior perforated substance, a cribriform plate of grey matter at the base of the brain through which they enter the basal ganglia — the surgical landmark that identifies them, and the plane where an aneurysm or a hypertensive bleed at the bifurcation tears them.
bloodSupply.after: Parent inflow is MCA for lateral branches and ACA for medial branches. Functional end-artery behaviour does not establish a complete absence of every microscopic anastomosis.

before.findings: Rupture of a lateral lenticulostriate artery causes sudden contralateral hemiplegia and hemisensory loss with gaze deviation toward the lesion and, when large, depressed consciousness and transtentorial herniation — the commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.

before.syndrome: Lacunar infarction with a pure motor or pure sensory syndrome
before.findings: Lipohyalinosis of a single perforator produces a small infarct in the internal capsule, corona radiata or pons: a pure motor hemiparesis, a pure sensory stroke, ataxic hemiparesis or a dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome — with no cortical signs (no aphasia, no neglect, no field defect).
before.vascular: Lenticulostriate or other deep perforating arteries (small-vessel disease)

before.findings: Repeated, stereotyped episodes of pure motor or sensorimotor deficit that resolve within minutes, followed by a permanent lacunar infarct in the same territory — a stuttering occlusion of a single lenticulostriate artery that must be recognized as impending stroke.
before.vascular: A single lenticulostriate perforator (middle cerebral artery)

before.findings: Bleeding from the caudothalamic groove perforators ruptures into the lateral ventricle, producing headache, meningism, a reduced level of consciousness and hydrocephalus rather than a focal hemiplegia.
before.vascular: Medial lenticulostriate and Heubner territory perforators

after.findings: A small capsular lesion may cause pure motor or sensorimotor deficits, ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria-clumsy hand without typical cortical signs. Pure sensory stroke classically localizes to thalamic rather than lenticulostriate territory.
after.vascular: Striate / other deep perforators according to location

after.findings: Hypertension-related small-vessel injury can cause basal ganglia haemorrhage with contralateral weakness or sensory loss; large haemorrhages may extend into ventricles or cause mass effect.

afferent: Proximal middle cerebral artery (vasc-middle-cerebral-artery, M1 segment) for the lateral group
Proximal anterior cerebral artery (vasc-anterior-cerebral-artery, A1 segment) for the medial group, of which the recurrent artery of Heubner is the largest and most constant branch
efferent: Lateral group: through the putamen to the internal capsule (posterior limb), the adjacent caudate body and the lateral globus pallidus

Medial group (Heubner): to the caudate head, the nucleus accumbens/ventral striatum and the anterior limb of the internal capsule — the territory whose loss produces the abulia of an anterior cerebral infarct

No anastomoses at the target: the perforators are functional end arteries, which is the anatomical reason small vessel occlusion produces a discrete lacune rather than a collateralized partial infarct

afferent: MCA M1 for the lateral group
ACA branches, including variable-origin Heubner artery, for the medial group
efferent: Parts of caudate, putamen, pallidum and internal capsule; distribution overlaps anterior choroidal and other perforators

contextNote.before: Authored from the v8 vessel inventory (docs/VASC_INVENTORY.md §3/§3.1, task vasc-acquire — BodyParts3D 4.0, CC BY 4.0): the archive we already own carries per-artery meshes, and its §3 table maps them to this very record id. The record is complete without the mesh — the territory and syndrome mappings below are the semantic content. This record is a two-vessel functional concept (lateral group from the MCA, medial group including Heubner's artery from the ACA) rather than a single named trunk, and it is classified `paired` because both groups are bilateral; the `origin3d` anchor sits at the anterior perforated substance. Meshes: no dedicated BP3D concept exists. The nearest elements are the anterolateral central branches of the middle cerebral artery (`FJ1662`/`FJ1662M`, `FJ1663`/`FJ1663M`, FMA 50376–50378), which the inventory files as MCA `half+support` rather than as their own record; the remaining lenticulostriate elements are inside its 44-element "generic MCA branch/zone" group. The record is therefore documented as a two-vessel functional concept whose geometry the render task takes from the MCA branch set.

function.before: The deep perforating arteries that supply the basal ganglia and the internal capsule: the lateral group arises from the proximal (M1) middle cerebral artery and pierces the anterior perforated substance to run through the putamen to the internal capsule, while the medial group (including the recurrent artery of Heubner) arises from the anterior cerebral artery and supplies the caudate head, the nucleus accumbens and the anterior limb of the capsule. They are end arteries — there are no anastomoses at their destinations — and they are the vessels of lacunar infarction and of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage, which is why the same anatomy explains both the commonest ischaemic and the commonest haemorrhagic deep lesion.
function.after: Umbrella term for striate perforators supplying parts of the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Lateral lenticulostriate branches usually arise from proximal MCA; medial striate branches arise from ACA, with the recurrent artery of Heubner usually near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2. Deep perforator territories have limited collateralization and are vulnerable to small-vessel infarction or haemorrhage. The separate lateral and medial records provide group detail; the model does not encode a universal branch count.

records.name: Anterior choroidal artery

bloodSupply.before: Supplied by its parent carotid trunk; the artery runs in the ambient cistern below the optic tract, immediately above the posterior communicating artery, and is at risk during temporal-lobe surgery, aneurysm clipping and choroid plexus surgery (its injury causes an infarct of the internal capsule and a post-operative hemiplegia).
bloodSupply.after: Inflow usually from the ICA. Cisternal branches supply deep neural tissue; plexal branches supply choroid plexus, not the CSF cavity itself.

before.syndrome: Anterior choroidal artery infarct (the capsular triad)
before.findings: Contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia occur together because the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the thalamocortical sensory fibres and the optic radiation all fall within the territory; the incomplete forms (pure motor, pure sensory, or a quadrantanopia alone) are more common than the full triad.

before.syndrome: Hippocampal and amygdalar infarction with memory loss
before.findings: Involvement of the uncal, hippocampal and amygdalar branches adds a memory deficit and, occasionally, seizures to the capsular findings — the anatomical reason the anterior choroidal territory appears in the clinical notes of the amygdala, hippocampus and temporal horn.

before.syndrome: Anterior choroidal aneurysm and surgical risk
before.findings: Aneurysms of the anterior choroidal artery are rare but their clipping risks the artery itself; because it is an end-artery territory with no useful anastomoses, occlusion during surgery produces an immediate, dense capsular hemiplegia.

after.findings: The classical combination is contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss; partial syndromes are common and depend on capsular and visual pathway involvement.

The artery can be at risk during aneurysm or medial temporal/intraventricular procedures. Occlusion can injure eloquent deep tissue; outcome is variable rather than invariably a complete dense hemiplegia.

The record is complete without the mesh — the territory and syndrome mappings below are the semantic content. It is in the atlas record set because its territory is cited repeatedly by the existing structure records (internal capsule, optic radiation, hippocampus, pallidum) and it is one of the classic syndrome-producing perforators. function.before: A small but surgically notorious artery arising from the internal carotid just above the posterior communicating artery: it runs backward below the optic tract, gives off the uncal, hippocampal and pallidal branches, and enters the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle through the choroidal fissure to supply the choroid plexus. Its territory is a compact bundle of functionally unrelated structures — the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic radiation (retrolenticular part), the globus pallidus, the hippocampus, the amygdala, the tail of the caudate and the temporal-horn plexus — which is why its occlusion produces the 'capsular triad' of hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia rather than a single clean syndrome.
function.after: Usually arises from the supraclinoid ICA distal to the PCoA and courses posteriorly near the optic tract before entering the choroidal fissure/temporal horn plexus. Supplies variable parts of the posterior internal capsule, optic tract/geniculocalcarine pathway, pallidum and medial temporal structures, and lateral-ventricular choroid plexus. Individual territory overlaps neighbouring perforators and choroidal arteries.

records.name: Medial posterior choroidal artery

bloodSupply.before: Supplied by the posterior cerebral artery; the arteries run in the velum interpositum and the choroidal fissure, adjacent to the internal cerebral veins, and they are the feeding vessels of choroid plexus tumours and the target of pre-operative embolization.
bloodSupply.after: Inflow from variable proximal PCA branches, commonly P1 or P2. Medial and lateral posterior choroidal territories are distinct but can overlap.

before.findings: Choroid plexus papillomas and carcinomas, and intraventricular meningiomas of the trigone, are fed by the posterior choroidal arteries (and the anterior choroidal artery anteriorly); recognizing the pedicle is what makes embolization and surgical control possible.
before.vascular: Posterior choroidal arteries (with the anterior choroidal artery)

before.findings: Occlusion produces infarction of the posterior thalamus and the adjacent plexus, adding hemisensory loss, visual field defects and memory disturbance to the picture of a posterior cerebral artery infarct; isolated occlusion is uncommon because the artery arises from the PCA itself.

before.syndrome: Intraventricular haemorrhage from the choroidal vessels
before.findings: The choroidal arteries are the source of intraventricular haemorrhage in the premature (germinal matrix) and of blood in the ventricles in adults with hypertension or vascular malformation; blood in the ventricle is what produces hydrocephalus.
before.vascular: Choroidal arteries (with the germinal matrix in neonates)

after.findings: Injury may affect thalamic/epithalamic tissue or choroid plexus depending on the branches involved. Exact sensory, visual or memory findings cannot be inferred from this single schematic course.
Choroidal arteries may feed intraventricular tumors; medial/lateral posterior and anterior choroidal contributions vary with tumor location.

afferent: Posterior cerebral artery (vasc-posterior-cerebral-artery) — the medial artery from the proximal P2 segment, the lateral from the distal P2
efferent: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle (body, atrium/glomus and temporal horn) and of the third ventricle — the vascular pedicle of the plexus in the posterior half of the ventricular system
Perforating branches to the pulvinar, the medial and lateral geniculate bodies, the habenula and the posterior thalamus

afferent: PCA, with variable P1/P2 origin
efferent: Third-ventricular choroid plexus and variable medial thalamic/epithalamic branches
Anastomotic contributions to adjacent choroidal territory; the lateral posterior choroidal arteries are a distinct group

function.before: The choroidal supply of the posterior circulation: the medial posterior choroidal artery arises from the P2 segment of the posterior cerebral artery and runs medially above the tectum to the third ventricle and the interventricular foramen region, while the lateral posterior choroidal artery arises more distally and runs laterally into the lateral ventricle to supply the choroid plexus of the body, the atrium (its glomus) and the temporal horn. Together they supply the choroid plexus of the lateral and third ventricles, the posterior thalamus and habenula region, and the adjacent fornix and pulvinar — the territory that makes the plexus a vascular as well as a CSF structure.
function.after: One or more PCA branches that curve around the midbrain toward the pineal/habenular region and tela choroidea of the third ventricle. Medial posterior choroidal branches supply third-ventricular choroid plexus and variable medial/posterior thalamic and epithalamic tissue. The distinct lateral posterior choroidal group enters the lateral-ventricular choroidal fissure and contributes to body/atrial plexus supply; it is not fully represented by this medial course.

records.name: Corticospinal tract (lateral)

before.syndrome: Pure motor hemiparesis (lacunar infarct of the posterior limb)
before.findings: Contralateral face-arm-leg weakness without cortical sensory or visual signs; UMN pattern (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign)
before.vascular: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery

before.findings: Contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid), with ipsilateral hypoglossal palsy and contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception from the adjacent medial lemniscus
Quadriparesis/quadriplegia with preserved vertical eye movements and blinking — bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers destroyed while the tegmentum is spared
Ipsilateral UMN weakness below the lesion (lateral column crossed at the decussation above), with ipsilateral DCML and contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss

after.syndrome: Corticospinal lesion above the pyramidal decussation
after.findings: Contralateral limb weakness; associated face weakness requires corticobulbar involvement. Capsular injury can produce a pure motor syndrome, but the pattern depends on lesion extent.
Ipsilateral upper motor neuron weakness below the lesion; a hemicord lesion also affects other sensory and motor pathways.

decussation.before: Pyramidal decussation at lvl-pyramid-decuss (cervicomedullary junction): ~85–90% of fibers cross to form the lateral CST; ~10% continue uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract and cross segmentally in the anterior white commissure
decussation.after: Most fibres (approximately 85-90%, with individual variation) cross at the caudal medullary pyramidal decussation to form the lateral tract. Anterior corticospinal fibres are a separate, mainly axial pathway with bilateral/segmental projections.

function.before: Carries the commands for voluntary, fractionated movement from the motor cortex to the contralateral spinal cord; fibers descend as a continuous bundle through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the middle three-fifths of the crus cerebri, the basis pontis, and the pyramid, then decussate. Lesions above the pyramidal decussation cause contralateral upper-motor-neuron signs; lesions below cause ipsilateral signs.
function.after: Major descending pathway for voluntary limb movement, especially fractionated distal movements. Injury may produce weakness and upper motor neuron signs; acute lesions can initially cause reduced tone and reflexes.

geometryNote.after: Authored teaching geometry in custom atlas units; not patient coordinates, tractography, validated fibre boundaries, or a complete connection graph. The curve depicts selected course segments only.

origin.before: Primary motor (M1), premotor and supplementary motor cortex → posterior limb of the internal capsule
origin.after: Layer V neurons of primary motor, premotor, supplementary motor and somatosensory/parietal cortex; fibres descend through corona radiata, posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi, ventral pons and medullary pyramids.

target.after: Contralateral spinal interneurons and anterior horn motor neurons after pyramidal crossing, with a major role in distal limb and skilled hand movement.

records.name: Corticobulbar tract

before.syndrome: Unilateral cortical/capsular lesion (e.g. middle cerebral artery infarct)
before.findings: Contralateral lower facial weakness with forehead sparing (bilateral upper-facial innervation); tongue deviates toward the weak side on protrusion
Bilateral corticobulbar damage → dysarthria, dysphagia, emotional incontinence, hyperreflexic jaw jerk with a spastic tongue
before.note: Classically after bilateral strokes, motor neuron disease, or multiple sclerosis

before.findings: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral lower facial/tongue weakness — corticobulbar and corticospinal fibers in the crus damaged beside the exiting third nerve

after.findings: Often contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing; forehead sparing is a useful pattern, not an absolute diagnostic rule.
May cause pseudobulbar dysarthria, dysphagia, brisk jaw reflex and emotional lability.
May impair contralateral genioglossus; protruded tongue can deviate toward the weak side, away from a unilateral cortical lesion. Bilateral innervation can limit the deficit.

decussation.before: No tract-level decussation — individual fibers project bilaterally to most cranial motor nuclei; exceptions dominated by contralateral innervation: the lower facial division (facial nucleus) and hypoglossal nucleus (partial)
decussation.after: Projections cross at several brainstem levels and are predominantly bilateral. Lower facial motor neurons and genioglossus receive important contralateral input; this is not a single compact decussation.

function.before: Delivers cortical commands to brainstem motor nuclei. Because most nuclei receive bilateral input, unilateral lesions cause little deficit; the exceptions produce the classic signs: contralateral lower facial weakness with forehead sparing (upper face is bilaterally innervated) and tongue deviation away from the cortical lesion (genioglossus is predominantly contralaterally innervated).
function.after: Contributes to voluntary orofacial, swallowing and speech movements through cranial motor networks. Bilateral innervation gives partial redundancy, with clinically important exceptions.

somatotopy.after: Orofacial representation lies mainly in inferolateral motor cortex; descending fibres pass through the genu/adjacent internal capsule. Brainstem projections are distributed rather than a precisely mapped single tube.

records.name: Corticopontine tract

before.findings: With corticospinal/corticobulbar fibers, the corticopontine bundles are destroyed by ventral pontine infarction; cerebellar modulation of the limbs is lost bilaterally

Symmetric demyelination of the basis pontis (corticopontine + corticospinal + pontine nuclei) → spastic quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy, fluctuating consciousness after rapid correction of hyponatremia
before.note: Classically 2–6 days after over-rapid sodium correction

after.findings: Supratentorial or pontine injury can contribute to ataxia, often together with weakness or other deficits. Side depends on the site relative to the crossed pontocerebellar projection; an isolated tract syndrome is difficult to establish.

decussation.before: Pontocerebellar fibers cross in the basis pontis to reach the contralateral middle cerebellar peduncle
decussation.after: Corticopontine fibres themselves principally terminate ipsilaterally. Crossing belongs to the downstream pontocerebellar projection, not to this tract.

function.before: The largest corticofugal projection: it funnels cortical intent into the pontine relay and onward through the middle cerebellar peduncle, giving the cerebellum a precisely timed copy of the movement plan for coordination and error correction. Damage disrupts cerebellar modulation of voluntary movement on the contralateral side (double-crossed cerebellar output restores contralaterality clinically).
function.after: Relays widespread cortical information to pontine nuclei, forming the input limb of corticopontocerebellar circuits involved in coordination and motor learning.

records.name: Rubrospinal tract

before.findings: With corticospinal interruption above the red nucleus, an intact rubrospinal pathway drives upper-limb flexion and lower-limb extension; loss of rubrospinal influence (lesion below the red nucleus) yields extensor (decerebrate) posturing
before.note: Rubrospinal sparing explains why decorticate rigidity carries a better prognosis than decerebrate rigidity

before.syndrome: Corticospinal lesions with relative flexor sparing
before.findings: In chronic hemiparesis the flexor synergy of the arm (and spastic dystonia) reflects residual rubrospinal and reticulospinal drive acting without corticospinal control
Red-nucleus infarction with CN III palsy → ipsilateral third-nerve palsy plus contralateral ataxia/tremor; the rubrospinal exit path is damaged with the nucleus

after.findings: Posturing can occur with severe hemispheric or brainstem injury. Classical rubrospinal explanations are teaching models and do not establish the exact lesion level or prognosis in an individual.

decussation.before: Ventral tegmental decussation (of Forel) immediately caudal to the red nucleus — fibers cross ventromedially and descend contralaterally
decussation.after: Crosses soon after leaving the red nucleus at the ventral tegmental decussation (Forel) in the midbrain.

function.before: Facilitates flexor tone of the contralateral upper limb as an alternative descending motor route; in humans it is modest in size but clinically important because it explains postures after brainstem lesions. Its preservation above a midbrain lesion produces flexed upper limbs in decorticate posturing.
function.after: A descending lateral motor pathway with an uncertain and relatively limited role in humans. Animal flexor-control mechanisms should not be treated as a complete explanation of human movement or posturing.

geometryNote.after: Authored teaching geometry in custom atlas units; not patient coordinates, tractography, validated fibre boundaries, or a complete connection graph. The curve depicts selected course segments only.

modality.before: Somatic motor — excitatory facilitation of contralateral upper-limb flexors (and inhibition of extensors)
modality.after: Descending somatic motor pathway; human functional contribution is limited and uncertain, and animal flexor-control mechanisms do not establish a human rule.

origin.before: Magnocellular red nucleus (rostral midbrain tegmentum); driven by cerebellar (dentate/interposed via SCP) and cortical input
origin.after: Magnocellular (caudal) division of the red nucleus in the midbrain.

records.name: Tectospinal tract

before.syndrome: Dorsal midbrain lesions (e.g. pineal region tumor)
before.findings: Loss of reflexive head orienting toward peripheral stimuli accompanies the gaze palsies of Parinaud syndrome; isolated tectospinal deficits are not clinically testable in isolation
before.note: Of the paired descending midbrain tracts, tectospinal lesions are the least clinically evident — noted for completeness

before.findings: Diminished quick head-turning reflexes; overshadowed by corticospinal deficits in the same territory

after.findings: Head/eye orienting abnormalities may accompany collicular or brainstem network lesions; a characteristic isolated human tectospinal syndrome is not established.

decussation.before: Dorsal tegmental decussation (of Meynert) in the caudal midbrain, dorsal to the medial lemniscus
decussation.after: Crosses in the dorsal tegmental decussation (Meynert) in the midbrain, then descends near the medial longitudinal fasciculus.

function.before: Mediates automatic head turning and postural adjustments of the neck toward sudden peripheral visual, auditory, or somatosensory stimuli, cooperating with tectobulbar fibers to the ocular motor nuclei for coordinated gaze-and-head orienting.
function.after: Participates in orienting head/neck movements toward sensory stimuli. Its isolated clinical contribution in humans is uncertain.

origin.before: Deep layers of the superior colliculus (midbrain tectum)
origin.after: Deep layers of the superior colliculus, integrating sensory signals relevant to orienting.

records.name: Lateral vestibulospinal tract

before.findings: Loss of cortical/red-nucleus influence releases the lateral vestibulospinal system → powerful ipsilateral extensor tone in all four limbs
before.note: Experimental dorsomedial medulla transection between the red nucleus and Deiters' nucleus reproduces this

before.findings: Ipsilateral loss of extensor postural tone with falling toward the lesion (as in acute vestibular neuritis involving Deiters' nucleus); combined lateral medullary lesions add ataxia
before.vascular: Vertebral / posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory (caudal extent)

after.findings: Brainstem injury involving vestibular nuclei and descending pathways may contribute to imbalance and falling; vertigo and nystagmus involve additional vestibular circuits.
A peripheral vestibular nerve disorder can alter vestibulospinal drive secondarily; it does not imply a lesion of the Deiters nucleus.

decussation.before: None — uncrossed; descends ipsilaterally in the ventral funiculus, anterior to the rubrospinal and spinocerebellar fibers
decussation.after: Predominantly uncrossed descent; downstream spinal networks have broader bilateral interactions.

function.before: Translates otolith (gravito-inertial) signals into increases in ipsilateral antigravity extensor tone, correcting posture when the body tilts. Hyperactivity of Deiters' nucleus and its tract underlies the extensor hypertonus of decerebrate rigidity.
function.after: Uses vestibular information to help maintain posture and balance, including facilitation of extensor/antigravity activity.

geometryNote.after: Authored teaching geometry in custom atlas units; not patient coordinates, tractography, validated fibre boundaries, or a complete connection graph. The curve depicts selected course segments only.

origin.before: Lateral vestibular (Deiters') nucleus at the lateral angle of the fourth-ventricle floor, caudal pons
origin.after: Lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters) near the pontomedullary region.

before.findings: Ocular tilt reaction and head-tilt with impaired vestibulocollic reflexes; ipsiversive lateropulsion when the medial vestibulospinal/MLF complex is infarcted

decussation.after: Contains crossed and uncrossed projections, descending bilaterally in association with the medial longitudinal fasciculus (descending MLF).

function.before: Couples canal signals to neck (and upper limb) motor neurons so the head is stabilized in space during body and eye movements — the spinal limb of the vestibulocollic reflex. It is the downward continuation of the MLF fiber system.
function.after: Supports vestibulocollic reflexes and stabilization of head position. Ascending vestibulo-ocular fibres are related but have different targets.

records.name: Reticulospinal tract (pontine and medullary)

before.findings: Loss of cortical control unmasks exaggerated reticulospinal drive → velocity-dependent hypertonus, clonus, and synergies in the contralateral limbs
before.note: The spasticity of upper-motor-neuron lesions is largely reticulospinal (not corticospinal) in mechanism

before.syndrome: Autonomic dysreflexia / neurogenic shock (cord or brainstem lesions)
before.findings: Interruption of descending reticulospinal (autonomic) fibers abolishes supraspinal vasomotor control — hypotension with high cord lesions, or dysreflexic hypertension below
before.note: Medullary reticulospinal fibers also carry respiratory and cardiovascular modulation

before.findings: Involvement of the medullary reticular formation disturbs ipsilateral autonomic (hypo/anidrosis, cardiovascular lability) and postural control alongside the classic sensory findings

after.findings: Reticulospinal circuits may contribute to residual movement and abnormal synergies after corticospinal injury; these outcomes involve multiple descending and spinal mechanisms.
Often causes mixed motor/postural deficits; isolated reticulospinal lesions are difficult to identify clinically.

decussation.before: None — predominantly ipsilateral descent with bilateral terminal arborization through commissural reticular neurons
decussation.after: Distributed crossed and uncrossed projections; no single obligatory decussation.

function.before: Provides the tonically active postural and muscle-tone background on which corticospinal movements ride: pontine output facilitates antigravity extensors, medullary output suppresses them; both adjust axial posture during voluntary movement and carry descending autonomic (vasomotor, sphincter) control. After corticospinal injury, reticulospinal hyperexcitability is a main driver of post-stroke spasticity.
function.after: Contributes to posture, gait, anticipatory adjustments and voluntary movements. A simple pontine-excitatory/medullary-inhibitory split does not capture the full system.

geometryNote.after: Authored teaching geometry in custom atlas units; not patient coordinates, tractography, validated fibre boundaries, or a complete connection graph. The curve depicts selected course segments only.

modality.before: Postural and autonomic somatic motor — the medial descending (parapyramidal) system setting muscle tone, posture, and autonomic outflow
modality.after: Descending somatic motor/postural networks; contributions to muscle tone, locomotion and coordinated movement.

origin.before: Pontine reticular formation (oral/caudal pontine nuclei) and medullary reticular formation (gigantocellular/medial nuclei)
origin.after: Pontine and medullary reticular formation, containing heterogeneous descending neuronal populations.

records.name: Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)

before.findings: Unilateral MLF lesion: on attempted lateral gaze away from the lesion, the ipsilateral (adducting) eye fails or lags with preserved convergence; abducting nystagmus in the contralateral eye; skew deviation may accompany
before.note: Classic demyelinating lesion in young adults (multiple sclerosis); small-vessel stroke in older patients

before.findings: Combined PPRF/abducens plus ipsilateral MLF lesion → the only surviving horizontal movement is abduction of the contralateral eye
Bilateral MLF lesions → bilateral adduction failure with exotropia and abduction nystagmus

after.findings: Impaired adduction of the eye ipsilateral to the MLF lesion during horizontal gaze, often with contralateral abducting nystagmus. Convergence is frequently preserved, but not always.
An ipsilateral MLF lesion plus abducens-nucleus or PPRF damage causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and INO; only contralateral eye abduction remains horizontally.

decussation.before: Internuclear fibers decussate within the oculomotor/trochlear complexes for yoking of the contralateral medial rectus; no tract-level decussation — the bundle itself is paramedian and paired
decussation.after: Abducens internuclear axons cross in the pons soon after leaving the abducens nucleus, then ascend in the opposite MLF to medial-rectus neurons of CN III. Other MLF components include crossed and uncrossed vestibular projections.

function.before: The wiring harness of conjugate gaze: abducens internuclear neurons carry the command for ipsilateral lateral rectus contraction up the MLF to the contralateral medial-rectus (CN III) neurons, and vestibular nuclei use the same bundle to drive vestibulo-ocular reflexes in all planes. Tectobulbar fibers add saccadic head-orienting commands.
function.after: Coordinates ocular motor nuclei with one another and with vestibular inputs. It is a mixed internuclear bundle rather than a single sensory or motor tract.

geometryNote.after: Authored teaching geometry in custom atlas units; not patient coordinates, tractography, validated fibre boundaries, or a complete connection graph. The curve depicts selected course segments only.

origin.before: Vestibular nuclei (medial/superior) and abducens internuclear neurons; receives tectobulbar contributions from the superior colliculus and a caudal continuation of the medial vestibulospinal fibers
origin.after: Vestibular nuclei and brainstem ocular motor internuclear neurons; horizontal gaze interneurons arise in the abducens nucleus.

records.name: Central tegmental tract

before.findings: Trans-synaptic degeneration of the inferior olive after CTT (or red nucleus/dentate) injury → palatal myoclonus, pendular nystagmus, ocular myorhythmia months after the initial lesion
before.note: Classic delayed complication of pontine or tegmental hemorrhage/infarct

before.findings: Myoclonus syndromes (palatal, ocular, skeletal) from disruption of the dentate–red nucleus–olive circuit at any leg, including the central tegmental tract

after.findings: Interruption of afferent connections to the olive can cause delayed ipsilateral olivary degeneration after central tegmental injury, sometimes with palatal/oculopalatal tremor. Not every affected patient has tremor; isolated olivocerebellar output injury does not produce the same deafferentation pattern.

decussation.before: No intrinsic decussation — the tract is an ipsilateral tegmental conduit within the Mollaret triangle
decussation.after: The rubro-olivary component is principally uncrossed. Dentatorubral input crosses via the superior cerebellar peduncle; olivocerebellar output crosses to the opposite cerebellar cortex via the inferior peduncle.

function.before: Links the red nucleus to the inferior olive as the central leg of the dentatorubro-olivary loop that calibrates cerebellar motor learning; it also carries reticular fibers between the midbrain and lower brainstem. Lesions produce hypertrophic olivary degeneration with palatal/tremor myorhythmia.
function.after: The rubro-olivary component forms part of the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit. The return route involves olivary climbing fibres to cerebellar cortex and deep-nuclear circuitry, not a simple direct olive-to-dentate synapse.

geometryNote.after: Authored teaching geometry in custom atlas units; not patient coordinates, tractography, validated fibre boundaries, or a complete connection graph. The curve depicts selected course segments only.

origin.before: Red nucleus (parvocellular, ipsilateral) and midbrain reticular formation
origin.after: Includes descending fibres from the parvocellular (rostral) red nucleus; other ascending/reticular fibres occupy the central tegmental region.

records.name: Hypothalamospinal (sympathetic) tract

before.findings: Ipsilateral miosis, mild ptosis, facial anhidrosis; pupil dilates poorly to hydroxyamphetamine (central lesion) and the anhidrosis involves face/arm/ trunk depending on level
before.note: Distinguish from preganglionic (second-order) and postganglionic (third-order) Horner by pharmacologic testing and anhidrosis distribution

before.findings: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome accompanies facial pain/temperature loss, dysphagia, dysphonia, and ataxia when the lateral tegmental sympathetic fibers are infarcted

after.findings: Ipsilateral miosis, mild ptosis and variable anhidrosis can accompany lateral brainstem or spinal injury. Horner syndrome also has peripheral preganglionic/postganglionic causes.

With intact postganglionic terminals, hydroxyamphetamine can dilate a central or preganglionic Horner pupil; dilation is reduced in a postganglionic lesion. Timing and other limitations prevent this from being an absolute rule.
after.note: Educational mechanism, not a recommendation for self-testing or a substitute for clinical assessment.

decussation.before: None — uncrossed; descends ipsilaterally through the lateral brainstem tegmentum
decussation.after: The clinically localized descending oculosympathetic pathway is mainly ipsilateral; broader hypothalamic autonomic projections are distributed.

function.before: Carries hypothalamic sympathetic commands to the spinal preganglionic neurons that drive pupil dilation, lid elevation (Müller muscle), facial sweating, and vasomotor tone. Interruption anywhere along its course produces ipsilateral central Horner syndrome — ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis without extraocular or visual loss.
function.after: Descending autonomic control includes sympathetic drive to the pupil, eyelid smooth muscle and sweating through a three-neuron oculosympathetic chain.

geometryNote.after: Authored teaching geometry in custom atlas units; not patient coordinates, tractography, validated fibre boundaries, or a complete connection graph. The curve depicts selected course segments only.

origin.before: Posterolateral hypothalamus (paraventricular and lateral hypothalamic area)
origin.after: Hypothalamic autonomic regions, including pathways descending through the lateral brainstem.

somatotopy.after: Lateral brainstem descent is a teaching localization, not a precisely delimited fibre bundle or fine map.

target.before: Descends through the lateral brainstem tegmentum to the cervical cord, where the pathway continues to the intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord (T1–L2) and its ciliospinal centre of Budge (C8–T2) for the oculosympathetics — drawn in this atlas only to the cervicomedullary junction, because no spinal-cord geometry is committed
target.after: Spinal sympathetic preganglionic neurons. The oculosympathetic component reaches upper thoracic intermediolateral neurons (chiefly T1-T2), then sympathetic chain and superior cervical ganglion.
